Note that changing the table
size (``M``) triggers a recalculation of the lookup table and can temporarily lead to inconsistent
backend selection for new traffic until all nodes have converged and completed their agent restart.

stem: Which statement best describes a benefit of Maglev consistent hashing as presented in the excerpt?

options.text: It improves resiliency in case of failures and provides better load balancing properties because nodes added to the cluster make consistent backend selection throughout the cluster for a given 5-tuple without having to synchronize state with other nodes.
It eliminates the need for any load balancer by assigning backends at TCP connect time.
It reduces memory consumption on each Cilium-managed node compared to the random algorithm.
It guarantees that backend reassignments are exactly zero on backend removal.

explanation: The excerpt states that Maglev improves resiliency in case of failures and provides better load balancing properties since nodes added to the cluster will make consistent backend selection throughout the cluster for a given 5-tuple without having to synchronize state with the other nodes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says in-cluster (E-W) sockets are assigned directly, but Maglev is for external traffic and does not eliminate the load balancer.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that enabling Maglev will have higher memory consumption compared to the default random algorithm.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states at most 1% difference in reassignments, not exactly zero.

citations.title: Maglev Consistent Hashing
citations.quote:
This improves resiliency in case of
failures. As well, it provides better load balancing properties since Nodes added to the cluster will
make consistent backend selection throughout the cluster for a given 5-tuple without
having to synchronize state with the other Nodes.

stem: An engineer is comparing Maglev with the default loadBalancer.algorithm=random. Which statement about memory consumption is correct according to the excerpt?

options.text: Enabling Maglev will have a higher memory consumption on each Cilium-managed node compared to the default of loadBalancer.algorithm=random, because random does not need the extra lookup tables.
Enabling Maglev will have a lower memory consumption because it uses a single lookup table per cluster.
Memory consumption is identical because both algorithms use the same lookup tables.
Maglev memory consumption depends only on the number of nodes, not on the table size.

explanation: The excerpt states that enabling Maglev will have a higher memory consumption on each Cilium-managed node compared to the default of loadBalancer.algorithm=random given random does not need the extra lookup tables.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says Maglev has higher memory consumption, not lower.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says random does not need the extra lookup tables, so consumption is not identical.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that memory consumption depends only on the number of nodes; it mentions the extra lookup tables.

citations.title: Maglev Consistent Hashing
citations.quote:
Note that enabling Maglev will have a higher memory consumption on each Cilium-managed Node compared
to the default of ``loadBalancer.algorithm=random`` given ``random`` does not need the extra lookup
tables.

stem: An engineer writes an egress gateway policy that lists two gateway nodes under `egressGateways`. A colleague asks whether the source endpoints matched by the policy will spread their traffic across both gateways. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Each matched endpoint egresses through a single gateway, chosen from the list, not through all of them.
Traffic is load-balanced across all gateways in the list, one connection per gateway.
Only the first entry in the list is used; the remaining entries are ignored until the first node fails.
The policy is rejected because multiple gateways require a separate policy per gateway.

explanation: The excerpt states that with multiple gateways the matched source endpoints still egress through a single gateway rather than all of them, and that endpoints are assigned to a gateway based on its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says endpoints egress through a single gateway, not all of them, so there is no spreading of traffic across the list.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes a first-entry-only or failover behaviour; assignment is based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt opens by saying it is possible to select multiple gateway nodes in the same policy, so such a policy is not rejected.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
When using multiple gateways the source endpoints matched by the policy will still egress traffic
    through a single gateway, not all of them.

stem: A platform team has an egress gateway policy with several entries in `egressGateways`. They add a new node that matches one of the `nodeSelector` fields. What does the excerpt say will happen to the endpoints matched by the policy?

options.text: The list of gateways will change and the endpoints will be reassigned.
Nothing changes, because endpoint-to-gateway assignment is fixed for the lifetime of the policy.
The policy stops matching endpoints until it is reapplied manually.
All endpoints immediately move to the newly added node.

explanation: The excerpt says that if a node matching one of the `nodeSelector` fields is added or removed, the list of gateways will change and the endpoints will be reassigned.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt only promises stable assignment for an endpoint's lifetime as long as the matched gateway nodes do not change; adding a matching node is such a change.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes reassignment of endpoints, not loss of policy matching.
optionRationale.d: Reassignment is described, but the excerpt does not say all endpoints move to the new node; assignment is based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
If a
    ``nodeSelector`` field is added, removed, or modified, or if a node matching one of the
    ``nodeSelector`` fields is added or removed, the list of gateways will change and the endpoints
    will be reassigned.

stem: Which field is used to configure multiple gateway nodes within a single egress gateway policy?

options.text: `egressGateways`
`egressGateway`
`nodeSelector`
`gatewayNodes`

explanation: The excerpt states that when selecting multiple gateway nodes in the same policy, the gateway nodes can be configured using the `egressGateways` list field.

optionRationale.b: `egressGateway` is the singular field; the excerpt says entries on the `egressGateways` list have the same configuration options as it, but it is not the list field itself.
optionRationale.c: `nodeSelector` is a field inside each list entry, not the field that holds the list of gateways.
optionRationale.d: `gatewayNodes` is not mentioned anywhere in the excerpt.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
In this case, the gateway nodes
can be configured using the ``egressGateways`` list field.

stem: How does the excerpt say endpoints are assigned to a gateway when a policy selects multiple gateway nodes?

options.text: Based on the gateway's CiliumEndpoint's UID.
Based on the order of entries in the `egressGateways` list.
Based on the source endpoint's node name.
Based on a round-robin scheme across the matched gateway nodes.

explanation: The excerpt says the endpoints will be assigned to a gateway based on its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives the CiliumEndpoint's UID as the basis, not the position of entries in the list.
optionRationale.c: No node-name-based assignment for the source endpoint is described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Round-robin is not mentioned; the excerpt describes assignment based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
The endpoints will be assigned to a gateway based on
    its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

stem: An engineer is comparing a policy with a single `egressGateway` field against one with an `egressGateways` list. Which statement about the configuration options of the list entries is correct according to the excerpt?

options.text: Entries on the `egressGateways` list have the exact same configuration options as the `egressGateway` field, and the same restrictions apply to each item.
Entries on the `egressGateways` list support a reduced set of options compared with the `egressGateway` field.
Entries on the `egressGateways` list support additional options that the `egressGateway` field does not.
The `egressGateways` list has no restrictions, unlike the `egressGateway` field.

explanation: The excerpt says entries on the `egressGateways` list have the exact same configuration options as the `egressGateway` field, and that the same restrictions apply to each item of the list.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the options are exactly the same, not reduced.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the options are exactly the same, not extended.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says the same restrictions as with the `egressGateway` field apply to each item of the list.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
Entries on this list have the exact same
configuration options as the ``egressGateway`` field

stem: An endpoint has been egressing through one of several gateway nodes selected by a policy. The cluster's gateway nodes matched by the `nodeSelector` fields remain unchanged. What does the excerpt say about that endpoint's gateway for the rest of its lifetime?

options.text: It should use the same gateway during its lifetime as long as the matched gateway nodes do not change.
It will be rotated to a different gateway periodically to balance load.
It will be reassigned whenever any other endpoint in the cluster is created.
It will always use the gateway with the lowest CiliumEndpoint UID in the cluster.

explanation: The excerpt says an endpoint should use the same gateway during its lifetime as long as the gateway nodes matched by the `nodeSelector` fields do not change.

optionRationale.b: No periodic rotation is described; stability is tied to the matched gateway nodes not changing.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt ties reassignment to changes in the `nodeSelector` fields or the matched nodes, not to creation of other endpoints.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt refers to assignment based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID but does not describe always choosing the lowest UID in the cluster.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
Hence, an endpoint should use the same gateway during its lifetime
    as long as the gateway nodes matched by the ``nodeSelector`` fields don't change.

stem: An engineer wants to query flow events from pods running on every node of a cluster through a single Hubble endpoint, rather than contacting each node individually. Which Hubble component provides this multi-node capability?

options.text: Hubble Relay, which consumes the gRPC API of each Hubble instance to provide an API covering events from across the entire cluster
The Peer service, which itself aggregates and serves all flow events from every node
The Hubble server, which by default forwards events from all other nodes to the local client
The peer manager, which exposes the Observer service directly to external callers

explanation: The excerpt states that Hubble Relay brings multi-node support, leveraging the Peer service to obtain information about Hubble instances and consuming their gRPC API to provide a richer API covering events from across the entire cluster. The Peer service supplies information about instances; it is Relay that consumes their APIs and serves the aggregated view.

optionRationale.b: The Peer service is used by Relay to obtain information about Hubble instances, not to aggregate and serve flow events itself.
optionRationale.c: The Hubble server instances make their API available per node; the excerpt does not describe the server forwarding other nodes' events.
optionRationale.d: The peer manager provides callers with the list of peers and handles reconnection; it is Relay that implements the Observer service for multi-node.

citations.title: Hubble Relay
citations.quote:
It leverages the Peer service to obtain information about Hubble instances and
consume their gRPC API in order to provide a more rich API that covers events
from across the entire cluster

stem: A cluster administrator is planning a rollout and wants to know when Hubble Relay became a stable feature rather than a technology preview. What does the excerpt say?

options.text: It was introduced as a technology preview in Cilium v1.8 and declared stable in Cilium v1.9
It was introduced as a technology preview in Cilium v1.9 and declared stable in Cilium v1.10
It was stable from its first release in Cilium v1.8, with no preview phase
It was introduced as a technology preview in Cilium v1.7 and declared stable in Cilium v1.8

explanation: The excerpt records that Hubble Relay was first introduced as a technology preview with the release of Cilium v1.8 and was declared stable with the release of Cilium v1.9.

optionRationale.b: The versions are shifted by one: the preview was v1.8 and stability came in v1.9.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly describes an initial technology preview phase, so it was not stable from the first release.
optionRationale.d: Both version numbers are earlier than those given in the excerpt.

citations.title: Hubble Relay
citations.quote:
Hubble Relay was first introduced as a technology preview with the release of
Cilium v1.8 and was declared stable with the release of Cilium v1.9.

stem: Hubble Relay needs to keep track of which Hubble instances exist in the cluster and to recover when one becomes unavailable. Which description matches the mechanism in the excerpt?

options.text: A peer manager maintains a persistent connection with every Hubble peer, provides callers with the list of peers, and attempts to reconnect when a caller reports a peer unreachable
A peer manager polls each Hubble peer on a fixed interval and removes unreachable peers permanently from the cluster
Hubble Relay connects only to the local node's Hubble instance and relies on that instance to fan out to the others
The Peer service holds the persistent connections to each Hubble peer and reports unreachable peers to Relay

explanation: The excerpt describes a peer manager that maintains a persistent connection with every Hubble peer, provides callers with the list of peers, and, when a caller reports a peer unreachable, attempts to reconnect.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes reconnection attempts, not permanent removal, and does not mention polling on a fixed interval.
optionRationale.c: Relay connects to every node in a cluster, not only the local one.
optionRationale.d: The Peer service is what Relay leverages to obtain information about Hubble instances; the persistent connections and reconnection behaviour belong to the peer manager.

citations.title: Hubble Relay
citations.quote:
it
maintains a persistent connection with every Hubble peer in a cluster with a
peer manager. This component provides callers with the list of peers. Callers
may report when a peer is unreachable, in which case the peer manager will
attempt to reconnect.

stem: A security review asks how access to the Hubble server API is restricted when it is exposed on a TCP port. What does the excerpt say about this?

options.text: By default, Hubble server endpoints are secured using mutual TLS (mTLS) in order to limit access to Hubble Relay only
By default, Hubble server endpoints are unauthenticated and rely on network policy to restrict access
By default, Hubble server endpoints use server-side TLS only, so any client with the CA certificate can connect
By default, Hubble server endpoints are secured using mTLS, but access is open to any client holding a certificate

explanation: The excerpt states that, by default, Hubble server endpoints are secured using mutual TLS (mTLS) when exposed on a TCP port, in order to limit access to Hubble Relay only.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes mTLS protection by default, not unauthenticated endpoints.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt specifies mutual TLS, which requires client certificates, not server-side TLS alone.
optionRationale.d: The stated purpose of mTLS is to limit access to Hubble Relay only, not to admit any certificate holder.

citations.title: Hubble Relay
citations.quote:
By default,
Hubble server endpoints are secured using mutual TLS (mTLS) when exposed on a
TCP port in order to limit access to Hubble Relay only.

stem: An operator is troubleshooting why Hubble Relay cannot reach a Hubble instance on a particular node and wants to confirm the port the Hubble server API listens on by default. Which port does the excerpt give?

options.text: Port 4244
Port 4245
Port 443
Port 8080

explanation: The excerpt says that, as Hubble Relay connects to every node in a cluster, the Hubble server instances must make their API available, by default on port 4244.

optionRationale.b: This is a different port number not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: This is a different port number not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: This is a different port number not mentioned in the excerpt.

citations.title: Hubble Relay
citations.quote:
the Hubble server
instances must make their API available (by default on port 4244).

stem: An organisation runs several Kubernetes clusters joined with ClusterMesh and wants a single view of Hubble events spanning all of them. According to the excerpt, which component makes this possible?

options.text: Hubble Relay, whose richer API can cover events from across the entire cluster or even multiple clusters in a ClusterMesh scenario
The peer manager, which federates events between clusters and exposes them through the Observer service
The Hubble server, which by default spans multiple clusters when ClusterMesh is enabled
The Peer service, which aggregates events from all clusters and serves them to callers

explanation: The excerpt says Relay provides a richer API that covers events from across the entire cluster, or even multiple clusters in a ClusterMesh scenario.

optionRationale.b: The peer manager maintains connections and supplies the list of peers; the multi-cluster event coverage is attributed to Relay's API.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the Hubble server as making its API available per node; it does not say the server spans clusters by default.
optionRationale.d: The Peer service is used by Relay to obtain information about Hubble instances, not to aggregate and serve events across clusters.

citations.title: Hubble Relay
citations.quote:
provide a more rich API that covers events
from across the entire cluster (or even multiple clusters in a ClusterMesh
scenario).

stem: You are running Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. You enable the Cilium Gateway API with host network mode through Helm, and a colleague asks what happened to the LoadBalancer type Service mode. What is the result?

options.text: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode, because the two are mutually exclusive.
Both modes remain active, and Cilium chooses between them per request at runtime.
Host network mode is rejected unless the LoadBalancer type Service mode is disabled first in a separate step.
The LoadBalancer type Service mode stays enabled but is limited to IPv6 listeners only.

explanation: The excerpt states that enabling the Cilium Gateway API host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode, and that the two are mutually exclusive. No separate manual step is required, and there is no per-request selection between the modes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both remain active with runtime selection.
optionRationale.c: The disabling happens automatically on enabling host network mode; the excerpt describes no separate prerequisite step.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no such IPv6-only limitation on the LoadBalancer type Service mode; it simply says the mode is disabled.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium Gateway API host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

stem: A platform team wants cross-cluster service discovery that follows a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard and gives them status condition reporting plus a dedicated `clusterset.local` DNS domain. Which Cluster Mesh option should they choose?

options.text: MCS-API, because it is the SIG Multicluster standard with higher-level features such as status condition reporting and the `clusterset.local` domain
Global Services, because they are the only option that provides a dedicated DNS domain
Global Services, because MCS-API cannot report status conditions
Neither; cross-cluster service discovery requires both options to be enabled together

explanation: The excerpt states that MCS-API is a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard based on ServiceExport and ServiceImport, and that it provides higher-level features such as consistent global service properties, status condition reporting and a dedicated `clusterset.local` DNS domain. Global Services are described as Cilium-specific cross-cluster load-balancing driven from Service annotations, so they are not the standard-based option.

optionRationale.b: The dedicated ``clusterset.local`` DNS domain is attributed to MCS-API, not to Global Services.
optionRationale.c: Status condition reporting is listed as an MCS-API feature, so this reverses the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says you can use either option, or both, depending on your needs — not that both are required.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
MCS-API  is a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard
based on the ServiceExport and ServiceImport resources. It provides higher-level
features such as consistent global service properties, status condition reporting,
and a dedicated ``clusterset.local`` DNS domain

stem: An engineer needs cross-cluster load-balancing configured directly from Cilium Service annotations, and wants granular control over how backends are shared between clusters. Which option fits, and why?

options.text: MCS-API, because it exposes Service annotations for backend sharing
Global Services, because they provide Cilium-specific cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations and allow more granular control
MCS-API, because it is the only option that supports differing Service properties per cluster
Global Services, because they replace the need for any Service annotations

explanation: The excerpt describes Global Services as providing Cilium-specific cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations, and notes they are useful when you want different Service properties in each cluster or more granular control over how backends are shared.

optionRationale.a: Annotation-driven load-balancing is attributed to Global Services, not MCS-API.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt associates differing Service properties per cluster with Global Services, not MCS-API.
optionRationale.d: Global Services work directly from Service annotations, so they do not remove the need for them.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
Global Services  provide Cilium-specific
cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations.

stem: A cluster uses MCS-API and the team wants the `clusterset.local` DNS domain to work without manually editing CoreDNS configuration. According to the excerpt, what makes this possible?

options.text: CoreDNS auto-configuration, which Cilium can manage automatically when it is enabled
Global Services annotations, which inject the DNS domain
ServiceExport resources, which configure CoreDNS directly
ServiceImport resources, which replace CoreDNS entirely

explanation: The excerpt says the dedicated `clusterset.local` DNS domain requires CoreDNS configuration that Cilium can manage automatically when CoreDNS auto-configuration is enabled.

optionRationale.b: Global Services are described as annotation-based load-balancing, not as the mechanism for the DNS domain.
optionRationale.c: ServiceExport is named as a resource underlying MCS-API, not as the CoreDNS configuration mechanism.
optionRationale.d: ServiceImport is named as a resource underlying MCS-API; the excerpt does not say it replaces CoreDNS.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
which requires CoreDNS configuration
that Cilium can manage automatically when CoreDNS auto-configuration is enabled.

stem: A team is deciding between the two Cluster Mesh options for cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing. What does the excerpt say about using them?

options.text: Only MCS-API may be used; Global Services must be disabled first
Only Global Services may be used; MCS-API is mutually exclusive with it
You can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment
Both must always be enabled, since neither works on its own

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium supports two options for cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing with Cluster Mesh, and that you can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt presents MCS-API as one of two supported options, not the only permitted one.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not make the options mutually exclusive; it allows either or both.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says either or both, not that both are mandatory.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote: You can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment.

stem: An engineer reads that MCS-API is built on two Kubernetes resources. Which pair does the excerpt name?

options.text: ServiceExport and ServiceImport
ServiceMonitor and ServiceImport
ServiceExport and GlobalService
ServiceImport and CiliumService

explanation: The excerpt states that MCS-API is a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard based on the ServiceExport and ServiceImport resources.

optionRationale.c: GlobalService is not named as an MCS-API resource; Global Services are a separate option.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
MCS-API  is a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard
based on the ServiceExport and ServiceImport resources.

stem: You are defining a security policy for the Star Wars demo and want it to apply to the deathstar pods no matter which node they are scheduled on or when they are started. What does Cilium use to identify the pods the policy applies to?

options.text: The endpoint IP addresses of the pods
The labels assigned to the pods
The Kubernetes namespace of the pods
The node hostname the pods are running on

explanation: Cilium applies policies based on pod labels, so the policy reaches the right pods irrespective of where or when they run in the cluster. Endpoint IP addresses are explicitly described as irrelevant for defining security policies.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention namespaces as the selection mechanism; it describes label-based selection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says policies apply irrespective of where the pod is running, so node hostname is not the mechanism.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote:
endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security
policies. Instead, you can use the labels assigned to the pods to define

stem: You apply a policy that restricts deathstar landing requests to ships carrying the label org=empire. You then run a landing request from a tiefighter pod, which has that label. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request hangs and must be killed with Control-C.
The request is rejected with a connection refused error.
The request succeeds and returns 'Ship landed'.
The request succeeds only after the policy is deleted.

explanation: The excerpt shows that after applying the policy, only the tiefighter pods with the org=empire label succeed, and the sample output for the tiefighter request is 'Ship landed'.

optionRationale.a: The hanging behaviour is described for the xwing request, not the labelled tiefighter.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe a connection refused error; the blocked request hangs instead.
optionRationale.d: The tiefighter request succeeds with the policy in place, as shown in the sample session.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: Now if we run the landing requests again, only the *tiefighter* pods with the label ``org=empire`` will succeed.

stem: After applying the L3/L4 policy in the demo, you run the same landing request from an xwing pod. What happens?

options.text: The request returns 'Ship landed' immediately.
The request hangs, and you must press Control-C or wait for it to time out.
The request is allowed because reply packets are always permitted.
The request is allowed because xwing pods are matched by the endpointSelector.

explanation: The excerpt states that the xwing pods will be blocked, and that the request will hang, so you press Control-C to kill the curl request or wait for it to time out.

optionRationale.a: 'Ship landed' is the response for the labelled tiefighter pod, not the blocked xwing.
optionRationale.c: Stateful connection tracking applies to reply packets within an allowed connection, not to a new request from a pod the policy blocks.
optionRationale.d: The policy whitelists traffic from pods with the org=empire label; the xwing request is blocked.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: This request will hang, so press Control-C to kill the curl request, or wait for it to time out.

stem: A policy allows the frontend to reach the backend. What does Cilium's stateful connection tracking do about the backend's reply packets?

options.text: It requires a separate explicit policy rule for every reply packet.
It drops reply packets unless the backend also carries the org=empire label.
It automatically allows all required reply packets within the context of the same TCP/UDP connection.
It allows reply packets only on a different TCP/UDP connection.

explanation: Because Cilium performs stateful connection tracking, once policy allows the frontend to reach the backend, all required reply packets that are part of the backend replying to the frontend within the same TCP/UDP connection are automatically allowed.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says replies are automatically allowed, not that each needs its own rule.
optionRationale.b: The org=empire label is specific to the demo policy, not a condition of connection tracking.
optionRationale.d: The automatic allowance is scoped to the same TCP/UDP connection, not a different one.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote:
Cilium performs stateful *connection tracking*, meaning that if policy allows
the frontend to reach backend, it will automatically allow all required reply
packets that are part of backend replying to frontend within the context of the
same TCP/UDP connection.

stem: Which field do CiliumNetworkPolicies use to match on pod labels in order to identify the sources and destinations to which the policy applies?

options.text: endpointSelector
podSelector
labelFilter
ipSelector

explanation: The excerpt states that CiliumNetworkPolicies match on pod labels using an 'endpointSelector' to identify the sources and destinations to which the policy applies.

optionRationale.c: labelFilter is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: ipSelector is not mentioned, and endpoint IP addresses are described as irrelevant for defining policies.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: CiliumNetworkPolicies match on pod labels using an "endpointSelector" to identify the sources and destinations to which the policy applies.

stem: The demo policy filters only on IP protocol and TCP protocol. What is such a policy commonly called?

options.text: An L7 HTTP policy
An L3/L4 network security policy
A DNS-based policy
A cluster-wide egress policy

explanation: The excerpt explains that a policy filtering only on IP protocol (network layer 3) and TCP protocol (network layer 4) is often referred to as an L3/L4 network security policy.

optionRationale.a: L7 is not mentioned; the policy filters on layers 3 and 4 only.
optionRationale.c: DNS-based filtering is not described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe the policy as cluster-wide or egress-specific.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: This is a simple policy that filters only on IP protocol (network layer 3) and TCP protocol (network layer 4), so it is often referred to as an L3/L4 network security policy.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement on nodes where the native devices differ between machines, though every device name begins with the prefix eth. They want NodePort services reachable through those devices without listing each name individually. Which Helm option value should they use?

options.text: devices=eth+
nodePort.directRoutingDevice=eth+
devices='eth0,eth1,eth2'
nodePort.range="10000\,32767"

explanation: The excerpt states that if the devices do not match across different nodes, the wildcard option can be used, for example devices=eth+, which matches any device starting with the prefix eth. The directRoutingDevice option concerns the single device used for direct routing between Cilium nodes, not the set of devices on which NodePort services are exposed.

optionRationale.b: The wildcard is available for directRoutingDevice too, but that option selects the direct routing device, not the devices through which NodePort services are made accessible.
optionRationale.c: This lists explicit device names, which the excerpt says must be named the same on all Cilium managed nodes — precisely the problem the team has.

stem: An administrator sets nodePort.directRoutingDevice=eth+ on a cluster where several devices match that wildcard. How does Cilium choose the direct routing device?

stem: A cluster's kube-apiserver has been configured to use the NodePort range 10000-32767 instead of the Kubernetes default. What must be done on the Cilium side?

options.text: Pass the same range to Cilium via nodePort.range, for example nodePort.range="10000\,32767".
Nothing; Cilium always assumes the default range of 30000-32767.
Set nodePort.autoProtectPortRanges to false so the new range is accepted.
Set nodePort.bindProtection to false so the new range is accepted.

explanation: The excerpt states that if kube-apiserver was configured to use a non-default NodePort port range, then the same range must be passed to Cilium via the nodePort.range option, giving nodePort.range="10000\,32767" for a range of 10000-32767.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives 30000-32767 only as the default Kubernetes NodePort range; it explicitly requires passing a non-default range to Cilium.
optionRationale.c: autoProtectPortRanges controls whether the NodePort range is appended to the reserved ports, not whether a non-default range is communicated to Cilium.
optionRationale.d: bindProtection controls whether application bind(2) requests to NodePort service ports are prevented, not the port range configuration.

stem: On a node, the configured NodePort range overlaps with the ephemeral port range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range. What does Cilium do by default, and why?

options.text: It appends the NodePort range to net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports, to prevent a NodePort service from hijacking traffic of a host local application whose source port matches the service port.
It shrinks the ephemeral port range so that the two ranges no longer overlap.
It refuses to start the Cilium agent until the overlap is removed manually.
It disables NodePort services on that node until the overlap is resolved.

explanation: The excerpt says that if the NodePort port range overlaps with the ephemeral port range, Cilium will append the NodePort range to the reserved ports, which is needed to prevent a NodePort service from hijacking traffic of a host local application whose source port matches the service port.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes appending to the reserved ports, not modifying the ephemeral port range itself.
optionRationale.c: No such refusal is described; the excerpt describes an automatic modification of the reserved ports.
optionRationale.d: NodePort services are not disabled; the protection is applied through the reserved ports list.

If the NodePort port range overlaps with the ephemeral port range

stem: An application running in the host network namespace of a Cilium node attempts a bind(2) to a port that is used by a NodePort service. What does the application typically observe by default, and which setting opts out of this behaviour?

options.text: A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.bindProtection to false opts out.
A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.autoProtectPortRanges to false opts out.

A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.directRoutingDevice opts out.

explanation: The excerpt states that by default the NodePort implementation prevents application bind(2) requests to NodePort service ports, with the application typically seeing a bind: Operation not permitted error, and that expert users can opt out by switching nodePort.bindProtection to false.

optionRationale.b: autoProtectPortRanges controls the modification of the reserved ports list, not the prevention of bind(2) requests.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the bind being prevented with an error, not succeeding with redirection.
optionRationale.d: directRoutingDevice selects the device used for direct routing; it does not govern bind protection.

stem: You are tracing socket load-balancing events with Hubble and want to confirm that a client's connection to a ClusterIP service is being translated to a backend pod. In the Hubble output, which event indicates the flow after the service address has been translated to the selected endpoint?

stem: A cluster administrator is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that includes a `toPorts` entry with both an `http` rule list and a `dns` rule list for the same port. What is the outcome?

options.text: The policy is rejected, because mixing different port level rule types in a single port is disallowed.
Both rule sets are applied, with HTTP evaluated before DNS.
The DNS rules are silently ignored and only the HTTP rules take effect.
The policy is accepted but the port is treated as having no layer 7 rules.

explanation: The `L7Rules` structure is a union: exactly one of the protocol-specific fields must be set per port, and mixing different port level rule types is disallowed. Supplying both `http` and `dns` for the same port therefore makes the policy invalid.

optionRationale.b: The union design forbids combining members on one port, so they are not both applied in any order.
optionRationale.c: Silently dropping one member is not what the excerpt describes; mixing is disallowed outright.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that if none are specified no additional port level rules apply, but here two conflicting types are specified, which is a rejection case.

per port.

stem: Two `toPorts` rules in a policy have identical `PortProtocol` values and select an overlapping set of endpoints. One carries HTTP layer 7 rules and the other carries DNS layer 7 rules. What happens?

options.text: The layer 7 rules are combined, with HTTP taking precedence over DNS.
The policy is rejected, because the layer 7 rule types differ.
Only the first rule encountered is used and the second is discarded.
Both rules are applied independently to the endpoints without interaction.

explanation: When multiple `toPorts` rules with identical `PortProtocol` select an overlapping list of endpoints, layer 7 rules are combined only if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

optionRationale.a: Combining happens only for rules of the same type; differing types cause rejection, not precedence.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes combining or rejecting, not first-match discarding.
optionRationale.d: Overlapping selection with identical `PortProtocol` triggers the combine-or-reject rule, so they are not treated independently.

stem: A layer 7 HTTP rule list contains three separate rules. An incoming HTTP request matches only the second of them. What is the result?

The request is dropped at the network layer without any application response.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: matching at least one rule is sufficient.
optionRationale.c: There is no requirement for the first rule to match; any single match suffices.
optionRationale.d: For layer 7 violations the excerpt says an application protocol specific access denied message is crafted where possible, not a silent packet drop.

optionRationale.c: The fields are marked optional and the excerpt explicitly covers the case where none are specified.

stem: An engineer runs Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement with socket-LB enabled. A pod has an established connected UDP socket to a Service backend, and that backend is then deleted. What does the Cilium agent do?

options.text: It forcefully terminates the application socket connected to the deleted backend so the application can be load-balanced to active backends.
It leaves the socket untouched and silently drops all further packets from that socket until the application closes it.
It rewrites the socket's destination to the Service cluster IP and keeps the connection alive indefinitely.
It disables socket-LB for that pod and falls back to iptables masquerading for the remainder of the connection.

explanation: The excerpt states that when socket-LB is enabled, pods can keep sending traffic to a deleted backend, and Cilium handles this by forcefully terminating application sockets connected to deleted backends so applications can be load-balanced to active backends.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says Cilium forcefully terminates such sockets, not that it leaves them and drops packets.
optionRationale.c: No such rewriting of the destination to the cluster IP is described; the described action is termination of the socket.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe disabling socket-LB or falling back to iptables in this situation.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
Cilium agent
      handles such scenarios by forcefully terminating application sockets that are connected
      to deleted backends, so that the applications can be load-balanced to active backends.

stem: A cluster uses Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement with socket-LB, and the administrator wants the socket termination behaviour for deleted backends to also cover all protocols, enabling `lb-sock-terminate-all-protos`. Which additional kernel config does the excerpt say this requires?

options.text: `CONFIG_INET_TCP_DIAG`
`CONFIG_INET_UDP_DIAG`
`CONFIG_INET_DIAG_DESTROY`
`CONFIG_INET_DIAG`

explanation: The base functionality requires `CONFIG_INET_DIAG`, `CONFIG_INET_UDP_DIAG` and `CONFIG_INET_DIAG_DESTROY`; the excerpt adds that if `lb-sock-terminate-all-protos` is enabled, the functionality additionally requires `CONFIG_INET_TCP_DIAG`.

optionRationale.b: ``CONFIG_INET_UDP_DIAG`` is one of the three configs required by the base functionality, not the additional one for all protocols.
optionRationale.c: ``CONFIG_INET_DIAG_DESTROY`` is part of the base set of required configs, not the additional one.
optionRationale.d: ``CONFIG_INET_DIAG`` is part of the base set of required configs, not the additional one.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
If ``lb-sock-terminate-all-protos`` is enabled the functionality will additionally
      require kernel config ``CONFIG_INET_TCP_DIAG``.

stem: An operator is running Cilium's DSR NodePort mode and observes problems in an environment where TCP Fast Open (TFO) is enabled. According to the excerpt, what is recommended?

options.text: Switch to `snat` mode.
Disable the eBPF kube-proxy replacement and use iptables kube-proxy.
Enable BPF-based masquerading instead of iptables masquerading.
Enable the socket-LB feature so that TFO traffic is translated in the cgroup hooks.

explanation: The excerpt states that DSR NodePort mode does not currently operate well with TCP Fast Open enabled, and recommends switching to `snat` mode in that situation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt recommends switching to ``snat`` mode, not abandoning the eBPF kube-proxy replacement.
optionRationale.c: BPF-based masquerading is recommended over iptables when using BPF-based NodePort, but it is not the remedy given for TFO with DSR.
optionRationale.d: socket-LB is described in relation to service translation and libceph, not as a fix for TFO with DSR NodePort.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
Cilium's DSR NodePort mode currently does not operate well in environments with
      TCP Fast Open (TFO) enabled. It is recommended to switch to ``snat`` mode in this
      situation.

optionRationale.c: This commit is listed without an SMB-only qualifier.
optionRationale.d: This commit is listed without an SMB-only qualifier.

stem: A pod is configured with a `hostPort` that overlaps with the configured NodePort range, on a cluster using Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement. What does the excerpt say happens?

options.text: The `hostPort` setting is ignored and a warning is emitted to the Cilium agent log.
The Pod is rejected by the Cilium agent and remains in a pending state.
The NodePort range is automatically extended so that both configurations can coexist.
The `hostPort` takes precedence and the overlapping NodePort is disabled.

explanation: The excerpt states that the eBPF kube-proxy replacement does not allow `hostPort` configurations for Pods that overlap with the configured NodePort range; in such a case the `hostPort` setting is ignored and a warning is emitted to the Cilium agent log.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the setting being ignored with a warning, not the Pod being rejected.
optionRationale.c: No automatic extension of the NodePort range is described.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the ``hostPort`` setting is ignored, not that it takes precedence.

stem: Which statement about transport protocol support in Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement matches the excerpt?

options.text: SCTP is not supported except in a few basic cases, and only TCP and UDP are fully supported as a transport for services at this time.
SCTP is fully supported, while UDP is supported only in a few basic cases.
TCP, UDP and SCTP are all fully supported as service transports.
Only SCTP is fully supported as a service transport, with TCP and UDP limited to basic cases.

explanation: The excerpt says the eBPF kube-proxy replacement does not support SCTP except in a few basic cases, and that only TCP and UDP are fully supported as a transport for services at this time.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt reverses this: SCTP is the limited protocol, and UDP is fully supported.
optionRationale.c: SCTP is explicitly excluded from full support.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says TCP and UDP are fully supported, not SCTP.

citations.quote:

stem: You have created a single VNet peering from cluster one's virtual network to cluster two's virtual network using `az network vnet peering create` with `--allow-vnet-access`. What connectivity does this give you?

options.text: Outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two only; the reverse direction needs a second peering.
Full bi-directional traffic, because a single peering is always symmetric.
No traffic at all until a route table is attached to both virtual networks.
Only traffic between the control planes, not node-to-node traffic.

explanation: The excerpt states that the first peering command allows outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two, and that bi-directional traffic requires adding a peering in the other direction as well.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says virtual networks can't connect by default and that bi-directional traffic requires a peering in the other direction too, so one peering is not symmetric.
optionRationale.c: No route table is mentioned anywhere in the excerpt; the peering itself is what enables cross-VNet communication.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no distinction between control-plane and node traffic; it speaks of outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
This allows outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two. To allow
bi-directional traffic, add a peering to the other direction as well.

stem: An engineer has run the peering command from cluster one to cluster two and now wants node-to-node traffic between the clusters to work in both directions. What must be done next according to the excerpt?

options.text: Add a peering from cluster two to cluster one, using cluster one's VNet ID as the remote VNet.
Re-run the same command with `--allow-vnet-access` removed so the peering becomes symmetric.
Delete the first peering, since two peerings on the same pair of VNets conflict.
Nothing further; node-to-node traffic is already possible after the first peering.

explanation: The excerpt shows a second `az network vnet peering create` command that peers cluster two's VNet back to cluster one, looking up cluster one's VNet ID, and then states that node-to-node traffic between clusters is now possible.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt never suggests removing `--allow-vnet-access`; both example commands include it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say the first peering must be deleted; it says to add a peering to the other direction as well.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says node-to-node traffic is possible only after the second, reverse peering is added.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
To allow
bi-directional traffic, add a peering to the other direction as well.

stem: In the excerpt's first peering command, how is the remote virtual network supplied to `az network vnet peering create`?

options.text: Via `--remote-vnet "${VNET_ID}"`, where `VNET_ID` was obtained with `az network vnet show --query id -o tsv`.
Via `--vnet-name`, which is set to the remote cluster's network name.
Via `--resource-group`, which points at the remote cluster's resource group.
Via `--name`, which is set to the remote peering's name.

explanation: The excerpt first exports `VNET_ID` using `az network vnet show` with `--query id -o tsv`, then passes it to the peering command as `--remote-vnet "${VNET_ID}"`.

optionRationale.b: `--vnet-name` is set to the local cluster's network (`${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net`), not the remote one.
optionRationale.c: `-g`/`--resource-group` is set to the local cluster's group (`${CLUSTER1}-group`).
optionRationale.d: `--name` names the peering itself (`peering-${CLUSTER1}-to-${CLUSTER2}`), not the remote VNet.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
--remote-vnet "${VNET_ID}" \
     --allow-vnet-access

stem: Which statement best describes the default state of virtual network connectivity and the mechanism the excerpt uses to change it?

options.text: Virtual networks can't connect by default; cross VNet communication is enabled by creating bi-directional peering.
Virtual networks are connected by default and peering is only needed to restrict traffic.
Virtual networks connect automatically once both clusters exist in the same subscription.
Cross VNet communication requires a VPN gateway rather than peering.

explanation: The excerpt opens by stating that virtual networks can't connect to each other by default and that cross VNet communication is enabled by creating bi-directional peering.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: connection is not the default, and peering enables communication rather than restricting it.
optionRationale.c: No automatic connection based on subscription is described; the excerpt requires explicit peering commands.
optionRationale.d: VPN gateways are not mentioned; the excerpt names peering as the mechanism.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
Virtual networks can't connect to each other by default. You can enable cross
VNet communication by creating bi-directional "peering".

stem: After completing the peering in both directions, what does the excerpt conclude about the state of the clusters with respect to Cilium Cluster Mesh?

options.text: Node-to-node traffic between clusters is now possible and all requirements for clustermesh are met.
Node-to-node traffic is possible but a further step is still required before clustermesh requirements are met.
Clustermesh is already fully enabled by the peering commands themselves.
Node-to-node traffic remains impossible until a load balancer is provisioned.

explanation: The excerpt states that node-to-node traffic between clusters is now possible and that all requirements for clustermesh are met, with enabling clustermesh explained elsewhere.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says all requirements for clustermesh are met, not that a further requirement remains.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says enabling clustermesh is explained in gs_clustermesh, so the peering commands do not themselves enable it.
optionRationale.d: Load balancers are not mentioned in the excerpt at all.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
Node-to-node traffic between clusters is now possible. All requirements for
clustermesh are met.

stem: When creating the reverse peering from cluster two to cluster one, which resource group and VNet name does the excerpt's command target?

options.text: `-g "${CLUSTER2}-group"` with `--vnet-name "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net"`.
`-g "${CLUSTER1}-group"` with `--vnet-name "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net"`.
`-g "${CLUSTER2}-group"` with `--vnet-name "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net"`.
`-g "${CLUSTER1}-group"` with `--vnet-name "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net"`.

explanation: In the second command block the peering is created in cluster two's resource group and VNet, with cluster one's VNet ID used as the remote VNet.

optionRationale.b: Those are the local values used in the first command block, which peers cluster one to cluster two.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt pairs cluster two's resource group with cluster two's VNet name, not cluster one's.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt pairs cluster one's resource group with cluster one's VNet name in the first block, not the reverse block.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
-g "${CLUSTER2}-group" \
     --name "peering-${CLUSTER2}-to-${CLUSTER1}" \
     --vnet-name "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net"

stem: An operator notices that every pod in a Deployment is receiving its own distinct security identity rather than sharing one identity across the application. The pods carry a label whose value is a deployment timestamp. What does the excerpt recommend to address this?

options.text: Limit the set of identity-relevant labels so that labels such as timestamps are not evaluated for identity.
Convert the timestamp label into an annotation so that Cilium ignores it automatically.
Add an inclusive label pattern for the timestamp label so that it is grouped across pods.
Disable identity allocation entirely for the namespace containing the Deployment.

explanation: The excerpt states that operators with larger environments should limit the set of identity-relevant labels to avoid frequent creation of new security identities, and gives timestamps and hashes as examples of labels that are not useful for policy enforcement or visibility. Such labels, when included in evaluation, cause Cilium to generate a unique identity for each pod instead of a single identity for all pods of a service or application.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that annotations are ignored automatically; it lists an exclusive pattern for annotation labels, and nothing about converting labels to annotations.
optionRationale.c: An inclusive pattern restricts relevance to matching labels; it does not group a per-pod unique value into a shared identity.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about disabling identity allocation for a namespace.

citations.title: Limiting Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote:
We recommend that operators with larger environments limit the set of
identity-relevant labels to avoid frequent creation of new security identities.

stem: An operator adds a single inclusive label pattern to the identity-relevant label configuration. Which of the following label patterns is then automatically added to the configuration?

options.text: `app\.kubernetes\.io`
`!pod-template-hash`
`!topology\.kubernetes\.io`
`!annotation.*`

explanation: The excerpt says that once at least one inclusive label pattern is added, only labels matching the inclusive configuration may be considered relevant, and a set of inclusive label patterns is automatically added, including `app\.kubernetes\.io` to include all `app.kubernetes.io` labels.

optionRationale.b: ``!pod-template-hash`` is an exclusive pattern from the default exceptions list, not one of the automatically added inclusive patterns.
optionRationale.c: ``!topology\.kubernetes\.io`` is an exclusive pattern from the default exceptions list, not one of the automatically added inclusive patterns.
optionRationale.d: ``!annotation.*`` is an exclusive pattern from the default exceptions list, not one of the automatically added inclusive patterns.

citations.title: Limiting Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote:
Additionally, when at least one inclusive label pattern is
configured, the following inclusive label patterns are automatically added to
the configuration:

stem: How does Cilium distinguish an exclusive label pattern from an inclusive one in the identity-relevant label configuration?

options.text: Exclusive patterns are identified by the presence of the `!` character.
Exclusive patterns are identified by a leading `-` character.
Exclusive patterns are identified by the absence of any wildcard character.
Exclusive patterns are identified by being written in upper case.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the listed label patterns are all exclusive label patterns, defining which label keys should be ignored, and that these are identified by the presence of the `!` character. Configurations without the `!` character are inclusive label patterns.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the ``!`` character, not a leading ``-``, as the marker.
optionRationale.c: Wildcards appear in both kinds of pattern, so their absence is not the distinguishing marker.
optionRationale.d: Case is not mentioned as a distinguishing feature anywhere in the excerpt.

citations.title: Limiting Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote:
The above label patterns are all *exclusive label patterns*, that is to say
they define which label keys should be ignored. These are identified by the
presence of the ``!`` character.

stem: By default, which of the following does Cilium ignore when evaluating labels for identities?

options.text: All `k8s.io` labels
All `app.kubernetes.io` labels
All `reserved:` labels
All `io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster` labels

explanation: The excerpt lists the default exceptions to the rule that all labels are relevant for identities, and `!k8s\.io` is among them, described as ignoring all `k8s.io` labels.

optionRationale.b: ``app\.kubernetes\.io`` appears in the list of inclusive patterns automatically added when an inclusive pattern is configured, not in the default ignore list.
optionRationale.c: ``reserved:.*`` appears in the automatically added inclusive patterns, not in the default ignore list.
optionRationale.d: ``io\.cilium\.k8s\.policy\.cluster`` appears in the automatically added inclusive patterns, not in the default ignore list.

citations.title: Limiting Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote: ``!k8s\.io``                                        Ignore all ``k8s.io`` labels

stem: An operator configures at least one inclusive label pattern. What effect does this have on which labels are considered relevant for identities?

options.text: Only labels that match the inclusive label configuration may be considered relevant for identities.
All labels remain relevant, and the inclusive patterns are added on top of the defaults.
The inclusive patterns replace the exclusive patterns, so all previously ignored labels become relevant.
No labels are considered relevant until an exclusive pattern is also configured.

explanation: The excerpt states that once at least one inclusive label pattern is added, only labels that match the inclusive label configuration may be considered relevant for identities, and that certain inclusive patterns are then added automatically.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says only matching labels may be considered relevant, not that all labels remain relevant.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say the exclusive patterns are replaced; it describes the inclusive patterns as restricting relevance.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about requiring an exclusive pattern before any label becomes relevant.

citations.title: Limiting Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote:
Once at least one inclusive label pattern is added, only
labels that match the inclusive label configuration may be considered relevant
for identities.

stem: In a CiliumBGPAdvertisement using advertisementType CiliumPodIPPool, what does the selector field do?

stem: An engineer installs Cilium with the Hubble Exporter configured, but has not set a value for `hubble-export-file-path`. What is the state of the Hubble Exporter?

options.text: It is disabled until a file path value is set for `hubble-export-file-path`.
It is enabled and writes flows to a default rotated file.
It is enabled and writes flows to `stdout` by default.
It is enabled but only exports flows once the Cilium pod is restarted.

explanation: The excerpt states that the Hubble Exporter is enabled with a ConfigMap property and is disabled until a file path value is set for `hubble-export-file-path`. There is no default path or default `stdout` behaviour described.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives no default file path; the exporter stays disabled until a path value is set.
optionRationale.c: `stdout` is a value you can define for `hubble-export-file-path`, not a default that applies when the key is unset.
optionRationale.d: Restarting the Cilium pods is mentioned only in the context of disabling the static configuration, not of enabling the exporter.

citations.quote:

stem: A platform team runs Kata Pods on a Cilium cluster with VXLAN enabled. Users report packet drops between traditional pods and Kata Pods, which the team traces to fragmentation. Which workaround does the excerpt describe as preferred?

options.text: Lower the MTU value in the Cilium ConfigMap so that the KataPod receives a lower device MTU.
Add an initContainer with NET_ADMIN to the KataPod deployment to adjust the route MTU inside the inner pod.
Disable VXLAN on the cluster so that no additional networking overhead is applied to the default route MTU.
Set the runtimeClassName of the KataPod to a value that copies the default route MTU into the inner namespace.

explanation: The excerpt states that there are two possible workarounds, with (b) being preferred, and (b) is to modify the KataPod deployment by adding an initContainer with NET_ADMIN to adjust the route MTU inside the inner pod. It is preferred because it aligns the KataPod configuration with all other pods and does not harm other connection types, being self-contained in the KataPod itself.

optionRationale.a: This is workaround (a), which the excerpt explicitly does not recommend because of its impact on all other communications.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt never suggests disabling VXLAN; it only mentions VXLAN as an example of overhead (+50B).
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the default route MTU is ignored during inner namespace creation, and no runtimeClassName value changes that.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote: There are currently two possible workarounds, with (b) being preferred:

stem: During creation of the outer Container Networking Namespace, Cilium creates the eth0 interface and then adjusts the default route MTU. How is that default route MTU computed?

options.text: It is copied directly from the inner eth0 device MTU created by Kata.
It is set to the MTU specified in the Cilium ConfigMap, without any adjustment.
It is computed as device MTU minus the overhead given by the Cilium configuration.
It is computed as device MTU plus the overhead given by the Cilium configuration.

explanation: The excerpt says Cilium adjusts the default route MTU, computed as device MTU - overhead, to account for the additional networking overhead given by the Cilium configuration, for example +50B for VXLAN and +80B for WireGuard.

optionRationale.a: The direction is the reverse: Kata copies the outer eth0 device MTU to the inner eth0, not the other way round.
optionRationale.b: The ConfigMap MTU is one possible source of the device MTU, but the route MTU is then reduced by the overhead.
optionRationale.d: The overhead is subtracted, not added, as shown by the example 1500B - 50B = 1450.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote: adjusts the ``default route MTU`` (computed as ``device MTU - overhead``) to account

stem: A KataPod is created inside the VM that Kata runs in the outer Container Networking Namespace. What does Kata copy into the inner Container Networking Namespace's eth0?

options.text: Only the outer eth0 device MTU, while the default route MTU is ignored.
Both the outer eth0 device MTU and the default route MTU.
Only the default route MTU, while the outer eth0 device MTU is ignored.
Neither value; the inner namespace inherits the MTU of the underlying network.

explanation: The excerpt states that during the inner Container Networking Namespace creation only the outer eth0 device MTU is copied over by Kata to the inner eth0, while the default route MTU is ignored. This is the root cause of possible fragmentation between traditional pods and KataPods.

optionRationale.b: The default route MTU is explicitly ignored, not copied.
optionRationale.c: It is the device MTU that is copied and the route MTU that is ignored, the opposite of this option.
optionRationale.d: Kata copies the outer eth0 device MTU; it does not fall back to the underlying network MTU.

only the outer ``eth0 device MTU`` (1) is copied over by Kata to
the inner ``eth0``, while the ``default route MTU`` (2) is ignored.

stem: An engineer wants to find the correct route MTU value to configure inside a KataPod. According to the excerpt, how can that value be obtained?

options.text: By reading the device MTU from the Cilium ConfigMap and using it unchanged.
By issuing ip route on a Cilium Pod or inside a traditional pod, or by computing it manually.
By issuing ip route inside the inner Container Networking Namespace of the KataPod.
By adding 50B to the outer eth0 device MTU for VXLAN overhead.

explanation: The excerpt says the correct route MTU value can be either manually computed or retrieved by issuing ip route on a Cilium Pod (or inside a traditional pod).

optionRationale.a: The ConfigMap MTU is the device MTU, not the route MTU, which is reduced by the overhead.
optionRationale.c: The inner namespace is precisely where the route MTU is not set correctly, so it is not the suggested source.
optionRationale.d: Overhead is subtracted from the device MTU, not added to it.

either manually computed or retrieved by issuing ``ip route`` on a Cilium Pod
(or inside a traditional pod).

stem: Why does the excerpt not recommend lowering the MTU value in the Cilium ConfigMap as a fix for KataPod fragmentation?

options.text: Because the Cilium ConfigMap MTU is ignored by the Kata runtime when creating the inner eth0.
Because it would prevent the KataPod from receiving a lower device MTU at all.
Because the lower device MTU value would be set on all Cilium-managed interfaces, affecting all other types of communications.
Because it would require adding an initContainer with NET_ADMIN to every traditional pod.

explanation: The excerpt says workaround (a) is not recommended as it would have a relevant impact on all the other types of communications (for example traditional pod-to-pod and pod-to-node) due to the lower device MTU value being set on all the Cilium-managed interfaces.

optionRationale.a: The ConfigMap MTU does influence the outer device MTU; the problem is its cluster-wide effect, not that it is ignored.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt says this workaround would allow the KataPod to have a lower device MTU, so it does take effect.
optionRationale.d: The initContainer approach is workaround (b), not a consequence of workaround (a).

due to the lower device MTU value being set on all the
   Cilium-managed interfaces.

stem: An engineer is planning a Cluster Mesh between three clusters. One cluster runs Cilium 1.18.x, a second runs 1.17.x, and a third runs 1.16.x. What does the excerpt say about this combination?

options.text: It is acceptable, because all three versions are within two minor releases of each other.
It is not acceptable, because 1.18.x can connect to 1.17.x or 1.19.x, but not 1.16.x.
It is acceptable, because only the datapath mode must match across clusters.
It is not acceptable, because all clusters must run exactly the same Cilium version.

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium versions must differ by no more than one minor release, and gives the example that 1.18.x can connect to 1.17.x or 1.19.x but not 1.16.x. The third cluster at 1.16.x therefore breaks the requirement.

optionRationale.a: The permitted spread is one minor release, not two; the excerpt explicitly excludes 1.16.x for a 1.18.x cluster.
optionRationale.c: Matching datapath mode is a separate requirement; the version rule is stated independently and is still violated.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt allows a difference of one minor release, so identical versions are not required.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements
citations.quote:
The Cilium versions of all clusters must differ by no more than one minor
  release. For example, Cilium ``1.18.x`` can connect to clusters running
  Cilium ``1.17.x`` or ``1.19.x``, but not ``1.16.x``.

stem: A platform team is preparing two clusters for Cluster Mesh. Cluster A was installed with Cilium defaulting to arch_overlay mode, while cluster B was installed with Cilium defaulting to native_routing mode. What is the consequence according to the excerpt?

options.text: The clusters can be meshed, provided their PodCIDR ranges are unique.
The clusters can be meshed, because the datapath mode is chosen per node rather than per cluster.
The clusters cannot be meshed, because all clusters must be configured with the same datapath mode.
The clusters can be meshed, but only if a VPN tunnel is established between them.

explanation: The excerpt's first requirement is that all clusters must be configured with the same datapath mode, noting that Cilium may default to arch_overlay or native_routing depending on the cloud environment. A mismatch between the two clusters therefore fails this prerequisite.

optionRationale.a: Unique PodCIDR ranges are a separate requirement and do not remedy a datapath mode mismatch.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the datapath mode as a per-cluster configuration, not a per-node choice.
optionRationale.d: Peering or VPN tunnels address node IP connectivity, which is a different requirement from datapath mode.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements

All clusters must be configured with the same datapath mode. Cilium install
  may default to arch_overlay or native_routing mode depending on
  the specific cloud environment.

stem: Which statement about Cilium version compatibility across clusters in a Cluster Mesh is supported by the excerpt?

options.text: Cilium 1.18.x can connect to clusters running 1.17.x or 1.19.x, but not 1.16.x.
Cilium 1.18.x can connect to any cluster running 1.16.x or later.
All clusters must run the identical patch release of Cilium.
Cilium 1.18.x can connect only to clusters running 1.18.x.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says 1.16.x cannot connect to a 1.18.x cluster.
optionRationale.c: The rule is expressed in minor releases, and the example uses the 1.18.x form rather than requiring identical patch releases.
optionRationale.d: A one-minor-release difference is permitted, so 1.17.x and 1.19.x are also allowed.

  Cilium ``1.17.x`` or ``1.19.x``, but not ``1.16.x``.

stem: An engineer is validating addressing before enabling Cluster Mesh. Which requirement does the excerpt place on PodCIDR ranges?

options.text: They must be identical in every cluster so that pods keep the same addresses.
They must be non-conflicting and unique IP addresses across all clusters and all nodes.
They must be allocated from the node's InternalIP subnet.
They must be routable over the public internet between clusters.

explanation: The excerpt requires that PodCIDR ranges in all clusters and all nodes be non-conflicting and unique IP addresses.

optionRationale.a: Identical ranges would conflict, which is the opposite of the stated requirement.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not tie PodCIDR allocation to the InternalIP subnet; it only requires uniqueness and non-conflict.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt mentions peering or VPN tunnels between node networks, not public internet routability of PodCIDRs.

citations.quote:
PodCIDR ranges in all clusters and all nodes must be non-conflicting and
  unique IP addresses.

stem: Two clusters are to be meshed, and the engineer must ensure nodes can reach each other. According to the excerpt, what must be true of node connectivity?

options.text: Nodes must have IP connectivity between each other using the configured InternalIP for each node.
Nodes must have IP connectivity using the PodCIDR assigned to each node.
Nodes must share a single flat Layer 2 network with no tunnelling.
Nodes must be reachable through a load balancer exposed by each cluster.

explanation: The excerpt states that nodes in all clusters must have IP connectivity between each other using the configured InternalIP for each node, typically met by peering or VPN tunnels.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt specifies the configured InternalIP, not the PodCIDR, as the address used for node connectivity.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the requirement is typically met by peering or VPN tunnels, so a flat Layer 2 network is not required.
optionRationale.d: No load balancer mechanism is mentioned; the excerpt refers to peering or VPN tunnels between node networks.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements
citations.quote:
Nodes in all clusters must have IP connectivity between each other using the 
  configured InternalIP for each node.

stem: A security reviewer asks what must be permitted for a Cluster Mesh to function between clusters. What does the excerpt say?

options.text: Only ICMP must be allowed between the clusters.
All traffic between the clusters must be permitted without restriction.
The network between clusters must allow the inter-cluster communication, with the exact ports documented in the firewall_requirements section.
Only the Kubernetes API server port must be reachable between clusters.

explanation: The excerpt requires that the network between clusters allow the inter-cluster communication, and points to the firewall_requirements section for the exact ports.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt does not restrict the requirement to ICMP.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt refers to specific ports documented in the firewall_requirements section rather than permitting all traffic.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not single out the Kubernetes API server port; it defers to the firewall_requirements section.
