  exact ports are documented in the firewall_requirements section.

stem: An engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy for endpoints with label env=prod. They want to ensure that only source endpoints that also carry env=prod can reach those endpoints, but they do not want this rule alone to grant any access. Which field should they use to establish this base requirement?

options.text: fromRequires
fromEndpoints
toRequires
toEntities

explanation: The fromRequires field establishes label requirements that serve as a foundation for any fromEndpoints relationship. It does not grant access by itself; additional rules matching fromEndpoints are needed to allow traffic. toRequires is for egress policies, fromEndpoints grants access, and toEntities is a different egress construct.

optionRationale.b: fromEndpoints is used to allow traffic from specific endpoints, not to set base requirements that do not grant access.
optionRationale.c: toRequires is the egress counterpart used with toEndpoints, not for ingress fromEndpoints.
optionRationale.d: toEntities is an egress rule that allows traffic to entities, not a base requirement field.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
For this purpose, the ``fromRequires`` field can be used to establish label
requirements which serve as a foundation for any ``fromEndpoints``
relationship.

stem: A policy uses fromRequires to require that any source endpoint must have label env=prod to reach endpoints with label env=prod. The same policy also includes a fromEndpoints rule that allows traffic from endpoints with label role=frontend. Which source endpoints will be able to reach the env=prod endpoints?

options.text: Only endpoints that have both env=prod and role=frontend.
Any endpoint with role=frontend, regardless of env label.
Any endpoint with env=prod, regardless of role label.
No endpoints, because fromRequires blocks all traffic.

explanation: The fromRequires rule sets a base requirement that the source must have env=prod. The fromEndpoints rule allows traffic from role=frontend. Both conditions must be met, so only endpoints with both labels can connect. The excerpt confirms this: when combined, the endpoint becomes accessible from endpoints that have both labels env=prod and role=frontend.

optionRationale.b: The fromRequires requirement for env=prod remains in effect and is not overridden by the fromEndpoints rule.
optionRationale.c: The fromEndpoints rule only allows role=frontend, so env=prod alone is insufficient.
optionRationale.d: fromRequires does not block all traffic; it only adds a requirement that must be satisfied alongside other rules.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
when combined with the
example policy below, the endpoint with label ``env=prod`` will become
accessible from endpoints that have both labels ``env=prod`` and
``role=frontend``.

stem: An engineer is reviewing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that uses fromRequires to limit ingress to endpoints with label app=db. The policy also contains a fromEndpoints rule that allows traffic from app=web. The engineer worries that the fromEndpoints rule might limit the scope of the fromRequires requirement. What is the effect of combining these rules?

options.text: The fromRequires requirement stays in effect regardless of what the fromEndpoints rule allows.
The fromEndpoints rule overrides the fromRequires requirement for matching sources.
The fromRequires requirement only applies to traffic not matched by fromEndpoints.
The combination is invalid and the policy is rejected.

explanation: The excerpt states that other ingress and egress rules do not limit the scope of fromRequires or toRequires. Pairing them results in valid policy, but the requirements set in fromRequires stay in effect no matter what would otherwise be allowed by the other rules.

optionRationale.b: The fromEndpoints rule does not override fromRequires; the requirement remains.
optionRationale.c: fromRequires applies to all traffic for the endpoint selector, not just traffic not matched by fromEndpoints.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says pairing other rules with fromRequires results in valid policy.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
Pairing other
ingress and egress rules with a ``toRequires`` or ``fromRequires`` will result in valid
policy, but the requirements set in ``toRequires`` and ``fromRequires`` stay in effect
no matter what would otherwise be allowed by the other rules.

stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between fromRequires and fromEndpoints in a CiliumNetworkPolicy?

options.text: fromRequires sets additional constraints that must be met for the selected endpoints to be reachable, but does not grant access by itself; fromEndpoints rules are also needed to allow traffic.
fromRequires grants access to all endpoints that meet its constraints, making fromEndpoints unnecessary.
fromEndpoints sets base requirements, and fromRequires allows specific traffic.
fromRequires and fromEndpoints are mutually exclusive and cannot be used together.

explanation: The excerpt explains that fromRequires is a list of additional constraints which must be met for the selected endpoints to be reachable. These constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves, so to allow traffic there must also be rules which match fromEndpoints.

optionRationale.b: fromRequires does not grant access; it only sets requirements.
optionRationale.c: The roles are reversed: fromRequires sets base requirements, fromEndpoints allows traffic.
optionRationale.d: They are designed to be used together, as the excerpt shows.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
``fromRequires`` is a list of additional constraints which must
be met in order for the selected endpoints to be reachable. These additional
constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves, so to allow traffic
there must also be rules which match ``fromEndpoints``.

stem: An engineer is designing an egress policy for endpoints with label env=prod. They want to ensure that traffic can only go to destination endpoints that also have label env=prod, and they want this requirement to apply to all egress rules for those endpoints. Which field should they use?

options.text: toRequires
fromRequires
toEndpoints
fromEndpoints

explanation: For egress policies, the toRequires field is used with toEndpoints, analogous to fromRequires with fromEndpoints. toRequires establishes base requirements for egress traffic. fromRequires is for ingress, toEndpoints allows egress traffic, and fromEndpoints is for ingress.

optionRationale.b: fromRequires is for ingress policies, not egress.
optionRationale.c: toEndpoints is used to allow egress traffic to specific endpoints, not to set base requirements.
optionRationale.d: fromEndpoints is for ingress policies.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements

The same applies for
egress policies, with ``toRequires`` and ``toEndpoints``.

stem: A cluster is running Cilium 1.18. An engineer deploys a CiliumNetworkPolicy that uses the fromRequires field. What is the status of this field in this version?

options.text: It is deprecated as of Cilium 1.17.x and will be removed in Cilium 1.19.
It is fully supported and not deprecated.
It was removed in Cilium 1.17.x.
It is only available in Cilium 1.19 and later.

explanation: The excerpt states that the fromRequires and toRequires fields are deprecated as of Cilium 1.17.x and have been removed as of Cilium 1.19. Therefore, in Cilium 1.18 they are deprecated but still present.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says they are deprecated as of 1.17.x.
optionRationale.c: They are deprecated in 1.17.x, not removed; removal is in 1.19.
optionRationale.d: They are removed in 1.19, not introduced.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium with metrics enabled but has left `hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled` at `false`. They want Prometheus to discover the Cilium metrics endpoints without a ServiceMonitor. What does the chart provide for this?

options.text: Annotations on the Cilium components, including `prometheus.io/scrape: true` and `prometheus.io/port: 9962`.
A ServiceMonitor resource that Prometheus discovers automatically.

optionRationale.b: This is the effect of enabling node-to-node encryption, not the default behaviour.
optionRationale.c: The default covers pod-to-pod traffic; node-to-node is the additional mode that must be enabled.
optionRationale.d: Host-network traffic to the kube-apiserver is deliberately excluded from node-to-node encryption, and is certainly not encrypted by default.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
By default, WireGuard-based encryption only encrypts traffic between Cilium-managed
pods.

stem: An engineer enables WireGuard node-to-node encryption and expects every node in the cluster to participate. Which nodes will automatically opt out of node-to-node encryption?

options.text: Nodes carrying the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane label.
Nodes carrying the node-role.kubernetes.io/worker label.
Every node that has a CiliumNode CRD registered.
No nodes opt out; node-to-node encryption always applies cluster-wide.

explanation: Cilium automatically disables node-to-node encryption from and to Kubernetes control-plane nodes, identified by the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane label, which is the default value of the node-encryption-opt-out-labels option.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the control-plane label, not a worker label, as the opt-out selector.
optionRationale.c: A CiliumNode CRD exists for nodes generally and is not the opt-out criterion.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly describes an automatic opt-out, so participation is not cluster-wide by default.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
Cilium automatically disables node-to-node encryption from and to
  Kubernetes control-plane nodes, i.e. any node with the
  ``node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane`` label will opt-out of node-to-node
  encryption.

stem: A worker node reboots and generates a new WireGuard private key, so its public key must be updated. Why does Cilium exclude control-plane nodes from node-to-node encryption by default?

options.text: To avoid a bootstrapping problem where the connection used to update the WireGuard public key would itself be encrypted with the key about to be replaced.
Because control-plane nodes never run Cilium-managed pods and therefore need no encryption.
Because the kube-apiserver cannot process WireGuard-encrypted packets at all.
To reduce CPU overhead on control-plane nodes during key rotation.

explanation: The excerpt explains that encrypting the kube-apiserver connection with WireGuard creates a bootstrapping problem: the connection used to update the public key would be encrypted with the very key being replaced, which is problematic when a node changes its key after a reboot or re-provisioning.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt notes that pod-to-pod traffic for Cilium-managed pods on control-plane nodes is still encrypted, so such pods are contemplated.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not claim the kube-apiserver cannot process such packets; it describes a key-update bootstrapping problem.
optionRationale.d: The stated reason is avoiding lockout from the control plane, not CPU savings.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
This creates a bootstrapping problem where the
  connection used to update the WireGuard public key is itself encrypted with
  the public key about to be replaced.

stem: An engineer wants to force node-to-node encryption from and to control-plane nodes. Which configuration achieves this, and what is the consequence?

options.text: Set node-encryption-opt-out-labels to an empty label selector; the engineer must then always manually update a node's public key in its CiliumNode CRD when a worker node's public key changes.
Set node-encryption-opt-out-labels to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane; worker nodes then update their own public keys automatically.
Remove the control-plane label from every node; no manual key maintenance is then required.
Disable WireGuard entirely; node-to-node encryption is then applied to all nodes including the control plane.

explanation: The excerpt states that an empty label selector with node-encryption-opt-out-labels forces node-to-node encryption from and to control-plane nodes, and that this is not recommended because it requires always manually updating a node's public key in its CiliumNode CRD when a worker node's public key changes.

optionRationale.b: That is the default selector, which causes control-plane nodes to opt out rather than forcing encryption.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe removing labels as a mechanism, and manual key updates would still be needed.
optionRationale.d: Disabling WireGuard would remove encryption rather than extend it to the control plane.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
You may force node-to-node encryption from and to control-plane nodes by
  using an empty label selector with that option.

stem: Which ConfigMap option controls the label selector for matching control-plane nodes that shall not participate in node-to-node encryption, and what is its default?

options.text: node-encryption-opt-out-labels, defaulting to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane.
node-encryption-opt-out-labels, defaulting to an empty label selector.
node-to-node-encryption-labels, defaulting to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane.
encryption-opt-out-selector, defaulting to node-role.kubernetes.io/worker.

explanation: The excerpt names the node-encryption-opt-out-labels ConfigMap option and states that it defaults to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane.

optionRationale.b: An empty selector is the value used to force encryption on control-plane nodes, not the default.
optionRationale.c: The option name is node-encryption-opt-out-labels, not node-to-node-encryption-labels.
optionRationale.d: Neither the option name nor the worker label matches the excerpt.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
The label selector for matching the control-plane nodes which shall not
  participate in node-to-node encryption can be configured using the
  ``node-encryption-opt-out-labels`` ConfigMap option. It defaults to
  ``node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane``.

stem: Even with node-to-node encryption disabled on control-plane nodes, what does the excerpt say remains encrypted there?

options.text: The Kubernetes control-plane itself is usually still encrypted by Kubernetes using mTLS, and pod-to-pod traffic for Cilium-managed pods on those nodes is still encrypted via Cilium's WireGuard implementation.
Nothing remains encrypted on control-plane nodes once they opt out.
Only N/S load balancer traffic remains encrypted on control-plane nodes.
Only Egress Gateway replies remain encrypted on control-plane nodes.

explanation: The excerpt notes that even if WireGuard node-to-node encryption is disabled on those nodes, the Kubernetes control-plane is usually still encrypted by Kubernetes itself using mTLS, and pod-to-pod traffic for Cilium-managed pods on control-plane nodes is still encrypted via Cilium's WireGuard implementation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly lists two forms of traffic that remain encrypted.
optionRationale.c: N/S load balancer traffic is described as not encrypted in certain redirection configurations, not as the remaining protection.
optionRationale.d: Egress Gateway replies are described as not encrypted when XDP Acceleration is enabled, not as remaining protection.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
Note that even if
  WireGuard node-to-node encryption is disabled on those nodes, the Kubernetes
  control-plane itself is usually still encrypted by Kubernetes itself using
  mTLS and that pod-to-pod traffic for any Cilium-manged pods on the
  control-plane nodes are also still encrypted via Cilium's WireGuard
  implementation.

stem: You have deployed a node-local DNS cache as a normal pod and applied a Local Redirect Policy, but DNS queries from application pods are still being resolved by the cluster DNS service rather than the cache. Which verification step does the excerpt recommend to confirm the policy has been applied on the Cilium agent pods?

options.text: Run `cilium-dbg lrp list` inside a Cilium agent pod and check that the policy appears with its matching service.
Run `cilium-dbg service list | grep LocalRedirect` and check for a `ClusterIP` entry.
Curl `<node-local-dns pod IP>:9253/metrics` and check `coredns_dns_requests_total`.
Run `kubectl --namespace kube-system get pods --selector=k8s-app=node-local-dns` and check the READY column.

explanation: The troubleshooting section instructs you to check whether the local redirect policy has been applied correctly on all the cilium agent pods, using `cilium-dbg lrp list`. The output shows the LRP namespace, name, frontend type and matching service.

optionRationale.b: The service list check is a separate troubleshooting step, for confirming the local redirect service entry exists, not for confirming the policy was applied on the agents.
optionRationale.c: The metrics check is how you verify that traffic is now going to the cache after the pods are ready, not a troubleshooting step for a policy that has not taken effect.
optionRationale.d: Checking that the node-local DNS pods are running and ready is a different troubleshooting step, listed before the policy check.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote: Check if the local redirect policy has been applied correctly on all the cilium agent pods.

stem: After all `node-local-dns` pods report ready, you want to confirm that DNS requests from application pods are actually being redirected to the node-local cache. What does the excerpt say you should do?

options.text: Curl `<node-local-dns pod IP>:9253/metrics` and check that `coredns_dns_requests_total` increments as new DNS requests are issued.
Curl the `kube-dns` service VIP on port 53 and check that responses come from the cluster DNS pods.
Run `cilium-dbg lrp list` and confirm the frontend type is `clusterIP + all svc ports`.
Restart the node-local DNS DaemonSet pods and watch for a new local redirect service entry.

explanation: The excerpt states that you can verify redirection by checking the DNS cache's metrics `coredns_dns_requests_total` via curling `<node-local-dns pod IP>:9253/metrics`, and that the metric should increment as new DNS requests from application pods are redirected to the `node-local-dns` pod.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe curling the kube-dns VIP; it describes curling the node-local DNS pod IP on port 9253.
optionRationale.c: Listing the LRP shows the policy configuration, but the excerpt presents the metrics check as the way to verify that traffic now goes to the local node-cache.
optionRationale.d: Restarting the DaemonSet pods is given as a workaround for a missing local redirect service entry, not as a verification method.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote: You can verify by checking the DNS cache's metrics ``coredns_dns_requests_total`` via curling

stem: You are enabling the DNS node-cache in a Cilium cluster. According to the excerpt, why must a Local Redirect Policy be deployed rather than relying on the node-cache's default interception?

options.text: Because the node-cache's default interception of traffic to the cluster DNS service VIP is bypassed when Cilium handles service resolution at or before the veth interface of the application pod.
Because the node-cache cannot listen on a static IP unless an LRP rewrites its listening address.
Because Cilium blocks all traffic to the `kube-dns` service until an LRP names that service as its matching service.
Because the node-cache only serves TCP queries, so an LRP is needed to add UDP support.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the DNS node-cache listens on a static IP to intercept traffic to the cluster's DNS service VIP by default, but this will be bypassed when Cilium is handling service resolution at or before the veth interface of the application pod. Hence an LRP is deployed to steer DNS traffic to the node local dns cache.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the node-cache already listens on a static IP by default; the LRP is for steering traffic, not for changing the listening address.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt says Cilium blocks traffic to `kube-dns`; the issue is that the default interception is bypassed.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the LRP using both `dns` and `dns-tcp` port names, so the node-cache is not described as TCP-only.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote:
bypassed when Cilium is handling service resolution at or before the veth interface of the
application pod

stem: You are adapting the example Local Redirect Policy for a cluster whose DNS service and port names differ from the quick deployment yaml. Which adjustments does the excerpt say are needed?

options.text: Modify the LRP to specify your cluster DNS service, and modify the port names to match your deployment if they differ.
Change the LRP's namespace to the application pod namespace and keep the `dns` and `dns-tcp` port names.
Change the node-cache's static listening IP and leave the LRP unchanged.
Replace the LRP with a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that selects the `kube-dns` pods.

explanation: The excerpt notes that the example LRP uses `kube-dns` for the cluster DNS service and that you will need to modify the example LRP if your cluster DNS service is different; it also says the LRP uses the same port names `dns` and `dns-tcp` as the example quick deployment yaml and that you will need to modify those to match your deployment if they are different.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the namespace specified in the LRP is set to the same namespace as the cluster's dns service, not the application pod namespace.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention changing the node-cache's static listening IP; it points to modifying the LRP.
optionRationale.d: No `CiliumNetworkPolicy` replacement is mentioned; the excerpt describes deploying a Local Redirect Policy.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote: you will need to modify this example LRP to specify it.

stem: A colleague asks what happens to DNS queries from application pods in a Cilium cluster that has no node-local DNS cache. What does the excerpt say?

options.text: They get directed to cluster DNS pods backed by the `kube-dns` service.
They are dropped until a Local Redirect Policy is created.
They are answered by the Cilium agent itself at the veth interface.
They are sent to the node-local cache's static IP and time out.

explanation: The excerpt states that in the absence of a node-local DNS cache, DNS queries from application pods will get directed to cluster DNS pods backed by the `kube-dns` service.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes normal direction to cluster DNS pods, not dropping.
optionRationale.c: Cilium handling service resolution at or before the veth interface is described as bypassing the node-cache's interception, not as answering DNS queries itself.
optionRationale.d: Without a node-local cache there is no cache static IP to send queries to in the excerpt's description.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote:
In the absence of a node-local DNS cache, DNS queries from application pods
will get directed to cluster DNS pods backed by the ``kube-dns`` service.

stem: During troubleshooting you find that the local redirect service entry is missing, which the excerpt attributes to a possible race condition between applying the policy and the node-local DNS DaemonSet pod resources. What workaround does the excerpt suggest?

options.text: Restart the node-local DNS DaemonSet pods, and file a GitHub issue with a sysdump if the issue persists.
Delete and recreate the Local Redirect Policy, then re-run `cilium-dbg lrp list`.
Restart the Cilium agent pods so that the policy is reapplied on every node.
Curl `<node-local-dns pod IP>:9253/metrics` until `coredns_dns_requests_total` increments.

explanation: The excerpt says that if the service entry is missing there might have been a race condition in applying the policy and the node-local DNS DaemonSet pod resources, and that as a workaround you can restart the node-local DNS DaemonSet pods, filing a GitHub issue with a sysdump if the issue persists.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not suggest recreating the LRP; it suggests restarting the DaemonSet pods.
optionRationale.c: Restarting the Cilium agent pods is not mentioned as the workaround for a missing service entry.
optionRationale.d: The metrics check verifies redirection once things work; it is not the workaround for a missing service entry.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote: As a workaround, you can restart the node-local DNS DaemonSet pods.

stem: A Cilium agent's status output shows that the heartbeat key has not been updated in time, and this has now happened on three consecutive checks. What does Cilium conclude?

options.text: The quorum check is declared to have failed and Cilium is declared unhealthy.
The etcd cluster elects a new leader and the agent continues without any status change.
Cilium reports failure in cilium-dbg status and is restarted by the Kubernetes probes.
The agent stops watching the heartbeat key until the operator rewrites it.

explanation: The excerpt states that if the heartbeat key is not updated in time, the quorum check is declared to have failed and Cilium is declared unhealthy after 3 or more consecutive failures. The three-consecutive-failure threshold is therefore met.

optionRationale.b: Leader election and failover are how etcd itself handles an unhealthy endpoint; they are not the conclusion Cilium draws from a missed heartbeat.
optionRationale.c: Reporting failure in cilium-dbg status and being restarted by the probes is what happens when no etcd endpoints can be reached, not the heartbeat-based quorum check.
optionRationale.d: Agents watch the heartbeat key to validate their ability to receive key updates; the excerpt gives no behaviour of ceasing to watch it.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: If the heartbeat key is not updated in time, the quorum check is declared to have failed and Cilium is declared unhealthy after 3 or more consecutive failures.

stem: An operator notices that the interval at which Cilium performs its background etcd health check differs between a small cluster and a much larger one. According to the excerpt, what determines this interval?

options.text: The overall cluster size: the larger the cluster, the longer the interval.
The number of etcd endpoints that are currently unreachable.
The number of consecutive quorum failures recorded so far.
The lease ID assigned to the lock used for the write test.

explanation: The excerpt says the interval depends on the overall cluster size, and that the larger the cluster, the longer the interval.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not tie the interval to how many endpoints are unreachable; unreachable endpoints lead to reported failure instead.
optionRationale.c: Consecutive failures determine when Cilium is declared unhealthy, not the length of the check interval.
optionRationale.d: The lock lease ID appears in the example status output but is not stated to influence the interval.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: The interval depends on the overall cluster size. The larger the cluster, the longer the

stem: A Cilium agent can reach no etcd endpoints at all. What does the excerpt say will happen?

options.text: Cilium reports failure in cilium-dbg status, the Kubernetes liveness and readiness probe fail, and Cilium is restarted.
Cilium waits for three consecutive intervals before reporting anything, then declares loss of quorum.
The Cilium operator rewrites the heartbeat key so that agents can resume receiving updates.
etcd elects a new leader and the agent fails over to a healthy endpoint without any restart.

explanation: The excerpt states that if no etcd endpoints can be reached, Cilium reports failure in cilium-dbg status, which causes the Kubernetes liveness and readiness probe to fail and Cilium to be restarted.

optionRationale.b: The three-interval threshold applies to the quorum write test and the heartbeat check, not to the case where no endpoints can be reached.
optionRationale.c: The operator constantly writes to the heartbeat key, but the excerpt does not describe it as a remedy for total unreachability.
optionRationale.d: Leader election and failover describe etcd's own recovery when an endpoint becomes unhealthy, not the agent's behaviour when no endpoint is reachable.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: If no etcd endpoints can be reached, Cilium will report failure in ``cilium-dbg status``. This will cause the liveness and readiness probe of Kubernetes to fail and Cilium will be restarted.

stem: Which mechanism does Cilium use to validate that an agent is able to receive key updates from etcd?

options.text: The operator constantly writes to a heartbeat key and all agents watch for updates to it.
Each agent acquires and releases a lock to test a write operation requiring quorum.
Each agent polls the etcd leader directly and compares the reported lease ID.
The Kubernetes liveness probe queries etcd on the agent's behalf.

explanation: The excerpt describes the operator constantly writing to the heartbeat key cilium/.heartbeat, with all Cilium agents watching for updates, which validates the ability of an agent to receive key updates from etcd.

optionRationale.b: The lock acquisition and release tests a write operation requiring quorum; it is a separate check from validating receipt of key updates.
optionRationale.c: Polling the leader and comparing lease IDs is not described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: The liveness and readiness probes fail when Cilium reports failure; they are not described as querying etcd for the agent.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: The Cilium operator will constantly write to a heartbeat key (``cilium/.heartbeat``). All Cilium agents will watch for updates to this heartbeat key. This validates the ability for an agent to receive key updates from etcd.

stem: How does the excerpt distinguish the lock-based check from the heartbeat-based check in Cilium's background etcd health monitoring?

options.text: The lock check tests a write operation requiring quorum, while the heartbeat check validates that an agent can receive key updates from etcd.
The lock check validates receipt of key updates, while the heartbeat check tests a write operation requiring quorum.
The lock check is performed by the operator, while the heartbeat check is performed only by the Kubernetes probes.
The lock check runs only when no etcd endpoints can be reached, while the heartbeat check runs continuously.

explanation: The excerpt says a lock is acquired and released to test a write operation which requires quorum, and separately that agents watching the heartbeat key validates the ability for an agent to receive key updates from etcd.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two roles: the lock tests the quorum-requiring write, and the heartbeat validates receipt of key updates.
optionRationale.c: It is the operator that writes the heartbeat key, and the probes are not described as performing the lock check.
optionRationale.d: The lock check is not conditioned on total unreachability; that situation is covered by the reported failure in cilium-dbg status.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: A lock is acquired and released to test a write operation which requires quorum.

stem: You are using Cilium's Gateway API implementation and want to route traffic to a service that is exported from another cluster via Cilium's MCS-API implementation. Which backend kind should you specify in your HTTPRoute?

Gateway

explanation: The excerpt shows that Gateway-API supports MCS-API by specifying a ServiceImport backend, and the example HTTPRoute uses `kind: ServiceImport` in its backendRefs. Therefore, to route to a multi-cluster service, you should use ServiceImport as the backend kind.

optionRationale.b: A Service backend is the usual Kubernetes backend, but the excerpt specifically describes using a ServiceImport backend for MCS-API support.
optionRationale.c: EndpointSlice is mentioned only in the context of alternate Gateway-API implementations that rely on it; it is not a backend kind for MCS-API in this excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Gateway is the parentRef kind, not a backend kind for routing to a service.

stem: You are using a third-party Gateway API implementation that officially supports MCS-API and relies on EndpointSlice to operate, together with Cilium's MCS-API implementation. What must you configure in Cilium?

options.text: Enable EndpointSlice synchronization in Cilium.
Add the annotation `multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service` to the ServiceImport.
Switch to the Cilium Gateway API implementation.
Disable MCS-API support in the Gateway API implementation.

explanation: The excerpt states that if the alternate Gateway-API implementation relies on EndpointSlice to operate, you should configure Cilium to enable EndpointSlice synchronization. This is necessary for the third-party implementation to function with Cilium's MCS-API.

optionRationale.b: The annotation `multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service` is required for the Cilium Gateway API implementation to support MCS-API, not for a third-party implementation that relies on EndpointSlice.
optionRationale.c: Switching to Cilium's Gateway API implementation is not required; the excerpt describes using another implementation with Cilium MCS-API, provided it supports MCS-API and EndpointSlice synchronization is enabled if needed.
optionRationale.d: Disabling MCS-API support would defeat the purpose; the excerpt says the alternate implementation should officially support MCS-API.

If the alternate Gateway-API implementation relies on EndpointSlice to operate,
configure Cilium to enable EndpointSlice synchronization .

stem: You are using the Cilium Gateway API implementation with Cilium's MCS-API. A ServiceImport resource is missing the annotation `multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service`. What is the consequence according to the excerpt?

options.text: The Cilium Gateway API implementation will not support that MCS-API implementation.
The ServiceImport will be ignored by all Gateway API implementations.
Cilium will automatically add the annotation.
The HTTPRoute will fail to be created.

Therefore, without that annotation, the Cilium Gateway API implementation will not support that MCS-API implementation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say the ServiceImport is ignored by all implementations; it specifically discusses the Cilium Gateway API implementation's requirements.
optionRationale.c: There is no mention of Cilium automatically adding the annotation; the excerpt states the annotation must be present.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that the HTTPRoute creation fails; it only describes the support conditions for the Cilium Gateway API implementation.

implementations using an underlying Service associated with a ServiceImport, and with

stem: Which of the following is true about the Cilium Gateway API implementation's support for MCS-API?

It only supports MCS-API implementations that use EndpointSlice.

stem: An operator is running with an external IPAM plugin, and the platform team wants to alert on how long calls to that external IPAM API take, broken down by the operation performed and the response code returned. Which cilium-operator metric should the alert be built on?

options.text: `ipam_api_duration_seconds`
`ipam_resync_total`
`ipam_api_rate_limit_duration_seconds`
`ipam_allocation_duration_seconds`

explanation: `ipam_api_duration_seconds` is the metric described as the duration of interactions with the external IPAM API, and it carries the `operation` and `response_code` labels, which is exactly the breakdown the team needs.

optionRationale.b: ``ipam_resync_total`` counts synchronization operations with the external IPAM API; it is a count, not a duration, and carries no ``response_code`` label.
optionRationale.c: ``ipam_api_rate_limit_duration_seconds`` measures time spent rate limiting while accessing the external IPAM API, not the duration of the API interactions themselves, and its only label is ``operation``.
optionRationale.d: ``ipam_allocation_duration_seconds`` measures allocation latency and is labelled by ``type``, ``status`` and ``subnet_id``, not by ``operation`` and ``response_code``.

citations.title: IPAM
