stem: A cluster administrator wants to know how many nodes currently fall into each of the categories total, in-deficit and at-capacity, so that capacity can be reviewed per category. Which metric exposes this, and by which label is it broken down?

options.text: `ipam_nodes`, broken down by the `category` label
`ipam_available_ips`, broken down by the `target_node` label
`ipam_needed_ips`, broken down by the `target_node` label
`ipam_ip_allocation_ops`, broken down by the `subnet_id` label

explanation: `ipam_nodes` is described as the number of nodes by category, with the categories given as total, in-deficit and at-capacity, and its label is `category`.

optionRationale.b: ``ipam_available_ips`` reports the number of available IPs on a node, not a count of nodes per category.
optionRationale.c: ``ipam_needed_ips`` reports the number of IPs needed to satisfy allocation on a node, not a node count by category.
optionRationale.d: ``ipam_ip_allocation_ops`` counts IP allocation operations and is labelled by ``subnet_id``, not by node category.

citations.title: IPAM
citations.quote: ``ipam_nodes``                           ``category``                                                      Enabled    Number of nodes by category { total  in-deficit  at-capacity }

stem: An engineer is investigating slow IP releases and wants latency figures for releasing an IP or an interface, sliced by the type of operation, its status and the subnet involved. Which metric provides this?

options.text: `ipam_release_duration_seconds`
`ipam_allocation_duration_seconds`
`ipam_ip_release_ops`
`ipam_interface_creation_ops`

explanation: `ipam_release_duration_seconds` is described as release IP or interface latency in seconds and carries the `type`, `status` and `subnet_id` labels.

optionRationale.b: ``ipam_allocation_duration_seconds`` covers allocation latency, not release latency, even though it shares the same label set.
optionRationale.c: ``ipam_ip_release_ops`` counts IP release operations; it is a count, not a latency, and is labelled only by ``subnet_id``.
optionRationale.d: ``ipam_interface_creation_ops`` counts interface creation operations and is labelled only by ``subnet_id``.

citations.title: IPAM
citations.quote: ``ipam_release_duration_seconds``        ``type``, ``status``, ``subnet_id``                               Enabled    Release ip or interface latency in seconds

stem: A node is reported as short of addresses, and the operator must decide how many more IPs to allocate there. Which metric tells the operator the number of IPs needed to satisfy allocation on that node?

options.text: `ipam_needed_ips`
`ipam_used_ips`
`ipam_available_ips`
`ipam_nodes`

explanation: `ipam_needed_ips` is described as the number of IPs needed to satisfy allocation on a node, and it is labelled by `target_node` so the figure can be read per node.

optionRationale.b: ``ipam_used_ips`` reports the number of currently used IPs on a node, which is the current consumption rather than the shortfall to be satisfied.
optionRationale.c: ``ipam_available_ips`` reports the number of available IPs on a node, taking into account plugin specific NIC/Address limits, not the number needed.
optionRationale.d: ``ipam_nodes`` counts nodes by category and does not report IPs needed on a node.

citations.title: IPAM
citations.quote: ``ipam_needed_ips``                      ``target_node``                                                   Enabled    Number of IPs needed to satisfy allocation on a node.

stem: Which cilium-operator IPAM metric is described as the number of synchronization operations with the external IPAM API and carries no labels?

options.text: `ipam_resync_total`
`ipam_api_duration_seconds`
`ipam_api_rate_limit_duration_seconds`
`ipam_ip_allocation_ops`

explanation: `ipam_resync_total` is the metric described as the number of synchronization operations with the external IPAM API, and the excerpt lists no labels for it.

optionRationale.b: ``ipam_api_duration_seconds`` measures the duration of interactions with the external IPAM API and carries the ``operation`` and ``response_code`` labels.
optionRationale.c: ``ipam_api_rate_limit_duration_seconds`` measures rate limiting duration and carries the ``operation`` label.
optionRationale.d: ``ipam_ip_allocation_ops`` counts IP allocation operations and carries the ``subnet_id`` label.

citations.title: IPAM
citations.quote: ``ipam_resync_total``                                                                                      Enabled    Number of synchronization operations with external IPAM API

stem: A team wants to compare, per node, how many IPs are currently in use against how many remain available, bearing in mind plugin specific NIC and address limits. Which pair of metrics should they use?

options.text: `ipam_used_ips` and `ipam_available_ips`
`ipam_needed_ips` and `ipam_nodes`
`ipam_ip_allocation_ops` and `ipam_ip_release_ops`
`ipam_allocation_duration_seconds` and `ipam_release_duration_seconds`

explanation: `ipam_used_ips` gives the number of currently used IPs on a node and `ipam_available_ips` gives the number of available IPs on a node taking into account plugin specific NIC/Address limits; both are labelled by `target_node`.

optionRationale.b: ``ipam_needed_ips`` is the number needed to satisfy allocation and ``ipam_nodes`` counts nodes by category; neither reports used versus available IPs.
optionRationale.c: These two metrics count allocation and release operations, not the current used and available IP totals.
optionRationale.d: These two metrics report allocation and release latency in seconds, not IP counts.

citations.title: IPAM
citations.quote: ``ipam_available_ips``                   ``target_node``                                                   Enabled    Number of available IPs on a node (taking into account plugin specific NIC/Address limits).

stem: A platform team runs a microservices cluster in which pods are created and destroyed constantly during rolling updates. They currently secure traffic with iptables rules that match on IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports. What problem does the excerpt identify with this approach?

options.text: IP addresses frequently churn in dynamic microservices environments, so filtering on them struggles to scale alongside the application.
iptables cannot be loaded on modern Linux kernels once eBPF has been enabled on the node.
iptables rules can only match on HTTP headers, which the team is not yet using.
iptables requires the application to be modified so that it exposes its identity to the kernel.

explanation: The excerpt states that traditional approaches such as iptables filter on IP address and TCP/UDP ports, but IP addresses frequently churn in dynamic microservices environments, and the highly volatile container life cycle causes these approaches to struggle to scale side by side with the application.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt never says iptables cannot run alongside eBPF; it criticises the filtering model, not kernel compatibility.
optionRationale.c: The opposite is true: the excerpt says traditional approaches filter on IP address and TCP/UDP ports, and that Cilium can filter on application-layer protocols such as HTTP.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says eBPF works transparently without requiring the application to change in any way; it does not attribute an application-modification requirement to iptables.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
Traditional Linux network security approaches (e.g., iptables) filter on IP
address and TCP/UDP ports, but IP addresses frequently churn in dynamic
microservices environments.

stem: A security architect wants to distinguish between different kinds of application traffic between services, but finds that TCP port 80 carries a wide range of messages across those services. According to the excerpt, what does Cilium offer in this situation?

options.text: It can filter on application-layer protocols such as HTTP, in addition to providing traditional Layer 3 and Layer 4 segmentation.
It reassigns each service to a dedicated TCP port so that port-based rules become meaningful again.
It replaces TCP with a proprietary transport that carries identity information in every packet.
It restricts security enforcement to Layer 3 and Layer 4 only, leaving application traffic unclassified.

explanation: The excerpt explains that protocol ports can no longer differentiate application traffic for security purposes, and that Cilium can filter on application-layer (e.g. HTTP), providing stronger security isolation by operating at the HTTP layer in addition to traditional Layer 3 and Layer 4 segmentation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe port reassignment; it says ports can no longer be used to differentiate application traffic.
optionRationale.c: No proprietary transport is mentioned; the excerpt refers to lightweight protocols like HTTP and to filtering on application-layer.
optionRationale.d: This inverts the excerpt, which says Cilium operates at the HTTP layer in addition to Layer 3 and Layer 4 segmentation.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
can filter on application-layer (e.g. HTTP).  As a
result, Cilium not only makes it simple to apply security policies in a highly
dynamic environment by decoupling security from addressing, but can also
provide stronger security isolation by operating at the HTTP-layer in addition
to providing traditional Layer 3 and Layer 4 segmentation.

stem: According to the excerpt, on what basis does Cilium insert security visibility and enforcement, in contrast to traditional systems?

options.text: On service, pod or container identity rather than IP address identification.
On the IP address of the node hosting each container.
On the TCP or UDP port number used by each service.
On the MAC address of each virtual network interface.

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium retains the ability to transparently insert security visibility and enforcement, but does so based on service / pod / container identity, in contrast to IP address identification in traditional systems.

optionRationale.b: Node IP addresses are still IP-based identification, which the excerpt contrasts with Cilium's identity-based approach.
optionRationale.c: Port-based differentiation is the traditional model the excerpt says no longer works for application traffic.
optionRationale.d: MAC addresses are not mentioned anywhere in the excerpt.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
By leveraging Linux eBPF, Cilium retains the ability to transparently insert
security visibility + enforcement, but does so in a way that is based on
service / pod / container identity (in contrast to IP address identification in
traditional systems)

stem: An operations team is concerned that adopting eBPF-based networking will require developers to rewrite their applications. What does the excerpt say about this?

options.text: eBPF provides visibility and control in a completely transparent way, without requiring the application to change in any way.
Applications must be recompiled against the eBPF libraries before Cilium can observe them.
Only containerised workloads can be observed, so virtual machines must be migrated first.
Applications must expose a sidecar API so that eBPF programs can query their state.

explanation: The excerpt says eBPF enables visibility into and control over systems and applications at a granularity and efficiency not possible before, and does so in a completely transparent way, without requiring the application to change in any way.

optionRationale.b: Recompilation is not mentioned; the excerpt stresses that no application change is required.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says eBPF is equally well-equipped to handle containerised workloads as well as more traditional workloads such as virtual machines and standard Linux processes.
optionRationale.d: No sidecar API is described; the mechanism is described as transparent.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
It does so in a
completely transparent way, without requiring the application to change in any
way.

stem: Which statement about the range of workloads eBPF can handle is supported by the excerpt?

options.text: It is equally well-equipped for modern containerised workloads and for more traditional workloads such as virtual machines and standard Linux processes.
It is designed exclusively for containerised workloads and cannot observe virtual machines.
It supports virtual machines only when they run a container runtime inside them.
It supports standard Linux processes only after they are placed in a Kubernetes pod.

explanation: The excerpt states that eBPF is equally well-equipped to handle modern containerised workloads as well as more traditional workloads such as virtual machines and standard Linux processes.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the explicit mention of virtual machines and standard Linux processes as supported workloads.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt places no such condition on virtual machine support.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt mentions standard Linux processes directly, with no requirement for a Kubernetes pod.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
eBPF is equally well-equipped to handle modern containerized workloads as
well as more traditional workloads such as virtual machines and standard Linux
processes.

stem: A team worries that identity-based security enforcement will not cope as their microservices environment grows very large. What does the excerpt say about scalability?

options.text: The use of eBPF enables Cilium to achieve this in a way that is highly scalable even for large-scale environments.
Scalability is achieved only by sharding the cluster into many small clusters.
Scalability depends on keeping access control lists below a fixed rule count.
Scalability is limited because identity lookups must be performed by an external database.

explanation: The excerpt closes by stating that the use of eBPF enables Cilium to achieve all of this in a way that is highly scalable even for large-scale environments.

optionRationale.b: Cluster sharding is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt mentions hundreds of thousands of rules only as a burden on traditional approaches, not as a limit on Cilium.
optionRationale.d: No external identity database is described in the excerpt.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
The use of eBPF enables Cilium to achieve all of this in a way that is highly
scalable even for large-scale environments.

stem: Which of the following is listed in the excerpt as a reason why a root-privilege host attacker may have full privileges on the local host?

options.text: Pods running with `privileged: true` or significant capabilities such as `CAP_BPF`, `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, `CAP_NET_RAW`, or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`.
Pods running with a read-only root filesystem and no added capabilities.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy that selects the host namespace.
Enabling the cilium-operator's service account in a different namespace.

explanation: The excerpt lists root SSH or console access, a containerised workload that has escaped the container namespace as a privileged user, and pods running with privileged: true or significant capabilities such as CAP_BPF, CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW, or CAP_SYS_ADMIN.

optionRationale.b: A read-only root filesystem with no added capabilities is not mentioned as a source of root-equivalent access.
optionRationale.c: CiliumNetworkPolicy is not mentioned in the excerpt at all.
optionRationale.d: The operator service account is discussed as an attack vector once the node is compromised, not as a cause of root access.

citations.title: Root-equivalent Host Attacker
citations.quote:
Pods running with ``privileged: true`` or other significant
   capabilities like ``CAP_BPF``, ``CAP_NET_ADMIN``, ``CAP_NET_RAW``, or
   ``CAP_SYS_ADMIN``.

stem: You are connecting three clusters with Cluster Mesh, all using native routing. Each cluster's PodCIDRs are allocated from the 10.0.0.0/8 private address space. Which configuration satisfies the native routing CIDR requirement for this setup?

options.text: Set the native routing CIDR to the PodCIDR of each local cluster only, so that each cluster routes only its own pods natively.
Set the native routing CIDR to 10.0.0.0/8, for example with the Helm option --set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8.
Set the native routing CIDR to 0.0.0.0/0 so that all traffic is natively routed.
Leave the native routing CIDR unset and rely on the Cluster Mesh to derive it from the remote clusters.

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium in each cluster must be configured with a native routing CIDR covering all PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters, and that when cluster CIDRs come from 10.0.0.0/8, a native routing CIDR such as 10.0.0.0/8 should cover all clusters. The Helm form given is --set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8.

optionRationale.a: A CIDR limited to the local PodCIDR would not cover the PodCIDR ranges of the other connected clusters, which the excerpt requires.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives 10.0.0.0/8 as the example covering clusters allocated from that private space; 0.0.0.0/0 is not mentioned.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Cilium in each cluster must be configured with the CIDR; it does not describe any automatic derivation.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote:
Cilium in each cluster must be configured with a native routing CIDR that
  covers all the PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters.

stem: An engineer prefers to configure the native routing CIDR through the Cilium ConfigMap rather than Helm. Given clusters whose CIDRs are allocated from 10.0.0.0/8, which ConfigMap option matches the excerpt's example?

options.text: ipv4-native-routing-cidr=10.0.0.0/8
native-routing-cidr=10.0.0.0/8
ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8
cluster-pool-ipv4-cidr=10.0.0.0/8

explanation: The excerpt lists the ConfigMap option as ipv4-native-routing-cidr=10.0.0.0/8, alongside the Helm and cilium install forms which use the camel-case ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR.

optionRationale.b: This drops the ipv4- prefix that the excerpt's ConfigMap option carries.
optionRationale.c: This is the Helm and cilium install spelling given in the excerpt, not the ConfigMap option.
optionRationale.d: This option name does not appear in the excerpt.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote: ConfigMap option ``ipv4-native-routing-cidr=10.0.0.0/8``

stem: You have configured the native routing CIDR correctly across your clusters, but pods in one cluster still cannot reach pods in another. The excerpt notes that, in addition to nodes, pods in all clusters must have IP connectivity between each other. What does it say typically meets this requirement?

options.text: Enabling the native-routed datapath mode on every cluster.
Establishing peering or VPN tunnels between the networks of the nodes of each cluster.
Allowing all ports between the node networks with firewall rules.
Allocating all cluster CIDRs from the 10.0.0.0/8 private address space.

explanation: The excerpt states that pod IP connectivity between clusters is typically met by establishing peering or VPN tunnels between the networks of the nodes of each cluster.

optionRationale.a: Native routing is the datapath context of the section, but the excerpt does not present enabling it as the means of achieving pod IP connectivity.
optionRationale.c: Firewall rules allowing all ports are given as the means of meeting the separate requirement for pod-to-pod communication across any ports, not the IP connectivity requirement.
optionRationale.d: Allocating CIDRs from 10.0.0.0/8 is described as typical for cluster CIDRs, not as the mechanism providing pod IP connectivity.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote:
This
  requirement is typically met by establishing peering or VPN tunnels between
  the networks of the nodes of each cluster

stem: A security team asks what the network between clusters must permit for Cluster Mesh pods to communicate. According to the excerpt, what is required?

options.text: Only the ports used by the Cilium agents on each node.
Only the ports used by the Cluster Mesh control plane between clusters.
Pod-to-pod inter-cluster communication across any ports that the pods may use.
Only traffic between node IPs, since pod traffic is encapsulated.

explanation: The excerpt says the network between clusters must allow pod-to-pod inter-cluster communication across any ports that the pods may use, typically accomplished with firewall rules allowing pods in different clusters to reach each other on all ports.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt does not restrict the requirement to Cilium agent ports.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not mention a control plane port set; it speaks of any ports the pods may use.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt requires pod-to-pod communication, not merely node-to-node traffic.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote:
The network between clusters must allow pod-to-pod inter-cluster communication
  across any ports that the pods may use.

stem: Which statement best captures the native routing CIDR requirement for native-routed datapath modes in Cluster Mesh?

options.text: Each cluster must use a native routing CIDR that covers only its own PodCIDR range.
Each cluster must use a native routing CIDR that covers all the PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters.
Only the cluster acting as the mesh control point needs a native routing CIDR.
The native routing CIDR must be identical to the node network CIDR of each cluster.

explanation: The excerpt requires Cilium in each cluster to be configured with a native routing CIDR covering all the PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters.

optionRationale.a: Covering only the local PodCIDR range contradicts the requirement to cover all connected clusters' ranges.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says Cilium in each cluster must be configured with the CIDR, not just one cluster.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not equate the native routing CIDR with the node network CIDR.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote: covers all the PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters.

stem: You are preparing a cilium install command for a cluster whose PodCIDRs, like those of the other connected clusters, are allocated from 10.0.0.0/8. Which option does the excerpt give for setting the native routing CIDR with cilium install?

options.text: --set nativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8
--set ipv4-native-routing-cidr=10.0.0.0/8
--set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8
--native-routing-cidr 10.0.0.0/8

explanation: The excerpt lists the cilium install option as --set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8, the same camel-case form used for the Helm option.

optionRationale.a: This omits the ipv4 prefix present in the excerpt's option name.
optionRationale.b: This is the ConfigMap spelling from the excerpt, not the cilium install flag form.
optionRationale.d: This flag form does not appear in the excerpt.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote: ``cilium install`` option ``--set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8``

stem: A cluster runs Cilium in kvstore/etcd mode and the kvstore becomes unavailable. An engineer asks whether existing pods will keep having their network policy enforced. What does the excerpt say?

options.text: Policy enforcement for existing workloads/endpoints continues, because datapath operations do not depend on the kvstore.
Policy enforcement stops for all endpoints until the kvstore returns, because policy rules are read from etcd on every packet.
Policy enforcement continues only for endpoints whose security identity was allocated after the outage began.
Policy enforcement is suspended only for layer 7 policies, while layer 3 and layer 4 rules continue.

explanation: The excerpt lists all datapath operations among the operations which do not require kvstore availability, stating that packets continue to be forwarded and network policy rules continue to be enforced for existing workloads/endpoints.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: datapath forwarding, policy enforcement and visibility for existing workloads/endpoints do not depend on the kvstore.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt makes no such distinction by allocation time; it says all datapath operations for existing workloads/endpoints are unaffected.
optionRationale.d: Layer 7 proxies are mentioned only as possibly briefly unavailable if the agent must restart as part of the etcd_recovery_behavior, not as a policy-enforcement suspension.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
All datapath forwarding, policy enforcement and visibility functions for
existing workloads/endpoints do not depend on the kvstore.

stem: In an etcd-mode cluster, a new workload is scheduled onto a node and it re-uses a security identity that is already known. What does the excerpt warn may still happen?

options.text: Nothing is affected, because re-using a known identity removes all kvstore dependency for that endpoint.
Packet drops due to policy enforcement may be observed, because state propagation of the endpoint details to other nodes still depends on the kvstore.
The endpoint will be assigned a new security identity by the kvstore before any traffic is allowed.
The workload will be rescheduled to another node until the kvstore is reachable.

explanation: The excerpt states that even when a workload can be scheduled by re-using a known security identity, propagation of the endpoint details to other nodes still depends on the kvstore, so packet drops due to policy enforcement may be observed because other nodes are unaware of the new workload.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly says state propagation to other nodes still depends on the kvstore despite identity re-use.
optionRationale.c: Identity re-use is described as avoiding the need for a new allocation; the excerpt does not say a new identity is assigned.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes packet drops due to policy enforcement, not rescheduling of the workload.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
If a
  workload can be scheduled due to re-using a known security identity, then
  state propagation of the endpoint details to other nodes will still depend on
  the kvstore

stem: Which of the following is listed in the excerpt as an operation for which the kvstore is strictly required when running in etcd mode?

options.text: Forwarding of packets for existing endpoints
Application of network policy updates
Registration of new nodes in the kvstore
Processing of updates to services

explanation: Node discovery is listed under the operations for which the kvstore is strictly required: new nodes must register themselves in the kvstore.

optionRationale.a: Forwarding for existing endpoints is listed under operations which do not require kvstore availability.
optionRationale.b: Network policy updates are listed as continuing to be processed and applied without the kvstore.
optionRationale.d: Services updates are listed under operations which do not require kvstore availability.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
Node discovery:
  New nodes require to register themselves in the kvstore.

stem: A Cilium agent in etcd mode starts up while the kvstore is unreachable. According to the excerpt, how does the agent behave?

options.text: It exits immediately without performing any operations until the kvstore appears.
It eventually fails, but still performs all possible operations while waiting for the kvstore to appear.
It falls back to CRD-mode automatically and continues indefinitely.
It blocks all datapath programming on its node until the kvstore connection succeeds.

explanation: The excerpt states that the agent will eventually fail if it cannot connect to the kvstore at bootstrap time, but it will still perform all possible operations while waiting for the kvstore to appear.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the agent still performs all possible operations while waiting, so it does not simply exit without doing anything.
optionRationale.c: No automatic fallback to CRD-mode is described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Datapath operations are listed as not requiring the kvstore, so blocking them is not what the excerpt describes.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
The Cilium agent will eventually fail if it can't connect to the kvstore at
  bootstrap time, however, the agent will still perform all possible operations
  while waiting for the kvstore to appear.

stem: Which statement best captures the difference between CRD-mode and kvstore/etcd mode as described in the excerpt?

options.text: In kvstore/etcd mode the kvstore becomes a vital component of overall cluster health, required to be available for several operations.
In CRD-mode the kvstore is still required, but only for multi-cluster state propagation.
In kvstore/etcd mode the kvstore is optional and only used for visibility functions.
Both modes require the kvstore equally; the only difference is where the CRDs are stored.

explanation: The excerpt says Cilium can run in CRD-mode and kvstore/etcd mode, and that in kvstore/etcd mode the kvstore becomes a vital component of overall cluster health because it must be available for several operations.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say the kvstore is required in CRD-mode; the kvstore requirements described apply when running in etcd mode.
optionRationale.c: The kvstore is described as vital in etcd mode, and visibility functions are listed among operations that do not depend on it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt distinguishes the modes and attaches the kvstore dependency to kvstore/etcd mode, not to both equally.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
When cilium is
running in kvstore/etcd mode, the kvstore becomes a vital component of the
overall cluster health as it is required to be available for several
operations.

stem: An operator notes that the Cilium agent had to restart as part of the etcd_recovery_behavior. According to the excerpt, what delays can this cause?

options.text: Permanent loss of all existing endpoints on the node.
Delays in processing of flow events and metrics, and short unavailability of layer 7 proxies.
Delays in applying network policy updates and service updates.
Delays in registering new nodes in the kvstore.

explanation: The excerpt states that if the agent requires to restart as part of the etcd_recovery_behavior, there can be delays in processing of flow events and metrics, and short unavailability of layer 7 proxies.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt mentions only delays and short unavailability, not permanent loss of endpoints.
optionRationale.c: Network policy updates and services updates are listed as continuing to be processed and applied, not as delayed by the restart.
optionRationale.d: Node registration is a kvstore-required operation, but the excerpt does not attribute delays in it to the agent restart.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
However, if the agent requires to restart as part of the
  etcd_recovery_behavior, there can be delays in:

  * processing of flow events and metrics
  * short unavailability of layer 7 proxies

stem: A platform team runs a cluster whose nodes are on Linux 5.15 and wants to enable BBR congestion control for Pods through Cilium's bandwidth manager. What does the excerpt say about this plan?

options.text: It will work, but only for Pods that stay in the host network namespace.
It will not work reliably, because BBR for Pods requires a v5.18.x or more recent Linux kernel.
It will work as long as eBPF Host-Routing is enabled, since the kernel version is irrelevant.
It will work, but only for Pods exposed behind Kubernetes Services.

explanation: The excerpt states plainly that BBR for Pods requires a v5.18.x or more recent Linux kernel, and repeats that a 5.18 or higher kernel is needed for BBR to work reliably for Pods. A 5.15 kernel therefore does not meet the requirement, and enabling eBPF Host-Routing does not remove the kernel constraint.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says that prior to that kernel, BBR was only working for sockets in the initial network namespace (hostns), which is the opposite of the claim that it would work for Pods there.
optionRationale.c: eBPF Host-Routing is described as an additional requirement, not a substitute for the kernel version; the excerpt explicitly ties reliability to a 5.18 or higher kernel.
optionRationale.d: Being exposed behind Services is given as the situation where BBR is particularly suitable, not as a workaround for an old kernel.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: BBR for Pods requires a v5.18.x or more recent Linux kernel.

stem: An engineer enables the bandwidth manager with BBR on a recent kernel but does not enable eBPF Host-Routing. According to the excerpt, what is the consequence?

options.text: The packet's socket association would be orphaned inside the host stack's forwarding/routing layer, so BBR cannot retain it until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device.
The kernel would stop retaining timestamps of network packets when switching from Pod to host network namespace.
Cilium would silently fall back to CUBIC for all Pods, and the status line would show EDT with BPF [CUBIC].
BBR would still work, but only for sockets in the initial network namespace.

explanation: The excerpt explains that BBR needs eBPF Host-Routing in order to retain the network packet's socket association all the way until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device in the host namespace, and that without it the association would be orphaned inside the host stack's forwarding/routing layer.

optionRationale.b: The timestamp retention issue is attributed to older kernels, not to the absence of eBPF Host-Routing.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe any automatic fallback to CUBIC or a CUBIC status line.
optionRationale.d: Working only for sockets in the initial network namespace is what the excerpt says about kernels prior to the fix, not about missing eBPF Host-Routing.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: BBR also needs eBPF Host-Routing in order to retain the network packet's socket association all the way until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device in the host namespace.

stem: Which command does the excerpt present for verifying whether the bandwidth manager with BBR has been enabled in Cilium?

options.text: kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep BandwidthManager
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg bpf bandwidth list
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg config get bbr
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep CongestionControl

explanation: The excerpt says the cilium status CLI command provides visibility through the BandwidthManager info line, and shows the command piping cilium-dbg status through grep BandwidthManager, producing a line such as EDT with BPF [BBR] [eth0].

optionRationale.b: No such subcommand appears in the excerpt; the verification is done through the status output.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention a config get command for BBR.
optionRationale.d: The info line to grep is named BandwidthManager, not CongestionControl.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: the ``cilium status`` CLI command provides visibility again through the ``BandwidthManager``

stem: A cluster is being created from scratch and the team expects to adopt BBR eventually. What does the excerpt recommend about when to select BBR?

options.text: Enable it later per node, since the setting only affects Pods created after it is applied on that node.
Select BBR upon initial Cilium installation when the cluster is created, so that all nodes and Pods homogeneously use BBR.
Enable BBR only after confirming that all external clients support it.
Enable BBR together with CUBIC on the same nodes to avoid retransmissions.

explanation: The excerpt states that ideally BBR is selected upon initial Cilium installation when the cluster is created, such that all nodes and Pods in the cluster homogeneously use BBR, since otherwise there could be potential unfairness issues for other connections still using CUBIC.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt notes that once enabled it uses BBR as a default for all newly spawned Pods, but its recommendation is homogeneous selection at installation, not per-node later rollout.
optionRationale.c: Client support is not raised as a condition; the excerpt recommends BBR particularly for Services serving external clients from the Internet.
optionRationale.d: CUBIC is mentioned only as the alternative still used by other connections, which creates potential unfairness issues, not as something to run alongside BBR.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: Ideally, BBR is selected upon initial Cilium installation when the cluster is created such that all nodes and Pods in the cluster homogeneously use BBR

stem: According to the excerpt, why do older kernels fail to make BBR work reliably for Pods?

options.text: They do not support the FQ queueing discipline on physical devices.
They do not retain timestamps of network packets when switching from Pod to host network namespace, so the kernel's pacing infrastructure does not function properly.
They lack the bandwidth manager's MQ/FQ setup entirely.
They cannot run eBPF programs in the host namespace.

explanation: The excerpt explains that older kernels do not retain timestamps of network packets when switching from Pod to host network namespace, and that due to this the kernel's pacing infrastructure does not function properly in general, not specific to Cilium.

optionRationale.a: FQ queueing discipline is mentioned in the context of eBPF Host-Routing, not as the reason older kernels fail.
optionRationale.c: The MQ/FQ base infrastructure is described as provided by Cilium's bandwidth manager, not as something missing from older kernels.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not claim older kernels cannot run eBPF programs in the host namespace.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: this is needed since older kernels do not retain timestamps of network packets when switching from Pod to host network namespace

stem: How does the excerpt characterise the benefit of BBR for Internet-facing traffic, and what caveat does it give?

options.text: BBR achieves higher bandwidths and lower latencies, but you might observe a higher rate of TCP retransmissions compared to CUBIC due to the nature of BBR's probing.
BBR achieves higher bandwidths and lower latencies, but only for sockets in the initial network namespace.
BBR reduces retransmissions compared to CUBIC, but increases queueing delays by 25x.
BBR achieves higher bandwidths only when CUBIC is disabled on the node's physical device.

explanation: The excerpt says BBR achieves higher bandwidths and lower latencies for Internet traffic, and notes that due to the nature of BBR's probing you might observe a higher rate of TCP retransmissions compared to CUBIC.

optionRationale.b: Restriction to the initial network namespace is described as the situation prior to the kernel fix, not as a caveat of BBR's benefit.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says queueing delays can be 25x lower, not higher, and does not claim BBR reduces retransmissions.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt gives no instruction to disable CUBIC on the physical device.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: Also note that due to the nature of BBR's probing you might observe a higher rate of TCP retransmissions compared to CUBIC.

stem: An engineer wants to write a policy that restricts traffic to and from the host namespace of specific nodes. Which resource shape does a host policy take?

options.text: A CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector instead of an EndpointSelector
A CiliumNetworkPolicy that uses an EndpointSelector instead of a NodeSelector
A CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses both a NodeSelector and an EndpointSelector
A CiliumHostPolicy custom resource with a nodeName field

explanation: Host policies are expressed as a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy in which the NodeSelector takes the place of the EndpointSelector.

optionRationale.b: A CiliumNetworkPolicy with an EndpointSelector is the ordinary namespaced endpoint policy form, not the host policy form described here.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the NodeSelector is used instead of an EndpointSelector, not alongside it.
optionRationale.d: No such resource as CiliumHostPolicy is mentioned; the host policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote:
Host policies take the form of a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy with a
NodeSelector instead of an EndpointSelector.

stem: A cluster runs a host policy whose NodeSelector matches three worker nodes. On each of those nodes, which traffic does the policy govern?

options.text: Only the host namespace, including host-networking pods, on each selected node
All pods on the selected nodes, whether or not they use host networking
Communications between non-host-networking pods and destinations outside the cluster
Only traffic leaving the cluster through the selected nodes' external interfaces

explanation: Host policies apply to every node matched by the NodeSelector, and on each such node they cover only the host namespace, which includes host-networking pods.

optionRationale.b: The policy applies to the host namespace, not to all pods on the node; non-host-networking pods are outside its scope.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly states that host policies do not apply to communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster.
optionRationale.d: The scope is the host namespace on the selected nodes, not merely egress through external interfaces.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote:
Host policies apply to all the nodes selected by their NodeSelector. In
each selected node, they apply only to the host namespace, including
host-networking pods.

stem: An engineer installs Cilium and wants host policies to be enforced, pinning the firewall to the eth0 device rather than relying on auto-detection. Which helm flags should be supplied?

options.text: --set devices='{eth0}' and --set hostFirewall.enabled=true
--set hostFirewall.enabled=true only, since the interface is always auto-detected
--set devices='{eth0}' only, since enabling the host firewall is implicit
--set hostFirewall.enabled=true and --enable-extended-ip-protocols=true

explanation: Installing host policies requires both the devices flag naming the interface Cilium is configured on and the flag that enables the host firewall.

optionRationale.b: Omitting the devices option leaves Cilium to auto-detect the interface, which is not what the engineer asked for; the host firewall flag alone does not pin the device.
optionRationale.c: The host firewall must be enabled explicitly with hostFirewall.enabled=true; the devices flag alone is insufficient.
optionRationale.d: The extended IP protocols flag concerns protocols without transport-layer ports, not the interface selection or host firewall enablement.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote:
Installation of Host Policies requires the addition of the following ``helm``
flags when installing Cilium:

stem: Which layer 7 rules may a host policy contain?

options.text: Layer 7 DNS rules only, and no other kinds of layer 7 rules
Layer 7 DNS rules and layer 7 HTTP rules
Any layer 7 rules supported by ordinary endpoint policies
No layer 7 rules at all; host policies are limited to layers 3 and 4

explanation: Host policies support layer 3 and layer 4 rules on ingress and egress, and layer 7 DNS rules, but no other layer 7 rule types.

optionRationale.b: HTTP is not among the permitted layer 7 rule types for host policies.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt restricts host policies to DNS among layer 7 rules, so the full endpoint policy set does not apply.
optionRationale.d: Layer 7 DNS rules are permitted, so it is wrong to say there are no layer 7 rules at all.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote:
They can also have
layer 7 DNS rules, but no other kinds of layer 7 rules.

stem: A host policy is in place and an operator needs VRRP traffic to be allowed on the nodes. What must be configured, and what happens to such traffic otherwise?

options.text: Set --enable-extended-ip-protocols to true; without it, the traffic is dropped with DROP_CT_UNKNOWN_PROTO
Add a layer 7 DNS rule for VRRP; without it, the traffic is rejected with a policy denial
Set hostFirewall.enabled=true; without it, VRRP traffic is silently allowed
Nothing needs configuring, because VRRP is handled as an ordinary UDP port

explanation: Protocols without transport-layer ports, such as VRRP, IGMP and tunnel/encapsulation protocols, require the extended IP protocols flag; by default such traffic is dropped with the DROP_CT_UNKNOWN_PROTO error.

optionRationale.b: VRRP is not a DNS rule matter, and layer 7 DNS rules are the only layer 7 rules host policies support.
optionRationale.c: hostFirewall.enabled is required to install host policies at all; it does not govern portless protocols.
optionRationale.d: VRRP has no transport-layer ports, which is precisely why the extended IP protocols flag is needed.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote:
In order to allow protocols such as VRRP, IGMP, and tunnel/encapsulation protocols
that don't have any transport-layer ports, set ``--enable-extended-ip-protocols``
flag to true. By default, such traffic is dropped with ``DROP_CT_UNKNOWN_PROTO`` error.

stem: How does the excerpt characterise host L7 DNS policies?

options.text: As a beta feature for which feedback and GitHub issues are invited
As a stable, generally available feature
As an alpha feature that is disabled by default
As a deprecated feature scheduled for removal

explanation: The excerpt labels host L7 DNS policies a beta feature and asks users to provide feedback and file a GitHub issue if problems occur.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt calls the feature beta, not generally available.
optionRationale.c: It is described as beta, and no default-disabled alpha status is stated.
optionRationale.d: No deprecation is mentioned; the excerpt invites feedback instead.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote: Host L7 DNS policies are a beta feature.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium Cluster Mesh across three clusters. One remote cluster's connection drops and is not restored. An engineer wants Cilium to stop sending global-service traffic to that cluster's backends after a defined period, rather than continuing to use cached information. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: Set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to a duration greater than zero, such as `"15m"`.
Leave `clustermesh.cacheTTL` at its default of `"0s"`, which revokes caches after the built-in grace period.
Set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to `"0s"` to force immediate revocation of cached data.
Disable global services on the unreachable cluster so its backends are removed from the cache.

explanation: The excerpt states that to mitigate stale backends you can configure a cache TTL, and that to enable it you set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to a duration greater than zero (e.g., `"15m"`). With a non-zero TTL, if the connection is lost and not re-established within that duration, Cilium revokes the cached data and stops load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's global-service backends.

optionRationale.b: The default ``"0s"`` disables the feature and means caches are never revoked, so no grace-period revocation occurs.
optionRationale.c: ``"0s"`` is the default that disables the feature; it does not force immediate revocation.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes configuring a cache TTL, not disabling global services on the remote cluster.

citations.title: Handling Unreachable Clusters
citations.quote: The default value is ``"0s"``, which disables this feature and means caches are never revoked.

stem: An operator notices that after a remote cluster in a Cluster Mesh became unreachable, global-service traffic is still being directed at backends in that cluster. No cache TTL has been configured. What explains this behaviour?

options.text: Cilium retains the last-known service information in its cache by default, which can lead to traffic being sent to stale or unreachable backends.
Cilium immediately revokes cached data for any cluster whose connection is lost, so the traffic must be coming from a local backend.
Cilium repopulates the remote cluster's services automatically on connection loss, restoring load-balancing to its backends.
Cilium stops load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's backends as soon as the connection drops, regardless of TTL.

explanation: By default, when a remote cluster becomes unreachable, Cilium retains the last-known service information in its cache, and this can lead to traffic being sent to stale or unreachable backends. Revocation only happens if a cache TTL greater than zero has been configured and the connection is not re-established within that duration.

optionRationale.b: Immediate revocation is not the default; the default ``"0s"`` means caches are never revoked.
optionRationale.c: Repopulation happens when connectivity is re-established, not on connection loss.
optionRationale.d: Stopping load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's backends requires a configured TTL and expiry of that duration.

citations.title: Handling Unreachable Clusters
citations.quote: By default, if a remote cluster becomes unreachable, Cilium will retain the last-known service information in its cache.

stem: How does the default value of `clustermesh.cacheTTL` affect cached service data for an unreachable remote cluster?

options.text: The default `"0s"` disables the feature, so caches are never revoked.
The default `"0s"` revokes caches immediately upon connection loss.
The default is `"15m"`, so caches are revoked after fifteen minutes.
The default `"0s"` means caches are revoked only for global services, not for other services.

explanation: The excerpt states that the default value is `"0s"`, which disables this feature and means caches are never revoked. A duration greater than zero must be set to enable revocation.

optionRationale.b: ``"0s"`` disables the feature rather than triggering immediate revocation.
optionRationale.c: ``"15m"`` is given only as an example of a value greater than zero, not as the default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no such distinction; ``"0s"`` means caches are never revoked.

citations.title: Handling Unreachable Clusters
citations.quote: which disables this feature and means caches are never revoked

stem: A remote cluster in a Cluster Mesh loses connectivity, and the operator has configured `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to `"15m"`. The connection is not re-established within that duration. What happens to global services?

options.text: Cilium automatically revokes the cached data for that cluster and stops load-balancing to the service backends in the unreachable cluster.
Cilium keeps the cached data indefinitely and continues load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's backends.
Cilium revokes the cached data but continues load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's backends until connectivity returns.
Cilium repopulates the remote cluster's services and resumes load-balancing to its backends.

explanation: With a cache TTL configured, if a remote cluster's connection is lost and not re-established within that duration, Cilium automatically revokes the cached data for that cluster. For global services, this means Cilium will stop load-balancing to the service backends in the unreachable cluster.

optionRationale.b: Indefinite retention is the behaviour when the TTL is left at the default ``"0s"``, not when a TTL is configured.
optionRationale.c: Revoking the cached data is precisely what causes load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's backends to stop.
optionRationale.d: Repopulation occurs when connectivity is re-established, which has not happened here.

citations.title: Handling Unreachable Clusters
citations.quote: If a remote cluster's connection is lost and not re-established within this duration, Cilium will automatically revoke the cached data for that cluster.

stem: After a period of unreachability during which cached data was revoked, connectivity to a remote cluster is re-established. What does Cilium do with that cluster's services?

options.text: The remote cluster's services are repopulated, and load-balancing to its backends resumes.
The remote cluster's services remain revoked until the cache TTL expires again.
The remote cluster's services are repopulated, but load-balancing to its backends stays disabled.
The remote cluster's services are repopulated only if `clustermesh.cacheTTL` is reset to `"0s"`.

explanation: The excerpt states that when connectivity is re-established, the remote cluster's services are repopulated, and load-balancing to its backends resumes.

optionRationale.b: Revocation is tied to the lost connection; re-establishing connectivity repopulates the services.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says load-balancing to its backends resumes, not that it stays disabled.
optionRationale.d: Resetting the TTL to ``"0s"`` would disable the revocation feature; it is not a condition for repopulation.

citations.title: Handling Unreachable Clusters
citations.quote: When connectivity is re-established, the remote cluster's services are repopulated, and load-balancing to its backends resumes.

stem: Which statement best contrasts the effect of a zero cache TTL with that of a non-zero cache TTL on an unreachable remote cluster?

options.text: With `"0s"` caches are never revoked, whereas a duration greater than zero causes cached data to be revoked if the connection is not re-established within that duration.
With `"0s"` caches are revoked immediately, whereas a duration greater than zero delays revocation until the connection is re-established.
With `"0s"` only global-service caches are revoked, whereas a duration greater than zero revokes all cached data.
With `"0s"` caches are revoked after fifteen minutes, whereas a duration greater than zero disables revocation.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the default `"0s"` disables the feature and means caches are never revoked, while setting `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to a duration greater than zero enables revocation of cached data when a lost connection is not re-established within that duration.

optionRationale.b: ``"0s"`` does not revoke immediately; it disables revocation entirely.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt draws no distinction by service type; ``"0s"`` means caches are never revoked.
optionRationale.d: The roles are reversed: ``"0s"`` disables the feature, and ``"15m"`` is an example of an enabling value.

citations.title: Handling Unreachable Clusters
citations.quote: To enable it, set ``clustermesh.cacheTTL`` to a duration greater than zero (e.g., ``"15m"``).

stem: A platform team runs Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation with the default settings. A client outside the cluster connects to a NodePort service whose backend pod runs on a different node. What does the node receiving the traffic do with the request?

options.text: It redirects the request to the remote backend on its behalf by performing SNAT, and replies from the backend make an extra hop back to that node for reverse translation.
It leaves the packet untouched and the backend replies directly to the external client using the service IP/port as source.
It drops the request because the backend is remote and no tunnel protocol is configured.
It rewrites the destination to the service's externalIP and requires the MTU to be lowered before forwarding.

explanation: In the default SNAT mode, when the node determines the backend is remote, it redirects the request on its behalf by performing SNAT. The trade-off is that backend replies must make the extra hop back to that node for reverse SNAT translation before returning to the client. No MTU change is needed in this mode.

optionRationale.b: This describes DSR mode, which must be enabled explicitly via the loadBalancer.mode Helm option; it is not the default behaviour.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt says remote backends cause drops; the node forwards them using SNAT.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states SNAT does not require any additional MTU changes, and lowering the MTU is associated with DSR encoding, not SNAT.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: the node is redirecting the request to the remote backend on its behalf by performing SNAT. This does not require any additional MTU changes.

stem: An engineer wants Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation to let backends reply directly to external clients without the extra hop, and also wants policy at the backend node to be able to match on the client's source IP. Which change achieves both goals?

options.text: Set the loadBalancer.mode Helm option to dsr.
Set bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation to true.
Keep the default SNAT mode and enable the Geneve tunnel protocol.
Disable source/destination IP address checking in the public cloud provider.

explanation: Setting loadBalancer.mode to dsr makes Cilium operate in DSR mode, in which backends reply directly to the external client without the extra hop and the client's source IP is preserved so policy can match on it at the backend node.

optionRationale.b: That flag disables the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554; it has nothing to do with DSR or source IP preservation.
optionRationale.c: SNAT mode is precisely the mode in which the client's source IP is not preserved, so keeping it cannot meet the requirement.
optionRationale.d: Disabling address checking may be necessary for DSR to work in some clouds, but it does not itself switch Cilium into DSR mode.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: Another advantage in DSR mode is that the client's source IP is preserved, so policy can match on it at the backend node. In the SNAT mode this is not possible.

stem: A cluster uses DSR mode. Because a given backend can serve multiple services, the backend must know which service IP/port to use as the source when replying. How does Cilium convey this, and what is the cost?

options.text: It encodes the information into the packet using a dispatch mechanism, at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.
It performs reverse SNAT on the node that received the request, at no cost to the MTU.
It sets bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation to true, at the cost of losing client source IP preservation.
It relies on the cloud provider's source/destination IP address checking to supply the service IP/port.

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium encodes the service IP/port information into the packet using one of the dispatch mechanisms, at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.

optionRationale.b: Reverse SNAT on the receiving node is the SNAT mode behaviour that DSR avoids, and it is not how the service IP/port is conveyed.
optionRationale.c: That flag concerns the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554 and does not encode service information.
optionRationale.d: Cloud address checking must in some environments be disabled for DSR to work; it does not supply the service IP/port.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: Cilium encodes this information into the packet (using one of the dispatch mechanisms described below), at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.

stem: An operator is tuning a Cilium deployment and wants to avoid the MTU reduction that DSR would otherwise require for UDP traffic, while still using DSR for TCP. What does the excerpt say makes this possible?

options.text: For TCP services, Cilium only encodes the service IP/port for the SYN packet, not subsequent ones, which allows a hybrid mode using DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
Cilium encodes the service IP/port in every TCP packet, so the MTU reduction applies equally to TCP and UDP.
The loadBalancer.mode option accepts a per-protocol value that selects DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
Setting bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation to true removes the need for any MTU reduction.

explanation: The excerpt notes that for TCP services Cilium only encodes the service IP/port for the SYN packet, not subsequent ones, and that this optimisation allows a hybrid mode where DSR is used for TCP and SNAT for UDP to avoid an otherwise needed MTU reduction.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the stated optimisation, which limits encoding to the SYN packet for TCP.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the hybrid mode as an optimisation arising from SYN-only encoding, not as a per-protocol value of loadBalancer.mode.
optionRationale.d: That flag relates to the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554, not to MTU reduction for DSR.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: For TCP services, Cilium only encodes the service IP/port for the SYN packet, but not subsequent ones.

stem: A team deploys Cilium in DSR mode on AWS and finds that DSR does not work. According to the excerpt, what may need to be done in such a public cloud environment?

options.text: Source/destination IP address checking, which the environment implements, has to be disabled for DSR mode to work.
The loadBalancer.mode must be changed back to snat because DSR is unsupported on any public cloud.
bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation must be set to true so that DSR can function.
The tunnel protocol must be switched to VXLAN, since DSR requires it in cloud environments.

explanation: The excerpt states that in some public cloud provider environments that implement source/destination IP address checking (e.g. AWS), the checking has to be disabled in order for DSR mode to work.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say DSR is unsupported on public clouds; it describes a prerequisite for it to work.
optionRationale.c: That flag disables the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554 and is not presented as a requirement for DSR.
optionRationale.d: VXLAN is listed as supporting only the Geneve dispatch mode, not as a DSR requirement in clouds.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: In some public cloud provider environments that implement source / destination IP address checking (e.g. AWS), the checking has to be disabled in order for the DSR mode to work.

stem: Which statement best describes the default behaviour of Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation with respect to SNAT?

options.text: It operates in SNAT mode by default, redirecting requests to remote backends on the node's behalf and requiring replies to make an extra hop back for reverse SNAT translation.
It operates in DSR mode by default, with backends replying directly to external clients using the service IP/port as source.
It operates in a hybrid mode by default, using DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
It operates without any address translation by default, relying on the client to route replies.

explanation: By default the eBPF NodePort implementation operates in SNAT mode: the node redirects the request to the remote backend on its behalf by performing SNAT, and replies from the backend make the extra hop back to that node for reverse SNAT translation.

optionRationale.b: DSR mode is not the default; it is enabled by changing loadBalancer.mode to dsr.
optionRationale.c: The hybrid mode is described as an optimisation available with DSR, not as the default.
optionRationale.d: The default explicitly performs SNAT, so it is not translation-free.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: By default, Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation operates in SNAT mode.

stem: You are preparing AWS credentials for Cilium to use when connecting to the AWS API. The IAM policy attached to those keys must allow the operator to enumerate EC2 resources. Which policy statement matches the excerpt?

options.text: An Allow effect on the action `ec2:Describe*` with the resource set to `*`.
An Allow effect on the action `ec2:*` restricted to the specific VPC ARN.
An Allow effect on the action `ec2:DescribeInstances` only, with the resource set to `*`.
A Deny effect on `ec2:Describe*` with an Allow effect on all other EC2 actions.

explanation: The excerpt shows a policy whose statement has `"Effect": "Allow"`, `"Action": "ec2:Describe*"` and `"Resource": "*"`. Nothing narrower or broader is described.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt never mentions a VPC ARN or restricting the resource to one; the resource in the policy is `*`.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt uses the wildcard action `ec2:Describe*`, not the single action `ec2:DescribeInstances`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt contains no Deny statement; the only statement has an Allow effect on `ec2:Describe*`.

citations.title: AWS Access keys and IAM role
citations.quote:
"Effect": "Allow",
             "Action": "ec2:Describe*",
             "Resource": "*"

stem: You have obtained AWS access tokens and are now writing the Kubernetes Secret that Cilium will use. According to the excerpt, how must the values in the `data` section be supplied?

options.text: As plain text, with each empty string replaced by the raw credential value.
As base64-encoded strings, with each empty string replaced by the associated value.
As hex-encoded strings generated with the `base64` utility.
As references to a separate ConfigMap holding the raw values.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium on nodes whose devices are auto-detected, and Cilium selects more than a single device to expose NodePort. Some of those underlying device drivers support native XDP and others do not. Which `loadBalancer.acceleration` value lets them enable XDP on the supported devices only?

`best-effort`
`disabled`
`hybrid`

explanation: The excerpt describes exactly this multi-device situation: where some devices support XDP but others do not, XDP can be enabled on the supported devices by setting `loadBalancer.acceleration` to `best-effort`.

optionRationale.a: `native` enables the acceleration, but in a multi-device environment it requires every underlying device's driver to have native XDP support on all Cilium managed nodes.
optionRationale.c: `disabled` is the default and disables the acceleration entirely, so nothing would be enabled on the supported devices.

stem: An engineer enables XDP acceleration for NodePort handling and then tries to observe the packets that were pushed back out of the device for NodePort handling right at the XDP layer. Why does `tcpdump` not show them, and what should be used instead?

The packets are only visible when `loadBalancer.acceleration` is set to `disabled`, so the setting must be turned off first.

explanation: The excerpt notes that packets pushed back out of the device for NodePort handling right at the XDP layer are not visible in tcpdump because packet taps come at a much later stage in the networking stack, and that Cilium's monitor command or metric counters can be used instead for visibility.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt attributes the invisibility to the position of packet taps in the stack, not to encryption, and does not mention `cilium-dbg status` as a packet-visibility tool.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the packets are pushed back out of the device, so they do reach it; it recommends the monitor command or metric counters, not the API server.
optionRationale.d: Disabling the acceleration is not presented as a way to gain visibility; the excerpt recommends the monitor command or metric counters.

stem: A platform team is running Cilium 1.9 and wants to block traffic from a particular source to a set of Pods. They have not enabled any feature flags. What is the position with deny policies?

options.text: Deny policies are available and enabled by default, so they can be used without enabling anything.
Deny policies are available but must be explicitly enabled in the Cilium agent configuration before use.
Deny policies are only available from Cilium 1.10 onwards.
Deny policies are available only in Cilium Enterprise, not in the open-source release.

explanation: The excerpt states that deny policies are available and enabled by default since Cilium 1.9, so no additional enablement step is required.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says they are enabled by default, not that they require explicit enablement.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives Cilium 1.9 as the point from which they are available and enabled by default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no such distinction between editions.

Deny policies, available and enabled by default since Cilium 1.9, allows to

stem: A cluster has a Cilium Network Policy that allows traffic from a client Pod to a server Pod on port 80, and a separate deny policy that denies that same traffic. What is the outcome?

options.text: The traffic is allowed, because the allow policy was created first.
The traffic is denied, because deny policies take precedence over allow policies.
The traffic is allowed, because allow policies always win over deny policies.
The traffic is allowed or denied depending on which policy type is cluster-wide.

explanation: Deny policies take precedence over allow policies, and the excerpt makes clear this holds regardless of whether the allow policy is a Cilium Network Policy, a Clusterwide Cilium Network Policy or a Kubernetes Network Policy.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt gives no role to creation order; precedence is determined by policy type.
optionRationale.c: This reverses the stated precedence.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says deny takes precedence regardless of which of those policy kinds is involved.

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:
Deny policies take precedence over allow policies, regardless of whether they
are a Cilium Network Policy, a Clusterwide Cilium Network Policy or even a
Kubernetes Network Policy.

stem: A single deny policy is applied to a Pod that previously had no policies selecting it. What happens to that Pod's traffic?

options.text: Nothing changes until an allow policy also selects the Pod.
The Pod enters default-deny mode, just as it would with an allow policy.
Only the specifically denied traffic is blocked; all other traffic remains unrestricted.
The Pod is placed in default-allow mode with the deny rule applied as an exception.

explanation: The excerpt states that, similarly to allow policies, Pods enter default-deny mode as soon as a single policy selects them.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says a single policy selecting the Pod is enough to trigger default-deny mode.
optionRationale.c: Default-deny mode is not limited to the explicitly denied traffic.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes default-deny mode, not default-allow with exceptions.

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:

stem: An engineer wants to write a deny policy that blocks requests to one specific URL on an otherwise allowed service, and another that blocks traffic to a specific domain name. What does the excerpt say about this?

Neither is supported: deny policies do not support L7 enforcement or toFQDNs.
Denying a domain name is supported, but denying a URL is not.

explanation: The excerpt lists both as unsupported: deny policies do not support policy enforcement at L7 (specifically denying a URL) and do not support toFQDNs (specifically denying traffic to a specific domain name).

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says L7 enforcement, including denying a URL, is not supported.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says toFQDNs, i.e. denying traffic to a specific domain name, is not supported.

stem: A deny policy is deployed that denies ingress from "world" on all namespaces on all Pods managed by Cilium. What happens to existing inter-cluster policies?

Because there is a Layer 3 allow policy and no deny policy.
Because deny policies never apply to Layer 4 traffic.
Because port 81 is exempt from default-deny mode.

optionRationale.b: That is the excerpt's stated reason for ping to the server being allowed, not for curl to port 81.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows a deny policy at Layer 4 (80/TCP), so deny policies do apply at Layer 4.

stem: An operator has set both `spec.eni.subnet-ids` and `spec.eni.subnet-tags` on the CiliumNode. A new ENI must be allocated. How are the candidate subnets determined?

options.text: Only the subnets whose IDs appear in `subnet-ids` are candidates; the tags are ignored.
Only subnets that match every entry in `subnet-tags` are candidates; the IDs are ignored.
A subnet is a candidate only if its ID is in `subnet-ids` and it also matches all `subnet-tags`.
The two fields are merged, so a subnet is a candidate if it matches either the IDs or the tags.

explanation: The excerpt states that any subnet with an ID in `subnet-ids` is a candidate, that a subnet must match all `subnet-tags` to be a candidate, and explicitly that when `subnet-ids` is set, `subnet-tags` are ignored. So the ID list alone defines the candidates.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the precedence rule: the excerpt says `subnet-tags` are ignored when `subnet-ids` is set, not the other way round.
optionRationale.c: Requiring both would contradict the explicit statement that `subnet-tags` are ignored when `subnet-ids` is set.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes a precedence, not a union; matching either field is not how candidacy is decided.

stem: Neither `spec.eni.subnet-ids` nor `spec.eni.subnet-tags` is set. The operator first tries to place a new ENI in the same subnet as the instance's primary ENI, but that subnet has run out of available IPs. What does the operator try next?

options.text: It immediately creates the ENI in the largest subnet matching the VPC and Availability Zone.
It looks for a subnet in the same route table as the node's subnet.
It fails the allocation and waits for IPs to become free in the node's subnet.
It picks the subnet with the most available addresses across all Availability Zones in the VPC.

explanation: The excerpt describes a fallback chain: consult `spec.eni.node-subnet-id` to use the same subnet as the primary ENI, and if that is not possible, look for a subnet in the same route table as the node's subnet. Only if that also fails does it fall back to the largest matching subnet.

optionRationale.a: The largest matching subnet is the last fallback, reached only after the same-route-table attempt fails.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes further fallbacks rather than a failure when the node's subnet lacks IPs.
optionRationale.d: The fallback is constrained to subnets matching the VPC and Availability Zone, not all Availability Zones.

citations.title: ENI Creation

the operator will look for a subnet in the same
route table as the node's subnet.

stem: Several subnets satisfy the VPC, Availability Zone and any configured ID or tag criteria. How does the operator choose between them?

options.text: It selects the subnet with the lowest ID in lexicographic order.
It selects the subnet with the most available addresses.
It selects the subnet that was created most recently.
It selects the subnet with the fewest existing ENIs attached.

explanation: The excerpt states that if multiple subnets match, the subnet with the most available addresses is selected.

optionRationale.a: No ordering by ID is mentioned; the selection criterion is address availability.
optionRationale.c: Creation time is not part of the described selection criteria.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt refers to available addresses, not to the number of attached ENIs.

stem: A new ENI is being created for an instance whose existing ENIs occupy interface indexes 1, 2 and 4, and `spec.eni.first-interface-index` is set to 1. Which interface index is chosen?

options.text: 1, because it is the value of `spec.eni.first-interface-index`.
3, because it is the first unused index greater than `spec.eni.first-interface-index`.
5, because it is the next index after the highest one in use.
2, because it is the lowest index currently in use and will be reused.

explanation: The excerpt says all existing ENIs are scanned and the first unused index greater than `spec.eni.first-interface-index` is selected. With 1, 2 and 4 in use and a starting point of 1, the first unused index greater than 1 is 3.

optionRationale.a: Index 1 is already in use, and the rule requires an unused index greater than the configured value.
optionRationale.c: The rule takes the first unused index above the configured value, not the one after the highest index in use.
optionRationale.d: Indexes in use are not reused; the scan looks for an unused one.

all existing ENIs are scanned and the first unused index greater than
``spec.eni.first-interface-index`` is selected.

`AllocateAddress` and `AssociateAddress`

optionRationale.c: `ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute` is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: These calls relate to addresses, not to creating and attaching an ENI as described.

stem: An operator sets `spec.eni.security-groups` and also `spec.eni.security-group-tags` on the CiliumNode. Which security groups end up attached to the newly created ENI?

options.text: The security groups matching the tags, because tag matching takes precedence.
The union of the IDs in `spec.eni.security-groups` and the groups matching the tags.
The IDs listed in `spec.eni.security-groups`, because that field is consulted first.
The security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance, because both fields are set.

explanation: The excerpt gives an explicit order: `spec.eni.security-groups` is consulted first, and if it is set those are the Security Group IDs attached. The tag field and the `eth0` inheritance are only reached when the earlier fields are unset.

optionRationale.a: Tag matching is the second step and is not reached when `spec.eni.security-groups` is set.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes a precedence order, not a union of both sources.
optionRationale.d: Inheriting from `eth0` applies only when none of the two fields are set.
