stem: A pod is scheduled onto a node in a Cilium cluster. Which component is invoked by Kubernetes at that moment to trigger the datapath configuration that gives the pod networking, load-balancing and network policies?

options.text: The Cilium Operator, because it handles duties that must be performed once for the entire cluster.
The CNI plugin (`cilium-cni`), which interacts with the Cilium API of the node.
The debug CLI client (`cilium-dbg`), which accesses the eBPF maps directly.
The `cilium` command line tool, using `kubeconfig` information to reach the cluster.

explanation: The CNI plugin is the component Kubernetes invokes when a pod is scheduled or terminated on a node; it then talks to the node's Cilium API to trigger the datapath configuration for that pod. The operator handles cluster-wide duties, the debug CLI inspects the local agent, and the `cilium` CLI is for installing, managing and troubleshooting from outside the cluster.

optionRationale.a: The operator is described as handling duties logically handled once for the entire cluster, not as the component invoked per pod by Kubernetes.
optionRationale.c: ``cilium-dbg`` is for inspecting the state and status of the local agent and accessing eBPF maps, not for triggering pod datapath configuration.
optionRationale.d: The ``cilium`` CLI is typically installed remote from the cluster and is used for quick-installing, managing and troubleshooting, not invoked by Kubernetes on pod scheduling.

The CNI plugin (``cilium-cni``) is invoked by Kubernetes when a pod is

stem: An engineer wants to inspect the state and status of the Cilium agent on the node they are logged into, and to validate the state of the eBPF maps directly. Which tool is intended for this?

options.text: The `cilium` command line tool, installed remote from the cluster and using `kubeconfig`.
The Cilium Operator, which manages cluster-wide duties.
The debug CLI client (`cilium-dbg`), which interacts with the REST API of the agent on the same node.
The CNI plugin (`cilium-cni`), which is invoked when a pod is scheduled or terminated.

optionRationale.a: The ``cilium`` tool is a separate CLI for quick-installing, managing and troubleshooting Cilium on Kubernetes clusters, typically installed remote from the cluster.
optionRationale.b: The operator manages cluster-wide duties and is not a local inspection tool.
optionRationale.d: The CNI plugin is invoked by Kubernetes on pod scheduling or termination; it is not the inspection tool.

citations.title: Cilium

The debug CLI allows inspecting the
  state and status of the local agent. It also provides tooling to directly
  access the eBPF maps to validate their state.

stem: What is the role of the Cilium agent (`cilium-agent`) on a node?

options.text: It runs once for the entire cluster and allocates addresses for new workloads.
It is invoked by Kubernetes when a pod is scheduled or terminated, to configure that pod's datapath.
It is a command-line tool installed remote from the cluster that uses `kubeconfig` to reach the Kubernetes API.

It runs on each node, accepts configuration describing networking, service load-balancing, network policies and visibility requirements, and manages the eBPF programs the kernel uses to control network access in and out of containers.

explanation: The agent runs on each node, accepts configuration via Kubernetes or APIs covering networking, service load-balancing, network policies and visibility & monitoring, listens for events about containers and workloads starting and stopping, and manages the eBPF programs that control network access in and out of those containers.

optionRationale.a: That describes cluster-wide duties, which the excerpt attributes to the operator rather than the per-node agent.
optionRationale.b: That describes the CNI plugin, not the agent.
optionRationale.c: That describes the ``cilium`` command line tool, not the agent.

citations.title: Cilium
citations.quote: The Cilium agent (``cilium-agent``) runs on each node in the cluster.

stem: The Cilium Operator becomes temporarily unavailable in a cluster. According to the excerpt, what is the expected effect?

options.text: All forwarding and network policy decisions stop immediately, because the operator is in the critical path for them.

The cluster will generally continue to function, though depending on configuration there may be delays in address management and thus in scheduling new workloads, or failure to update the kvstore heartbeat key.
Every node's agent immediately restarts and all eBPF programs are removed.
The CNI plugin can no longer be invoked by Kubernetes for any pod on any node.

explanation: The operator is not in the critical path for forwarding or network policy decisions, and a cluster will generally continue to function if it is temporarily unavailable. Depending on configuration, however, its unavailability can delay address management (and therefore scheduling of new workloads) and can prevent the kvstore heartbeat key from being updated, leading agents to declare kvstore unhealthiness and restart.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: the operator is not in the critical path for any forwarding or network policy decision.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt mentions agents declaring kvstore unhealthiness and restarting as a consequence of a stale heartbeat key, not an immediate restart of every agent with removal of eBPF programs.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say the CNI plugin stops being invoked; it describes delays in address management and kvstore heartbeat issues.

citations.title: Cilium
citations.quote:
The Cilium operator is not in the critical path for
  any forwarding or network policy decision. A cluster will generally continue
  to function if the operator is temporarily unavailable.

stem: A platform team creates a LoadBalancer service with spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges set to 192.168.1.0/24. A pod in the same cluster then connects to the service's external address. What does Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement do with that connection?

options.text: It drops the connection because the pod's IP is not in the white-listed CIDR.
It allows the connection, because the field is ignored for access from inside the cluster.
It allows the connection only if the pod's IP falls within 192.168.1.0/24.
It rewrites the source ranges to include all pod CIDRs before evaluating the connection.

explanation: The excerpt states that when the service is accessed from inside a cluster, the kube-proxy replacement ignores the field whether or not it is set, so any pod or host process in the cluster can reach the LoadBalancer service internally. The source ranges therefore do not restrict in-cluster access.

optionRationale.a: The restriction applies to access from outside, not to in-cluster traffic, which is explicitly exempt.
optionRationale.c: The CIDR check is not applied to in-cluster access at all, so membership of the range is irrelevant here.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes no rewriting of source ranges; it says the field is ignored for internal access.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks

ignore the field regardless whether it is set.

stem: An engineer sets spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges on a LoadBalancer service and expects the same CIDR filtering to apply to the NodePort and ClusterIP services created alongside it. What is the default behaviour?

options.text: The CIDRs apply to the LoadBalancer service only, not to the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP services.
The CIDRs apply to the LoadBalancer and NodePort services, but not to the ClusterIP service.
The CIDRs apply to all three service types automatically.
The CIDRs apply to none of them until the src-ranges-policy annotation is set.

explanation: By default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges only apply to the LoadBalancer service, and not to the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP service that get installed along with it.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt makes no distinction granting NodePort the filter by default; both NodePort and ClusterIP are excluded.
optionRationale.c: Applying the ranges to all externally exposed types requires an explicit opt-in, not the default.
optionRationale.d: The default allow-list behaviour applies to the LoadBalancer service without any annotation.

stem: A team wants the CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges to filter traffic for NodePort and ClusterIP services as well as the LoadBalancer service. Which Helm setting enables this?

options.text: bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true

service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: all
bpf.nodePortSourceRanges=true

explanation: The excerpt says the propagation of white-listed CIDRs to all externally exposed service types can be enabled in Helm via bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.

optionRationale.b: This flag name does not appear in the excerpt; the documented Helm option is bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes.
optionRationale.c: src-ranges-policy accepts only allow or deny and controls allow-list versus deny-list, not which service types are filtered.
optionRationale.d: No such flag is mentioned; the excerpt names bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes.

stem: A security team wants to block traffic from a specific set of CIDRs while allowing all other traffic to a LoadBalancer service. How can this be achieved with Cilium?

options.text: Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny on the service and list the CIDRs in loadBalancerSourceRanges.
Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: allow and list the CIDRs in loadBalancerSourceRanges.
Set service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer and leave loadBalancerSourceRanges empty.
Enable bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true and list the CIDRs in loadBalancerSourceRanges.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the list can be turned into a deny-list, blocking traffic from certain CIDRs while allowing everything else, through the service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy annotation, which accepts allow or deny.

optionRationale.b: The allow value is the default allow-list behaviour, which permits only the listed CIDRs rather than blocking them.
optionRationale.c: The type annotation avoids creating corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services; it does not invert the CIDR list.
optionRationale.d: That Helm option propagates the ranges to other service types; it does not change allow-list into deny-list.

stem: A LoadBalancer service is created with no value set for spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges. What restriction does Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement apply to access from outside the cluster?

All external traffic is dropped until a CIDR is added.
Only traffic from the cluster's pod CIDR is permitted.
External traffic is restricted to the default deny-list.

optionRationale.b: The src-ranges-policy annotation with deny turns the CIDR list into a deny-list; it does not suppress service creation.
optionRationale.c: The allow value is the default allow-list behaviour and has no effect on creating NodePort or ClusterIP services.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the annotation set to LoadBalancer for this purpose, not NodePort.

stem: An engineer wants to see the exact source policy that produced a particular rule applied to endpoint 568. They run `cilium-dbg endpoint get 568` and note the labels of the rule. What is the correct next step to display that exact source policy?

options.text: Pass the labels to `cilium-dbg policy get`.
Run `cilium-dbg policy get` with no arguments.
Run `cilium-dbg endpoint list` and filter by the labels.
Run `cilium-dbg endpoint get 568 -o jsonpath='{range ..status.policy.realized.l4.ingress[*].derived-from-rules}{@}{"\n"}{end}'`.

explanation: The excerpt states that the labels listed by `cilium-dbg endpoint get` can be passed to `cilium-dbg policy get` to show that exact source policy.

optionRationale.b: A no-label `cilium-dbg policy get` returns the complete policy on the node, not the exact source policy.
optionRationale.c: `cilium-dbg endpoint list` is used to pair data with `cilium-dbg endpoint get`, but it does not fetch a policy by labels.
optionRationale.d: This command extracts the derived-from-rules labels, but it does not itself display the source policy; the labels must then be passed to `cilium-dbg policy get`.

The list of labels can be
passed to ``cilium-dbg policy get`` to show that exact source policy.

stem: While troubleshooting, an engineer runs `cilium-dbg policy get` without providing any labels. What does this command return?

options.text: The complete policy on the node.
Only the rules that have no labels.
An error because labels are required.
The policy for the endpoint with ID 568.

explanation: The excerpt notes that a no label `cilium-dbg policy get` returns the complete policy on the node.

optionRationale.b: Rules with no labels cannot be fetched alone; a no-label get returns the complete policy, not just those rules.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say an error occurs; it describes the result of a no-label get.
optionRationale.d: The command does not take an endpoint ID; it takes labels or none.

`cilium-dbg endpoint list`

`cilium-dbg endpoint get 568 -o jsonpath='{range ..status.policy.realized.l4.egress[*].derived-from-rules}{@}{"\n"}{end}'`

stem: An attacker gains code execution inside a container that was started with hostNetwork: true and hostPID: true, but the container runs without root privileges or capabilities. According to the threat model, which statement best describes this attacker's position?

options.text: They are a limited-privilege host attacker: they have direct access to the host PID or network namespace but cannot disable Cilium components or undermine the eBPF and other kernel state Cilium relies on.
They are a fully privileged attacker, because hostNetwork and hostPID containers always run with root-equivalent capabilities.
They are not considered an attacker at all, because Cilium ignores traffic from host-networked containers.
They are a remote attacker only, since host namespace access does not grant any ability to bypass Cilium's network controls.

explanation: The excerpt defines this attacker as having direct access to the host PID or network namespace (or both) but without root-equivalent privileges that would let them disable Cilium components or undermine the eBPF and other kernel state. It explicitly lists hostNetwork: true and hostPID: true containers as a way this level of access can arise.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says such containers may run without root privileges or capabilities, so host namespace access does not imply root equivalence.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that an attacker at this level would be able to bypass some of Cilium's network controls, so they are clearly in scope.
optionRationale.d: Host namespace access is precisely what the excerpt describes as the basis of this attacker's access, not a remote-only position.

citations.title: Limited-privilege Host Attacker
citations.quote:
the attacker is someone with the ability to run arbitrary
code with direct access to the host PID or network namespace (or both), but
without "root"-equivalent privileges that would allow them to disable Cilium
components or undermine the eBPF and other kernel state Cilium relies on.

stem: Which of the following is listed in the excerpt as a way a limited-privilege host attacker's level of access could arise?

options.text: A containerized workload that has escaped the container namespace but runs as a non-privileged user.
A user with root-equivalent privileges who disables Cilium components on the node.
A remote user who has no access to the node's PID or network namespace.
An operator who undermines the eBPF and other kernel state Cilium relies on.

explanation: The excerpt lists three ways this access could exist, including a containerized workload that has escaped the container namespace but as a non-privileged user.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt defines this attacker as lacking root-equivalent privileges that would allow disabling Cilium components.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt requires direct access to the host PID or network namespace, so a user without such access does not fit.
optionRationale.d: Undermining the eBPF and other kernel state is exactly what the excerpt says this attacker cannot do.

citations.title: Limited-privilege Host Attacker
citations.quote:
-  A containerized workload that has "escaped" the container namespace
   but as a non-privileged user.

stem: How does the excerpt characterise the threat to Cilium configuration and Cilium eBPF programs from a limited-privilege host attacker, compared with the threat to the Cilium agent?

options.text: Both the Cilium configuration and the Cilium eBPF programs are described as facing the same threat as the Cilium agent.
The Cilium configuration faces the same threat as the agent, but the eBPF programs are unaffected.
The eBPF programs face the same threat as the agent, but the Cilium configuration is unaffected.
Neither the Cilium configuration nor the eBPF programs face any threat from this attacker.

explanation: For both the Cilium configuration and the Cilium eBPF programs, the excerpt gives the same entry: same as for the Cilium agent.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives the eBPF programs the same threat as the agent, not an absence of threat.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives the Cilium configuration the same threat as the agent, not an absence of threat.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt assigns both the same threat as the Cilium agent, so neither is free of threat.

citations.quote:
Cilium           Same as for the Cilium

stem: A platform team runs a selectorless Service backed by two manually managed EndpointSlice objects. They annotate the slices with weights of 70 and 30, but traffic is still spread evenly across all backends. The Service has no lb-algorithm annotation and the cluster uses the default load-balancing algorithm. What is the most likely reason the weights are not applied?

options.text: Weights are only honored when the Service uses the Maglev algorithm, so the Service must use Maglev either globally or via service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm.
Weights must always add up to 100, and the values 70 and 30 were rejected as a pair.
The weight annotation must be placed on the Service rather than on each EndpointSlice.
Selectorless Services cannot use weights at all; a selector must be defined first.

explanation: The excerpt states that weights are only honored for the Service referenced by the EndpointSlice when it uses the Maglev load-balancing algorithm, whether configured globally or selected per service. Since the Service in this scenario uses the default algorithm and has no lb-algorithm annotation, the weights are not honored.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says weights are relative and do not need to add up to 100, so 70 and 30 are perfectly valid.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes weights being assigned on a per-EndpointSlice basis through the service.cilium.io/weight annotation, not on the Service.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says the feature is primarily intended for selectorless Services backed by multiple manually managed EndpointSlice objects.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
Weights are only honored for the Service referenced by that ``EndpointSlice``
when it uses the Maglev load-balancing algorithm, whether Maglev is configured
globally or selected per service through ``service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm``.

stem: An engineer wants to select the Maglev algorithm for a single Service using the service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm annotation rather than enabling Maglev globally. What must be true for this per-service selection to work?

options.text: The Service must be of type ClusterIP.
bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation must be set to true.
Each EndpointSlice must carry a weight annotation of at least 1.
The EndpointSlice addressType must be IPv4.

explanation: The excerpt states that per-service algorithm selection requires bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true. Without that setting, selecting Maglev through the annotation on a single Service will not take effect.

optionRationale.a: The example Service happens to be ClusterIP, but the excerpt does not make Service type a requirement for per-service algorithm selection.
optionRationale.c: A weight of 0 is valid and marks backends as being in maintenance, so a minimum weight of 1 is not required.
optionRationale.d: IPv4 appears in the example, but the excerpt does not tie per-service algorithm selection to the addressType.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote: Per-service algorithm selection requires ``bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true``.

stem: A Service is backed by two EndpointSlice objects with weights 70 and 30. Later, the operator changes the second EndpointSlice from weight 30 to weight 0. What is the effect on traffic?

options.text: The weight 0 is treated as invalid and ignored, so traffic continues at roughly 70/30.
The second slice's backends are removed immediately and all existing connections to them are terminated.
The second slice's backends enter maintenance: existing connections can continue, but new traffic goes entirely to the first slice's backends.
New traffic is split evenly between the two slices because a zero weight resets the distribution.

explanation: The excerpt explains that a weight of 0 marks those backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue while new traffic is steered to other backends. When the second slice is changed to 0, the first slice receives 100% of the new traffic share.

optionRationale.a: Zero is a valid value; the excerpt says valid values range from 0 to 65535, and invalid values are ignored, but 0 is not invalid.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt says existing connections can continue to use the maintenance backends, so they are not terminated.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the first slice now receives 100% of the new traffic share, not an even split.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
A weight of ``0`` marks those
backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue
while new traffic is steered to other backends.

stem: An engineer assigns a weight annotation to an EndpointSlice that contributes four backend addresses to a Service. How does the configured weight apply?

options.text: It applies to all backends in that EndpointSlice.
It applies only to the first backend listed in the EndpointSlice.
It is divided evenly among the backends in the EndpointSlice.
It applies only to backends that have no other annotations.

explanation: The excerpt states that the configured weight applies to all backends in a given EndpointSlice, so every address in that slice shares the same weight.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt makes no distinction between the first and subsequent backends; the weight covers all of them.
optionRationale.c: The weight is not divided among backends; it applies to all backends in the slice.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about other annotations affecting whether the weight applies.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote: The configured weight applies to all backends in a given ``EndpointSlice``.

stem: Which statement best describes how Cilium treats the numeric values supplied through the service.cilium.io/weight annotation?

options.text: Weights are absolute shares and must total exactly 100 across all slices of a Service.
Weights are relative, may range from 0 to 65535, and invalid values are ignored.
Weights are percentages capped at 100, and any value above 100 is clamped to 100.
Weights are relative but must be positive integers, so 0 is rejected as invalid.

explanation: The excerpt states that valid values range from 0 to 65535, that invalid values are ignored, and that weights are relative and do not need to add up to 100.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly says weights are relative and do not need to add up to 100.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives the valid range as 0 to 65535, not a percentage capped at 100.
optionRationale.d: Zero is a valid value that marks backends as being in maintenance, so it is not rejected.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
Valid values range from ``0`` to ``65535``. A weight of ``0`` marks those
backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue
while new traffic is steered to other backends. Invalid values are ignored.
Weights are relative and do not need to add up to ``100``.

stem: You have just applied a CiliumNetworkPolicy named to-groups-sample that uses ToGroups rules. Shortly afterwards you list the CiliumNetworkPolicies in the default namespace. What do you expect to see?

options.text: Only to-groups-sample, because ToGroups rules are resolved in memory and never materialised as policies.
to-groups-sample plus a second policy whose name is to-groups-sample-togroups- followed by a UUID, created automatically.
Only a policy named to-groups-sample-togroups- followed by a UUID; the original policy is replaced.
to-groups-sample plus a CiliumEndpoint named after the security group, holding the resolved CIDRs.

explanation: The excerpt states that every time a new policy with ToGroups rules is added, an equivalent policy (the derivative policy) is created. The sample listing shows both to-groups-sample and to-groups-sample-togroups-044ba7d1-f491-11e8-ad2e-080027d2d952, so the parent remains and the derivative is added alongside it.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt shows the derivative policy as a real CiliumNetworkPolicy object returned by kubectl get cnp, not an in-memory construct.
optionRationale.c: The listing shows the parent to-groups-sample still present with an age of 11s, so it is not replaced.
optionRationale.d: The derivative is a CiliumNetworkPolicy, not a CiliumEndpoint; the excerpt never mentions a CiliumEndpoint holding CIDRs.

stem: An engineer inspects the derivative policy generated for a ToGroups rule and wants to confirm which destination IPs the rule actually permits. Which part of the derivative policy holds that information?

options.text: metadata.OwnerReferences

optionRationale.b: status reports whether the policy is enforced yet and when it was last updated.
optionRationale.d: The endpointSelector identifies which endpoints the policy applies to, not the permitted destination IPs.

stem: A pod labelled any:class: xwing is selected by the derivative policy shown in the excerpt, and its realised policy enforcement is egress only. A connection attempt is made from that pod to an IP that is not 34.254.113.42/32 or 172.31.44.160/32. What is the result?

The connection is denied, because the pod can only connect to the two listed CIDRs.
The connection is allowed but logged, since the derivative policy only records CIDRs.
The connection is redirected to the nearest listed CIDR by the derivative policy.

optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt describes redirection of traffic to a listed CIDR.

stem: A security group's set of instance IPs changes after the derivative policy has already been created. What does the excerpt say happens to the list of IPs in the derivative policy?

options.text: It is frozen at creation time and requires deleting and recreating the parent policy.

explanation: The excerpt says the derivative policy contains the set of CIDRs corresponding to the ToGroups specification, and that the list of IPs is updated periodically.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes periodic updates, not a frozen list requiring recreation.

IPs is updated periodically.

stem: You are reviewing a derivative policy and want to trace it back to the ToGroups policy that caused it to be created. Which field of the derivative policy contains that information?

options.text: specs.Egress.ToCIDRSet
status.nodes

stem: A platform team wants Cilium to drop traffic destined for addresses that are not valid endpoints, and to do so as early as possible for maximum performance. Which Cilium datapath object should they rely on, and which hook does it use?

options.text: The prefilter object, which runs an XDP program and uses CIDR maps supplied by the Cilium agent to look up and drop or allow packets.
The Service object, which performs a map lookup on destination IP and port using the TC ingress hook.
The endpoint policy object, which maps packets to identities and enforces L3/L4 policy.
The socket operations hook, which runs on TCP events in the root cgroup.

explanation: The excerpt states that the prefilter object runs an XDP program and provides prefilter rules for best performance, using CIDR maps supplied by the Cilium agent so that a packet is either dropped, for example when the destination is not a valid endpoint, or allowed to be processed by the stack. The other objects either operate at a different hook or serve a different purpose.

optionRationale.b: The Service object does perform a map lookup on destination IP and optionally port, but it forwards matching packets to L3/L4 endpoints and is described as usable with the TC ingress hook, not as the XDP-based object that drops traffic for invalid destinations.
optionRationale.c: The endpoint policy object is described as the primary object responsible for mapping packets to identities and enforcing L3 and L4 policies, not as the XDP prefilter that drops traffic to non-endpoint destinations.
optionRationale.d: The socket operations hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events to monitor state transitions; it is not the XDP-based prefilter object.

stem: According to the excerpt, how does the socket operations hook differ in what it is attached to and what it reacts to, compared with the socket send/recv hook?

options.text: The socket operations hook is attached to a specific cgroup and runs on TCP events, while the socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket.
The socket operations hook is attached to a networking interface and runs on packet reception, while the socket send/recv hook runs after the networking stack has done initial processing.
The socket operations hook runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket, while the socket send/recv hook is attached to a specific cgroup and runs on TCP events.
The socket operations hook is attached to the host side of a veth pair, while the socket send/recv hook is attached to the root cgroup.

explanation: The excerpt describes the socket operations hook as attached to a specific cgroup and running on TCP events, whereas the socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket, at which point it can inspect the message and drop it, send it to the TCP layer, or redirect it to another socket.

optionRationale.b: Attachment to a networking interface and running on packet reception describes the XDP hook, and running after initial stack processing describes the TC ingress hook, not the socket hooks.
optionRationale.c: This reverses the two hooks: the cgroup-attached TCP-event hook is socket operations, and the per-send hook is socket send/recv.
optionRationale.d: The veth pair attachment is discussed in relation to the TC ingress hook for containers, and the root cgroup is where Cilium attaches the socket operations program, not the socket send/recv hook.

optionRationale.d: Map recreation is discussed in relation to enabling the setting on-the-fly, not as the cause of the memory trade-off.

The trade-off is higher memory usage given the per-CPU pools cannot be
shared anymore

stem: An engineer runs `cilium status` inside a Cilium pod to check whether eBPF host-routing is active. Which value of the "Host Routing" line confirms that it is?

options.text: "BPF"
"Enabled"
"Legacy"
"iptables"

explanation: The excerpt states that to validate whether the installation is running with eBPF host-routing you run `cilium status` and look for the line reporting the status for "Host Routing", which should state "BPF".

optionRationale.b: "Enabled" is a plausible-sounding status word but the excerpt specifies the value "BPF".
optionRationale.c: "Legacy" is associated with the legacy host-routing comparison in the benchmarks, not with the status value that confirms eBPF host-routing.
optionRationale.d: iptables is what eBPF host-routing bypasses; it is not the reported status value.

citations.title: eBPF Host-Routing

run ``cilium status``
in any of the Cilium pods and look for the line reporting the status for

stem: A cluster administrator is deploying Cilium and wants eBPF host-routing to be active. Which two prerequisites does the excerpt list for this feature?

options.text: eBPF-based kube-proxy replacement and eBPF-based masquerading
eBPF-based kube-proxy replacement and a service mesh
eBPF-based masquerading and IPsec encryption
A kernel with netfilter hooks and legacy host-routing disabled

explanation: Under the Requirements heading, the excerpt lists exactly two items: eBPF-based kube-proxy replacement and eBPF-based masquerading.

optionRationale.b: A service mesh is not a requirement; in fact the excerpt notes BPF Host Routing is incompatible with Istio.
optionRationale.c: IPsec is mentioned only in connection with a required kernel bugfix, not as a requirement for the feature.
optionRationale.d: Netfilter hooks are what eBPF host-routing bypasses, and the excerpt does not list them as a requirement.

* eBPF-based kube-proxy replacement
* eBPF-based masquerading

stem: A platform team depends on iptables rules being evaluated for traffic on their nodes. By default, with Cilium performing routing in eBPF, what happens to packets with respect to the regular network stack?

options.text: They still traverse some parts of the regular network stack, including all of the iptables hooks, which adds significant overhead.
They bypass the regular network stack entirely, so no iptables hooks are evaluated.
They traverse the regular network stack only when IPsec is enabled.
They are dropped unless bpf.hostLegacyRouting is set to true.

explanation: The excerpt explains that even when routing is performed by Cilium using eBPF, by default packets still traverse some parts of the regular network stack, ensuring all packets still traverse all of the iptables hooks, and that these add significant overhead.

optionRationale.b: Full bypass of iptables and the upper host stack is what eBPF host-routing introduces, not the default behaviour described.
optionRationale.c: IPsec is discussed only in relation to a kernel bugfix requirement, not as a condition for traversing the stack.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say packets are dropped; bpf.hostLegacyRouting is given as a workaround for netfilter-dependent features.

citations.title: eBPF Host-Routing
citations.quote:
Even when network routing is performed by Cilium using eBPF, by default network
packets still traverse some parts of the regular network stack of the node.
This ensures that all packets still traverse through all of the iptables hooks
in case you depend on them.

stem: An engineer is told that eBPF host-routing was introduced to fully bypass iptables and the upper host stack. In which Cilium release did this feature appear?

options.text: Cilium 1.9
Cilium 1.10
Cilium 1.19
Cilium 1.8

explanation: The excerpt states that eBPF-based host-routing was introduced in Cilium 1.9 to fully bypass iptables and the upper host stack.

optionRationale.b: 1.10 is a plausible later release but is not the version named in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: 1.19 is a trap: the blog URL contains "cilium-19", which refers to the 1.9 announcement, not a 1.19 release.
optionRationale.d: 1.8 is an earlier release than the one named in the excerpt.

citations.title: eBPF Host-Routing

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with eBPF host-routing and also uses GKE Workload Identities, which relies on netfilter hooks. Users report that the identity feature no longer works. What does the excerpt recommend as a workaround?

options.text: Configure `bpf.hostLegacyRouting=true` or leverage local-redirect-policy.
Disable eBPF-based masquerading on the nodes.
Upgrade the kernel package on the nodes.
Run `cilium status` and confirm the Host Routing line states "BPF".

explanation: Because eBPF host routing means packets no longer hit the netfilter tables in the host namespace, it is incompatible with features relying on netfilter hooks such as GKE Workload Identities; the excerpt says to configure `bpf.hostLegacyRouting=true` or leverage local-redirect-policy to work around this.

optionRationale.b: Masquerading is a requirement for the feature, not a workaround for netfilter incompatibility.
optionRationale.c: A kernel upgrade is advised for connectivity problems when using BPF Host Routing with IPsec, not for this netfilter issue.
optionRationale.d: Checking status only confirms the mode is active; it does not restore the netfilter-dependent feature.

citations.title: eBPF Host-Routing
citations.quote:
Therefore, it is incompatible
with features relying on netfilter hooks (for example, `GKE Workload Identities`_).
Configure ``bpf.hostLegacyRouting=true`` or leverage local-redirect-policy
to work around this limitation.

stem: A team enables BPF Host Routing together with IPsec and then observes connectivity problems. According to the excerpt, what should they check before reporting an issue?

options.text: That the kernel package on the nodes has been upgraded recently, because a kernel bugfix is required.
That eBPF-based masquerading has been disabled.
That the Host Routing status line reads "Legacy".
That Istio has been installed alongside Cilium.

explanation: The excerpt notes that when using BPF Host Routing with IPsec a kernel bugfix is required, and that if connectivity problems are observed you should ensure the kernel package on the nodes has been upgraded recently before reporting an issue.

optionRationale.b: eBPF-based masquerading is a requirement for the feature, not something to disable.
optionRationale.c: "Legacy" would indicate the feature is not active in the eBPF form; the excerpt asks for "BPF".
optionRationale.d: Istio is stated to be incompatible with BPF Host Routing, so installing it would not be a remedy.

citations.title: eBPF Host-Routing
citations.quote:
When using BPF Host Routing with IPsec, `a kernel bugfix <https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=c4327229948879814229b46aa26a750718888503>`_
is required. If you observe connectivity problems, ensure that the kernel
package on your nodes has been upgraded recently before reporting an issue.

stem: Which statement best captures what eBPF host-routing changes about packet handling on the host?

options.text: It fully bypasses iptables and the upper host stack and achieves a faster network namespace switch compared to regular veth device operation.
It keeps all packets traversing the iptables hooks but reduces their overhead.
It replaces the kernel's network stack with a userspace forwarding path.
It routes packets through the host netfilter tables more efficiently than legacy host-routing.

explanation: The excerpt says eBPF-based host-routing was introduced to fully bypass iptables and the upper host stack, and to achieve a faster network namespace switch compared to regular veth device operation.

optionRationale.b: Keeping packets traversing the iptables hooks describes the default behaviour that eBPF host-routing is meant to move away from.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes bypassing parts of the host stack, not replacing the stack with a userspace path.
optionRationale.d: eBPF host routing means packets no longer hit the netfilter tables in the host namespace, so it does not route them through those tables.

citations.title: eBPF Host-Routing
citations.quote:
in Cilium 1.9 to fully bypass iptables and the upper host stack, and to achieve
a faster network namespace switch compared to regular veth device operation.

stem: An engineer reads that eBPF host-routing is "automatically enabled if your kernel supports it". What does the excerpt say about the effect on iptables hooks in the host namespace once it is active?

options.text: Packets no longer hit the netfilter tables in the host namespace, making the feature incompatible with features relying on netfilter hooks.
Packets continue to hit all netfilter tables in the host namespace as before.
Packets hit the netfilter tables only in the pod namespace, not the host namespace.
Packets hit the netfilter tables only when local-redirect-policy is configured.

explanation: The excerpt states that eBPF host routing optimises host-internal packet routing and that packets no longer hit the netfilter tables in the host namespace, which is why it is incompatible with features relying on netfilter hooks.

optionRationale.b: That describes the default behaviour before eBPF host-routing, not the effect once it is active.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt speaks of the host namespace specifically and does not make this pod-namespace distinction.
optionRationale.d: local-redirect-policy is mentioned as a workaround for the limitation, not as a condition for hitting netfilter tables.

citations.title: eBPF Host-Routing
citations.quote:
eBPF host routing optimizes the host-internal packet routing, and packets no
longer hit the netfilter tables in the host namespace.

stem: A platform team runs a global service named rebel-base across two clusters. In cluster 1 they annotate the service with service.cilium.io/affinity=local, then run a curl against rebel-base from a pod in cluster 1. What do they observe?

options.text: Replies come only from pods in cluster 1, because the local endpoints are preferred.
Replies come from pods in both clusters, because the annotation only affects the cluster where it is set on the ServiceExport.
Replies come only from pods in cluster 2, because the annotation inverts the default preference.
Replies come from both clusters, but the local endpoints are marked as preferred in the endpoint list.

explanation: Setting the annotation to local makes the Global Service load-balance across healthy local backends, using remote endpoints only when all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy. The excerpt confirms that accessing the service from cluster 1 after applying the annotation yields replies from cluster 1 only.

optionRationale.b: The annotation does change behaviour for traffic originating in the annotated cluster; the excerpt shows replies from cluster 1 only, not from both clusters.
optionRationale.c: The value local prefers local endpoints; it is the value remote that makes replies come from cluster 2 only.
optionRationale.d: Preferring local endpoints means traffic is served by them, not that both clusters answer while local ones are merely marked preferred.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote: You will see replies from pods in ``cluster 1`` only.

stem: You are configuring a Cluster Mesh with Helm and want to avoid repeating the same remote-cluster information in every cluster's values file. You therefore place all remote clusters in a single `clusters.yaml` file that every cluster's values file references. Why does this work?

options.text: Because Cilium ignores the local cluster from the list of remote clusters, so the shared list is safe to apply everywhere.
Because Helm automatically strips the entry matching the release's own cluster name before rendering the chart.
Because the Cluster Mesh API server deduplicates the local cluster at runtime and rejects any connection to itself.
Because the shared file must be split into group files, one per cluster, before it can be applied.

explanation: The excerpt states that a single `clusters.yaml` holding all remote clusters avoids repeating information in every cluster's values file, and that this is possible since Cilium ignores the local cluster from the list of remote clusters. The other options describe mechanisms the excerpt does not mention.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt attributes this to Cilium ignoring the local cluster, not to Helm stripping entries during rendering.
optionRationale.c: No runtime deduplication by the API server is described; the reason given is that Cilium ignores the local cluster from the remote list.
optionRationale.d: Splitting into group files is offered as an option for building a partial mesh, not as a prerequisite for using a shared file.

citations.title: Configure Cluster Mesh with Helm
citations.quote:
The ``clusters.yaml`` file contains all the remote clusters so that you don't
have to repeat the same information in every cluster's values file. Note that
this is possible since Cilium ignores the local cluster from the list of remote
clusters.

stem: You are preparing the first EKS cluster for a Cilium Cluster Mesh deployment and are about to create the VPC that will host it. A colleague suggests using 172.17.0.0/16 as the CIDR block. What does the preparation guide advise, and why?

options.text: Avoid 172.17.0.0/16, because certain AWS services utilise this range and using it could cause potential issues.
Use 172.17.0.0/16, because it is the range reserved for the Cilium Cluster Mesh control plane traffic between clusters.
Avoid 172.17.0.0/16, because it is the default CIDR block that the create-vpc command assigns when no block is given.
Use 172.17.0.0/16, because the guide's example VPC is created with that block and the subnets are carved from it.

explanation: The guide explicitly warns against the 172.17.0.0/16 range when creating the VPC, stating that certain AWS services utilise this range, so using it could lead to potential issues. The example instead creates the VPC with 10.0.0.0/16.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says nothing about a reserved Cluster Mesh control plane range; the warning is about AWS services using the range.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe any default CIDR block for create-vpc; the example passes 10.0.0.0/16 explicitly.
optionRationale.d: The example VPC is created with 10.0.0.0/16, not 172.17.0.0/16, and the guide advises avoiding the latter.

citations.title: Install cluster one
citations.quote: Avoid using the ``172.17.0.0/16`` CIDR range for your VPC to prevent potential issues since certain `AWS services <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-cidr-blocks.html>`__ utilize this range.

stem: An engineer configures a Hubble metric with `flow:destinationContext=dns|ip`. For a particular flow the destination has no known DNS name. What label value is added to the metric for that flow?

options.text: The IP address of the destination, because the first non-empty value among the specified contexts is used.
An empty value, because the first listed context (`dns`) produced no value.
Both the DNS placeholder and the IP address, joined by the `|` symbol.
The value `reserved:world`, because an unresolved destination falls back to a reserved identity.

explanation: When several contexts are separated by `|`, the first non-empty value is added as the label. The excerpt gives exactly this example: the DNS name is tried first, and if none is known the IP address is used instead.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states the first non-empty value is used, so an empty first context does not stop the fallback.
optionRationale.c: The `|` symbol is the separator used in the configuration, not a joiner of values in the resulting label.
optionRationale.d: `reserved:world` is a reserved identity mentioned only in the context of the `reserved-identity` option, not a fallback for unresolved DNS.

citations.title: Context Options
citations.quote:
When multiple are specified, then the first non-empty value is added to the
metric as a label.

stem: A metric is configured with both `sourceContext` and `sourceEgressContext`. Which statement describes how the `source` label is determined for egress traffic?

options.text: `sourceEgressContext` takes precedence over `sourceContext` for egress traffic.
`sourceContext` takes precedence over `sourceEgressContext` for egress traffic.
The two options are merged, and the first non-empty value across both is used.
`sourceEgressContext` applies only to ingress traffic, so `sourceContext` governs egress.

explanation: The excerpt lists `sourceEgressContext` as configuring the `source` label for egress traffic and states explicitly that it takes precedence over `sourceContext`.

optionRationale.b: The precedence runs the other way: the egress-specific option overrides the general one.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes precedence, not a merge of the two options.
optionRationale.d: `sourceEgressContext` is defined for egress traffic; the ingress-specific option is `sourceIngressContext`.

citations.title: Context Options
citations.quote: ``sourceEgressContext`` - Configures the ``source`` label on metrics for egress traffic (takes precedence over ``sourceContext``).

stem: An engineer wants the metric to carry the Kubernetes pod name and namespace in the form `namespace/pod` as the source context value. Which value should be given to `sourceContext`?

options.text: `pod`
`pod-name`
`namespace`
`workload`

explanation: In the table of possible context values, `pod` is described as the Kubernetes pod name and namespace name in the form of `namespace/pod`.

optionRationale.b: `pod-name` gives only the Kubernetes pod name, without the namespace.
optionRationale.c: `namespace` gives only the Kubernetes namespace name.
optionRationale.d: `workload` gives the workload name and namespace, not the pod name and namespace.

citations.title: Context Options
citations.quote: ``pod``               Kubernetes pod name and namespace name in the form of ``namespace/pod``.

stem: How does `labelsContext` differ from `sourceContext` and `destinationContext` when adding context to a metric?

options.text: `labelsContext` puts the listed labels into different label values, whereas the source and destination contexts put different values into the same metric label.
`labelsContext` puts the listed labels into the same metric label, whereas the source and destination contexts use separate labels.
`labelsContext` accepts only a single value, while the source and destination contexts accept several separated by `|`.
`labelsContext` applies only to ingress traffic, while the source and destination contexts apply to both directions.

explanation: The excerpt states that, unlike `sourceContext` and `destinationContext`, `labelsContext` puts the listed labels into different label values rather than different values into the same metric label.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the distinction described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: `labelsContext` takes a list of labels, separated by `,`, not a single value.
optionRationale.d: No ingress-only restriction on `labelsContext` is stated in the excerpt.

citations.title: Context Options
citations.quote:
Unlike ``sourceContext`` and ``destinationContext``, instead
of different values being put into the same metric label, the ``labelsContext`` puts them into different label values.

stem: You run `kubectl get gateway -A` and see a Gateway in namespace `website` whose CLASS column shows `cilium`, but the PROGRAMMED column is empty. According to the excerpt, what should you check first?

options.text: Make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.
Make sure that the Gateway API CRDs are installed.
Make sure a LoadBalancer implementation is present, since no IP appears.
Run `kubectl describe httproute` to inspect the attached routes.

explanation: The excerpt states that if the `Programmed true` indicator is missing, you should make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration. The class is already `cilium`, so the class check does not apply, and the missing-address and missing-CRD checks address different symptoms.

optionRationale.b: Missing CRDs would show up as the Gateway API resource type not being found, not as a missing Programmed indicator.
optionRationale.c: The LoadBalancer check is tied to a gateway having no address, not to the Programmed indicator.
optionRationale.d: Describing an HTTPRoute is the route-checking step, which the excerpt says to do when the Gateway is functional.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: If the ``Programmed true`` indicator is missing, make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.

stem: A colleague reports that `kubectl get gateway -A` lists a Gateway with class `cilium` and a PROGRAMMED value of `True`, but the ADDRESS column is blank. What does the excerpt say this indicates, and what should be checked?

options.text: Cilium has not prepared a configuration for the Gateway; Gateway API must be enabled in the Cilium configuration.
A LoadBalancer service is not assigned to the gateway; you might be missing a LoadBalancer implementation, and you can check the service with `kubectl get service`.
The referenced secrets were not found; the `ResolvedRefs` condition will be false.
The Gateway API CRDs are not installed; the Cilium Operator will log an error.

explanation: The excerpt explains that if the gateway has an address, a LoadBalancer service is assigned to the gateway, and that if no IP appears you might be missing a LoadBalancer implementation. It also suggests checking the service with `kubectl get service`. Since PROGRAMMED is `True`, Cilium has already prepared a configuration.

optionRationale.a: A missing Programmed indicator is the symptom for that check, but here PROGRAMMED is `True`.
optionRationale.c: `ResolvedRefs` concerns referenced secrets and is a status condition, not the explanation given for a missing address.
optionRationale.d: Missing CRDs would surface as the Gateway API resource type not being found, not as a blank address.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote:
If the gateway has an address, it means that a LoadBalancer service is assigned to the gateway.
 If no IP appears, you might be missing a LoadBalancer implementation.

stem: When you run `kubectl describe gateway <name>`, which condition type does the excerpt say means that the Gateway configuration was programmed into Envoy?

options.text: `Accepted`
`ResolvedRefs`
`Programmed`
`Attached Routes`

explanation: The excerpt lists the status conditions for gateway and listener and defines `Programmed` as the condition meaning the Gateway configuration was programmed into Envoy.

optionRationale.a: `Accepted` means the Gateway configuration was accepted, not that it was programmed into Envoy.
optionRationale.b: `ResolvedRefs` means all referenced secrets were found and have permission for use.
optionRationale.d: `Attached Routes` appears under Listeners and is a count, not a condition type.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: ``Programmed``: the Gateway configuration was programmed into Envoy.

stem: You are checking an HTTPRoute and want to confirm that the services it references were found and are valid. Which condition type in the HTTPRoute status should you look at?

options.text: `Accepted`
`ResolvedRefs`
`Programmed`
`Controller Name`

explanation: For HTTPRoute status, the excerpt notes `ResolvedRefs` as the condition meaning the referenced services were found and are valid references.

optionRationale.a: `Accepted` means the HTTPRoute configuration was correct and accepted, not that its service references were validated.
optionRationale.c: `Programmed` is described for the Gateway and its listeners, not as the HTTPRoute condition for service references.
optionRationale.d: `Controller Name` is a field in the status output, not a condition type.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: ``ResolvedRefs``: The referenced services were found and are valid references.

stem: An engineer is writing a client that calls the Observer service's GetFlows endpoint and supplies both an allow list and a deny list of flow filters. What will the returned stream contain?

options.text: All flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list.
Only flows that match every filter in both the allow list and the deny list.
All flows matched by the deny list, with the allow list applied only when the deny list is empty.
An error, because allow and deny filters cannot be combined in a single request.

explanation: The excerpt states that when both allow and deny filters are specified, the result contains all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list. It also notes that when multiple flow filters are provided, only one of them has to match for a flow to be included or excluded, so requiring every filter to match is wrong.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the stated semantics: the excerpt says only one of multiple filters has to match, not that all must match.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the deny list as subtracting from the allow list result, not as the primary selection with the allow list as a fallback.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt says the two filter types are mutually exclusive; it explicitly describes what happens when both are specified.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: When both allow and deny filters are specified, the result will contain all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list.

stem: A user wants to know which namespaces have had network flows recently, without streaming individual flow events. Which Observer RPC endpoint should they call, and what does it return?

options.text: GetNamespaces, which returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour.
GetNodes, which returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour.
ServerStatus, which returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour.
GetFlows, which returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour.

explanation: The excerpt assigns the namespace listing to GetNamespaces: it returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour. The other endpoints have different roles: GetNodes reports per-instance metrics and information, ServerStatus summarises GetNodes, and GetFlows streams flow events.

optionRationale.b: GetNodes returns metrics and other information related to each Hubble instance, not namespaces.
optionRationale.c: ServerStatus returns a summary of the information in GetNodes, not a namespace list.
optionRationale.d: GetFlows returns a stream of flow related events, not a list of namespaces.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: ``GetNamespaces`` returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour.

stem: An engineer is told that the Observer service exposes endpoints for Cilium agent events and Cilium datapath debug events. How do these endpoints differ from GetFlows?

options.text: GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents are similar to GetFlows except they do not implement filtering capabilities.
GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents are similar to GetFlows but add allow list and deny list filtering on top of it.
GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents are not part of the Observer service and are served by a separate principal service.
GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents return only a summary of GetNodes rather than event data.

explanation: The excerpt says the Observer service also provides GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents to expose data about Cilium agent events and Cilium datapath debug events respectively, and that both are similar to GetFlows except they do not implement filtering capabilities.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the distinction: the excerpt says these endpoints do not implement filtering, whereas GetFlows does.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly places both endpoints within the Observer service.
optionRationale.d: Summarising GetNodes is the role of ServerStatus, not of these event endpoints.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote:
Both are similar to ``GetFlows``
except they do not implement filtering capabilities.

stem: A developer reads that the ring buffer's internal buffer length is a bit mask of ones plus one, with one slot reserved for the writer. From a user's perspective, what is the effective capacity of the ring buffer?

options.text: One less than a power of 2.
Exactly a power of 2.
One more than a power of 2.
An arbitrary value that is not constrained to a power of 2.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the internal buffer size is always a power of 2 with 1 slot reserved for the writer, and that in effect, from a user perspective, the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

optionRationale.b: A power of 2 describes the internal buffer size, not the user-visible capacity, which loses one slot to the writer.
optionRationale.c: The reserved slot is subtracted, not added, so the capacity is below a power of 2 rather than above it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the internal buffer size is always a power of 2, so the capacity is constrained accordingly.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote:
In effect, from a user perspective,
the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

stem: You run the fortio load generator against echo-service with the command `fortio load -c 2 -qps 0 -n 20 http://echo-service:8080`. Reviewing the output, you notice that not every request succeeded. What does the excerpt say this indicates?

options.text: The 503 response code seen on some requests triggers a circuit breaker.
The 503 response code indicates that fortio itself failed to resolve the Service IP address.
The 503 response code is a warmup artefact and does not affect the circuit breaker.
The 503 response code shows that the number of concurrent connections was too low to trip anything.

explanation: The excerpt states that some requests returned 503 and that this triggers a circuit breaker. The other options introduce causes and interpretations that the excerpt does not support.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the Service resolving to 10.96.182.43:8080, so resolution did not fail; nothing links 503 to DNS.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt makes no claim that 503s are warmup artefacts; it explicitly ties the 503 to tripping the circuit breaker.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the opposite direction of reasoning: the 503s are what trigger the breaker, and the next step is to raise concurrency to 4.

citations.title: Tripping Envoy Circuit Breaker

stem: You run `hubble observe --pod deathstar --protocol http` after generating traffic from the `tiefighter` and `xwing` pods. Which flows appear in the output?

options.text: Only the HTTP request and response that were forwarded, plus the HTTP request that was dropped; the `xwing` connection attempts do not appear.
All flows to the `deathstar` pod, including the `xwing` TCP SYN attempts, because `--protocol http` is ignored when a pod filter is present.
Only the dropped flows, because `--protocol http` implicitly sets the verdict to DROPPED.
Only the `xwing` flows, because the `tiefighter` requests were allowed and therefore not observed.

explanation: The excerpt shows that filtering on the application layer (L7, HTTP) to the `deathstar` pod returns the forwarded POST request, its forwarded 200 response, and the dropped PUT request. The `xwing` attempts appear only in the separate `--verdict DROPPED` output, where they are recorded as `Policy denied DROPPED (TCP Flags: SYN)` rather than as HTTP flows.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt presents `--protocol http` as a filter on the application layer (L7, HTTP), and the resulting output contains no `xwing` entries, so the filter is not ignored.
optionRationale.c: The `--protocol http` output includes two FORWARDED entries, so the filter does not imply a DROPPED verdict.
optionRationale.d: The `--protocol http` output contains the `tiefighter` request and response, so allowed traffic is observed.

stem: An engineer runs `cilium monitor` on a cluster where no L7 rules have been configured, and sees only L3/L4 packet events. She wants the tooling to surface DNS and HTTP flow details for Pods in the `default` namespace. What must she do?

options.text: Create a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that specifies L7 rules, having first enabled L7 Proxy support.
Restart the Cilium agent with L7 proxy support disabled, since L7 visibility is a datapath-only feature.
Add an `endpointSelector` matching `k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: default` to a policy with only L3/L4 `toEndpoints` rules.
Run `hubble observe` with the `-t l7` filter, which by itself causes Cilium to start proxying matching traffic.

explanation: The excerpt states that L7 visibility requires enabling L7 Proxy support and that you enable visibility for L7 traffic by creating a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that specifies L7 rules. Merely filtering output or writing L3/L4-only rules does not make L7 flows visible.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the feature requires enabling L7 Proxy support, not disabling it, and describes L7 visibility as depending on redirection to the proxy.
optionRationale.c: A policy with only L3/L4 rules does not specify L7 rules, and the excerpt ties L7 visibility to policies that specify L7 rules.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt presents `hubble observe -f -t l7 -o compact` as a way to view L7 flow details once the policy is in place, not as the mechanism that enables proxying.

stem: You are validating a Cilium and SPIRE integration. You run `spire-server entry show -parentID spiffe://spiffe.cilium/ns/cilium-spire/sa/spire-agent` and the output reports two entries. Which pair of SPIFFE IDs do those entries carry?

`spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/17947` and `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-operator`
`spiffe://spiffe.cilium/ns/cilium-spire/sa/spire-agent` and `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/17947`
`spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-agent` and `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/17947`

explanation: The excerpt states that the Cilium agent and operator should have a registered delegate Identity with the SPIRE Server, and the sample output for the parent ID `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/ns/cilium-spire/sa/spire-agent` shows exactly two entries, whose SPIFFE IDs are `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-agent` and `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-operator`.

optionRationale.b: The identity-based SPIFFE ID belongs to the echo workload entry, not to the delegate entries shown for the spire-agent parent ID.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available, and they want the Cilium ingress controller's Envoy listener reachable directly on the host network. After enabling host network mode via Helm, what happens to the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode?

options.text: It is automatically disabled, because the two modes are mutually exclusive.
It remains active and both modes serve traffic simultaneously on different ports.
It is converted into a shared Ingress listener on port 8080.
It is left untouched but must be disabled manually before host network mode takes effect.

explanation: The excerpt states that enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode, and that the two are mutually exclusive. No manual step is required, and the modes cannot run together.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both serve traffic at once.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes converting the Service mode into a shared listener; the Service mode is simply disabled.
optionRationale.d: The disabling is automatic, not a manual prerequisite.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium ingress controller host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

stem: A cluster runs the Cilium ingress controller in dedicated mode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. An engineer creates a new Ingress resource for host network exposure but omits the per-Ingress host listener port annotation. What is the consequence according to the excerpt?

options.text: The annotation is mandatory in this situation, so the Ingress resource must set ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port.
The Ingress resource silently falls back to the shared listener on port 8080.
The Ingress resource inherits the port from ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort.
The Ingress resource is rejected only if the global mode is shared rather than dedicated.

explanation: The excerpt says the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation is mandatory if the global mode is configured to dedicated, or if the Ingress resource sets the loadbalancer-mode annotation to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the annotation as mandatory in this case, not as having a silent fallback.
optionRationale.c: The sharedListenerPort Helm flag belongs to the shared Ingress method, not to the dedicated per-Ingress annotation.
optionRationale.d: The mandatory condition applies when the global mode is dedicated, which is the opposite of what this option claims.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: This annotation is mandatory if the global Cilium ingress controller mode is configured to ``dedicated`` (``ingressController.loadbalancerMode``) or the ingress resource sets the ``ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode`` annotation to ``dedicated`` and multiple ``Ingress`` resources are deployed.

stem: How does the excerpt distinguish the shared Ingress and dedicated Ingress methods for specifying host network ports?

options.text: Shared Ingress ports are set globally via Helm flags, while dedicated Ingress ports are set per Ingress resource via annotations.
Shared Ingress ports are set per Ingress resource via annotations, while dedicated Ingress ports are set globally via Helm flags.
Both methods use only the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation, differing solely in the port range.
Both methods use only Helm flags, differing solely in whether TLS passthrough is enabled.

explanation: The excerpt lists two methods: Shared Ingress, configured globally via Helm flags such as sharedListenerPort, httpPort, httpsPort and tlsPassthroughPort; and Dedicated Ingress, configured per Ingress resource via annotations such as ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two methods as described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: The annotation belongs to the dedicated method only; the shared method uses Helm flags.
optionRationale.d: The shared method uses Helm flags, but the dedicated method uses annotations, not flags.

Choose a port number lower than 1023 so that it is reserved for the ingress controller.
Choose exactly 8080, since any other value is unsupported.
Choose any port, as the excerpt gives no constraint on the value.

stem: An engineer exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service in a cluster that uses kube-proxy, and the backend application must see the original client IP. Which Service setting does the excerpt say is the only way to ensure source IP visibility in this situation?

options.text: Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on the Service.
Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` on the Service.
Leave `externalTrafficPolicy` unset so that Kubernetes defaults it to `Local`.
Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` and disable the `healthCheckNodePort`.

explanation: The excerpt states that with `Local`, nodes route only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, and that in clusters using `kube-proxy` this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

optionRationale.b: ``Cluster`` is described as allowing the node to masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say that leaving the field unset defaults it to ``Local``; it only describes the two relevant settings.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the ``healthCheckNodePort`` is automatically set by Kubernetes when ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` is set, and does not suggest disabling it.

Because of this, in clusters that use
  ``kube-proxy``, this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium ingress configuration (Ingress and Gateway API) and wants the backend pod to keep the client IP visible. What does the excerpt say about the need to set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` for this purpose?

options.text: It is required, because Cilium forwards ingress traffic to Envoy using masquerading.
It is not necessary, because Cilium always forwards ingress traffic to the local node and to Envoy via TPROXY, and the source IP remains visible via `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address`.
It is required only for Gateway API, while Ingress works with `Cluster`.
It is not necessary, but only if the `healthCheckNodePort` is manually configured.

explanation: The excerpt says that for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says ingress traffic is forwarded to Envoy using TPROXY, which transparently forwards packets, not masquerading.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt treats Ingress and Gateway API together and does not distinguish them on this point.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not make source IP visibility conditional on manually configuring the ``healthCheckNodePort``.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services

However, for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, **it is not
necessary** to configure ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` to keep the source IP
visible to the backend pod

stem: An engineer sets `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on a general Loadbalancer Service and wants to know how to check whether a given node has local pods running. According to the excerpt, what behaviour should the request to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` show?

options.text: It returns 200 on every node in the cluster regardless of local pods.
It returns 200 on nodes that have local pods running, and non-200 on nodes that don't.
It returns non-200 on nodes that have local pods running, and 200 on nodes that don't.
It returns 200 only on the node that holds the Service's ClusterIP.

explanation: The excerpt describes the contract for `externalTrafficPolicy` local: the node opens the `healthCheckNodePort`, and requests to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` return 200 on nodes with local pods running and non-200 on nodes without.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly distinguishes nodes with and without local pods, so the result is not uniform.
optionRationale.c: This inverts the described behaviour: 200 is returned where local pods are running.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt ties the check to local pods, not to the location of the ClusterIP.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
``http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz`` will return 200 on nodes that
  have local pods running, and non-200 on nodes that don't.

stem: Which statement best describes the `Cluster` setting of `externalTrafficPolicy` as presented in the excerpt?

options.text: The node routes only to Pods on the local node and never masquerades the source IP.
The node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, and the node may masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see it.
The node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly and always preserves the source IP.
The node routes only to endpoints on other nodes, preserving the source IP through TPROXY.

explanation: The excerpt says that with `Cluster` the node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, upstream loadbalancers expect to be able to send traffic to any node, and the node may masquerade the source IP, meaning the backend pod may not see it.

optionRationale.a: That describes the ``Local`` setting, not ``Cluster``.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the node may masquerade the source IP under ``Cluster``, so preservation is not guaranteed.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe routing only to endpoints on other nodes.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
``Cluster``: Node will route to all endpoints across the cluster evenly. This
  has a couple of other effects: Firstly, upstream loadbalancers will expect to
  be able to send traffic to any node and have it end up at a backend Pod, and
  the node *may* masquerade the source IP.

stem: An operator running Cilium ingress config sets `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on the Service that exposes Envoy and expects the usual per-node health check behaviour. What does the excerpt say Cilium does for such Services?

options.text: Cilium ensures that every node in the cluster will pass the `healthCheckNodePort` check, so that external load balancers forward correctly.
Cilium disables the `healthCheckNodePort` for ingress Services because TPROXY makes it redundant.
Cilium passes the check only on nodes that have local Envoy pods, exactly as for general Loadbalancer Services.
Cilium requires the operator to configure `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` before the check can pass.

explanation: The excerpt states that for any Services that expose Cilium's Envoy, Cilium will ensure that when `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` is set, every node in the cluster will pass the `healthCheckNodePort` check so that external load balancers forward correctly.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say the port is disabled; it says Cilium ensures every node passes the check.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt notes that Cilium implements the general behaviour for Loadbalancer Services but that it is a bit different for Cilium ingress config.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not require switching to ``Cluster`` for the check to pass.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
Also, for any Services that exposes Cilium's Envoy, Cilium will ensure that
when ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` is set, every node in the cluster will
pass the ``healthCheckNodePort`` check, so that external load balancers will
forward correctly.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium alongside Istio in ambient mode. They want Cilium L7 HTTP policy to govern traffic for a particular workload, but that workload is currently enrolled in Istio ambient. What must they do so that Cilium can enforce L7 policy on that workload?

options.text: Remove the workload from Istio ambient, either by removing the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` label from the namespace or by annotating the pod with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`.
Set `mtls.mode=DISABLE` in an Istio PeerAuthentication resource for that workload.
Keep the workload in ambient but enable Cilium L7 policy alongside Istio L7 policy so both enforce HTTP rules.
Change the Istio ambient redirection port from 15008 to a port Cilium can inspect.
