stem: An engineer sets spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges on a LoadBalancer service and expects the same CIDR restriction to apply to the NodePort and ClusterIP services created alongside it. With default Cilium behaviour, what actually happens?

The CIDRs apply to all three service types automatically.
The CIDRs are rejected unless bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes is set to true.

explanation: By default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges only apply to the LoadBalancer service, not to the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP service installed along with it.

optionRationale.b: The default does not extend to NodePort either; only the LoadBalancer service is covered.
optionRationale.c: Applying the CIDRs to all externally exposed types requires opting in, for example via bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say the field is rejected; it describes a default scoping behaviour and two ways to change it.

stem: A team wants the CIDR list in loadBalancerSourceRanges to block traffic from certain CIDRs while allowing everything else. Which annotation and value achieve this?

options.text: service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny

service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer
bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true

explanation: Cilium supports turning the list into a deny-list through the service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy annotation, which accepts allow or deny; setting it to deny blocks traffic from the listed CIDRs while allowing the rest.

optionRationale.b: The allow value is the default behaviour, which treats the list as an allow-list rather than a deny-list.
optionRationale.c: The service.cilium.io/type annotation is used to avoid creating corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, not to invert the CIDR policy.
optionRationale.d: bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes is a Helm option that propagates the CIDRs to all externally exposed service types; it does not turn the list into a deny-list.

stem: A platform team has a global service in cluster 1 with `service.cilium.io/affinity` set to `local`. All local backends in cluster 1 are healthy. A client in cluster 1 curls the global service. What does it observe?

options.text: Replies come only from pods in cluster 1, because the local endpoints are preferred while they remain available and healthy.
Replies come from pods in both clusters, because the affinity annotation only affects endpoints in the remote cluster.
Replies come only from pods in cluster 2, because `local` means the local cluster is excluded from load-balancing.
Replies alternate strictly between cluster 1 and cluster 2, because `local` enables round-robin across clusters.

explanation: With the annotation value `local`, the Global Service load-balances across healthy local backends and only uses remote endpoints if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy. The excerpt's step 2 confirms that from cluster 1 you will see replies from pods in cluster 1 only.

optionRationale.b: The annotation does affect which endpoints are preferred; the excerpt shows cluster 1 clients getting replies from cluster 1 only, not from both clusters.
optionRationale.c: `local` prefers endpoints from the local cluster, not the remote one; `remote` is the value that prefers remote endpoints.

The route has been programmed into Envoy by the Cilium Gateway controller.

explanation: For HTTPRoute status, the excerpt lists `ResolvedRefs` as meaning the referenced services were found and are valid references. `Accepted` is the condition covering whether the HTTPRoute configuration was correct and accepted.

optionRationale.b: That is the meaning of the `Accepted` condition type for an HTTPRoute, not `ResolvedRefs`.
optionRationale.c: That description belongs to `ResolvedRefs` on the Gateway's status conditions, which concerns referenced secrets, not the HTTPRoute's service references.

stem: A Gateway's status shows a condition with Status set to false, and you want to understand why. Which fields does the excerpt say give more information?

The `Attached Routes` count on the listener.

optionRationale.c: `Controller Name` and `Parent Ref` identify the controller and the parent gateway reference, not the reason for a false condition.

stem: An engineer is running a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available, and wants the Cilium ingress controller's Envoy listener reachable directly on the host network. options.text: The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode is automatically disabled, because the two modes are mutually exclusive.
A LoadBalancer Service is still created, but it is bound only to the loopback interface.
A NodePort Service is retained alongside the host listener so that both paths remain available.
The Service type is switched to ExternalName so that the host listener can be reached by DNS name.

explanation: Host network mode and the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode cannot coexist: enabling host network mode automatically disables the Service-based mode. The listener is then exposed on all interfaces rather than on a Service.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 and/or ::), not restricted to loopback, and says nothing about retaining a LoadBalancer Service.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the two modes are mutually exclusive, so a NodePort Service is not retained alongside the host listener.
optionRationale.d: No ExternalName Service type is mentioned anywhere in the excerpt; the Service mode is disabled, not converted.

stem: An engineer enables host network mode and wants the shared HTTP listener to be reachable on a host port different from the shared listener port, while leaving the other shared listeners on the default. Which Helm value should be set?

ingressController.hostNetwork.httpPort
ingressController.hostNetwork.tlsPassthroughPort
ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port

optionRationale.c: tlsPassthroughPort applies to the shared TLS passthrough listener, not the HTTP listener.

stem: A cluster runs the Cilium ingress controller in dedicated mode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. An engineer creates a new Ingress resource for host network exposure but omits the per-Ingress port annotation. What is the consequence?

options.text: The Ingress falls back to the shared listener port 8080, which is shared across all Ingress resources.
The Ingress is rejected because the host-listener-port annotation is mandatory in this situation.
The Ingress is accepted, but the port clashes are resolved automatically by Cilium.
The Ingress uses the tlsPassthroughPort value as its host listener port.

explanation: The ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation is mandatory when the global mode is dedicated, or when the Ingress sets the loadbalancer-mode annotation to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed. optionRationale.a: Although the default port is 8080, the excerpt states it can only be used for a single Ingress resource as it needs to be unique per Ingress resource, so it cannot be shared across all of them.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt warns that misconfiguration might result in port clashes and instructs the operator to configure unique ports; it does not describe automatic resolution.
optionRationale.d: tlsPassthroughPort is a Helm value for the shared TLS passthrough listener, not a fallback for a dedicated Ingress host listener port.

options.text: The Cilium proxy (HTTP) interferes with Istio's mTLS-based HTTPs connections; you must disable Istio's mTLS authentication by configuring a new policy.
The L4 policy was applied to the wrong namespace; you must reapply it in the `red` namespace.
Istio is in `PERMISSIVE` mode; you must switch it to `STRICT` mode so that mTLS is enforced.
The `/ip` path is not permitted by the Cilium proxy; you must add `/deny` to the allowed paths.

optionRationale.c: ``PERMISSIVE`` is the default described earlier and is not presented as the cause of the 503 responses.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium alongside Istio in ambient mode. They want Cilium L7 HTTP policy to govern traffic for a particular workload, but that workload is currently enrolled in Istio ambient. What must they do so that Cilium can enforce L7 policy on that workload's traffic?

options.text: Remove the workload from Istio ambient, either by removing the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` label from the namespace or by annotating the pods with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`.
Set `mtls.mode=DISABLE` in an Istio PeerAuthentication resource for that workload.
Leave the workload in ambient mode but enable Cilium L7 policy, since Cilium can inspect traffic tunneled over port 15008.
Configure `hostNetwork: true` on the istiod pods so that Cilium can reach the workload's sidecar.

explanation: In ambient mode, the way to make a workload subject to Cilium L7 policy is to take it out of Istio ambient, either by removing the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` label from the namespace or by annotating the pods with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`. Otherwise Istio encrypts the traffic with mTLS and Cilium cannot access it for L7 policy enforcement. Disabling mTLS via PeerAuthentication is the sidecar-mode remedy, not the ambient one.

optionRationale.b: ``mtls.mode=DISABLE`` under PeerAuthentication is the instruction given for sidecar mode, not for ambient mode.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that traffic tunneled and encrypted by Istio over port 15008 gives Cilium no visibility into source, destination or any L7 information, so leaving the workload in ambient does not work.
optionRationale.d: ``hostNetwork: true`` on istiod is a requirement for sidecar mode with automatic injection and Cilium overlay mode, unrelated to L7 policy enforcement.

optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Cilium has no visibility into the actual source and destination, not merely the L7 information.

stem: An engineer exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service and wants the backend Pod to see the client's original address. She is using Cilium Ingress and is deciding whether she must set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on that Service. What does the excerpt say about this requirement?

options.text: It is not necessary, because Cilium ingress traffic is always sent to the local node and forwarded to Envoy via TPROXY, keeping the source IP visible through `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address`.
It is mandatory, because only `Local` prevents masquerading of the source IP for any Service that exposes Envoy.
It is mandatory, because `Cluster` causes the node to always masquerade the source IP for ingress traffic.
It is not necessary, because Cilium rewrites the source IP into the `healthCheckNodePort` response headers instead.

explanation: The excerpt states that for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod, via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields. It explains that all ingress traffic bound for a Service that exposes Envoy always goes to the local node and is always forwarded to Envoy using the Linux Kernel TPROXY function.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite for Cilium ingress config: `Local` is not necessary to keep the source IP visible. The masquerading point applies to the general `Cluster` description, not as a mandate for Envoy-exposing Services.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the node *may* masquerade the source IP under `Cluster`, not that it always does, and it explicitly says `Local` is not necessary for Cilium ingress config.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt mentions `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` as the fields carrying the source IP, not the `healthCheckNodePort` response headers.

stem: A cluster runs `kube-proxy` and exposes a Service with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`. An operator wants to know how to check, from outside the cluster, whether a given node has local Pods behind that Service. According to the excerpt, what behaviour should she expect?

options.text: A request to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` returns 200 on nodes with local Pods running and non-200 on nodes without them.
A request to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` returns 200 on every node in the cluster regardless of local Pods.
A request to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` returns non-200 on nodes with local Pods and 200 on nodes without them.
No such port is opened; the operator must inspect EndpointSlices to determine local Pod presence.

explanation: The excerpt describes part of the contract for `externalTrafficPolicy` local: the node opens a port (the `healthCheckNodePort`, automatically set by Kubernetes when `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` is set), and requests to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` return 200 on nodes that have local Pods running and non-200 on nodes that do not.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says non-200 is returned on nodes without local Pods, so 200 on every node is wrong. The always-passing behaviour is described separately for Services exposing Cilium's Envoy.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the reverse: 200 on nodes with local Pods, non-200 on nodes without.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says the node will open the `healthCheckNodePort`, so claiming no such port exists contradicts it.

the node will

stem: How does the excerpt contrast the `Local` and `Cluster` settings of `externalTrafficPolicy` for a Loadbalancer or NodePort Service?

options.text: `Local` routes only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, whereas `Cluster` routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly and the node may masquerade the source IP.
`Local` routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, whereas `Cluster` routes only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP.
`Local` routes only to Pods on the local node but always masquerades the source IP, whereas `Cluster` never masquerades the source IP.
`Local` and `Cluster` differ only in the health check port number that Kubernetes assigns automatically.

explanation: The excerpt gives two relevant settings. `Local`: nodes route traffic only to Pods running on the local node, without masquerading the source IP. `Cluster`: the node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, and the node may masquerade the source IP, which in many cases may mean the backend pod does not see the source IP.

optionRationale.b: This swaps the two definitions; the excerpt assigns even cluster-wide routing to `Cluster` and local-only routing to `Local`.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says `Local` routes without masquerading the source IP, and that `Cluster` *may* masquerade it, not that it never does.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the `healthCheckNodePort` as automatically set when `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` is set; it does not present port numbering as the difference between the two settings.

stem: A Cilium Egress Gateway policy uses an egressGateway nodeSelector with matchLabels testLabel: testVal. Three nodes in the cluster carry that label and are named node-c, node-a and node-b. Which node acts as the gateway node for the policy?

options.text: node-a, because the first node in lexical ordering based on node name is selected when several nodes match.
node-c, because the most recently created matching node is selected.
All three nodes act as gateway nodes and share the SNAT traffic.
No node is selected, because a nodeSelector matching more than one node is ambiguous and the policy is ignored.

explanation: When several nodes match the label set given in nodeSelector, Cilium picks the first node in lexical ordering based on node name. Among node-a, node-b and node-c, that is node-a.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says nothing about creation time; the tie-break is lexical ordering by node name.
optionRationale.c: A single gateway node is selected per policy; the excerpt describes selecting one node, not sharing traffic across all matches.
optionRationale.d: An ambiguous match is resolved by lexical ordering, not by ignoring the policy. The excerpt only says policies specifying both egressIP and interface are ignored.

stem: A node is being shut down for maintenance. BGP Graceful Restart is enabled, and the node's BGP peer supports Graceful Restart with Notification as defined in RFC 8538. After the node is unselected from the CiliumBGPClusterConfig node selector, when will the peer withdraw routes towards the node?

options.text: After the Stale Timer defined in RFC 8538 expires.
Immediately after the node is unselected, because the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification to the peer.
Only after the node has been fully shut down and the BGP session times out.
Never, because Graceful Restart keeps the routes in place until the peer is reconfigured manually.

explanation: With Graceful Restart enabled and a peer that supports Graceful Restart with Notification, the peer withdraws routes only once the Stale Timer defined in RFC 8538 expires.

optionRationale.b: Immediate withdrawal after unselecting the node is the behaviour when the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification, because the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification.
optionRationale.c: The withdrawal is driven by the Stale Timer on the peer, not by the node finishing its shutdown.
optionRationale.d: Routes are eventually withdrawn; Graceful Restart delays the withdrawal rather than preventing it.

stem: An engineer drains a node, then unselects it from the CiliumBGPClusterConfig node selector so that all BGP sessions on the node shut down, and then shuts the node down straight away without waiting for the BGP peer to remove its routes. What is the consequence described for Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster?

options.text: Ongoing traffic for those Services is broken, because the peer may still send traffic to the node.
Nothing happens, because draining the node already removed all Pods from the Service endpoints.
The BGP peer immediately withdraws all routes, so no traffic is affected.
The Services are converted to externalTrafficPolicy=Local until the node returns.

explanation: The peer may still send traffic to the node during the period before it removes routes, so shutting the node down without waiting breaks ongoing traffic of externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster Services.

optionRationale.b: Draining removes Pods from Service endpoints, but the peer can still direct traffic to the node until it withdraws routes.
optionRationale.c: Immediate withdrawal is not guaranteed; it depends on Graceful Restart settings and the peer's implementation.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes no such conversion of the external traffic policy.

stem: On ingress, how does the L3 Encryption object obtain the key needed to decrypt a packet?

stem: A Cilium agent is running on a node and a container's traffic must be monitored and policy enforced on everything the container sends out. The container is connected to the host through a veth pair. Which attachment point does Cilium use to achieve this?

options.text: The XDP hook in the networking driver, which runs on packet reception before any other processing.
The TC ingress hook of the host side of the veth pair.
The socket operations hook attached to the root cgroup, which runs on TCP events.
The socket send/recv hook, which runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket.

explanation: Cilium attaches to the TC ingress hook on the host side of the veth pair, which lets it monitor and enforce policy on all traffic exiting a container. XDP runs at the earliest point in the driver on packet reception and is suited to filtering and DDoS protection, while the socket hooks operate on TCP socket events and send operations rather than on the veth device.

optionRationale.a: XDP is the earliest hook in the networking driver and is described as ideal for filtering and DDoS protection, not as the veth attachment point for container egress policy.
optionRationale.c: The socket operations hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events such as ESTABLISHED transitions; it is not the veth attachment point described for container traffic.
optionRationale.d: The socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation of a TCP socket and is used to accelerate datapath redirects, not to attach to the host side of a veth pair.

stem: A three-node cluster has both IPv4 and IPv6 enabled and IPsec encryption is active. No key rotation is in progress. An engineer runs `cilium-dbg encrypt status` in a Cilium Pod and sees `Keys in use: 8`. What does this indicate?

options.text: The key count is as expected for this cluster configuration.
The key count is too high; it should be 4 because there are three nodes.
The key count is too low; it should be 12 because there are three nodes and two IP families.
The key count indicates that a key rotation is currently ongoing.

explanation: The number of keys in use should be 2 per remote node per enabled IP family. In a three-node cluster with both IPv4 and IPv6 enabled and no key rotation, there should be 8 keys in use on each node, so 8 is correct.

optionRationale.b: The expected count is 2 per remote node per IP family, not 2 per node overall; with three nodes and two families the expected count is 8, not 4.
optionRationale.c: The expected count is 2 per remote node per IP family, giving 8 for three nodes and two families, not 12.
optionRationale.d: During a key rotation the count can double to 4 per remote node per IP family, which would give 16 here, not 8; 8 is the normal value.

citations.title: Troubleshooting

optionRationale.d: `XfrmOutPolBlock` is an XFRM error counter for packets Cilium dropped that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text; it is not the first thing to check when Pods fail to start.

stem: A request to an Ingress-backed service is failing. An engineer SSHes to a Kubernetes node and sends a request to localhost on the node port shown for the LoadBalancer service. The response comes back with the header `server: envoy`. What does this indicate?

The Cilium agent is not running on that node.

stem: A Cilium-managed pod on a node is the source of a TCP connection. The connection completes its handshake and moves into the ESTABLISHED state, and the peer is a node-local process. Which behaviour does Cilium exhibit at that moment?

options.text: The socket operations program, attached to the root cgroup, detects the ESTABLISHED transition and, because the socket has a node local peer, attaches a socket send/recv program to the socket.
The XDP program attached to the container's veth pair drops the packet so that the connection must be re-established through the proxy.
The L3 Encryption object performs a map lookup on the destination IP and marks the socket for encryption before any further processing.
The Service object performs a map lookup on the destination IP and port and forwards the packet to one of the configured L3/L4 endpoints.

explanation: Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations program to the root cgroup and uses it to monitor TCP state transitions, specifically ESTABLISHED. When a socket transitions into ESTABLISHED and the TCP socket has a node local peer (possibly a local proxy), a socket send/recv program is attached.

optionRationale.b: XDP runs at the earliest point in the networking driver on packet reception and is used for filtering such as dropping malicious traffic; it is not what reacts to a TCP state transition on an established socket.
optionRationale.c: The L3 Encryption object's map lookup on the destination IP happens on egress to decide whether a packet should be encrypted; it is not triggered by a socket entering ESTABLISHED.
optionRationale.d: The Service object does a map lookup on destination IP and optionally port for packets received by that object and forwards to L3/L4 endpoints; it is not the component that attaches a program on an ESTABLISHED transition.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations
  program to the root cgroup and uses this to monitor for TCP state transitions,
  specifically for ESTABLISHED state transitions.

stem: A Cilium operator configures a Hubble metric with `flow:destinationContext=dns|ip`. A flow targets a pod whose DNS name is not known to Hubble. What value is placed in the metric's `destination` label?

options.text: The IP address of the target, because the first non-empty value among the specified contexts is used.
An empty string, because the first context in the list (`dns`) produced no value.
Both the DNS name and the IP address, separated by a `|` symbol.
The literal string `dns|ip`, because multiple contexts cannot be combined for a single label.

explanation: When multiple contexts are specified for source or destination, they are separated by `|` and the first non-empty value is added to the metric as a label. With `dns|ip`, Hubble first tries the DNS name; if none is known, it falls back to the IP address.

optionRationale.b: The fallback behaviour means an empty value is not used when a later context can supply a value.
optionRationale.c: Only one value is chosen; the `|` separates candidate contexts, not output values.
optionRationale.d: The `|` is a separator in the configuration, not a literal label value.

stem: A pod in a Cilium cluster with transparent encryption enabled is permitted by policy to initiate traffic to destinations outside the cluster. A new pod is created on a remote node, and the local node has not yet learned that the new pod's IP address belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint. The local pod sends packets to that IP address during this window. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It sends them unencrypted, because it has to assume the destination IP address is outside of the cluster.
It drops them until the endpoint information has propagated, then retries them encrypted.
It encrypts them using the local node's key and re-encrypts them with the remote node's key once it learns the endpoint.
It encrypts them using the encryption key of the remote node, which it fetches on demand for each new destination.

explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether a destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that a particular IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or newly joined remote Cilium host, it must assume the destination is outside the cluster, so the initial packets go out unencrypted. Only once the endpoint information has propagated does Cilium begin encrypting packets using the encryption key of the remote node.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes a time window in which packets are sent unencrypted; it does not describe dropping and later retrying them.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says encryption uses the key of the remote node once the endpoint is known; it does not describe double encryption with the local key.
optionRationale.d: The key of the remote node is used once Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node, not fetched on demand before that.

stem: An engineer wants to stop pods in a Cilium cluster from sending unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster, so that the window in which packets to not-yet-discovered remote endpoints leave unencrypted is closed. Which approach does Cilium describe as a workaround?

options.text: Define an egress policy that either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities, or allows egress outside the cluster only to a subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.
Define an ingress policy that drops all traffic from reserved:world identities, so that pods never receive replies from outside the cluster.
Enable encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled so that all egress traffic leaving the node is encrypted.
Set encryption.strictMode.egress.allowRemoteNodeIdentities to true so that no traffic can leave the cluster unencrypted.

explanation: The excerpt gives two mitigations. The first is to ensure the endpoint is not allowed to send unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster, achieved by an egress policy that either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities or only allows egress to addresses outside the cluster for a subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.

optionRationale.b: The workaround is framed as an egress policy restricting where pods may send traffic, not an ingress policy on reserved:world.
optionRationale.c: Strict mode ingress concerns cluster-internal ingress traffic arriving other than through the WireGuard tunnel; it is not the egress workaround described.
optionRationale.d: allowRemoteNodeIdentities is a fallback that permits unencrypted traffic associated with a node identity; it does not prevent unencrypted egress.

addresses using ``toCIDR``, ``toCIDRSet`` and ``toFQDN`` rules.

stem: Encryption strict mode ingress is enabled on a node. Which statement about its scope and requirements matches the described behaviour?

options.text: Any cluster-internal ingress traffic that did not arrive on the node through the WireGuard tunnel is dropped; it is supported with both tunnel and native routing modes and requires WireGuard encryption.
Any cluster-internal ingress traffic that did not arrive on the node through the WireGuard tunnel is dropped; it is supported with both WireGuard and IPsec encryption.
Node-to-node encryption for WireGuard is protected by strict mode ingress, which enforces on all traffic destined for the node.
It is supported when chaining Cilium on top of other CNI plugins, provided all pod-routable interfaces are managed by Cilium.

explanation: When encryption strict mode ingress is enabled, any cluster-internal ingress traffic that did not arrive on the node through the WireGuard tunnel is dropped, preventing unencrypted pod traffic from reaching local endpoints. It is supported with both tunnel and native routing modes and requires WireGuard encryption; it is not supported with IPsec.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that strict mode ingress requires WireGuard encryption and is not supported with IPsec.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt lists as a limitation that node-to-node encryption for WireGuard is not protected by strict mode ingress; enforcement only applies to cluster-internal pod traffic destined for local endpoints.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that strict mode ingress is currently not supported when chaining Cilium on top of other CNI plugins.

stem: A Cilium cluster uses transparent encryption. An endpoint is permitted to initiate traffic to targets outside the cluster. A new pod is created on a remote node, and before information about that endpoint has propagated, the local endpoint sends packets to the new pod's IP address. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It sends them unencrypted, because it must assume the destination IP address is outside the cluster.
It drops them until the endpoint information has propagated to every node.
It encrypts them using the local node's key and re-encrypts them once the remote node is known.
It encrypts them using the encryption key of the remote node, which is fetched on demand for each packet.

explanation: Transparent encryption decides whether to encrypt by using the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to determine whether the destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that an IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or a newly joined remote Cilium host, it has to assume the destination is outside the cluster, so the initial packets go out unencrypted. Only once the endpoint information has propagated does Cilium begin encrypting using the remote node's key.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the described behaviour involves dropping the packets; they are sent, but unencrypted, during the time window.
optionRationale.c: Cilium does not encrypt with the local key and then re-encrypt; it starts encrypting with the remote node's key once it knows the address is a remote endpoint.
optionRationale.d: The remote node's key is used only after Cilium has learned that the IP address is an endpoint on that remote node, not fetched per packet beforehand.

options.text: Define an egress policy that either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities, or allows egress outside the cluster only to a subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.
Define an ingress policy that drops all traffic arriving from reserved:world identities on every node.
Set encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled to true so that egress packets are encrypted before leaving the node.
Disable transparent encryption for the endpoint so that no packets are sent until the remote endpoint is discovered.

optionRationale.b: The workaround is expressed as an egress policy restricting traffic to reserved:world, not an ingress policy dropping traffic from it.
optionRationale.c: Strict mode ingress concerns cluster-internal ingress traffic arriving other than through the WireGuard tunnel; it is not the workaround described for this egress issue.

stem: A cluster administrator enables encryption strict mode egress by setting encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and supplying the expected pod CIDR in encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr. Which statement describes a limitation of this mode?

The pod CIDR must be IPv6, because strict mode egress only protects IPv6 traffic.
Strict mode egress requires IPsec and is not supported with WireGuard.
Strict mode egress is only supported when Cilium is chained on top of another CNI plugin.

explanation: Among the listed limitations of encryption strict mode egress is that the pod CIDR, and therefore the strict mode egress CIDR, must be IPv4; IPv6 traffic is not protected by strict mode and can be leaked.

optionRationale.b: The requirement is the reverse: the CIDR must be IPv4, and IPv6 traffic is the unprotected case.

stem: In a cluster with Istio ambient mode and Cilium, client and server applications are deployed across the red, blue, and green namespaces. By default, Istio operates in PERMISSIVE mode. A connectivity test is run from a client in the green namespace to a server in the blue namespace. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request succeeds with HTTP 200 because PERMISSIVE mode allows unsecured traffic.
The request fails with HTTP 000 because PERMISSIVE mode blocks traffic from unmanaged pods.
The request succeeds only if the client is in the same namespace as the server.
The request fails with HTTP 403 because PERMISSIVE mode enforces L7 policy.

explanation: By default, Istio works in PERMISSIVE mode, allowing both Istio-ambient-managed and Istio-unmanaged pods to send and receive unsecured traffic. Therefore, the connectivity test from green to blue should succeed with HTTP 200.

optionRationale.b: PERMISSIVE mode allows unsecured traffic; it does not block traffic from unmanaged pods.
optionRationale.c: PERMISSIVE mode allows traffic between different namespaces; there is no same-namespace restriction.
optionRationale.d: PERMISSIVE mode does not enforce L7 policy; it allows unsecured traffic.

client 'blue' to server 'blue'
client 'green' to server 'red'

explanation: The L4 policy restricts communication in the blue namespace to clients from blue and red namespaces. Therefore, a client from the green namespace to a server in the blue namespace is not allowed and is expected to fail.

optionRationale.c: Clients from the blue namespace are allowed to communicate with the blue namespace.
optionRationale.d: The policy only restricts communication in the blue namespace; communication to the red namespace is not restricted by this policy.

Istio is enforcing mTLS authentication.
The Cilium proxy is interfering with Istio's mTLS connections.
The L4 network policy is blocking the request.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with Istio in ambient mode. Web servers and clients are deployed across the red, blue and green namespaces, and connectivity checks from every client namespace to httpbin.red and httpbin.blue all return 200. An engineer then applies a Cilium L4 network policy that restricts communication in the blue namespace to clients located only in the blue and red namespaces. When the same connectivity checks are re-run, which result set should the engineer expect?

options.text: All six checks return 200, because Istio's PERMISSIVE mode allows unsecured traffic between managed and unmanaged pods.
The three checks to httpbin.red return 200; the checks from red and blue to httpbin.blue return 200; the check from green to httpbin.blue returns 000 and the command terminates with exit code 28.
The three checks to httpbin.red return 200; all three checks to httpbin.blue return 000 and each command terminates with exit code 28.
The checks from red and blue to httpbin.blue return 403, while the check from green to httpbin.blue returns 000.

explanation: The L4 policy restricts communication in the blue namespace to clients in the blue and red namespaces, so only the green client is blocked when reaching httpbin.blue. The expected output shows the green-to-blue check returning 000 with exit code 28, while the red and blue clients still reach httpbin.blue with 200 and all traffic to httpbin.red is unaffected. The 403 response appears only later, when an L7 policy is applied and a different URL path such as /deny is requested.

optionRationale.a: PERMISSIVE mode describes Istio's default handling of unsecured traffic between ambient-managed and unmanaged pods; it does not mean a Cilium L4 policy has no effect, and the checks do not all stay at 200.
optionRationale.c: This describes the outcome after the L7 policy is applied, when the Cilium HTTP proxy interferes with Istio's mTLS-based HTTPS connections and all communication with the blue namespace breaks. The L4 policy alone blocks only the green client.
optionRationale.d: A 403 is the response seen when accessing a different URL path such as /deny under the L7 policy; the L4 policy produces 000 with exit code 28 for the blocked client, not 403.

stem: An engineer wants to know how many simultaneous connections a single egress-gateway node can support to one common remote endpoint address using the same egress IP, when the node-port range is left at its default. What is that number, and how is it derived?

options.text: 32768, the difference between the maximum NAT node port value of 65535 and the default upper bound of --node-port-range, which is 32767.
65535, because the full NAT node port range is available to the egress-gateway.
32767, because that is the default upper bound of --node-port-range.
It is unlimited, because Cilium allocates a fresh egress IP for each new connection.

explanation: The limit is the difference between the maximum NAT node port value (65535) and the upper bound of --node-port-range, which defaults to 32767, giving 65535 - 32767 = 32768 possible connections to a common remote endpoint address using the same egress IP.

optionRationale.b: 65535 is the maximum NAT node port value, but the ports up to the --node-port-range upper bound are not available for this, so the full range cannot be used.
optionRationale.c: 32767 is the default upper bound of --node-port-range, which is subtracted from 65535 rather than being the answer itself.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes a hard limit on SNAT map capacity, not unlimited allocation of egress IPs.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote: The limit is equal to the difference between max NAT node port value (65535) and the upper bound of ``--node-port-range`` (default: 32767).

stem: An engineer runs the NAT statistics command on an egress-gateway node and sees a row whose connection count is approaching 32768. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: It may indicate SNAT connection overflow issues, since the count is approaching the default connection limit.
It is expected and harmless, because the statistics are recalculated every 30 seconds.
It shows that the egress-gateway has run out of egress IPs and must allocate more.
It indicates that the remote endpoint is refusing connections because of the firewall.

explanation: A row with a very large connection count, approaching the default connection limit of 32768, may indicate SNAT connection overflow issues.

optionRationale.b: The 30-second recalculation explains delays in the statistics being updated, not why a near-limit count would be harmless.
optionRationale.c: The limit concerns source port mappings in the SNAT map, not a shortage of egress IPs.
optionRationale.d: The firewall is described as permitting traffic that matches the egress IP; the excerpt does not attribute high counts to firewall refusals.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote: If you observe one or more row having a very large connection count (i.e. approaching the default connection limit: 32768), then this may indicate SNAT connection overflow issues.

stem: A cluster uses Cilium's egress-gateway with an egress IP of 10.1.0.0 masquerading connections to a backend at 10.2.0.0:8080. Many clients connect to that same backend through the same egress-gateway node. How does Cilium's datapath distinguish these connections from one another?

options.text: Each connection is mapped using a unique source port.
Each connection is assigned a unique egress IP from the egress-gateway pool.
Each connection is given a distinct destination port on the remote endpoint.
Each connection is tracked by a per-client tunnel identifier in the SNAT map.

explanation: Because all clients share the same tuple of egress IP, remote endpoint IP and remote endpoint port, Cilium's datapath maps each connection to this destination using a unique source port. The egress IP stays the same, and the destination address and port are unchanged, so neither of those can be the distinguishing factor.

optionRationale.b: The scenario fixes a single egress IP of 10.1.0.0 for these connections; the datapath does not hand out a new egress IP per connection.
optionRationale.c: The remote endpoint port is 8080 for all of these connections and is not varied to distinguish them.
optionRationale.d: No per-client tunnel identifier is described; the distinguishing mechanism is the source port in the SNAT mapping.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote: In Cilium's datapath, each connection to this destination will be mapped using a unique source port.

stem: An engineer is told that an egress-gateway node can handle 32768 possible connections to a common remote endpoint address using the same egress IP. Which calculation produces that figure?

options.text: The difference between the max NAT node port value (65535) and the upper bound of --node-port-range (default: 32767).
The difference between the max NAT node port value (65535) and the lower bound of --node-port-range (default: 1024).
The sum of the max NAT node port value (65535) and the upper bound of --node-port-range (default: 32767).
The upper bound of --node-port-range alone (default: 32767), rounded up to the next power of two.

explanation: The limit is the difference between the maximum NAT node port value of 65535 and the upper bound of --node-port-range, which defaults to 32767, giving 65535 - 32767 = 32768 connections.

optionRationale.b: The default lower bound of the node port range is not the figure used; the calculation uses the upper bound of --node-port-range.
optionRationale.c: The two values are subtracted, not added; adding them would give a figure far above 32768.
optionRationale.d: The limit is a difference between two values, not the upper bound of the range on its own.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote: The limit is equal to the difference between max NAT node port value (65535) and the upper bound of ``--node-port-range`` (default: 32767).

stem: Clients on a cluster make a very large number of connections through an egress-gateway node to the same remote endpoint, using the same egress IP. What does Cilium warn will happen if the SNAT map reaches capacity?

options.text: Old connections will no longer be tracked, causing connectivity issues.
The egress-gateway will automatically allocate a second egress IP to share the load.
New connections will be routed directly from the client pod without masquerading.
The remote endpoint will be removed from the egress-gateway policy and traffic will be dropped at the firewall.

explanation: When too many connections are made through the egress-gateway node and the SNAT map reaches capacity, old connections are no longer tracked, which causes connectivity issues. High SNAT port mapping utilisation can also cause failures because the SNAT mapping cannot find available source ports.

optionRationale.b: No automatic allocation of an additional egress IP is described; the remedy is a manual change such as splitting traffic across different egress IPs.
optionRationale.c: Connections are not described as falling back to unmasqueraded routing; the failure manifests as lost tracking and port exhaustion.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the description removes the remote endpoint from policy or involves the firewall dropping traffic as the mechanism.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote: If too many connections are made through the egress-gateway node, Cilium's SNAT map can reach capacity, which will result in old connections not being tracked, causing connectivity issues.

stem: An engineer wants to inspect the connection tuples with the highest SNAT usage on a Cilium agent. Which command is used, and how many such tuples does the agent store stats for?

options.text: kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg shell -- db/show nat-stats, covering the top 30 connection tuples.
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg shell -- db/show nat-stats, covering the top 10 connection tuples.
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg bpf nat list, covering the top 30 connection tuples.
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg monitor --type nat, covering all connection tuples.

explanation: The Cilium agent stores stats about the top 30 connection tuples, accessible inside a cilium agent container using the cilium-dbg utility with the command shown, which runs db/show nat-stats in the cilium-dbg shell.

optionRationale.b: The number of stored tuples is 30, not 10.
optionRationale.c: The subcommand given is db/show nat-stats run through the cilium-dbg shell, not bpf nat list.
optionRationale.d: cilium-dbg monitor --type nat is not the command described, and the stats cover only the top 30 tuples rather than all of them.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote: Cilium agent stores stats about the top 30 such connection tuples, this can be accessed inside a cilium agent container using the ``cilium-dbg`` utility.

stem: An engineer runs the nat-stats command on an agent and sees a row whose connection count is approaching 32768. What does this suggest, and what is the only solution?

options.text: It may indicate SNAT connection overflow, and the only solution is to reduce the number of connections being SNATed through the egress-gateway.
It may indicate SNAT connection overflow, and the only solution is to raise the max NAT node port value above 65535.
It indicates a stale stats cache, and the only solution is to wait for the next recalculation.
It indicates a firewall misconfiguration, and the only solution is to widen the firewall rule to accept additional source IPs.

explanation: A very large connection count approaching the default limit of 32768 may indicate SNAT connection overflow issues. Because the problem results from hitting a hard limit on egress-gateway functionality, the only solution is to reduce the number of connections SNATed through an egress-gateway, for example by creating fewer new connections or splitting traffic across different egress IPs and/or remote endpoint addresses.

optionRationale.b: The max NAT node port value is given as 65535; raising it is not presented as a solution.
optionRationale.c: The stats are recalculated periodically, but a high count is a genuine signal of overflow rather than a caching artefact.
optionRationale.d: The firewall is not the cause; the limit is a hard limit in Cilium's egress-gateway functionality.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote: If you observe one or more row having a very large connection count (i.e. approaching the default connection limit: 32768), then this may indicate SNAT connection overflow issues.

stem: An engineer checks nat-stats shortly after a burst of new connections and finds the counts lower than expected. What explains the delay before the figures reflect the new connections?

options.text: The stats are re-calculated every 30 seconds by default.
The stats are re-calculated every 5 minutes by default.
The stats are only refreshed when the Cilium agent is restarted.
The stats are streamed continuously, so any discrepancy means the connections were never SNATed.

explanation: The stats are re-calculated every 30 seconds by default, so there is a delay between new connections occurring and the stats being updated.

optionRationale.b: The default recalculation interval is 30 seconds, not 5 minutes.
optionRationale.c: Recalculation happens periodically rather than only on agent restart.
optionRationale.d: The stats are not continuous; the documented default is a 30-second recalculation, which accounts for the delay.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote: **Note**: These stats are re-calculated every 30 seconds by default. So there is a delay between new connections occurring and when the stats are updated.

stem: A Cilium egress-gateway is configured so that connections to a backend at 10.2.0.0:8080 are masqueraded using egress IP 10.1.0.0. A firewall in front of the backend permits only traffic whose source IP is 10.1.0.0. Many clients in the cluster open connections to that same backend, and over time the egress-gateway node begins to drop or fail to establish new connections to 10.2.0.0:8080. An engineer inspects the agent and finds that the SNAT map has reached capacity. Which action is consistent with resolving this condition?

options.text: Reduce the number of connections being SNATed through the egress-gateway, for example by having clients create fewer new connections or by splitting traffic across different egress IPs and/or remote endpoint addresses.
Raise the upper bound of --node-port-range above 65535 so that the SNAT map can hold more entries.
Increase the interval at which the agent recalculates nat-stats so that stale entries are evicted sooner.
Add the backend's address to the firewall allow-list under a second source IP so that both 10.1.0.0 and the node IP are accepted.

explanation: The excerpt states that because the problem is a result of hitting a hard limit on Cilium's Egress Gateway functionality, the only solution is to reduce the number of connections that are being SNATed through an egress-gateway, which can be done by having clients avoid creating as many new connections, or by lowering the amount of connections going to the same remote address (with a common egress IP) by splitting up traffic via different egress IPs and/or remote endpoint addresses. The other options either misstate the limit, confuse the stats refresh interval with eviction, or change the firewall rather than the connection volume.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives the limit as the difference between the max NAT node port value (65535) and the upper bound of --node-port-range (default: 32767); it does not present raising the range as a remedy, and the maximum port value is 65535.
optionRationale.c: The 30-second figure refers to how often the nat-stats are re-calculated, not to any eviction of SNAT entries; changing it would not enlarge the SNAT map.
optionRationale.d: The firewall already permits source IP 10.1.0.0; the failure is caused by SNAT map capacity on the egress-gateway node, not by the firewall rejecting the egress IP.

stem: An engineer creates a ServiceExport named rebel-base in namespace prod on cluster A. The same namespace prod exists on clusters B and C, but no ServiceExport is created there. What is the effect of the ServiceExport on cluster A?

options.text: The Service is exported to all clusters, provided that the Service Namespace is present on those clusters.
The Service is exported only to clusters that already have a matching ServiceExport.
The Service is exported only to the local cluster until a ServiceImport is created manually.
The ServiceExport has no effect until a ServiceImport resource is created in each cluster.

explanation: Creating a ServiceExport exports the Service to all clusters, as long as the Service Namespace is present on those clusters. No matching ServiceExport or manual ServiceImport is required on the other clusters.

optionRationale.b: A ServiceExport on one cluster is enough; the excerpt does not require a matching ServiceExport on every cluster.
optionRationale.c: The export is not limited to the local cluster; it reaches all clusters where the namespace exists.
optionRationale.d: ServiceImport resources are created automatically, not manually, and the export does not wait for them.

stem: Two clusters each export a Service named rebel-base in namespace prod. The ServiceExports are created at different times. What does Cilium create for this set of exported Services, and how are their endpoints treated?

options.text: A ServiceImport is created automatically, and the Endpoints from both exported Services are merged and made globally available.
A separate ServiceImport is created per cluster, and each keeps only its local Endpoints.
No ServiceImport is created until an engineer manually defines one, and endpoints remain cluster-local.
A ServiceImport is created only for the oldest ServiceExport, and the newer export's endpoints are discarded.

explanation: For each set of exported Services with the same name and namespace, a ServiceImport is created automatically, and all Endpoints from those exported Services are merged and made globally available.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes one ServiceImport per set of exported Services with the same name and namespace, not one per cluster.
optionRationale.c: ServiceImport creation is automatic, not manual.
optionRationale.d: Endpoints from all exported Services with the same name and namespace are merged; they are not discarded based on age.

explanation: Cilium reconciles SessionAffinity into the ServiceImport. On conflict it sets a conflict condition on the corresponding ServiceExport status and resolves the conflict based on ServiceExport creation time from oldest to newest.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes setting a conflict condition and resolving by creation time, not rejecting the newer ServiceExport.
optionRationale.c: A conflict is resolved to one set of properties, not merged so that both values are honoured.
optionRationale.d: The resolution order is oldest to newest, not newest to oldest.

stem: Which resource must an engineer create in order to export a Service through the Multi-Cluster Services API?

options.text: A ServiceExport resource
A ServiceImport resource
A derived-$hash Service
A Cilium Global Service

stem: A platform team exports a Service named payments in namespace finance from three clusters by creating a ServiceExport in each cluster. The ServiceExport in cluster A was created first, the one in cluster B second, and the one in cluster C third. The three exported Services disagree on the SessionAffinity property. What does Cilium do?

options.text: It sets a conflict condition on the corresponding ServiceExport status and resolves the conflict based on ServiceExport creation time, so the value from cluster A is used.
It rejects the ServiceExport in clusters B and C, leaving only the ServiceExport in cluster A active.
It merges the SessionAffinity values into a union and applies the union to the ServiceImport.
It resolves the conflict based on ServiceExport creation time from newest to oldest, so the value from cluster C is used.

explanation: Cilium globally reconciles SessionAffinity into the ServiceImport. When exported Services conflict on such a property, Cilium sets a conflict condition on the corresponding ServiceExport status and resolves the conflict based on ServiceExport creation time from oldest to newest, so the oldest ServiceExport (cluster A) wins.

optionRationale.b: Cilium does not reject the later ServiceExports; it records a conflict condition and still resolves the property.
optionRationale.c: A union is applied to Ports, not to SessionAffinity.
optionRationale.d: The resolution order is oldest to newest, not newest to oldest.

stem: An engineer sets `clean-cilium-bpf-state` to `true` in the Cilium ConfigMap and restarts the Cilium daemon. What is the effect on existing endpoints and connections?

options.text: All eBPF state is removed from the filesystem on startup; endpoints are restored with the same IP addresses, but ongoing connections may be briefly disrupted and loadbalancing decisions are lost, so active connections via the loadbalancer will break.

eBPF state is preserved, but endpoints are assigned new IP addresses and all connections are re-established automatically.
Only the eBPF state related to loadbalancing is removed; endpoints and ongoing connections are unaffected.

explanation: The `clean-cilium-bpf-state` option removes all eBPF state from the filesystem on startup. Endpoints are restored with the same IP addresses, but ongoing connections may be briefly disrupted and loadbalancing decisions will be lost, so active connections via the loadbalancer will break. The eBPF state is reconstructed from original sources, and the option should be turned off again after restarting the daemon.

optionRationale.b: This describes `clean-cilium-state`, which removes all Cilium state including unrecoverable endpoint state and CNI configuration files, and is irreversible.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that endpoints are restored with the same IP addresses, not new ones, and that connections may be disrupted.
optionRationale.d: The option removes all eBPF state, not just loadbalancing state, and it does affect ongoing connections.

stem: A cluster administrator needs to completely reset Cilium state, including endpoint state and CNI configuration files, because of a serious issue. They set `clean-cilium-state` to `true` and restart Cilium. What happens to existing endpoints that were managed by Cilium?

options.text: They continue to operate as before, but Cilium will no longer manage them and they may stop working without warning; they must be deleted and reconnected to allow the new Cilium instance to manage them.
They are automatically deleted and recreated by Cilium with new IP addresses.
They are restored with the same IP addresses and continue to be managed by Cilium without interruption.
They are migrated to a new Cilium instance and remain fully managed.

explanation: The `clean-cilium-state` option removes all Cilium state, including unrecoverable information such as all endpoint state, as well as recoverable state such as eBPF state pinned to the filesystem, CNI configuration files, library code, links, routes, and other information. This operation is irreversible. Existing endpoints currently managed by Cilium may continue to operate as before, but Cilium will no longer manage them and they may stop working without warning. After using this operation, endpoints must be deleted and reconnected to allow the new instance of Cilium to manage them.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not state that endpoints are automatically deleted and recreated; it says they must be deleted and reconnected manually.
optionRationale.c: This describes `clean-cilium-bpf-state`, not `clean-cilium-state`; the latter removes all state and is irreversible.

stem: An engineer wants to reduce per-packet latency by pre-allocating map entries, accepting the trade-off of up-front memory allocation. Which ConfigMap option should they set to `true`?

options.text: `preallocate-bpf-maps`
`debug`
`monitor-aggregation`
`clean-cilium-bpf-state`

explanation: The `preallocate-bpf-maps` option enables pre-allocation of map entries, which reduces per-packet latency at the expense of up-front memory allocation. It should be set to `true` to optimize for latency. Note that if this value is modified, connectivity may be temporarily disrupted for endpoints with active connections during the next Cilium startup.

optionRationale.b: `debug` enables verbose logging and configures eBPF programs to emit more visibility events; it does not pre-allocate map entries.
optionRationale.c: `monitor-aggregation` controls coalescing of tracing events in `cilium-dbg monitor`; it does not affect map pre-allocation.

It generates a tracing event on every send packet.

The `none` level generates a tracing event on every receive and send packet, and the `low` level generates a tracing event on every send packet.

stem: An engineer sets `monitor-aggregation` to `medium` and wants to ensure that, on average, one tracing event is sent during a specific interval, assuming new packets are sent at least once per interval. Which option controls this interval?

`monitor-aggregation`
`debug`
`preallocate-bpf-maps`

explanation: The `monitor-aggregation-interval` option defines the interval to report tracing events. It is only applicable for `monitor-aggregation` levels `medium` or higher. Assuming new packets are sent at least once per interval, this ensures that on average one event is sent during the interval.

optionRationale.b: `monitor-aggregation` sets the aggregation level (none, low, medium, maximum), not the reporting interval.
optionRationale.c: `debug` enables verbose logging and visibility events; it does not control the tracing event interval.
optionRationale.d: `preallocate-bpf-maps` controls pre-allocation of map entries to reduce latency; it does not control the tracing event interval.

stem: An engineer sets `monitor-aggregation` to `maximum` in the Cilium ConfigMap and expects the most aggressive coalescing available. What tracing behaviour results?

It generates a tracing event on every send packet only.

optionRationale.c: That is the behaviour of `low`, which generates an event on every send packet.

stem: An engineer sets `monitor-aggregation` to `low` and enables socket load-balancing. Which description matches the resulting tracing behaviour?

stem: How does the Cilium ingress controller expose its Envoy listener on the host when host network mode is enabled?

options.text: On all interfaces, using 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.
Only on the loopback interface, using 127.0.0.1.
Only on the node's primary IP address, selected at startup.
On a ClusterIP address allocated by the LoadBalancer Service.

explanation: In host network mode the listener is exposed on all interfaces, with 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.

optionRationale.b: The listener is not restricted to loopback.

stem: A team wants to change the host network port used by the shared Cilium ingress controller Envoy listener away from its default. What guidance applies to the port number they choose?

options.text: They should choose a port number higher than 1023.
They must choose a port number lower than 1024.
They must choose port 8080, since it cannot be changed.
They must choose a port that is unique per Ingress resource.

explanation: The sharedListenerPort flag sets the host network port for the Envoy listener, with a default of 8080. If it is changed, a port number higher than 1023 should be chosen, referring to binding to a privileged port.

optionRationale.b: The guidance is the opposite: choose a port higher than 1023.
optionRationale.c: The default is 8080, but the value can be changed.
optionRationale.d: Uniqueness per Ingress resource applies to the dedicated per-Ingress annotation, not to the shared listener port.

stem: A platform team runs a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. They enable the Cilium ingress controller in host network mode via Helm. What happens to the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode for the ingress controller?

It remains enabled and both modes expose the Envoy listener simultaneously.
It is converted into a ClusterIP Service that forwards to the host network listener.
It is left unchanged but must be disabled manually before host network mode can take effect.

explanation: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode; the two are mutually exclusive, so no manual step is required.

optionRationale.b: The two modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both expose the listener at once.

Only on the node IP address used by the Cilium agent.
On all interfaces, using 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.
Only on the interfaces selected by the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation.

stem: A team enables host network mode for the Cilium ingress controller and wants to change the global host network port used by the shared Envoy listener. They set ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort. What is the default value of this setting, and what constraint applies if it is changed?

options.text: The default is 80, and any value may be chosen because the listener runs as root.
The default is 8080, and a changed value should be a port number higher than 1023.
The default is 443, and a changed value must be lower than 1024.
The default is 0, which means a random port is chosen on every restart.

explanation: The sharedListenerPort defaults to 8080, and if changed the engineer should choose a port number higher than 1023 to avoid binding to a privileged port.

optionRationale.a: The default is 8080, not 80, and the guidance is to pick a port above 1023.
optionRationale.c: The default is 8080, not 443, and the guidance is for ports above 1023, not below 1024.
optionRationale.d: The default is 8080; 0 is the unset value for the httpPort, httpsPort and tlsPassthroughPort settings, not for sharedListenerPort.

A port allocated dynamically by the Cilium agent.
The value of sharedListenerPort, because an unset or 0 httpsPort falls back to it.
No HTTPS listener is created when httpsPort is 0.

explanation: For the shared HTTPS listener, if httpsPort is unset or 0, sharedListenerPort is used. The same fallback applies to httpPort and tlsPassthroughPort.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt gives no special treatment for 443; the fallback is sharedListenerPort.
optionRationale.b: No dynamic allocation is described; the fallback is a specific configured value.
optionRationale.d: A value of 0 means the fallback is used, not that the listener is omitted.

ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode
ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort
ingress.cilium.io/host-network-port

explanation: The per-Ingress annotation for the host network port is ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port. Its default is 8080, but it must be unique per Ingress resource.

optionRationale.b: ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode selects shared or dedicated mode; it does not set the port.
optionRationale.c: This is a Helm value for the global shared listener, not a per-Ingress annotation.

stem: The global Cilium ingress controller mode is configured to dedicated via ingressController.loadbalancerMode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. What must each Ingress resource provide, and why?

options.text: Nothing extra; the controller assigns a unique port automatically to each Ingress resource.

The ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation, because the port must be unique per Ingress resource and the annotation is mandatory in dedicated mode when multiple Ingress resources are deployed.
The ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode annotation set to shared, so that all Ingress resources reuse one port.
A NodePort Service per Ingress resource, because host network mode is disabled in dedicated mode.

explanation: In dedicated mode, or when an Ingress sets ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed, the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation is mandatory because the port must be unique per Ingress resource.

optionRationale.a: No automatic assignment is described; the annotation is mandatory in this situation.
optionRationale.c: Setting the mode to shared contradicts the dedicated configuration and does not satisfy the requirement.
optionRationale.d: Host network mode is not disabled in dedicated mode, and no NodePort Service per Ingress is described.

stem: A cluster uses Istio in sidecar mode with automatic sidecar injection, and Cilium in overlay mode using VXLAN. What must be true of the istiod pods so that they are reachable by the API server?

options.text: The istiod pods must be running with hostNetwork: true.
The istiod pods must be annotated with ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled.
The istiod pods must have mtls.mode=DISABLE set in a PeerAuthentication resource.
The istiod pods must be removed from the istio.io/dataplane-mode namespace label.

explanation: When Istio sidecar mode with automatic sidecar injection is used together with Cilium overlay mode (VXLAN or GENEVE), istiod pods must be running with hostNetwork: true in order to be reachable by the API server.

optionRationale.b: The ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled annotation is used in ambient mode to remove pods from Istio ambient, not to make istiod reachable by the API server.
optionRationale.c: mtls.mode=DISABLE under PeerAuthentication is used to disable Istio mTLS for workloads managed by Cilium L7 policy, not to make istiod reachable.
optionRationale.d: The istio.io/dataplane-mode label relates to Istio ambient mode, not to sidecar mode with Cilium overlay mode.

stem: When Istio L7 HTTP policy controls are used with Cilium and Istio deployed together, which statement is correct?

options.text: Policy is managed in Istio, and disabling mTLS between workloads is not required.
Policy is managed in Cilium, and mTLS must be disabled between workloads.
Policy is managed in both Cilium and Istio, and mTLS must be disabled between workloads.
Policy is managed in Istio, and mTLS must be disabled between workloads.

explanation: If Istio L7 HTTP policy controls are used, policy is managed in Istio and disabling mTLS between workloads is not required.

optionRationale.b: With Istio L7 HTTP policy controls, policy is managed in Istio, not Cilium, and disabling mTLS is not required.
optionRationale.c: Using both Cilium and Istio L7 HTTP policy controls at the same time is not recommended, and disabling mTLS is not required when Istio manages policy.
optionRationale.d: Disabling mTLS between workloads is not required when Istio L7 HTTP policy controls are used.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote: If using Istio L7 HTTP policy controls, policy will be managed in Istio and disabling mTLS between workloads is not required.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium and Istio together in sidecar mode. They want Cilium to enforce L7 HTTP policy for a set of workloads. What must they do to the Istio configuration for those workloads?

options.text: Set mtls.mode=DISABLE in a PeerAuthentication resource that applies to those workloads.
Set mtls.mode=STRICT in a PeerAuthentication resource that applies to those workloads.
Remove the istio.io/dataplane-mode label from the namespace.
Annotate the pods with ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled.

explanation: In sidecar mode, Cilium L7 HTTP policy can only see traffic that Istio has not encrypted with mTLS. The required step is to disable Istio mTLS for the affected workloads by configuring mtls.mode=DISABLE under Istio's PeerAuthentication.

optionRationale.b: STRICT would enforce mTLS, which is the opposite of what is needed for Cilium to inspect L7 traffic.
optionRationale.c: Removing the istio.io/dataplane-mode label is the ambient-mode step, not the sidecar-mode step.
optionRationale.d: The ambient.istio.io/redirection annotation is used in ambient mode, not sidecar mode.

stem: Cilium and Istio are deployed together in ambient mode. An engineer wants Cilium to enforce L7 HTTP policy for a particular workload that is currently part of the Istio ambient mesh. Which action removes that workload from Istio ambient so that Cilium can enforce L7 policy?

options.text: Annotate the pod with ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled.
Set mtls.mode=DISABLE in a PeerAuthentication resource for the workload.
Run istiod with hostNetwork: true.
Enable Istio L7 HTTP policy controls for the workload.

explanation: In ambient mode, a workload is removed from Istio ambient either by removing the istio.io/dataplane-mode label from the namespace or by annotating the pod with ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled. The annotation is one of the two permitted ways.

optionRationale.b: mtls.mode=DISABLE under PeerAuthentication is the sidecar-mode step, not the ambient-mode step.
optionRationale.c: hostNetwork: true on istiod is required for API server reachability with Cilium overlay mode, not for removing a workload from ambient.
optionRationale.d: Enabling Istio L7 policy controls would put policy management in Istio, which is the opposite of what is wanted here.

citations.title: Istio configuration
