stem: In a deployment where Istio ambient mode uses mTLS together with Istio L7 HTTP policy controls, how does Cilium NetworkPolicy apply to traffic between the Istio-managed, mTLS-secured workloads?

options.text: Cilium enforces L7 policy on the decrypted HTTP requests inside the tunnel.
Cilium NetworkPolicy applies to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic, but Cilium has no visibility into the actual source and destination or any L7 information.
Cilium NetworkPolicy does not apply at all because the traffic is encrypted.
Cilium enforces policy only on traffic entering from non-Istio-managed workloads.

explanation: When Istio mTLS is used in ambient mode with Istio L7 policy controls, traffic between ambient workloads is encrypted and tunnelled by Istio over port 15008. Cilium NetworkPolicy still applies to that encrypted and tunnelled L4 traffic, but Cilium cannot see the real source and destination or any L7 details.

optionRationale.a: Cilium has no visibility into L7 information for this tunnelled and encrypted traffic.
optionRationale.c: Cilium NetworkPolicy still applies to the encrypted and tunnelled L4 traffic; it is not bypassed entirely.
optionRationale.d: Traffic from non-Istio-managed workloads is a separate case; the question asks about traffic between Istio-managed workloads.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote:
Cilium NetworkPolicy will still apply to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic entering and leaving the Istio-managed pods,
  but Cilium will have no visibility into the actual source and destination of that tunneled and encrypted L4 traffic, or any L7 information.

stem: A team is deciding where to manage L7 HTTP policy for workloads that are part of an Istio mesh. They want to use Istio L7 HTTP policy controls rather than Cilium's. What does this choice require regarding mTLS between the workloads?

options.text: mTLS must be disabled between the workloads.
mTLS must be set to STRICT in a PeerAuthentication resource.
Disabling mTLS between the workloads is not required.
The workloads must be removed from Istio ambient mode.

explanation: If Istio L7 HTTP policy controls are used, policy is managed in Istio and disabling mTLS between workloads is not required. The mTLS-disabling step applies only when Cilium L7 policy is used.

optionRationale.a: Disabling mTLS is the requirement for using Cilium L7 policy, not Istio L7 policy.
optionRationale.b: The text does not require STRICT mTLS for this choice; it says disabling mTLS is not required.
optionRationale.d: Removing workloads from ambient is the step for using Cilium L7 policy in ambient mode, not for using Istio L7 policy.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote: If using Istio L7 HTTP policy controls, policy will be managed in Istio and disabling mTLS between workloads is not required.

stem: An engineer is deploying Cilium in overlay mode using VXLAN together with Istio in sidecar mode and automatic sidecar injection. What must be true of the istiod pods so that they are reachable by the API server?

options.text: They must run with hostNetwork: true.
They must be annotated with ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled.
They must have mtls.mode=DISABLE set in a PeerAuthentication resource.
They must be labelled with istio.io/dataplane-mode.

explanation: With Istio sidecar mode and automatic sidecar injection combined with Cilium overlay mode (VXLAN or GENEVE), istiod pods must run with hostNetwork: true in order to be reachable by the API server.

optionRationale.b: The ambient.istio.io/redirection annotation is for removing pods from Istio ambient, not for making istiod reachable.
optionRationale.c: mtls.mode=DISABLE is the step for using Cilium L7 policy in sidecar mode, not a requirement for istiod reachability.
optionRationale.d: The istio.io/dataplane-mode label relates to ambient mode membership, not to istiod reachability.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote: together with Cilium overlay mode (VXLAN or GENEVE), ``istiod`` pods must be running with ``hostNetwork: true`` in order to be reachable by the API server.

stem: Why is it not recommended to use both Cilium and Istio L7 HTTP policy controls at the same time?

options.text: Because Istio would encrypt all traffic over port 15008.
To avoid split-brain problems.
Because Cilium cannot enforce L4 policy when Istio is present.
Because istiod would not be reachable by the API server.

explanation: The guidance is that either Cilium or Istio L7 HTTP policy controls can be used, but using both at the same time is not recommended in order to avoid split-brain problems.

optionRationale.a: Port 15008 tunnelling is a specific ambient mTLS behaviour, not the stated reason for avoiding dual L7 policy control.
optionRationale.c: Cilium NetworkPolicy still applies to L4 traffic in the relevant scenarios; the stated reason is split-brain.
optionRationale.d: istiod reachability concerns hostNetwork with overlay mode, not the reason for avoiding dual L7 policy control.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote:
Either Cilium or Istio L7 HTTP policy controls can be used, but it is not recommended to use **both** Cilium and Istio L7 HTTP policy
  controls at the same time, to avoid split-brain problems.

stem: An engineer deploys the Cloud City demo and runs `kubectl get pods,svc` to check progress. Which pair of pods does the output show, and what label does the pod running the gRPC door manager service carry?

options.text: `cc-door-mgr` with label `app=cc-door-mgr`, and `terminal-87` with label `app=public-terminal`.
`cc-door-server` with label `app=cc-door-server`, and `terminal-87` with label `app=public-terminal`.
`cc-door-mgr` with label `app=door-manager`, and `terminal-87` with label `app=terminal`.
`cc-door-mgr` with label `app=cc-door-mgr`, and `terminal-87` with label `app=cc-door-mgr`.

explanation: The demo launches two pods: `cc-door-mgr`, a single pod running the gRPC door manager service with label `app=cc-door-mgr`, and `terminal-87`, the public network access terminal, which uses the gRPC client code to communicate with the door management services and carries the label `app=public-terminal`.

optionRationale.b: `cc-door-server` is the name of the Kubernetes Service, not the door manager pod, and no such label is given for it.
optionRationale.c: The labels are `app=cc-door-mgr` and `app=public-terminal`; neither `app=door-manager` nor `app=terminal` appears.
optionRationale.d: The terminal pod is labelled `app=public-terminal`, not `app=cc-door-mgr`; the two pods carry different labels.

citations.title: Deploy the Demo Application
citations.quote: - **cc-door-mgr**: A single pod running the gRPC door manager service with label ``app=cc-door-mgr``.

stem: A team is deploying the Cloud City gRPC demo. They want to confirm that the deployment has finished and the setup is ready before applying any security policy. What does the material say about how to track progress and when the setup is ready?

options.text: Run `kubectl get svc,pods`; each pod passes through several states until it reaches `Running`, at which point the setup is ready.
Run `kubectl describe deployment`; the setup is ready as soon as the Deployment reports `Available`.
Run `kubectl get svc,pods`; the setup is ready as soon as the Service `cc-door-server` has a ClusterIP assigned.
Run `kubectl logs` against `terminal-87`; the setup is ready when the terminal prints the door access code.

explanation: Kubernetes deploys the pods and service in the background, and running `kubectl get svc,pods` informs you about the progress of the operation. Each pod goes through several states until it reaches `Running`, at which point the setup is ready.

optionRationale.b: The material names `kubectl get svc,pods` as the way to check progress, not `kubectl describe deployment`, and readiness is tied to pods reaching `Running`.
optionRationale.c: A ClusterIP being assigned is not the stated readiness condition; readiness is when each pod reaches `Running`.
optionRationale.d: No such log check or access-code output is described; the stated method is `kubectl get svc,pods`.

citations.title: Deploy the Demo Application
citations.quote:
Running
``kubectl get svc,pods`` will inform you about the progress of the operation.
Each pod will go through several states until it reaches ``Running`` at which
point the setup is ready.

explanation: The service listing shows `svc/cc-door-server` with ClusterIP `10.0.0.72` and `PORT(S)` of `50051/TCP`.

stem: An engineer needs to know which gRPC call on the Cloud City `DoorManager` service is used to set an access code that opens or locks a door. Which RPC is defined for that purpose?

options.text: `SetAccessCode(DoorAccessCodeRequest) returns (DoorActionReply)`
`RequestMaintenance(DoorMaintRequest) returns (DoorActionReply)`
`GetStatus(DoorRequest) returns (DoorStatusReply)`
`GetName(DoorRequest) returns (DoorNameReply)`

explanation: The `DoorManager` service definition includes `SetAccessCode`, commented as setting the access code to open or lock the door, taking a `DoorAccessCodeRequest` and returning a `DoorActionReply`.

optionRationale.b: `RequestMaintenance` is for requesting maintenance on the door, not for setting an access code.
optionRationale.c: `GetStatus` only finds out whether the door is open or closed; it does not set anything.
optionRationale.d: `GetName` returns the human readable name of the door, which is unrelated to access codes.

stem: A toFQDNs rule uses the matchPattern value *.cilium.io. Which domain name does this pattern match?

options.text: sub.cilium.io
cilium.io
sub.sub.cilium.io
app.cilium.io.example.com

explanation: A single asterisk within a domain allows zero or more valid DNS characters except the dot separator. Therefore *.cilium.io matches sub.cilium.io but not cilium.io or sub.sub.cilium.io.

optionRationale.b: The pattern *.cilium.io does not match cilium.io because the asterisk does not cover the absence of a subdomain label before the dot.
optionRationale.c: The pattern *.cilium.io does not match sub.sub.cilium.io because the asterisk does not cross the dot separator.
optionRationale.d: The pattern *.cilium.io matches names ending in .cilium.io, not names that merely contain cilium.io followed by further labels.

citations.title: DNS based
citations.quote:
``*.cilium.io`` will match ``sub.cilium.io`` but not
    ``cilium.io`` or ``sub.sub.cilium.io``.

stem: A toFQDNs rule uses the matchPattern value **.cilium.io. Which domain name does this pattern match?

options.text: test.app.cilium.io
cilium.io
cilium.io.test
app.cilium.com

explanation: The **. prefix is a special wildcard that matches all cascaded subdomains in the prefix. Therefore **.cilium.io matches both app.cilium.io and test.app.cilium.io, but not cilium.io itself.

optionRationale.b: The **.cilium.io pattern does not match cilium.io, because the wildcard covers subdomains only.
optionRationale.c: The pattern is anchored to the cilium.io suffix, so a name with cilium.io as a leading label does not match.
optionRationale.d: The pattern requires the cilium.io suffix, so a name ending in cilium.com does not match.

citations.title: DNS based
citations.quote:
``**.cilium.io`` pattern will match both
    ``app.cilium.io`` and ``test.app.cilium.io`` but not ``cilium.io``.

stem: An engineer is preparing a kind cluster to test the standalone DNS proxy. They have already built the standalone DNS proxy image locally and created the kind cluster with Cilium installed from source. They now need to make the locally built image available inside the kind cluster. Which command should they run?

options.text: kind load docker-image quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest
make docker-standalone-dns-proxy-image
kubectl rollout restart ds -n kube-system cilium
cilium upgrade --chart-directory='./install/kubernetes/cilium' --set='l7Proxy=true'

explanation: The step for loading the standalone DNS proxy image into kind uses `kind load docker-image quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest`. The image must first be built with `make docker-standalone-dns-proxy-image`, but that command builds the image rather than loading it into the kind cluster.

optionRationale.b: This command builds the standalone DNS proxy container image from source; it does not load the image into the kind cluster.
optionRationale.c: This command restarts the Cilium agent DaemonSet to apply configuration changes; it does not load an image into kind.
optionRationale.d: This command upgrades Cilium with Helm settings to enable the standalone DNS proxy; it does not load a locally built image into the kind cluster.

citations.quote: Load the standalone DNS proxy image you built into the kind cluster:

stem: When upgrading Cilium to enable the standalone DNS proxy, which Helm value sets the DNS proxy port used by both the Cilium agent and the standalone DNS proxy?

options.text: dnsProxy.proxyPort=10094
l7Proxy=true
standaloneDnsProxy.enabled=true
standaloneDnsProxy.image.pullPolicy=Never

explanation: The excerpt states that `dnsProxy.proxyPort=10094` sets the DNS proxy port used by both the agent and standalone DNS proxy.

optionRationale.b: `l7Proxy=true` enables L7 proxy support required for DNS policy enforcement, not the DNS proxy port.
optionRationale.c: `standaloneDnsProxy.enabled=true` enables the standalone DNS proxy but does not set the port.
optionRationale.d: `standaloneDnsProxy.image.pullPolicy=Never` is used to reference the locally-built image, not to set the DNS proxy port.

citations.quote: ``dnsProxy.proxyPort=10094`` sets the DNS proxy port used by both the agent and standalone DNS proxy

stem: A test pod labelled `org=alliance` is running in a cluster where the standalone DNS proxy is enabled and a DNS policy allows queries to `cilium.io` and its subdomains while blocking all other queries. An engineer runs `kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup example.com.` and receives a response indicating the server can't find `example.com: REFUSED`. Why is the query refused?

options.text: Because `example.com` is not in the allowed DNS policy rules.
Because the standalone DNS proxy is not running.
Because the test pod does not have the label `org=alliance`.
Because the Cilium agent is down.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the query to `example.com` is refused because it is not in the allowed DNS policy rules. The policy allows only `cilium.io` and its subdomains.

optionRationale.b: The scenario states the standalone DNS proxy is enabled; the refusal is due to policy, not the proxy being down.
optionRationale.c: The test pod is described as labelled `org=alliance`, which matches the policy selector.
optionRationale.d: The Cilium agent being down is not mentioned in this scenario; the refusal is due to the DNS policy rules.

citations.title: Building and Deploying
citations.quote: The query to ``example.com`` is refused because it's not in the allowed DNS policy rules.

stem: A Cilium cluster uses transparent encryption. A pod is permitted to initiate traffic to destinations outside the cluster. A new Cilium-managed endpoint is created on a remote node, but the local node has not yet learned that the endpoint's IP address belongs to that remote node. What happens to packets the pod sends to that IP address during this window?

options.text: Cilium sends the initial packets unencrypted because it must assume the destination IP is outside the cluster.
Cilium drops the packets until the endpoint information has propagated.
Cilium encrypts the packets using the local node's encryption key.
Cilium encrypts the packets using the remote node's encryption key as soon as the endpoint is created.

explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether a destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that a particular IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or newly joined remote Cilium host, it has to assume the destination is outside the cluster and will send the initial packets unencrypted. Only once the information has propagated and Cilium knows the IP is an endpoint on a remote node does it start encrypting using the remote node's key.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes a time window during which packets are sent unencrypted, not dropped.
optionRationale.c: Encryption, once it begins, uses the encryption key of the remote node, not the local node.
optionRationale.d: Encryption with the remote node's key starts only after the endpoint information has propagated, not immediately on endpoint creation.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
In such a case there is a time window during which Cilium will send out the
initial packets unencrypted, as it has to assume the destination IP address is
outside of the cluster.

stem: An engineer wants to prevent a pod from sending unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster, without enabling encryption strict mode. Which approach is described as a workaround?

options.text: Define an egress policy that either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities, or only allows egress to a subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.
Set encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled to true so that all cluster-internal ingress traffic must arrive through the WireGuard tunnel.
Set encryption.strictMode.egress.allowRemoteNodeIdentities to true to permit unencrypted traffic to node identities.
Switch to direct routing mode so that the node CIDR and pod CIDR do not overlap.

explanation: The excerpt states that one workaround is to ensure the endpoint is not allowed to send unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster. This can be achieved by defining an egress policy which either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities, or only allows egress traffic to addresses outside the cluster to a certain subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.

optionRationale.b: Strict mode ingress concerns cluster-internal ingress traffic arriving at local endpoints, not egress to arbitrary external targets.
optionRationale.c: Setting allowRemoteNodeIdentities to true allows unencrypted traffic to node identities; it does not restrict egress to arbitrary external targets.
optionRationale.d: Direct routing mode with non-overlapping node and pod CIDRs is a requirement for disabling dynamic lookups in strict mode egress, not a workaround for unencrypted egress to arbitrary targets.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
One workaround for this issue is to ensure that the endpoint is not allowed to
send unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside of the cluster.

stem: An engineer enables encryption strict mode egress by setting encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and configuring the expected pod CIDR as encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr. Which statement about the limitations of this mode is correct?

options.text: The pod CIDR and therefore the strict mode egress CIDR must be IPv4; IPv6 traffic is not protected and can be leaked.
The pod CIDR must be IPv6, because IPv4 traffic is not protected by strict mode egress.
Strict mode egress requires IPsec encryption and is not supported with WireGuard.
Strict mode egress is supported only when Cilium is chained on top of another CNI plugin.

explanation: The excerpt lists as a limitation that the pod CIDR and therefore the encryption strict mode egress CIDR must be IPv4, and that IPv6 traffic is not protected by the strict mode and can be leaked.

optionRationale.b: The requirement is the opposite: the CIDR must be IPv4, and IPv6 is the unprotected case.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not state that strict mode egress requires IPsec; the IPsec restriction is mentioned for strict mode ingress.
optionRationale.d: Chaining on top of other CNI plugins is mentioned as a limitation of strict mode ingress, not egress.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
The pod CIDR and therefore the encryption strict mode egress CIDR must be
  IPv4. IPv6 traffic is not protected by the strict mode and can be leaked.

stem: A cluster uses encryption strict mode ingress. Which limitation applies to this mode?

options.text: Node-to-node encryption for WireGuard is not protected by strict mode ingress; enforcement only applies to cluster-internal pod traffic destined for local endpoints.
Strict mode ingress protects node-to-node WireGuard encryption but not cluster-internal pod traffic.
Strict mode ingress is supported only with IPsec and not with WireGuard.
Strict mode ingress requires the pod CIDR to be IPv4 and leaks IPv6 traffic.

explanation: The excerpt states that node-to-node encryption for WireGuard is not protected by strict mode ingress, and that enforcement only applies to cluster-internal pod traffic destined for local endpoints.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the limitation: node-to-node WireGuard encryption is the unprotected case, while cluster-internal pod traffic to local endpoints is enforced.
optionRationale.c: Strict mode ingress requires WireGuard encryption and is not supported with IPsec, the opposite of this option.
optionRationale.d: The IPv4 requirement and IPv6 leak are limitations of strict mode egress, not strict mode ingress.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
Node-to-node encryption for wireguard is not protected by strict mode 
  ingress. Enforcement only applies to cluster-internal pod traffic destined
  for local endpoints.

stem: A network security team wants Cilium to inspect TLS-encrypted traffic destined for an external service. They generate an internal CA private key and CA certificate, then create a private key and certificate signing request for the destination, and use the CA private key to sign the certificate. What must also be done so that client workloads accept the inspected connection?

options.text: Install the internal CA certificate on each client workload so that they trust certificates signed by that CA.
Provide the internal CA private key to Cilium so that it can sign certificates on the fly.
Configure each client workload to trust the destination service's original certificate instead of the internal CA.
Disable TLS verification on the client workloads for the destination service.

explanation: In the friendly interception model, the network security team creates an internal certificate authority and uses it to create alternative certificates for external destinations. For clients to accept these certificates, each client workload must trust the new certificate authority; otherwise the client's TLS library will reject the connection as invalid. The excerpt states: 'This model requires each client workload to also trust this new certificate, otherwise the client's TLS library will reject the connection as invalid.' Therefore, the CA certificate must be installed on the clients.

optionRationale.b: The CA private key is used only to create certificates, which can be done offline; it does not need to be provided to Cilium.
optionRationale.c: The client must trust the internal CA, not the destination's original certificate, because Cilium presents a certificate signed by the internal CA.
optionRationale.d: Disabling TLS verification is not mentioned and would undermine the authentication that TLS provides.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model
citations.quote: This model requires each client workload to also trust this new certificate, otherwise the client's TLS library will reject the connection as invalid.

stem: In a Cilium TLS inspection setup, which statement best describes the role of the internal certificate authority?

options.text: It is an entity trusted to create proof that a given network service is who it claims to be, and it signs certificates for external destinations so that Cilium can act as those destinations.
It is a public certificate authority that automatically issues certificates for any destination without additional configuration.
It is a component that stores private keys for individual destination services as Kubernetes secrets.
It is a mechanism that encrypts all traffic between Cilium and the destination service without terminating TLS.

explanation: The excerpt defines a Certificate Authority as 'an entity that is trusted to create proof that a given network service (e.g., www.cilium.io) is who they say they are.' In the friendly interception model, the network security team creates their own internal certificate authority to create alternative certificates for external destinations. Cilium then uses a certificate signed by this internal CA to act like the destination service and terminate the TLS connection.

optionRationale.b: The internal CA is created by the network security team, not a public authority, and it is used for specific destinations where inspection is desired.
optionRationale.c: Private keys for individual destination services are stored as Kubernetes secrets, but that is separate from the CA's role.
optionRationale.d: Cilium terminates the TLS connection and initiates a new one; it does not merely encrypt traffic without termination.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model
citations.quote: the network security team creates their own "internal certificate authority" that can be used to create alternative certificates for external destinations.

stem: When configuring Cilium for TLS inspection, what must be provided to Cilium regarding certificate authorities?

options.text: The set of CAs that Cilium should trust when validating the new TLS connection to the destination service.
The private key of the internal CA so that Cilium can generate certificates on demand.
The private keys for all client workloads so that Cilium can impersonate them.
The public key of the destination service so that Cilium can verify its identity.

explanation: Because Cilium terminates the initial TLS connection from the client and creates a new TLS connection to the destination, it must be told which certificate authorities to trust when validating that new connection. The excerpt states: 'Cilium must be told the set of CAs that it should trust when validating the new TLS connection to the destination service.'

optionRationale.b: The CA private key does not need to be provided to Cilium at all; it is used only to create certificates, which can be done offline.
optionRationale.c: Client private keys are not mentioned as being provided to Cilium.
optionRationale.d: The destination's public key is not what Cilium needs; it needs the set of trusted CAs.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model
citations.quote: Cilium must be told the set of CAs that it should trust when validating the new TLS connection to the destination service.

stem: How does the TLS inspection model used by Cilium for network security monitoring differ from the standard TLS authentication model?

options.text: In the standard model, a trusted certificate authority proves the identity of the destination service; in the Cilium inspection model, the network security team creates an internal CA to issue alternative certificates for external destinations, which clients must trust.
In the standard model, clients do not verify certificates; in the Cilium inspection model, clients verify certificates against the internal CA.
In the standard model, the destination service signs its own certificates; in the Cilium inspection model, the client signs certificates for the destination.
In the standard model, a public CA is always used; in the Cilium inspection model, the internal CA is optional and only used for logging.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the TLS model relies on a Certificate Authority that is trusted to create proof that a network service is who it claims to be, preventing impostors. For friendly interception, Cilium uses a model similar to traditional firewalls with TLS inspection: the network security team creates their own internal certificate authority to create alternative certificates for external destinations, and each client workload must trust this new certificate. This allows the firewall to act as the destination and inspect traffic.

optionRationale.b: In the standard TLS model, clients do verify certificates; the excerpt states that otherwise the client's TLS library will reject the connection as invalid.
optionRationale.c: In the standard model, a CA signs certificates, not the destination itself; in the Cilium model, the internal CA signs certificates, not the client.
optionRationale.d: The internal CA is not optional for inspection; it is required to create alternative certificates, and it is used for interception, not just logging.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model
citations.quote: In the case of "friendly interception" for network security monitoring, Cilium uses a model similar to traditional firewalls with TLS inspection capabilities:  the network security team creates their own "internal certificate authority" that can be used to create alternative certificates for external destinations.

stem: An Elasticsearch cluster serves two kinds of client: `outpost` clients that only need to upload troop logs, and an `empire-hq` client that only needs search access to both the `troop_logs` and `spaceship_diagnostics` indices. An engineer wants to apply least privilege security to this cluster. Which statement best describes the goal?

options.text: Give each client access only to the particular indices it needs, and limit the operations each client may perform on each index.
Give every client full access to all indices, but log every request so that misuse can be audited later.
Restrict all clients to search operations only, so that no client can create or modify any index.
Give the `outpost` clients access to both indices and the `empire-hq` client access only to `troop_logs`.

explanation: Least privilege for Elasticsearch clusters means granting each client access only to the particular indices it needs and limiting the operations it may perform on each index. The `outpost` clients need only to upload troop logs, while `empire-hq` needs search access to both indices.

optionRationale.b: Full access for all clients is the opposite of least privilege; auditing does not limit what a compromised client can do.
optionRationale.c: Search-only for everyone would prevent the `outpost` clients from uploading troop logs, which they legitimately need to do.
optionRationale.d: This reverses the stated needs: `outpost` needs only troop-log upload, and `empire-hq` needs search access to both indices.

citations.title: Security Risks for Elasticsearch Access
citations.quote: For Elasticsearch clusters the **least privilege security** challenge is to give clients access only to particular indices, and to limit the operations each client is allowed to perform on each index.

stem: In an Elasticsearch deployment, the `outpost` clients are intended only to upload troop logs, and the `empire-hq` client is intended only to search both the `troop_logs` and `spaceship_diagnostics` indices. An engineer notes that the outposts are physically exposed and could be captured. What risk does this create for the Elasticsearch data?

options.text: Once an outpost is compromised, its client can be used to search and manipulate the critical data in Elasticsearch.
A compromised outpost can only read the `troop_logs` index, because upload credentials never permit search.
A compromised outpost can disrupt Elasticsearch only by exhausting storage with repeated uploads of troop logs.
A compromised outpost has no effect on Elasticsearch, because the `empire-hq` client is the only one with search access.

explanation: The outposts are described as weak spots that are susceptible to capture. Once compromised, the clients can be used to search and manipulate the critical data in Elasticsearch, which is exactly what the simulated attack demonstrates.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that a compromised client can search and manipulate critical data; it does not limit the compromise to reading troop logs.
optionRationale.c: Storage exhaustion is not mentioned; the stated risk is searching and manipulating critical data.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says a compromised outpost client can be used to search and manipulate critical data, so it does affect Elasticsearch.

citations.title: Security Risks for Elasticsearch Access
citations.quote: From the security perspective, the outposts are weak spots and susceptible to be captured by the rebels. Once compromised, the clients can be used to search and manipulate the critical data in Elasticsearch.

stem: Rebels have captured an `outpost` client. Running `kubectl exec outpost -- python search.py`, they retrieve hits from both the `spaceship_diagnostics` index and the `troop_logs` index. They then run `kubectl exec outpost -- python update.py`, which reports uploading spaceship diagnostics with `stats` set to `[OK] [ENGINE OK @SPEED 5000 km/s]`. What has the compromised outpost achieved?

options.text: It has searched all the indices and manipulated the diagnostics data, changing the `stats` for the tiefighter spaceship.
It has only read data, because the `update.py` script failed to modify the diagnostics.
It has modified the `troop_logs` index, leaving the spaceship diagnostics untouched.
It has changed the `spaceshipid` of the tiefighter, so the diagnostics now belong to a different spaceship.

explanation: The excerpt describes the rebels first searching all the indices and then manipulating the diagnostics data from a compromised outpost. The `update.py` run changes the `stats` for the tiefighter spaceship, a change that is hard to detect but has adverse impact.

optionRationale.b: The `update.py` output shows the diagnostics being uploaded with altered `stats`, so the data was modified, not merely read.
optionRationale.c: The manipulation targets `spaceship_diagnostics`, not `troop_logs`.
optionRationale.d: The `spaceshipid` remains `3459B78XNZTF`; what changes is the `stats` field.

citations.quote: In the commands below, the rebels first search all the indices and then manipulate the diagnostics data from a compromised outpost.

stem: An engineer applies a manifest that creates a Deployment for each of three microservices and a Service named deathstar. The Service is intended to load-balance traffic to the deathstar pods across two replicas. Which label selector must the deathstar Service use for this to work?

options.text: org=empire, class=deathstar
org=empire, class=tiefighter
org=alliance, class=xwing
k8s-app=kube-dns

explanation: The deathstar Deployment is identified with the labels (org=empire, class=deathstar), and the deathstar-service load-balances traffic to all pods carrying that label pair. The other label pairs belong to the tiefighter and xwing deployments, and k8s-app=kube-dns is the label shown on the DNS endpoints, not on the deathstar pods.

optionRationale.b: org=empire, class=tiefighter identifies the tiefighter landing-request client, not the deathstar webservice pods.
optionRationale.c: org=alliance, class=xwing identifies the alliance ship's client service, not the deathstar pods.
optionRationale.d: k8s-app=kube-dns appears on the coredns endpoints in the endpoint list, not on the deathstar pods.

stem: A single-node cluster has Cilium installed and kube-dns working. An engineer deploys the demo application and then runs `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg endpoint list`. What will the output show?

options.text: All endpoints in the cluster, because the command targets the Cilium DaemonSet and this is a single-node installation.
Only the endpoints running on the same node as the selected Cilium pod, because endpoint listing is always node-local.
Only the deathstar endpoints, because the demo application is the most recently deployed workload.
No endpoints, because endpoint listing requires a multi-node installation.

explanation: The excerpt states that in a single-node installation the command `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg endpoint list` lists them all, whereas in a multi-node installation only the endpoints on the same node are listed. Since the scenario is a single-node cluster, every endpoint is shown.

optionRationale.b: Node-local listing is the behaviour described for a multi-node installation, not a single-node one.
optionRationale.c: The command lists endpoints generally; nothing in the excerpt restricts output to the most recently deployed workload.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the command as listing all endpoints in a single-node installation, so it does not require multiple nodes.

tiefighter

The tiefighter and xwing are landing-request client services, and kube-dns is the DNS component that must be operating correctly before deployment.

optionRationale.b: tiefighter represents a landing-request client service on a typical empire ship, not the port 80 webservice.
optionRationale.c: xwing represents a similar client service on an alliance ship, not the port 80 webservice.

stem: An engineer wants to restrict which gRPC methods a set of pods can invoke on a service. How is each gRPC method mapped to an HTTP request so that a Cilium HTTP-aware filter can be applied?

options.text: Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.
Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP GET call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.
Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /<method-name>/cloudcity.DoorManager.
Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP PUT call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.

explanation: Since gRPC is built on top of HTTP, each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>, which allows a Cilium HTTP-aware filter to permit only a subset of methods.

optionRationale.b: gRPC methods are mapped to POST calls, not GET calls.
optionRationale.c: The URL form places the service name before the method name: /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.
optionRationale.d: gRPC methods are mapped to POST calls, not PUT calls.

``/cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>``.

stem: How does Cilium's response to a denied gRPC request differ from that of a traditional firewall?

options.text: Cilium operates at the API layer and can explicitly reply with a custom gRPC status code 7 PERMISSION_DENIED, whereas a traditional firewall would drop packets indistinguishably from a network failure.
Cilium drops packets silently, whereas a traditional firewall returns a gRPC status code.
Cilium returns an HTTP 403 Forbidden response, whereas a traditional firewall returns a TCP reset.
Cilium logs the denied request but allows it through, whereas a traditional firewall blocks it.

explanation: Because Cilium operates at the API layer, it can explicitly reply with a custom gRPC status code 7 PERMISSION_DENIED, indicating that the request was intentionally denied for security reasons, unlike a traditional firewall which would just drop packets in a way indistinguishable from a network failure.

optionRationale.b: The roles are reversed: Cilium replies with a gRPC status code, while a traditional firewall drops packets.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt mentions gRPC status code 7 PERMISSION_DENIED, not HTTP 403 Forbidden.
optionRationale.d: Cilium denies the request; it does not allow it through.

citations.title: Securing Access to a gRPC Service with Cilium
citations.quote:
unlike
a traditional firewall which would just drop packets in a way indistinguishable
from a network failure, because Cilium operates at the API-layer, it can
explicitly reply with a custom gRPC status code 7 PERMISSION_DENIED

stem: An engineer is troubleshooting an Ingress resource in a Cilium cluster. They SSH to a Kubernetes node and send a request to the NodePort that the LoadBalancer service forwards to. The response includes the header `server: envoy` and a 503 status. What does this indicate about the request path?

options.text: The request is being redirected to the Cilium Envoy proxy successfully.
The request never reached the node port and was dropped by the cloud load balancer.
The Cilium Envoy proxy is not running on the node, so the request was handled by the backend service directly.
The request bypassed the proxy and was forwarded directly to the backend service, which returned 503.

explanation: The presence of the `server: envoy` header in the HTTP response shows that the request was successfully redirected to the Cilium Envoy proxy. A 503 from Envoy still confirms the proxy handled the request; the next step is to check backend health and CEC provisioning.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that the first step, from cloud LoadBalancer to node port, is out of Cilium scope, but a response with `server: envoy` proves the request reached the proxy, so it did reach the node port.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt lists a missing Envoy proxy as a common root cause, but if the proxy were not running, the response would not carry the `server: envoy` header.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the request gets forwarded to the Cilium Envoy proxy and then proxied to the backend; a direct backend response would not include `server: envoy`.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If you see a response similar to the above, it means that the request is being
redirected to proxy successfully. The http response will have one special header
``server: envoy`` accordingly.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium on a cluster whose nodes are protected by a firewall that blocks all ICMP traffic and all TCP traffic on port 4240 between nodes. No other health-related rules are configured. What is the effect on the cluster?

options.text: Cilium continues to operate, but it cannot provide health information about the nodes.
Cilium fails to start on the nodes until ICMP Type 0/8, Code 0 is permitted.
Cilium continues to operate and health monitoring falls back to UDP port 8472.
Cilium continues to operate but pod-to-pod traffic is blocked until port 4240 is opened.

explanation: Health monitoring via ICMP and TCP 4240 is recommended but optional. If the firewall permits neither method, Cilium still operates, but health information is unavailable.

optionRationale.b: Cilium does not require these rules to start; they are recommended but optional.
optionRationale.c: UDP 8472 is the VXLAN overlay port, not a fallback for health monitoring.
optionRationale.d: Port 4240 is for cilium-health monitoring, not for pod-to-pod traffic forwarding.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote: If the firewall does not permit either of these methods, Cilium will still operate fine but will not be able to provide health information.

stem: An engineer deploys Cilium with WireGuard encryption on nodes behind a restrictive firewall. Which port must the firewall allow for the WireGuard tunnel endpoint?

options.text: UDP 8472
TCP 4240
UDP 6081

explanation: When WireGuard is in use, UDP port 51871 must be allowed.

optionRationale.b: UDP 8472 is the default VXLAN overlay port, not the WireGuard port.
optionRationale.c: TCP 4240 is used for cilium-health monitoring.
optionRationale.d: UDP 6081 is the Geneve overlay port.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote: If you are using WireGuard, you must allow UDP port 51871.

stem: A cluster uses Cilium in VXLAN overlay network mode on Linux hosts that have not been reconfigured from the default. Which UDP port must be open among all nodes to enable the overlay?

options.text: UDP 8472
UDP 6081
TCP 4240

explanation: In VXLAN overlay mode, Cilium uses Linux's default VXLAN port 8472 over UDP unless Linux has been configured otherwise, and that port must be open among all nodes.

optionRationale.b: UDP 6081 is the port used by Geneve overlay mode, not VXLAN.
optionRationale.c: UDP 51871 is the WireGuard encryption tunnel endpoint.
optionRationale.d: TCP 4240 is for cilium-health monitoring, not the overlay.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote: If you are using VXLAN overlay network mode, Cilium uses Linux's default VXLAN port 8472 over UDP, unless Linux has been configured otherwise.

stem: A team runs Cilium with IPsec enabled on AWS, where Security Groups do not allow ESP traffic by default. What must be done for the deployment to work?

options.text: Ensure the firewall allows ESP traffic through.
Open UDP port 51871 between all nodes.
Open UDP port 8472 between all nodes.
Open TCP port 4240 between all nodes.

explanation: For IPsec-enabled deployments, ESP traffic must be permitted by the firewall; AWS Security Groups do not allow it by default.

optionRationale.c: UDP 8472 is the VXLAN overlay port, not the IPsec requirement.
optionRationale.d: TCP 4240 is for cilium-health monitoring.

citations.quote: For IPsec enabled Cilium deployments, you need to ensure that the firewall allows ESP traffic through.

stem: A node has 8 vCPUs and 30 GiB of memory. Cilium is started with `--bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio: 0.0025`. What is the resulting size of Cilium's connection tracking BPF maps on that node?

options.text: 131072 entries
262144 entries
284560 entries
569120 entries

explanation: With `--bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio: 0.0025`, the table shows that on a node with 8 vCPUs and 30 GiB of memory, Cilium sets its connection tracking maps to 284560 entries. The value 262144 is what kube-proxy would set for its own table on the same node, and 131072 is the minimum floor that applies on smaller nodes.

optionRationale.a: 131072 is the minimum number of entries Cilium uses regardless of memory, which applies to the smaller nodes in the table, not to an 8 vCPU / 30 GiB node.
optionRationale.b: 262144 is the kube-proxy connection tracking entry count for an 8 vCPU / 30 GiB node, not the Cilium count.
optionRationale.d: 569120 is the Cilium connection tracking entry count for a 16 vCPU / 60 GiB node.

stem: An engineer wants to raise the maximum number of entries in Cilium's NAT BPF map on a node. Which `cilium-agent` command line option is provided for this purpose?

options.text: `--bpf-nat-global-max`
`--bpf-ct-global-tcp-max`
`--bpf-lb-map-max`
`--bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio`

explanation: The excerpt lists `--bpf-nat-global-max` among the command line options that can override the upper capacity limit of certain BPF maps, and the NAT map is the one whose limit this option controls. The other options target different maps or set a memory-based ratio rather than a fixed capacity.

optionRationale.b: `--bpf-ct-global-tcp-max` overrides the connection tracking map limit, not the NAT map limit.
optionRationale.c: `--bpf-lb-map-max` overrides the load balancer map limit, not the NAT map limit.
optionRationale.d: `--bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio` sets a ratio of total system memory used to size several large maps at startup; it is not a per-map capacity option for the NAT map.

citations.title: eBPF Maps
citations.quote:
A given capacity can be set using
``--bpf-auth-map-max``, ``--bpf-ct-global-tcp-max``, ``--bpf-ct-global-any-max``,
``--bpf-nat-global-max``, ``--bpf-neigh-global-max``, ``--bpf-policy-map-max``,
``--bpf-fragments-map-max`` and ``--bpf-lb-map-max``.

stem: A cluster is handling a large number of fragmented datagrams. Which statement describes the default capacity limit for fragmentation maps in Cilium?

options.text: The IPv4 and IPv6 fragmentation maps each default to 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node.
The IPv4 and IPv6 fragmentation maps each default to 16k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node.
The IPv4 fragmentation map defaults to 8k and the IPv6 fragmentation map defaults to 16k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node.
The IPv4 and IPv6 fragmentation maps share a single default limit of 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node.

explanation: The table lists both IPv4 Fragmentation and IPv6 Fragmentation with a default limit of 8k, and the scale implication is a maximum of 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node for each map. The 16k figure belongs to other maps such as the masquerade and egress policy maps.

optionRationale.b: 16k is the default limit for the IPv4 Masq, IPv6 Masq, Egress Policy and Node maps, not the fragmentation maps.
optionRationale.c: Both fragmentation maps have the same default limit of 8k; the excerpt does not give IPv6 a larger default.
optionRationale.d: The table lists the two fragmentation maps separately, each with its own 8k limit, rather than a single shared limit.

citations.title: eBPF Maps
citations.quote:
IPv4 Fragmentation       node             8k                Max 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node
IPv6 Fragmentation       node             8k                Max 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node

stem: A Cilium datapath designer wants a BPF program that inspects packet data at the earliest possible moment after reception, before any other networking-stack processing, so that malicious traffic can be dropped with the best possible performance. Which BPF hook should the program be attached to?

options.text: The XDP hook
The traffic control ingress hook
The socket operations hook
The socket send/recv hook

explanation: XDP sits at the earliest point in the networking driver and runs the program upon packet reception, directly on the packet data before any other processing, which the excerpt describes as the best possible packet processing performance and ideal for filtering programs that drop malicious or unexpected traffic.

optionRationale.b: The tc ingress hook is also attached to a networking interface but runs after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet, so it is not the earliest point.
optionRationale.c: The socket operations hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events, not on packet reception in the driver.
optionRationale.d: The socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket, which is far removed from packet reception.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
The XDP BPF hook is at the earliest point possible in the networking driver
  and triggers a run of the BPF program upon packet reception.

stem: An engineer is choosing between the XDP hook and the traffic control ingress hook for a program that must apply L3/L4 endpoint policy and redirect traffic to endpoints. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two hooks?

options.text: The tc ingress hook runs after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet and has access to most of the metadata associated with a packet, making it ideal for local node processing such as L3/L4 endpoint policy.
The tc ingress hook runs before the networking stack has done any processing of the packet, which is why it is preferred for dropping malicious traffic at the driver.
The XDP hook runs after the L3 layer of the stack and therefore has access to more packet metadata than the tc ingress hook.
The XDP hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events, whereas the tc ingress hook is attached to a networking interface.

explanation: The excerpt states that tc ingress programs are attached to a networking interface, same as XDP, but run after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet, before the L3 layer, with access to most of the packet metadata, which makes the hook ideal for local node processing such as applying L3/L4 endpoint policy and redirecting traffic to endpoints.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the ordering: tc ingress runs after initial processing, not before any processing; running at the driver is the XDP position.
optionRationale.c: XDP is the earliest hook in the driver, not a hook that runs after the L3 layer.
optionRationale.d: The cgroup-attached hook that runs on TCP events is the socket operations hook, not XDP.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
BPF programs attached to the traffic
  control (tc) ingress hook are attached to a networking interface, same as
  XDP, but will run after the networking stack has done initial processing
  of the packet.

stem: Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations program to the root cgroup to monitor TCP state transitions. Which state transition is specifically monitored, and what happens when a socket enters that state?

options.text: The ESTABLISHED transition is monitored, and if the TCP socket has a node local peer a socket send/recv program is attached.
The LISTEN transition is monitored, and a socket send/recv program is detached from the socket.
The ESTABLISHED transition is monitored, and the packet is passed to the Linux xfrm layer for decryption.
The CLOSED transition is monitored, and the socket is redirected to another socket.

explanation: The excerpt says Cilium uses the root-cgroup socket operations program to monitor TCP state transitions, specifically ESTABLISHED, and that when a socket transitions into ESTABLISHED state and has a node local peer (possibly a local proxy) a socket send/recv program is attached.

optionRationale.b: The monitored transition named is ESTABLISHED, and the action described is attaching a program, not detaching one.
optionRationale.c: Passing packets to the Linux xfrm layer belongs to the L3 Encryption object, not the socket operations hook.
optionRationale.d: CLOSED is not the transition named, and redirecting to another socket is a capability of the socket send/recv hook on send operations.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations
  program to the root cgroup and uses this to monitor for TCP state transitions,
  specifically for ESTABLISHED state transitions.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with eBPF-based masquerading enabled. An engineer inspects the node and finds that the eBPF masquerading program is attached to eth0 and eth1. A pod on that node sends a packet to an address outside the cluster, and the packet leaves through a device that does not run the masquerading program. What happens to the packet?

options.text: It is masqueraded to the IPv4 address of the output device, because the program is attached to at least one device on the node.
It is not masqueraded, because masquerading can take place only on devices which run the eBPF masquerading program.
It is masqueraded by falling back to iptables-based masquerading for that device.
It is dropped, because eBPF masquerading requires every output device to run the program.

explanation: The eBPF masquerading program only acts on the devices it is attached to. A packet sent from a pod to an outside address is masqueraded only if the output device runs the program, so a packet leaving through a device without the program is not masqueraded.

optionRationale.a: Attachment to eth0 and eth1 says nothing about a different output device; the program must run on the device the packet actually leaves through.
optionRationale.c: No iptables fallback per device is described; the eBPF implementation is a distinct mode.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says such packets are not masqueraded, not that they are dropped.

citations.title: eBPF-based
citations.quote:
Masquerading can take place only on those devices which run the eBPF
masquerading program.

stem: An engineer enables eBPF-based masquerading with the bpf.masquerade=true helm option and does not set the devices option. Which devices will the eBPF masquerading program be attached to?

options.text: All devices on the node, regardless of any other feature.
Only the device carrying the default route.
The devices selected by the BPF NodePort device detection mechanism.
No devices until the devices option is set explicitly.

explanation: When the devices option is not specified, the program is automatically attached to the devices selected by the BPF NodePort device detection mechanism. The devices helm option exists to change this manually.

optionRationale.a: Attachment is not to every device; it follows the NodePort device detection mechanism unless overridden.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the BPF NodePort device detection mechanism, not the default-route device.
optionRationale.d: Attachment happens automatically; an explicit devices setting is only needed to change it manually.

citations.title: eBPF-based
citations.quote:
If not specified, the program will be automatically
attached to the devices selected by :ref:`the BPF NodePort device detection
mechanism <Nodeport Devices>`.

stem: A platform team enables the eBPF-based ip-masq-agent with ipMasqAgent.enabled=true and supplies a configuration file that sets nonMasqueradeCIDRs but leaves masqLinkLocal unset. Which additional CIDR is appended to the non-masquerade CIDR list?
explanation: For IPv4, if masqLinkLocal is not set or is set to false, 169.254.0.0/16 is appended to the non-masquerade CIDRs list. The IPv6 equivalent, fe80::/10, is appended only when masqLinkLocalIPv6 is not set or false.

optionRationale.b: fe80::/10 is the IPv6 link-local range, appended based on masqLinkLocalIPv6 rather than masqLinkLocal.
optionRationale.c: 10.0.0.0/8 is one of the default non-masquerade CIDRs provisioned when the configuration file is empty, not the appended link-local range.
optionRationale.d: 240.0.0.0/4 is likewise one of the default non-masquerade CIDRs, not the appended link-local range.

citations.title: eBPF-based
citations.quote:
In addition, if the ``masqLinkLocal`` is not set or set to false, then
``169.254.0.0/16`` is appended to the non-masquerade CIDRs list.

stem: An engineer runs a Fortio load test against http://echo-service:8080 with the flags `-c 2 -qps 0 -n 20`. The run completes and the summary reports `Code 200 : 19 (95.0 %)` and `Code 503 : 1 (5.0 %)`. What does the presence of the 503 response indicate?

options.text: A circuit breaker has been triggered.
The Fortio pod could not resolve the Service DNS name.
The echo-service pods are all unhealthy and removed from the Service endpoints.
The load test exceeded the 20-call limit and Fortio rejected the extra request.

explanation: The excerpt states that seeing a 503 response code in the output means a circuit breaker has been triggered. The single 503 among 20 calls is therefore the signal that the breaker tripped.

optionRationale.b: Name resolution succeeded: the output shows the address resolved to 10.96.182.43:8080, so DNS failure is not the cause.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the output indicates endpoint removal; the requests reached the Service and returned a mix of 200 and 503.
optionRationale.d: Fortio ran exactly 20 calls as requested; the 503 is a response code from the Service, not a rejection of an over-limit call.

citations.title: Tripping Envoy Circuit Breaker
citations.quote:
From the above output, you can see that the response code of some requests is 503, 
which triggers a circuit breaker.

stem: An engineer wants Fortio to call http://echo-service:8080 with four concurrent connections and send 20 requests. Which command achieves this?

options.text: kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 4 -qps 0 -n 20 http://echo-service:8080
kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 2 -qps 0 -n 20 http://echo-service:8080
kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 4 -qps 0 -n 4 http://echo-service:8080
kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 20 -qps 0 -n 4 http://echo-service:8080

explanation: The excerpt shows that the `-c` flag sets the number of concurrent connections and the `-n` flag sets the number of requests. Four connections and 20 requests therefore require `-c 4 -qps 0 -n 20`.

optionRationale.b: This uses `-c 2`, which is two concurrent connections, not four.
optionRationale.c: This uses `-n 4`, which sends four requests rather than 20.
optionRationale.d: This swaps the values, using 20 connections and 4 requests.

stem: A Fortio load test is run against http://echo-service:8080 with `-c 2 -qps 0 -n 20`. The output includes the line `Sockets used: 3 (for perfect keepalive, would be 2)`. What does the parenthetical part of this line tell the engineer?

options.text: With perfect keepalive, two sockets would have been used.
With perfect keepalive, three sockets would have been used.
Two sockets were reused and one was closed by the circuit breaker.
The test would have needed two more sockets to avoid the 503 response.

explanation: The line reports that three sockets were used and notes that for perfect keepalive it would be two, so the ideal figure with perfect keepalive is two sockets.

optionRationale.b: Three is the number actually used, not the perfect-keepalive figure.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not attribute socket counts to the circuit breaker closing connections.
optionRationale.d: The parenthetical gives the ideal count as two, not two additional sockets.

citations.title: Tripping Envoy Circuit Breaker
citations.quote: Sockets used: 3 (for perfect keepalive, would be 2)

stem: An engineer needs the name of the Fortio pod stored in an environment variable so that later commands can reference it. Which command does this?

options.text: export FORTIO_POD=$(kubectl get pods -l app=fortio -o 'jsonpath={.items[0].metadata.name}')
export FORTIO_POD=$(kubectl get pods -l app=echo-service -o 'jsonpath={.items[0].metadata.name}')
export FORTIO_POD=$(kubectl get svc -l app=fortio -o 'jsonpath={.items[0].metadata.name}')

stem: An engineer runs a Fortio load test from a pod against http://echo-service:8080 using the flags `-c 2 -qps 0 -n 20`. The run completes and the summary reports `Code 200 : 19 (95.0 %)` and `Code 503 : 1 (5.0 %)`. What does the single 503 response indicate in this run?

options.text: A circuit breaker has been triggered.
The Fortio pod could not resolve the Service name, so one request never left the client.
The load generator exhausted its 20-call budget before the last request was sent.
The connection was reused for all requests, so one socket was reported as an error.

explanation: The run with two concurrent connections produced one 503 among the 20 calls, and a 503 response code is what indicates that a circuit breaker has been triggered. The remaining 19 calls returned 200, so the Service was reachable and the run completed all 20 calls.

optionRationale.b: The output shows the name resolved to 10.96.182.43:8080, so name resolution was not the cause of the 503.
optionRationale.c: The run reports that all 20 calls were made, so the call budget was not exhausted.
optionRationale.d: Socket reuse is reported separately as a connection statistic and is not what a 503 response code signifies.

stem: In a cluster with Istio ambient mode and Cilium, client and server applications are deployed across the red, blue and green namespaces. No Cilium network policies have been applied yet. A connectivity test is run from a client in the green namespace to a server in the blue namespace. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request succeeds with HTTP 200 because Istio is in PERMISSIVE mode by default.
The request fails with HTTP 000 because Cilium blocks traffic between namespaces by default.
The request succeeds with HTTP 200 only if a Cilium L4 policy explicitly allows it.
The request fails with HTTP 403 because Istio ambient mode denies unauthenticated traffic.

explanation: Istio works in PERMISSIVE mode by default, allowing both Istio-ambient-managed and Istio-unmanaged pods to send and receive unsecured traffic. Therefore, without any Cilium policy, the green client can reach the blue server and receives HTTP 200.

optionRationale.b: Cilium does not block traffic by default; the excerpt shows all initial checks succeed.
optionRationale.c: No Cilium L4 policy is required for the initial success; PERMISSIVE mode allows it.
optionRationale.d: HTTP 403 is seen only after an L7 policy is applied and a different URL path is accessed; it is not the default behaviour.

stem: A cluster runs 200 clusterIP Services. On average each Service selects 8 Pod backends and exposes 2 port/protocol entries. Using the sizing heuristic given for Cilium's service LB maps, roughly how many LB map entries are required?

options.text: About 3,200 entries
About 400 entries
About 1,600 entries
About 64,000 entries

explanation: The heuristic multiplies the number of LB services by the average number of endpoints per service and the average number of port/protocols per service: 200 × 8 × 2 = 3,200 entries. The 64k figure is the default map size set by `--bpf-lb-map-max`, not an estimate of the entries this workload needs.

optionRationale.b: This multiplies only the number of services by the average number of ports (200 × 2), omitting the endpoints per service.
optionRationale.c: This multiplies the number of services by the average number of endpoints (200 × 8), omitting the port/protocol factor.
optionRationale.d: This is the default value of the ``--bpf-lb-map-max`` flag, not the result of the sizing heuristic for this workload.

stem: An engineer is planning a Cilium installation and expects the cluster to grow substantially, with some Services selecting very large sets of Pod backends. Which statement about sizing the service LB maps is correct?

options.text: The simple heuristic is sufficient in all cases because endpoint counts per service are always normally distributed.
The heuristic assumes selected Pods and port/protocol entries per service are roughly normally distributed, so large outliers may require a more detailed estimate.
Map size can be safely increased at any time after installation, because Cilium repopulates the new map without affecting connections.
The map size is fixed at 64k entries and cannot be changed by any flag.

explanation: The heuristic is only an approximation: it assumes the number of selected Pods and port/protocol entries per service are roughly normally distributed, and the text notes that use cases with large outliers may need a more detailed estimate. Resizing later is also risky, since changing the map size parameter and restarting Cilium causes connection disruptions while the new map is repopulated.

optionRationale.a: The text explicitly warns that outliers such as a service selecting a very large set of Pod backends may require a more detailed estimate.
optionRationale.c: The text states the opposite: resizing after the maps exist and restarting Cilium results in connection disruptions as the new map is repopulated.
optionRationale.d: The maps are configured via the ``--bpf-lb-map-max`` flag, which is set to 64k by default but is a configurable parameter.

stem: An engineer is preparing a cluster for a Cilium upgrade and wants to confirm that the CiliumNetworkPolicies already deployed will be accepted by the new version. Which action should the engineer take before starting the upgrade?

optionRationale.c: Disabling policy enforcement is not part of the validation procedure and would not establish that the policies are valid.

Delete the Deployment and reinstall Cilium from scratch.

stem: A cluster runs Istio with its default peer authentication behaviour, and some pods in the mesh have no Istio sidecar injected. A client pod without a sidecar sends a request to a server pod that is managed by Istio. What is the expected outcome?

options.text: The request is rejected because Istio requires every pod in the cluster to carry a sidecar before any traffic is accepted.
The request succeeds, because Istio's default PERMISSIVE mode allows both Istio-managed pods and pods without sidecars to send and receive traffic between each other.
The request succeeds only if Cilium is installed with the socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly Helm value set to true.
The request is redirected to the Cilium HTTP proxy, which returns 403 until an L7 network policy is applied.

explanation: Istio's default peer authentication mode is PERMISSIVE, which permits traffic between Istio-managed pods and pods that have no sidecar, in both directions. Nothing in the prerequisites about Cilium's Helm values changes this behaviour, and the Cilium proxy only becomes relevant once an L7 network policy is applied.

optionRationale.a: PERMISSIVE mode explicitly tolerates pods without sidecars, so a sidecar is not a precondition for traffic to be accepted.
optionRationale.c: The socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly value is a Cilium installation prerequisite, not a condition that governs whether Istio accepts traffic from a pod without a sidecar.
optionRationale.d: The Cilium HTTP proxy interference described arises only after a Cilium L7 network policy is applied, not by default.

stem: A platform team runs a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. They enable the Cilium ingress controller in host network mode via Helm. What happens to the LoadBalancer and NodePort Service modes for the ingress controller?

explanation: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode, since the two modes are mutually exclusive. The listener is then exposed on all interfaces, not on loopback only.

ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort, set as an annotation on the Ingress resource.
ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port, which may be shared by all Ingress resources as long as it is above 1023.

stem: In host network mode, an engineer sets ingressController.hostNetwork.httpsPort to a non-zero value while leaving sharedListenerPort at its default. How does the shared HTTPS listener behave?

stem: A platform team exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service and sets externalTrafficPolicy: Local. They want to confirm that only nodes with local backend pods are considered healthy by an external load balancer. Which behaviour should they expect from the health check endpoint?

options.text: Requests to http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz return 200 on nodes that have local pods running, and non-200 on nodes that do not.
Requests to http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz return 200 on all nodes regardless of whether they have local pods running.
Requests to http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz return 200 only on the node that is the leader for the Service.
Requests to http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz return 200 only if kube-proxy is not installed.

explanation: With externalTrafficPolicy: Local, Kubernetes automatically sets healthCheckNodePort, and the node opens that port. The contract is that /healthz returns 200 on nodes with local pods and non-200 on nodes without. Cilium implements this for general Loadbalancer Services, though it behaves differently for Cilium ingress config.

optionRationale.b: This would defeat the purpose of the health check, which is to let external load balancers avoid nodes without local backends.
optionRationale.c: There is no leader concept for this health check; it is per-node based on local pod presence.
optionRationale.d: The health check behaviour is independent of kube-proxy; kube-proxy is mentioned only in relation to source IP visibility.

stem: An engineer is running a cluster with kube-proxy and wants to ensure that backend pods see the original client source IP for traffic arriving through a Loadbalancer Service. Which externalTrafficPolicy setting must they use?

options.text: Local
Cluster
Either Local or Cluster; both preserve the source IP.
Neither; source IP visibility is not possible with kube-proxy.

explanation: In clusters that use kube-proxy, externalTrafficPolicy: Local is the only way to ensure source IP visibility, because nodes route only to local pods without masquerading the source IP. With Cluster, the node may masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see it.

optionRationale.b: Cluster allows routing to all endpoints and the node may masquerade the source IP, so the backend may not see the client IP.
optionRationale.c: Only Local guarantees no masquerading in kube-proxy clusters; Cluster does not.
optionRationale.d: Source IP visibility is possible with Local, so this is false.

stem: How does Cilium forward ingress traffic bound for a Service that exposes Envoy to the backend?

options.text: It always forwards to Envoy on the local node using the Linux Kernel TPROXY function.
It uses kube-proxy iptables rules to load-balance across all endpoints in the cluster.
It uses externalTrafficPolicy to decide between local and remote endpoints before forwarding.
It forwards to Envoy only when externalTrafficPolicy is set to Cluster.

explanation: Cilium always sends ingress traffic for a Service exposing Envoy to the local node and always forwards it to Envoy using TPROXY, which transparently forwards packets to the backend. This is why the externalTrafficPolicy behaviour differs for Cilium ingress.

optionRationale.b: Cilium does not rely on kube-proxy iptables for this; it uses TPROXY on the local node.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states traffic always goes to the local node and is forwarded via TPROXY, regardless of externalTrafficPolicy.
optionRationale.d: The forwarding via TPROXY is unconditional for such Services, not dependent on Cluster policy.

explanation: With externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster, the node routes to all endpoints across the cluster and may masquerade the source IP. Consequently, in many cases the backend pod does not see the source IP. This is in contrast to Local, which does not masquerade.

optionRationale.c: healthCheckNodePort is associated with Local, not a condition for source IP preservation in Cluster mode.

stem: A team exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a Loadbalancer Service with externalTrafficPolicy set to Cluster. What effect does this setting have on routing and source IP?

options.text: The node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, and the node may masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see the source IP.
The node routes only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, guaranteeing source IP visibility.
The node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly and never masquerades the source IP, so the backend pod always sees the source IP.
The node routes only to Pods on the local node and always masquerades the source IP.

explanation: With externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster, the node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly. Upstream load balancers expect to be able to send traffic to any node and have it reach a backend Pod, and the node may masquerade the source IP. Consequently, the backend pod may not see the source IP.

optionRationale.b: This describes the Local setting, not Cluster.
optionRationale.c: Cluster does not guarantee source IP visibility; the node may masquerade the source IP.
optionRationale.d: This combines the routing behaviour of Local with masquerading, which is not what Cluster does.
