stem: A Cilium cluster uses transparent encryption. An endpoint is permitted to initiate traffic to targets outside the cluster. A new pod is created on a remote node, but the local node has not yet learned that the pod's IP address belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint. During this time, the endpoint sends packets to that IP address. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It sends them unencrypted, because it must assume the destination IP address is outside the cluster.
It drops them until the endpoint information has propagated.
It encrypts them using the local node's encryption key.
It encrypts them using the encryption key of the remote node.

explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether a destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that a particular IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or newly joined remote Cilium host, it has to assume the destination is outside the cluster, so the initial packets are sent unencrypted. Only once the information has propagated and Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node does it start encrypting packets using the encryption key of the remote node.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the initial packets are sent out unencrypted, not dropped; dropping would be a policy action, not the described encryption behaviour.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that once the endpoint is known, encryption uses the encryption key of the remote node, not the local node's key.
optionRationale.d: Encryption with the remote node's key begins only after Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node; before that, packets are unencrypted.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
In such a case there is a time window during which Cilium will send out the
initial packets unencrypted, as it has to assume the destination IP address is
outside of the cluster.

stem: An Elasticsearch cluster serves three clients: `outpost` uploads troop logs, `spaceship` uploads diagnostics, and `empire-hq` searches both indices. The security team wants to apply least privilege so that each client can only perform its intended operations. Which statement best describes the least privilege goal for this cluster?

options.text: Give clients access only to particular indices and limit the operations each client is allowed to perform on each index.
Give all clients full access to all indices but log every operation for auditing.
Restrict all clients to read-only access on all indices to prevent data manipulation.
Allow clients to access any index but limit them to a single operation type, such as search or upload.

explanation: Least privilege for Elasticsearch clusters means restricting each client to the specific indices it needs and limiting the operations it can perform on those indices. The other options either grant excessive access or apply overly broad restrictions that do not match the stated goal.

optionRationale.b: Full access to all indices violates least privilege, even with auditing.
optionRationale.c: Read-only access for all clients would prevent the outpost and spaceship from uploading logs and diagnostics.
optionRationale.d: Limiting to a single operation type across any index does not restrict access to particular indices as required.

citations.title: Security Risks for Elasticsearch Access
citations.quote: For Elasticsearch clusters the **least privilege security** challenge is to give clients access only to particular indices, and to limit the operations each client is allowed to perform on each index.

stem: In an Elasticsearch deployment, the `outpost` client is intended only to upload troop logs, while the `empire-hq` client is intended only to search both the `troop_logs` and `spaceship_diagnostics` indices. An attacker compromises the `outpost` client and runs a script that searches all indices and then updates the `spaceship_diagnostics` data, changing the `stats` field for a tiefighter spaceship from a critical engine burn warning to an OK status. What is the primary security risk demonstrated by this scenario?

options.text: A compromised client can search and manipulate critical data in Elasticsearch because it is not restricted to its intended index and operations.
The `empire-hq` client can no longer search the indices because the `outpost` client has modified the data.
The `spaceship` client will fail to upload diagnostics because the `outpost` client has updated the same index.
The Elasticsearch cluster will reject the update because the `outpost` client lacks write permissions by default.

explanation: The scenario shows that once an outpost is compromised, the client can be used to search and manipulate critical data because it is not limited to its intended index and operations. The other options describe effects not supported by the excerpt.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not state that empire-hq loses search ability; the risk is unauthorised access by the compromised client.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention upload failures for the spaceship client due to the outpost's actions.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the outpost successfully updating the diagnostics data, so the cluster does not reject the update by default.

citations.title: Security Risks for Elasticsearch Access
citations.quote: Once compromised, the clients can be used to search and manipulate the critical data in Elasticsearch.

stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy contains a single rule whose endpointSelector matches pods labelled app=frontend. The rule supplies an ingress section but no egress section. A pod labelled app=frontend receives an inbound connection and also makes an outbound connection. What does the rule do?

options.text: It applies at ingress only; egress is unaffected because the egress section was omitted.
It applies at both ingress and egress, because omitting a section makes it default to allowing all traffic in that direction.
It has no effect at all, because a rule must provide both ingress and egress to be valid.
It applies at egress only, because the ingress section is ignored unless egress is also present.

explanation: Each rule is split into an ingress section and an egress section, and either one or both may be provided. An omitted or empty ingress section means the rule does not apply at ingress, and likewise for egress. Here only ingress was supplied, so the rule is enforced on traffic entering the selected pods and does not apply at egress.

optionRationale.b: Omission of a section means the rule does not apply in that direction; it does not create an allow-all default.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that either ingress, egress, or both can be provided, so a single section is sufficient.
optionRationale.d: The direction supplied was ingress, and it is the egress section that is absent, so the rule cannot apply at egress.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote:
Either ingress, egress, or both can be
provided. If both ingress and egress are omitted, the rule has no effect.

stem: An engineer is following the steps to test the standalone DNS proxy and has just built the standalone DNS proxy container image from source. Which command loads that locally built image into the kind cluster?

options.text: kind load docker-image quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest
make kind && make kind-image && make kind-install-cilium
kubectl rollout restart ds -n kube-system cilium
cilium upgrade --chart-directory='./install/kubernetes/cilium' --set='l7Proxy=true'

explanation: After building the image, the next step is to load it into the kind cluster using `kind load docker-image quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest`.

optionRationale.b: This command creates a kind cluster and builds/installs Cilium from source; it does not load the standalone DNS proxy image.
optionRationale.c: This restarts the Cilium agent DaemonSet to apply configuration changes; it does not load an image into kind.
optionRationale.d: This upgrades Cilium with Helm settings to enable the standalone DNS proxy; it does not load the image into the kind cluster.

citations.quote: Load the standalone DNS proxy image you built into the kind cluster:

stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy selects pods with app=client and contains an egress rule with toFQDNs.matchPattern set to `*.cilium.io`. The DNS proxy observes a response for `cilium.io` and another for `sub.sub.cilium.io`. Which of these names will have its IPs inserted into the generated L3 rule?

options.text: Neither `cilium.io` nor `sub.sub.cilium.io`.
Both `cilium.io` and `sub.sub.cilium.io`.
`cilium.io` only.
`sub.sub.cilium.io` only.

explanation: The pattern `*.cilium.io` uses a single `*` that matches zero or more valid DNS characters except the `.` separator. It therefore matches `sub.cilium.io` but not `cilium.io` (no leading label) and not `sub.sub.cilium.io` (two labels before the dot). To cover cascaded subdomains the `**.` prefix would be needed.

optionRationale.b: A single `*` does not span the `.` separator, so neither name is covered.
optionRationale.c: `*.cilium.io` requires at least the wildcard label to be present; the bare apex `cilium.io` is explicitly excluded.
optionRationale.d: `sub.sub.cilium.io` has two labels before `cilium.io`, which a single `*` cannot match.

citations.title: DNS based
citations.quote:
``*`` within a domain allows 0 or more valid DNS characters, except for the
    ``.`` separator. ``*.cilium.io`` will match ``sub.cilium.io`` but not
    ``cilium.io`` or ``sub.sub.cilium.io``.

stem: An engineer wants to write a Cilium HTTP-aware filter that permits only certain gRPC methods on a service. How is each gRPC method mapped to an HTTP request that the filter can match?

options.text: Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.
Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP GET call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.
Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /<method-name>/cloudcity.DoorManager.
Each gRPC method is mapped to a raw TCP connection on port 50051 with no HTTP URL.

explanation: Since gRPC is built on top of HTTP, a gRPC call is mapped to an HTTP URL, and each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>. A Cilium HTTP-aware filter can then white-list the permitted URLs.

optionRationale.b: The mapping uses HTTP POST, not GET.
optionRationale.c: The order is /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>, not the reverse.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL, so a URL is involved.

citations.title: Securing Access to a gRPC Service with Cilium
citations.quote:
Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form
``/cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>``.

stem: A network security team wants Cilium to inspect TLS traffic destined for an external service. They generate a CA private key and CA certificate, then create a certificate for the destination signed by that CA. When Cilium terminates the client's TLS connection and opens a new TLS connection to the real destination, what must Cilium be configured with so that it can validate the destination's certificate?

options.text: The set of CAs that Cilium should trust when validating the new TLS connection to the destination service.
The CA private key used to sign the destination certificate.
The private key of the destination service, stored as a Kubernetes secret.
A client certificate signed by the internal CA, installed on each client workload.

explanation: Because Cilium terminates the initial TLS connection and creates a new one to the destination, it must be told which CAs to trust when validating that new connection. The CA private key is not needed by Cilium; it is used only to create certificates, which can be done offline.

optionRationale.b: The CA private key is used only to create certificates and does not need to be provided to Cilium at all.
optionRationale.c: Private keys for individual destination services are stored as Kubernetes secrets, but that is not what Cilium needs to validate the destination's certificate.
optionRationale.d: Clients need the CA certificate installed to trust certificates signed by that CA, but a client certificate is not what Cilium uses to validate the destination.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model
citations.quote:
Cilium must be told the set of CAs that it
   should trust when validating the new TLS connection to the destination service.

stem: In a Cilium TLS inspection deployment, which statement correctly describes the sensitivity of the CA private key and the CA certificate?

options.text: The CA private key must be kept safe because anyone with access to it can inspect TLS-encrypted traffic, whereas certificates are public information and not sensitive.
The CA certificate must be kept secret because it can be used to decrypt traffic, whereas the CA private key is public.
Both the CA private key and the CA certificate must be kept secret because either can be used to sign new certificates.
Neither the CA private key nor the CA certificate is sensitive because Cilium does not need either of them.

explanation: The CA private key is highly sensitive: anyone with access to it can inspect TLS-encrypted traffic. Certificates, by contrast, are public information and are not sensitive.

optionRationale.b: The CA certificate is public information, not a secret, and the private key is the sensitive component.
optionRationale.c: Only the private key is sensitive; certificates are public information.
optionRationale.d: The private key is extremely sensitive, and Cilium does need to be told which CAs to trust.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model
citations.quote:
it is EXTREMELY important that you keep the above private keys safe, as anyone
    with access to this private key will be able to inspect TLS-encrypted traffic (certificates on the other
    hand are public information, and are not at all sensitive).

stem: How does Cilium handle the start of additional pods labelled role=frontend once the first such pod has already been given an identity that is permitted to initiate connections to the identity of the role=backend pod?

options.text: It resolves the identity via a key-value store, with no action performed on any cluster node hosting role=backend pods.
It installs a new IP address filter on every node hosting a role=backend pod before the pod is allowed to start.
It assigns a fresh, unique identity to each new pod, which must then be separately allowed to reach the role=backend identity.
It delays the new pod until every cluster node has been updated with the security rules for that pod.

explanation: Because Cilium bases security on a label-derived identity that can be shared between pods, starting further role=frontend pods only requires resolving that identity via a key-value store; nothing has to be done on the nodes hosting role=backend pods, and the start is delayed only until the identity is resolved.

optionRationale.b: Installing IP address filters on backend nodes is the traditional approach that Cilium replaces, not what Cilium does.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the identity can be shared between pods, so subsequent frontend pods reuse the existing identity rather than each needing a new one.
optionRationale.d: Updating security rules on all other cluster nodes is the costly step Cilium avoids; only identity resolution is required.

citations.title: Identity-Based
citations.quote:
The subsequent start of additional ``role=frontend`` pods
only requires to resolve this identity via a key-value store, no action has to
be performed on any of the cluster nodes hosting ``role=backend`` pods.

stem:
A CiliumNetworkPolicy named rule1 selects endpoints with org=empire and class=deathstar and allows ingress on TCP port 80 from endpoints labelled org=empire, with an HTTP rule permitting only POST /v1/request-landing. After the policy is applied, an engineer runs the following from the tiefighter pod:

$ kubectl exec tiefighter -- curl -s -XPUT deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/exhaust-port

What response should the engineer expect?

options.text: Access denied, because the L7 rule permits only POST /v1/request-landing and disallows all other calls, including PUT /v1/exhaust-port.
Panic: deathstar exploded, because the maintenance API is still reachable and the request is processed.
No output at all, because traffic from pods labelled org=empire is dropped before the HTTP layer is evaluated.
Ship landed, because the policy matches on the org=empire label of the source pod and ignores the HTTP method.

explanation: The policy extends the identity-aware rule with an HTTP-layer rule that allows only POST /v1/request-landing from org=empire endpoints. A PUT to /v1/exhaust-port therefore does not match the allowed request and is rejected at L7, returning "Access denied" rather than reaching the maintenance handler. The empty response is reserved for traffic from pods without the org=empire label, such as xwing, which is dropped before the HTTP layer is reached.

optionRationale.b: This is the outcome seen before any L7 policy is applied, when tiefighter has full access to deathstar's API; the L7 rule now blocks the PUT.
optionRationale.c: The silent, timing-out outcome applies to traffic from pods without the label org=empire, such as xwing, not to tiefighter, which matches the fromEndpoints selector.
optionRationale.d: The policy does not ignore the method: the http rule names method POST explicitly, so a PUT cannot be treated as allowed.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "rule1"
spec:
  description: "L7 policy to restrict access to specific HTTP call"
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      org: empire
      class: deathstar
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        org: empire
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "80"
        protocol: TCP
      rules:
        http:
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/v1/request-landing"

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
extends our original policy by limiting *tiefighter* to making only a POST /v1/request-landing
API call, but disallowing all other calls (including PUT /v1/exhaust-port).

stem: A cluster runs Cilium in direct routing mode. An engineer deploys the following Service, which selects DSR forwarding with IPIP dispatch, and labels only the node `node-a` with `service.cilium.io/node=beefy`. The nginx backend Pods, however, are scheduled on `node-b`, which does not carry that label. What is the result?

options.text: Traffic reaches the backend Pods, but their replies are sent back through the load balancing node because the backend node cannot rewrite the source to the service address.

The backend node cannot terminate the inbound IPIP traffic and rewrite the reply to be sourced from the service address, because the service is not present on that node, so DSR handling fails for those Pods.
The IPIP tunnel is never established and Cilium falls back to Geneve encapsulation, which carries the service IP and port to the backend.
The Service is rejected by the API server because `port` and `targetPort` differ, which IPIP dispatch does not permit.

explanation: With DSR the backend node takes part in service handling: it terminates the inbound IPIP traffic and rewrites the reply so that it is sourced from the service address and returned directly to the client. That requires the service to be present on the backend node, so when DSR IPIP is combined with selective service node exposure, the backend Pods must run on nodes that are part of the exposure set. Only nodes hosting neither the frontend nor any backend may be left out. Here the Pods sit on a node outside the exposure set, so the required handling cannot happen there.

optionRationale.a: DSR does not fall back to routing replies through the load balancing node; the backend node rewrites the reply itself, which is precisely what it cannot do without the service installed.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes no fallback from IPIP to Geneve; it states that selecting `loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip` automatically enables inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes.
optionRationale.d: The manifest sets both `port` and `targetPort` to `80`, so they match; the failure described comes from node exposure, not port validation.

attachments.title: The Service under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  annotations:
    service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer
    service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr
    service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm: maglev
    service.cilium.io/node: beefy
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: LoadBalancer

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
This requires the service to be present on the backend node. Therefore, when DSR
    IPIP is combined with `Selective Service Node Exposure`_, the backend Pods
    must run on nodes that are part of the exposure set

stem: A platform team has enabled Cilium's bandwidth manager on a cluster and wants to confirm, from the command line, that the feature is active and see which devices are enforcing egress bandwidth limitation. Which command and output line should they look at?

options.text: Run `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep BandwidthManager` and check the `BandwidthManager` line, which shows the mode and the devices.
Run `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium` and check that every Cilium Pod reports `READY 1/1`.
Run `cilium bpf bandwidth list` and check the token bucket entries for each Pod.
Run `kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'` and check that the Pod IPs fall within the native device subnets.

explanation: The `cilium status` CLI command provides visibility through the `BandwidthManager` info line, and it also dumps a list of devices on which the egress bandwidth limitation is enforced. The example output shows `BandwidthManager: EDT with BPF [BBR] [eth0]`, so this is the line to inspect.

optionRationale.b: Checking that the Cilium Pods are Running only verifies that the agents came up; it says nothing about whether the bandwidth manager feature is enabled.
optionRationale.c: No such command appears in the material; the documented way to verify the feature is the `BandwidthManager` info line from `cilium status`.
optionRationale.d: Reading Pod IPs does not report the bandwidth manager state or the devices on which egress limitation is enforced.

attachments.title: Verification output
attachments.body:
$ kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep BandwidthManager
 BandwidthManager:       EDT with BPF [BBR] [eth0]

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
In order to verify whether the bandwidth manager feature has been enabled in Cilium,
the ``cilium status`` CLI command provides visibility through the ``BandwidthManager``
info line. It also dumps a list of devices on which the egress bandwidth limitation
is enforced:

stem: A global service named rebel-base exists in a Cluster Mesh. In cluster 1, an engineer runs `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=remote --overwrite` and then, from cluster 1, runs `kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base`. Which pods reply?

options.text: Only pods in cluster 2, because the remote endpoints are now preferred.
Only pods in cluster 1, because the local endpoints remain preferred until the annotation is removed.
Pods in both clusters, because the annotation only takes effect on the cluster where the Service object is defined.
No pods reply, because setting the value to remote disables local backends entirely and the remote ones are not yet healthy.

explanation: Setting the affinity annotation to remote makes the remote endpoints the preferred destination, so traffic from cluster 1 is served by cluster 2's pods. The excerpt records that after changing the value to remote, accessing the global service from cluster 1 gives replies from pods in cluster 2 only, and the endpoint listing shows the remote backends marked as preferred.

optionRationale.b: This describes the effect of the local value, not remote; the annotation was overwritten with remote, so the preference flips to the remote endpoints.
optionRationale.c: The annotation is applied to the global service and changes which endpoints are preferred for access from cluster 1; the excerpt shows the replies changing immediately after the annotate command.
optionRationale.d: The remote value expresses a preference rather than disabling local backends, and the excerpt shows replies still arriving, from cluster 2.

attachments.title: Endpoint listing after setting affinity to remote in cluster 1

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote: 5. In cluster 1, change ``service.cilium.io/affinity`` value to ``remote`` for existing global service

stem: A kind cluster runs in cluster-pool IPAM mode with 10.0.0.0/8 as the cluster-wide pool and /24 per-node PodCIDRs. An engineer performs the Helm upgrade that switches to multi-pool IPAM mode and enables the operator migration, using ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools to create the default CiliumPodIPPool with the same CIDR and mask size. The operator has finished the migration, but no Cilium agent has been restarted yet. What does the engineer observe in each CiliumNode's spec.ipam at this point?

options.text: The podCIDRs field is still populated and pools is empty, because the per-node allocation only moves into pools once the agent restarts.
The podCIDRs field is gone and pools.allocated lists the same per-node CIDR as before, with pool set to default.
Both podCIDRs and pools.allocated are populated, each holding the same per-node CIDR, until the agent restart clears podCIDRs.
pools.allocated is empty and pools.requested lists the number of IPv4 addresses the node needs from the default pool.

explanation: Once the operator has performed the migration, each node has the same per-node CIDR allocated from the default multi-pool IP pool, and the CiliumNode records it under pools.allocated with pool: default rather than under spec.ipam.podCIDRs. The requested block only appears after the agent itself restarts in multi-pool mode.

optionRationale.a: This describes the state before the migration, when each CiliumNode stores its per-node allocation in spec.ipam.podCIDRs and pools is empty; the operator migration has already moved the allocation by the time described.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows the post-migration output with only pools.allocated present, not a period in which both fields carry the same CIDR.
optionRationale.d: The requested block with needed ipv4-addrs appears only after the agent restarts, not at the point where the operator has finished the migration.

attachments.title: CiliumNode IPAM state before the migration
attachments.body:
$ kubectl get ciliumnode kind-worker -o yaml | yq .spec.ipam
  podCIDRs:
    - 10.0.3.0/24
  pools: {}

attachments.title: CiliumNode IPAM state after the operator migration
attachments.body:
$ kubectl get ciliumnode kind-worker -o yaml | yq .spec.ipam
  pools:
    allocated:
      - cidrs:
          - 10.0.3.0/24
        pool: default

citations.quote:
After the operator performs the migration, each node has the same per-node CIDR

stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy named rule1 selects endpoints with org=empire, class=deathstar and allows ingress on TCP port 80 from endpoints labelled org=empire, with an HTTP rule permitting only POST /v1/request-landing. After the policy is applied, an engineer runs `kubectl exec tiefighter -- curl -s -XPUT deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/exhaust-port` and receives the response `Access denied`. What explains this result?

options.text: The L7 HTTP rule permits only POST /v1/request-landing, so the PUT to /v1/exhaust-port is disallowed while the connection itself is still allowed from an org=empire pod.
The PUT request is dropped at L3/L4 because tiefighter does not carry the label org=empire, so the connection times out.
The path /v1/exhaust-port does not match the exact URL /v1/request-landing, so Cilium rewrites the request to the permitted path and the API rejects it.
The policy only covers port 80, so the request on the service port is redirected to a port with no policy and denied by the deathstar application itself.

explanation: The policy extends the identity-aware rule with an HTTP-layer rule that allows only the POST /v1/request-landing call and disallows all other calls, including PUT /v1/exhaust-port. Because tiefighter carries org=empire, traffic from it is admitted at L3/L4, but the L7 rule rejects the PUT, which is why the response is `Access denied` rather than a timeout.

optionRationale.b: Traffic from pods without the label org=empire is the case that continues to be dropped and times out; tiefighter is an org=empire pod, so this does not apply.
optionRationale.c: Cilium does not rewrite requests to a permitted path; the HTTP rule simply permits or denies the request as made.
optionRationale.d: The policy is enforced by Cilium on the selected deathstar endpoints for TCP port 80; the denial comes from the L7 policy, not from redirection to an unpoliced port.

attachments.title: The policy applied to deathstar
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "rule1"
spec:
  description: "L7 policy to restrict access to specific HTTP call"
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      org: empire
      class: deathstar
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        org: empire
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "80"
        protocol: TCP
      rules:
        http:
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/v1/request-landing"

attachments.title: Result of the PUT request from tiefighter
attachments.body:
$ kubectl exec tiefighter -- curl -s -XPUT deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/exhaust-port
 Access denied

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
extends our original policy by limiting *tiefighter* to making only a POST /v1/request-landing
API call, but disallowing all other calls (including PUT /v1/exhaust-port).

stem: A cluster runs Istio alongside Cilium, which was installed with the Helm values `socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly` and `cni.exclusive=false`. Web servers and clients are deployed across the `red`, `blue` and `green` namespaces, and connectivity checks between all of them return 200. An L4 Cilium network policy is then applied that restricts communication in the `blue` namespace to clients located only in `blue` and `red`. When the same connectivity checks are re-run, which result set should you expect?

options.text: `client 'red' to server 'blue': 200`, `client 'blue' to server 'blue': 200`, `client 'green' to server 'blue': 000` with exit code 28
`client 'red' to server 'blue': 503`, `client 'blue' to server 'blue': 503`, `client 'green' to server 'blue': 000` with exit code 28
`client 'red' to server 'blue': 403`, `client 'blue' to server 'blue': 403`, `client 'green' to server 'blue': 403`
All six checks return 200, because Istio's default `PERMISSIVE` mode overrides the Cilium policy

explanation: The excerpt states that the Cilium-managed L4 policy restricts communication in the `blue` namespace to clients located only in `blue` and `red` namespaces, and the re-run checks show `red` and `blue` clients still reaching `httpbin.blue` with 200 while the `green` client gets 000 and the command terminates with exit code 28. The 503 responses appear only later, once the L7 HTTP policy is added and the Cilium proxy interferes with Istio's mTLS connections.

optionRationale.b: The 503 results belong to the later stage, after the L7 HTTP-based policy is applied and the Cilium proxy interferes with Istio's mTLS-based connections — not to the L4-only policy.
optionRationale.c: 403 is the code seen when a client in `red` requests the `/deny` path after mTLS is disabled and Cilium enforces the L7 policy; it is not the outcome of the L4 restriction on the `blue` namespace.
optionRationale.d: `PERMISSIVE` mode concerns Istio-managed and non-sidecar pods sending and receiving traffic; the excerpt shows the Cilium L4 policy does change the results, with the `green` client failing.

stem: A cluster runs in `multi-pool` IPAM mode with a single `CiliumPodIPPool` named `default` whose IPv4 CIDR is `10.10.0.0/16`. An engineer applies a change that replaces that CIDR with `10.20.0.0/16` while pods on two nodes still hold addresses from the old range. What does the Cilium operator do in response?

options.text: It logs a warning for each CIDR block still in use by a node but removed from the pool.
It refuses the update and reverts the pool to the previous CIDR.
It silently reassigns the affected pods to addresses from the new CIDR.
It deletes the `CiliumNodes` of the affected nodes automatically.

explanation: The excerpt states that the operator reports a warning for each CIDR block still in use by a node but removed from the pool, and shows the corresponding log lines with `msg="CIDR from pool still in use by node"`. The update itself is accepted; the operator does not revert it, reassign pod IPs, or delete `CiliumNodes` on its own — those are manual steps in the migration procedure.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the update being applied and the operator merely warning; nothing reverts the pool.
optionRationale.c: Reassigning IPs is done by evicting and rescheduling workloads, not by the operator silently.
optionRationale.d: Deleting `CiliumNodes` is a manual step performed with `kubectl delete cn` for each node group.

stem: An engineer wants to change the CIDR of an in-use `CiliumPodIPPool` in a `multi-pool` cluster. Which statement describes what is permitted when editing an existing `CiliumPodIPPools` resource?

options.text: New IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs can be added, but CIDRs already in use cannot be deleted or updated.
In-use CIDRs can be updated freely, but new CIDRs cannot be added to the pool.
Both adding new CIDRs and deleting in-use CIDRs are permitted, provided the operator is restarted first.
Neither adding new CIDRs nor changing in-use CIDRs is permitted; the pool must be recreated.

explanation: The excerpt states that it is possible to extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use. This restriction exists to prevent pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the rule: adding CIDRs is allowed, updating in-use ones is not.
optionRationale.c: Deleting in-use CIDRs is explicitly not possible, and restarting the operator does not lift the restriction.
optionRationale.d: Extending the pool with new CIDRs is explicitly possible, so a full recreation is not the only option.

stem: A CiliumBGPPeerConfig named cilium-peer sets authSecretRef: bgp-auth-secret, but no Secret of that name exists in the BGP secrets namespace. What is the result for the BGP session that references this configuration?

options.text: The session is established using an empty password, and the agent logs an error about the failed secret fetch.
The session is refused outright and the peer configuration is rejected by the Cilium Agent.
The agent falls back to a password taken from the CiliumBGPPeerConfig's own spec, if one is present.
The session is established only after the agent retries the secret fetch until it succeeds.

explanation: Cilium does not block the session when the referenced secret is missing: it proceeds with an empty password and records the problem in the agent log. The documented log line is `Failed to fetch secret "secretname": not found (will continue with empty password)`, which confirms both the empty password and the error log.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the session continues with an empty password rather than being refused, and nothing suggests the peer configuration is rejected.
optionRationale.c: The password is expected in a Secret key named `password`; the excerpt describes no fallback to a password stored in the peer configuration itself.
optionRationale.d: The agent does not retry until success — it continues with an empty password and logs the error.

stem: An engineer edits the Cilium ConfigMap in kube-system and sets labels to "io\.kubernetes\.pod\.namespace k8s-app app name", then saves it. The Operator is managing identities. What must the engineer do for the new label pattern setting to take effect?

options.text: Restart both the Cilium Operators and the Cilium Agents.
Restart only the Cilium Agents, because the Operator does not read the labels setting.
Nothing — the setting is picked up automatically once the ConfigMap is saved.
Delete and recreate all Cilium endpoints so that new identities are allocated.

explanation: The excerpt states that after saving the ConfigMap, if the Operator is managing identities, you must restart both the Cilium Operators and Agents to pick up the new label pattern setting. Restarting only the Agents is the procedure given for the case where the Agent is managing identities.

optionRationale.b: Restarting only the Cilium Agents is what the excerpt prescribes when the Agent, not the Operator, is managing identities.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly requires a restart after saving the ConfigMap; the setting is not picked up automatically.

stem: You export a Service called rebel-base from the payments namespace in two clusters by creating a ServiceExport in each. The two ServiceExports disagree on the session affinity setting. What does Cilium do?

options.text: It sets a conflict condition on the corresponding ServiceExport status and resolves the conflict based on ServiceExport creation time, oldest first.
It rejects the newer ServiceExport and leaves the ServiceImport with the properties of the oldest ServiceExport only.
It merges both values into the ServiceImport and sets a conflict condition on the ServiceImport status.
It stops reconciling the ServiceImport until an operator deletes one of the ServiceExports.

explanation: Cilium reconciles a fixed set of properties — including SessionAffinity — into the ServiceImport. When the exported Services conflict on any of those properties, Cilium records a conflict condition on the corresponding ServiceExport status and resolves the conflict by ServiceExport creation time, from oldest to newest. The documentation warns that a conflict may resolve to properties you did not intend, so you should eventually resolve conflicts between the exported Services yourself.

optionRationale.b: Cilium does not reject the newer ServiceExport; it sets a conflict condition on the ServiceExport status and still resolves the conflict by creation time.
optionRationale.c: The conflict condition is set on the ServiceExport status, not on the ServiceImport status.
optionRationale.d: Reconciliation is not suspended; Cilium resolves the conflict automatically, oldest ServiceExport first.

attachments.title: The ServiceExport created in each cluster
attachments.body:
apiVersion: multicluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
   kind: ServiceExport
   metadata:
      name: rebel-base

If any conflict arises on any of these properties, Cilium sets a conflict
condition on the corresponding ServiceExport status and resolves the conflict
based on ServiceExport creation time from oldest to newest.

stem: A CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy uses a serviceMatcher for a Service named my-service in namespace default. The policy's redirectBackend specifies toPorts with port "80" and protocol TCP, and localEndpointSelector matchLabels app=proxy. After the policy is applied, you run cilium-dbg service list in the Cilium pod on the node where the proxy pod runs and see the frontend 172.20.0.51:80 listed with Service Type LocalRedirect and a single backend. What does this tell you about the service entry?

options.text: The existing ClusterIP service entry created by Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement has been replaced with a LocalRedirect entry that may only have node-local backend pods.
The ClusterIP service entry is unchanged, and a second LocalRedirect entry has been added alongside it for the same frontend.
The service entry has been converted to a headless service whose backends are selected by the Kubernetes Service selector app=MyApp.
The service entry now load-balances across all backend pods in the cluster, including those on other nodes, because the localEndpointSelector widens the backend set.

explanation: Applying a serviceMatcher policy replaces the existing service entry that Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement created with a new entry of type LocalRedirect, and that entry may only have node-local backend pods. The output showing LocalRedirect with a single backend on the node running the proxy pod is consistent with this.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states the existing service entry is replaced, not that a second entry is added alongside it.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt turns the Service into a headless service; the Service remains a clusterIP Service and the entry type becomes LocalRedirect.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the LocalRedirect entry may only have node-local backend pods, so it does not load-balance across pods on other nodes.

attachments.title: The Local Redirect Policy applied
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy
metadata:
  name: "lrp-svc"
spec:
  redirectFrontend:
    serviceMatcher:
      serviceName: my-service
      namespace: default
  redirectBackend:
    localEndpointSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: proxy
    toPorts:
      - port: "80"
        protocol: TCP

stem: You are deploying the standalone DNS proxy into a kind cluster. You have already run `make docker-standalone-dns-proxy-image` and created the cluster with Cilium installed from source. Which command loads the image you built into the kind cluster?

options.text: kind load docker-image quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest
docker push quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest
kubectl apply -f quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest
make kind-image

explanation: The documented step for getting the locally built image into the kind cluster is `kind load docker-image quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest`. The build step produces a local image only, so it must be loaded into the kind nodes before the proxy pods can reference it.

optionRationale.b: Pushing to a registry is not part of the procedure; the image is used locally with `pullPolicy=Never`.
optionRationale.c: `kubectl apply` takes manifests, not container image references.
optionRationale.d: `make kind-image` is part of building and installing Cilium itself, not of loading the standalone DNS proxy image.

stem: You are upgrading Cilium to enable the standalone DNS proxy with a locally built image. Which combination of Helm settings is used so that the cluster references the locally built image rather than pulling one from a registry?

options.text: `standaloneDnsProxy.image.tag=latest` together with `standaloneDnsProxy.image.pullPolicy=Never`
`standaloneDnsProxy.image.tag=latest` together with `standaloneDnsProxy.image.pullPolicy=Always`
`standaloneDnsProxy.image.useDigest=true` together with `standaloneDnsProxy.image.pullPolicy=IfNotPresent`
`dnsProxy.proxyPort=10094` together with `l7Proxy=true`

explanation: The example upgrade sets `image.tag=latest` and `image.pullPolicy=Never`, and the notes state that these are used to reference the locally-built image. `pullPolicy=Never` prevents a registry pull, which is what makes the locally loaded image the one that runs.

optionRationale.b: `Always` would force a registry pull, defeating the purpose of using a locally built image.
optionRationale.c: The example explicitly sets `useDigest=false`, and `IfNotPresent` is not the documented pull policy for this setup.
optionRationale.d: These two flags make the proxy operational and enable L7 support, but they do not control which image is used.

attachments.title: The upgrade command in use
attachments.body:
$ cilium upgrade \
       --chart-directory='./install/kubernetes/cilium' \
       --set='l7Proxy=true' \
       --set='dnsProxy.proxyPort=10094' \
       --helm-set='standaloneDnsProxy.enabled=true' \
       --helm-set='standaloneDnsProxy.image.repository=quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy' \
       --helm-set='standaloneDnsProxy.image.tag=latest' \
       --helm-set='standaloneDnsProxy.image.useDigest=false' \
       --helm-set='standaloneDnsProxy.image.pullPolicy=Never'

stem: After applying the DNS policy shown, you run `kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup example.com.` from a pod labelled `org=alliance` and receive `** server can't find example.com: REFUSED`. Why is the query refused?

options.text: `example.com` is not covered by the allowed DNS rules in the policy, so the query is refused.
The pod is missing the `org=alliance` label required by the endpoint selector.
Port 53 traffic to kube-dns is blocked because the policy only permits port 80.
The standalone DNS proxy is not running, so all DNS resolution fails.

explanation: The policy allows only the listed names and patterns — `cilium.io`, `*.cilium.io` and `*.api.cilium.io` in the DNS rules — and the documentation states that the query to `example.com` is refused because it is not in the allowed DNS policy rules.

optionRationale.b: The test pod is created with the matching label `org=alliance`, so the selector is satisfied.
optionRationale.c: The policy does allow port 53 with protocol ANY to kube-dns; port 80 appears in the separate `toFQDNs` section.
optionRationale.d: A refused answer is an enforcement decision, not a failure to resolve; the proxy is answering the query.

attachments.title: The DNS policy applied to the cluster
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "tofqdn-dns-visibility"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      any:org: alliance
  egress:
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
       "k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace": kube-system
       "k8s:k8s-app": kube-dns
    toPorts:
      - ports:
         - port: "53"
           protocol: ANY
        rules:
          dns:
            - matchName: "cilium.io"
            - matchPattern: "*.cilium.io"
            - matchPattern: "*.api.cilium.io"

  - toFQDNs:
      - matchName: "cilium.io"
      - matchName: "sub.cilium.io"
      - matchName: "service1.api.cilium.io"
      - matchPattern: "special*service.api.cilium.io"
    toPorts:
      - ports:
         - port: "80"
           protocol: TCP

$ kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup example.com.
   Server:         10.96.0.10
   Address:        10.96.0.10#53

   ** server can't find example.com: REFUSED

stem: You deliberately break the Cilium agent by setting the `cilium-agent` image to a non-existent tag, and the agent pods enter `ImagePullBackOff`. From the test pod you then run `nslookup cilium.io` and `nslookup example.com`. What is the expected outcome?

options.text: `cilium.io` resolves and `example.com` is still refused, because the standalone DNS proxy enforces DNS policies independently of the agent.
Both queries fail, because DNS policy enforcement requires a running Cilium agent.
`cilium.io` resolves and `example.com` also resolves, because policy enforcement stops when the agent is down.
Both queries are refused, because the standalone DNS proxy cannot start without the agent.

explanation: The resilience test shows that the standalone DNS proxy continues to enforce DNS policies independently: the allowed `cilium.io` query succeeds and the non-allowed `example.com` query is still refused even when the agent is unavailable.

optionRationale.b: This is precisely the failure mode the standalone proxy is designed to avoid; the test demonstrates queries still work.
optionRationale.c: Enforcement does not lapse — the non-allowed domain is still refused.
optionRationale.d: The proxy keeps serving queries; it does not stop when the agent goes down.

attachments.title: The resilience test commands
attachments.body:
# Intentionally break the Cilium agent by using a non-existent image
    $ kubectl set image -n kube-system ds/cilium cilium-agent=quay.io/cilium/cilium:non-existent-image
    
    # Wait for agent pods to enter ImagePullBackOff state
    $ kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready=false pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium --timeout=60s
    
    # DNS queries for allowed domains should still work via standalone DNS proxy
    $ kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup cilium.io

    # Verify that policy enforcement still works - non-allowed domains are still refused
    $ kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup example.com

citations.title: Building and Deploying
citations.quote:
Both queries demonstrate that the standalone DNS proxy continues to enforce DNS policies
independently, allowing ``cilium.io`` and refusing ``example.com``, even when the agent is unavailable.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium 1.18. Two CiliumBGPAdvertisement objects both select the same LoadBalancer Service, and each sets a different large community. What communities does the resulting BGP advertisement carry?

options.text: Only the communities from the advertisement that appears last in the list of advertisements.
The union of the community elements from every matching advertisement.
Only the communities from the advertisement with the highest local preference.
No communities, because overlapping selectors are rejected and the advertisement is dropped.

explanation: Overlapping advertisement selectors are supported, and for communities the union of elements is taken across all matches. So both large communities end up on the advertisement.

optionRationale.a: Picking the last sequential match describes the behaviour prior to Cilium 1.18, not the current overlap handling.
optionRationale.c: Local preference has its own overlap rule (largest value wins); it does not decide which communities survive.
optionRationale.d: Overlapping selectors are supported today, so the advertisement is not dropped.

citations.title: Overlapping Advertisements
citations.quote:
Today, overlapping 
advertisement selectors are supported. Overlap handling varies by attribute:

stem: Two CiliumBGPAdvertisement objects match the same Service. One sets local preference 100 and the other sets local preference 200. What local preference is used in the resulting advertisement?

options.text: 100, the first match encountered.
200, the largest value across all matches.
150, the average of the matching values.
The value is left unset because the matches conflict.

explanation: For local preference, overlap handling selects the largest value observed across all matches, consistent with RFC 4271's requirement that the higher degree of preference be preferred.

optionRationale.a: First-match selection is not how overlap is resolved for local preference.
optionRationale.c: Averaging is not part of the described overlap handling.
optionRationale.d: Conflicting matches do not leave the attribute unset; a definite value is chosen.

citations.title: Overlapping Advertisements
citations.quote: * Local Preference: the largest value is selected

stem: A LoadBalancer Service named hello-world initially carries only the label app=hello-world, and two advertisements select on vpc1=true and vpc2=true respectively. What is the BGP advertisement state for this Service at that point?

options.text: It is advertised with the communities of the first advertisement only.
It is advertised with the communities of both advertisements.
It is not advertised at all, because neither selector matches.
It is advertised without any communities attached.

explanation: With no vpc1 or vpc2 label present, neither selector matches, which results in no matches and no BGP advertisements.

optionRationale.a: There is no match to begin with, so no advertisement is produced.
optionRationale.b: Both selectors require labels the Service does not yet have.
optionRationale.d: An unmatched Service is not advertised at all, rather than advertised bare.

attachments.title: The two advertisements
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
 kind: CiliumBGPAdvertisement
 metadata:
   name: bgp-advertisements
   labels:
     advertise: bgp
 spec:
   advertisements:
     - advertisementType: "Service"
       service:
         addresses:
           - LoadBalancerIP
       selector:
         matchExpressions:
           - { key: vpc1, operator: In, values: [ "true" ] }
       attributes:
         communities:
           large: [ "1111:1111:1111" ]
     - advertisementType: "Service"
       service:
         addresses:
           - LoadBalancerIP
       selector:
         matchExpressions:
           - { key: vpc2, operator: In, values: [ "true" ] }
       attributes:
         communities:
           large: [ "2222:2222:2222" ]

 hello-world   LoadBalancer   10.2.65.71   <pending>     8080:30569/TCP   43m   app=hello-world

stem: Using the two advertisements shown, an operator runs `kubectl label service hello-world vpc1=true` and then `kubectl label service hello-world vpc2=true`. Which communities does the resulting BGP advertisement set?

Only 2222:2222:2222, from the vpc2 advertisement.
Neither, because a Service may match only one advertisement.

explanation: Once both labels are present, both selectors match the Service, and the union of community elements is taken across all matches, so both large communities are set.

optionRationale.b: The vpc2 match does not exclude the vpc1 match; both apply.
optionRationale.d: Overlapping advertisement selectors are supported, so a Service can match more than one advertisement.

stem: Which community types may be used in the attributes of overlapping advertisements?

options.text: Only Large communities.
Only Standard and Large communities.
All possible combinations of Standard, Large and WellKnown communities.
Only WellKnown communities.

explanation: The documentation states that all possible combinations of communities (Standard, Large, WellKnown) are supported.

optionRationale.a: Large is not the only supported type.
optionRationale.b: WellKnown communities are also supported.
optionRationale.d: Standard and Large communities are also supported.

citations.title: Overlapping Advertisements
citations.quote:
All possible combinations of communities (``Standard``, ``Large``, ``WellKnown``) are 
supported.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium 1.18. Two CiliumBGPAdvertisement objects are installed, each with a Service advertisement selecting on LoadBalancerIP addresses. The first matches Services labelled vpc1=true and sets the large community 1111:1111:1111; the second matches Services labelled vpc2=true and sets the large community 2222:2222:2222. A Service named hello-world is labelled with both vpc1=true and vpc2=true. Which communities does the resulting BGP advertisement carry?

options.text: Only 2222:2222:2222, because the last sequential match wins.
Both 1111:1111:1111 and 2222:2222:2222, because the union of elements is taken across all matches.
Neither community, because a Service matching more than one advertisement is skipped.
Only 1111:1111:1111, because the first match in the list takes precedence.

explanation: Overlapping advertisement selectors are supported, and for communities the union of elements is taken across all matches. A Service carrying both labels therefore matches both advertisements and the resulting advertisement set carries both large communities. The last-sequential-match behaviour belongs to releases prior to Cilium 1.18, where overlapping matches were not expected.

stem: A team runs Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. They enable the Cilium ingress controller's host network mode through Helm. Which statement describes the resulting behaviour?

options.text: The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode is disabled automatically, and the Envoy listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6).
The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode remains active alongside host network mode, and the Envoy listener is exposed only on the node's primary interface.
The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode is disabled automatically, and the Envoy listener is exposed only on the loopback interface (127.0.0.1 for IPv4 and/or ::1 for IPv6).
Host network mode cannot be enabled unless a LoadBalancer Service is available, so the Helm installation fails.

explanation: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode, because the two are mutually exclusive, and the listener is then exposed on all interfaces — 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6. This suits environments where a LoadBalancer Service is unavailable, such as development clusters.

optionRationale.b: The two modes are mutually exclusive, so LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode is disabled rather than kept active, and the listener binds all interfaces rather than a single primary one.
optionRationale.c: The listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 and/or ::), not restricted to the loopback interface.
optionRationale.d: Host network mode is specifically useful where a LoadBalancer Service is unavailable, so it does not require one to exist.

stem: A cluster-wide policy named default-deny is applied. It selects every endpoint whose io.kubernetes.pod.namespace is not kube-system, and its only egress rule permits UDP port 53 to the kube-dns endpoints in kube-system with a DNS matchPattern of '*'. A client outside the cluster then requests the /details endpoint of an application exposed through Cilium Ingress. What is the result?

options.text: The request is denied, and the response returned to the client is HTTP 403.
The request is allowed, because the policy contains no ingress section and therefore only restricts egress.
The request is allowed, because the reserved:ingress identity is excluded from the endpointSelector.
The request is dropped at the TCP layer, so the client receives no HTTP response at all.

explanation: The policy denies all traffic by default, and the excerpt states that with it applied the request to /details is denied for external and in-cluster traffic. The captured session shows the client receiving an HTTP 403 Forbidden with server: envoy, so the denial is surfaced as an HTTP response rather than a silent connection failure.

optionRationale.b: The policy is described as blocking all traffic by default; the absence of an ingress section does not leave ingress unrestricted, and the observed result is a denial.
optionRationale.c: The endpointSelector excludes only the kube-system namespace; nothing in the policy exempts the reserved:ingress identity, which is handled by a separate policy later in the flow.
optionRationale.d: The captured output shows a complete HTTP exchange ending in 403 Forbidden, not a dropped connection.

attachments.title: The default-deny policy
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "default-deny"
spec:
  description: "Block all the traffic (except DNS) by default"
  egress:
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
        k8s-app: kube-dns
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: '53'
        protocol: UDP
      rules:
        dns:
        - matchPattern: '*'
  endpointSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
      operator: NotIn
      values:
      - kube-system

stem: After a default-deny policy has blocked traffic to an application behind Cilium Ingress, a second CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy named allow-ingress-egress is applied. It selects endpoints for which reserved:ingress exists and allows egress to the cluster entity. What effect does this have?

options.text: It allows the ingress proxy to reach endpoints in the cluster, so requests to /details succeed from both an external client and an in-cluster client.
It allows only external traffic, because the cluster entity covers endpoints outside the cluster rather than inside it.
It has no effect until the default-deny policy is deleted, because cluster-wide policies are evaluated in creation order.
It allows the ingress proxy to reach the cluster, but in-cluster clients remain blocked because they do not carry the reserved:ingress identity.

explanation: The policy grants egress from the reserved:ingress identity to all cluster identities, and the captured session shows both the external curl and the in-cluster client from deployment/client receiving the /details payload. The excerpt notes that allowing all traffic from reserved:ingress to all cluster identities is generally the more reliable option, since Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.

optionRationale.b: The policy targets the cluster entity, and the excerpt's own output shows the in-cluster client succeeding, so the rule is not limited to external traffic.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes creation-order evaluation or a requirement to delete the default-deny policy first; the allow policy takes effect alongside it.
optionRationale.d: The captured output shows the in-cluster client from deployment/client receiving the same JSON payload, so in-cluster traffic is no longer blocked.

  description: "Allow all the egress traffic from reserved ingress identity to any endpoints in the cluster"
  endpointSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: reserved:ingress
      operator: Exists
  egress:
  - toEntities:
    - cluster

stem: A default-deny CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy is in place and you are now adding a policy to let the Cilium Ingress proxy reach application endpoints. Which approach does the guidance favour, and why?

options.text: Allow all traffic from the reserved:ingress identity to all cluster identities, because Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.
Allow egress from reserved:ingress to specific identities only, because broad cluster access would bypass the default-deny policy.
Allow ingress to the application endpoints from the world entity, because the ingress proxy appears as world to those endpoints.
Allow egress from reserved:ingress to kube-dns on UDP port 53, because name resolution is the only requirement of the proxy.

explanation: The excerpt acknowledges that a NetworkPolicy selecting reserved:ingress and allowing egress to specific identities could also be used, but concludes that allowing all traffic from reserved:ingress to all cluster identities is probably more reliable, given that Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt presents the specific-identity approach as possible but less reliable than the broad cluster allowance, not as the favoured option.
optionRationale.c: The policy shown grants egress from reserved:ingress to the cluster entity; nothing in the excerpt describes the proxy as the world entity for this purpose.

stem: A cluster runs the Cilium BGP Control Plane with no aggregation fields configured on its CiliumBGPAdvertisement resources. A Service of type ClusterIP is assigned the address 10.96.14.37. What prefix does the BGP Control Plane advertise for that service VIP?

options.text: 10.96.14.0/24, the subnet containing the VIP
10.96.14.37/32, the exact route for the VIP
10.96.0.0/16, the cluster's service CIDR
Nothing is advertised until an aggregation length is set

explanation: Without any aggregation configuration, the BGP Control Plane advertises exact routes for service VIPs, which for an IPv4 address means a /32 prefix. The aggregation length fields exist precisely to change this default, so 10.96.14.37/32 is what is advertised here.

optionRationale.a: A /24 is what you would get by setting aggregationLengthIPv4 to 24, but no aggregation is configured in this scenario.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt never mentions advertising the whole service CIDR; the default is the exact VIP route.
optionRationale.d: Aggregation is optional; the default behaviour is to advertise exact routes, not to withhold them.

stem: The CiliumNetworkPolicy below is in use in a ClusterMesh. With `policy-default-local-cluster` set to `false`, which traffic does it allow?

Traffic from `bar` in the local cluster only

Two separate `fromEndpoints` entries, each with `matchLabels` naming `bar` and one cluster

optionRationale.b: Naming only `fixme-cluster-name-1` in `matchLabels` would exclude `bar` in the second cluster.
optionRationale.c: `Exists` allows every cluster, which is broader than the two clusters you want to select.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt presents the multi-cluster selection as a single `matchExpressions` clause with multiple values, not as separate entries.

   name: allow-from-bar
   namespace: default
 spec:
   description: "Allow ingress traffic from bar"
   endpointSelector:
     matchLabels:
       name: foo
   ingress:
   - fromEndpoints:
     - matchLabels:
         name: bar
       matchExpressions:

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with its eBPF kube-proxy replacement enabled. An engineer deploys a Pod that declares a hostPort but no hostIP. On which addresses on the node will that Pod be reachable?

options.text: Only on the loopback address, such as 127.0.0.1:hostPort.
On the node's detected local addresses used for NodePort services, and additionally through the loopback address on the node.
Only on the node's ExternalIP, because hostPort always prefers the public address.
On every address of every node in the cluster, because hostPort is cluster-wide.

explanation: When a hostPort is given without a hostIP, the Pod is exposed to the outside world using the same local addresses from the node that were detected and used for exposing NodePort services, and it is also reachable through the loopback address on the node.

stem: A cluster runs the CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy shown in the attachment. A pod with labels org=empire and class=mediabot in the default namespace is scheduled on node1 and sends traffic to an external address. What happens to that traffic?

options.text: It is routed through node2 and SNATed with the egress IP 10.168.60.100.
It is SNATed on node1 using the first IPv4 address of the interface enp0s8.
It leaves the cluster without SNAT because the destination 0.0.0.0/0 is not matched by the policy.
It is dropped because the pod is not on the gateway node.

explanation: The policy selects pods with org=empire and class=mediabot in the default namespace, and its nodeSelector restricts it to node1. Traffic from those pods on node1 to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 is routed through the gateway node labelled node.kubernetes.io/name: node2, which SNATs it with the egress IP 10.168.60.100.

optionRationale.b: The interface field is only an alternative to egressIP; here egressIP is set, so the interface is not used.
optionRationale.c: The policy explicitly lists 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 as destinationCIDRs, so all traffic leaving the cluster is matched.
optionRationale.d: The policy routes traffic through the gateway node; it does not drop traffic from pods on other nodes.

attachments.title: The egress gateway policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-sample
spec:
  # Specify which pods should be subject to the current policy.
  # Multiple pod selectors can be specified.
  selectors:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        org: empire
        class: mediabot
        # The following label selects default namespace
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: default
    nodeSelector: # optional, if not specified the policy applies to all nodes
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node1 # only traffic from this node will be SNATed
  # Specify which destination CIDR(s) this policy applies to.
  # Multiple CIDRs can be specified.
  destinationCIDRs:
  - "0.0.0.0/0"
  - "::/0"

  # Configure the gateway node.
  egressGateway:
    # Specify which node should act as gateway for this policy.
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node2

    # Specify the IP address used to SNAT traffic matched by the policy.
    # It must exist as an IP associated with a network interface on the instance.
    egressIP: 10.168.60.100

    # Alternatively it's possible to specify the interface to be used for egress traffic.
    # In this case the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses assigned to that interface will be used
    # as egress IP.
    # interface: enp0s8

A pod labelled org=empire, class=deathstar is running on a node in zone A, and a pod labelled org=empire, class=tiefighter is running on a node in zone B. The tiefighter pod sends a request to the deathstar pod on TCP port 80. What is the result?

options.text: The request is allowed, because the policy selects pods by their labels rather than by endpoint IP addresses.
The request is blocked, because the two pods are on different nodes and the policy only covers same-node traffic.
The request is blocked, because the tiefighter pod does not carry the class=deathstar label required by the endpointSelector.
The request is allowed only if the deathstar pod's IP address is also listed in the fromEndpoints section.

explanation: The policy selects the destination with endpointSelector matchLabels org=empire and class=deathstar, and admits traffic from any endpoint labelled org=empire on TCP port 80. Because Cilium matches on pod labels, the location of either pod within the cluster does not matter, so the tiefighter pod (org=empire) reaches the deathstar pod on port 80.

optionRationale.b: Cilium applies policies to the right pods based on labels irrespective of where they run in the cluster, so node placement is not a factor.
optionRationale.c: The class=deathstar label is required on the destination, which the deathstar pod has; the source only needs org=empire, which tiefighter has.

stem: After the CiliumNetworkPolicy below is applied, a tiefighter pod labelled org=empire sends a request to a deathstar pod on TCP port 80 and the request succeeds. The deathstar pod then sends its reply packets back to the tiefighter pod. What happens to those reply packets?

options.text: They are automatically allowed, because Cilium performs stateful connection tracking for the same TCP connection.
They are dropped unless a separate egress rule permitting them is added to the policy.
They are dropped unless the reply packets are explicitly listed in the fromEndpoints section.
They are allowed only if the reply packets also arrive on TCP port 80.

explanation: Cilium performs stateful connection tracking: once policy allows the frontend to reach the backend, all required reply packets that are part of the backend replying to the frontend within the same TCP/UDP connection are automatically allowed. optionRationale.d: The automatic allowance covers all required reply packets of the same connection, not only those arriving on the original destination port.

stem: An engineer is writing a Layer 7 DNS policy and wants queries for `sub.cilium.io` to be allowed, but queries for `cilium.io` itself must not be allowed by that same entry. Which `matchPattern` value achieves this?

`cilium.io`

optionRationale.b: Without the dot separator before `cilium.io`, the pattern would also match the bare name `cilium.io`, which the engineer wants to exclude.

It is refused, because `matchName` cannot be used for cluster-internal names and only `matchPattern` is evaluated.

stem: An engineer enables graceful restart on a CiliumBGPPeerConfig but does not set restartTimeSeconds. A Cilium Agent then restarts. How long does the peering router wait, by default, before removing the routes previously advertised by the Cilium BGP control plane?

options.text: 120 seconds
15 seconds
Until the Cilium Agent sends a new BGP OPEN message, with no timer involved
The routes are withdrawn immediately, because no RestartTime was configured

explanation: The excerpt gives the default explicitly: the default value of RestartTime is 120 seconds. The timer starts when the peer receives the TCP FIN and moves to Idle, and the routes are removed when it expires.

optionRationale.b: 15 seconds appears only in the example manifest as an explicitly configured restartTimeSeconds value, not as a default.
optionRationale.c: The peer starts its RestartTime timer on receiving the TCP FIN; the wait is bounded by that timer rather than by the next OPEN message.
optionRationale.d: Graceful restart is what prevents immediate withdrawal; the default timer still applies when restartTimeSeconds is omitted.

stem: A Cilium Agent managing BGP peering is restarted. The peering router receives a TCP FIN on the BGP session. What does the router do, and what happens to traffic in the datapath while the Agent restarts?

options.text: It changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer, while the datapath continues to forward traffic with no disruption.
It immediately withdraws all routes learned from Cilium, and forwarding stops until the Agent reconnects.
It keeps the session in Established state and ignores the FIN until a new BGP OPEN message arrives.
It changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer, but the datapath drops traffic until the session is re-established.

explanation: On receiving the TCP FIN the peer changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer. Because the peering router does not withdraw the routes immediately and the datapath continues to forward traffic during the Agent restart, there is no traffic disruption.

optionRationale.b: Immediate withdrawal is exactly what graceful restart avoids; the peer waits for the RestartTime timer instead.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the peer changes its BGP state to Idle on receiving the TCP FIN, so it does not stay in Established.
optionRationale.d: The state transition and timer are right, but the excerpt states the datapath continues to forward traffic during Agent restart, so there is no disruption.

starts its ``RestartTime`` timer.

stem: A platform team is sizing restartTimeSeconds for a cluster whose Cilium Agents take a variable and, in some cases, lengthy time to boot. What guidance applies to the value they choose?

options.text: Set it to a duration greater than the time taken by the Cilium Agent to boot up.
Set it to a duration shorter than the Agent boot time so that stale routes are cleared promptly.
Set it to exactly 120 seconds, since any other value is ignored by the peer.
Leave it unset, because the peer derives the value from the Agent's measured boot time.

explanation: The excerpt advises that, if using RestartTime, you should set it to a duration greater than the time taken by the Cilium Agent to boot up, since boot up time varies by deployment.

optionRationale.b: A value shorter than the boot time would let the timer expire and the routes be removed before the Agent is back, which is the opposite of the guidance.
optionRationale.c: 120 seconds is only the default; the parameter is configurable and the example sets 15.
optionRationale.d: The peer does not measure boot time; the value is advertised by Cilium and defaults to 120 seconds if not set.

you should set it to a duration greater than the time taken by the Cilium Agent to boot up.

stem: A cluster's Cilium Agent takes roughly 40 seconds to boot after a restart. You want the peering BGP router to keep the routes it learned from the Cilium BGP control plane for as long as possible during that restart, but you also want the peer to remove them if the Agent fails to come back. Which configuration should you apply?

options.text: A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and `restartTimeSeconds: 15`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and `restartTimeSeconds: 60`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: false` and `restartTimeSeconds: 60`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and no `restartTimeSeconds`, relying on the 120-second default

explanation: `RestartTime` is the time advertised to the peer within which the Cilium BGP control plane is expected to re-establish the BGP session after a restart, and on its expiration the peer removes the routes previously advertised. Because the Agent here needs about 40 seconds to boot, the value must be greater than that boot time, so 60 seconds is the suitable choice. A value of 15 seconds would expire before the Agent is back, and the default of 120 seconds is not the tightest fit for the stated requirement.

optionRationale.a: 15 seconds is shorter than the roughly 40-second boot time, so the peer's timer would expire and the routes would be removed before the session is re-established.
optionRationale.c: Graceful restart must be enabled for the capability to be advertised and for the peer to hold routes; disabling it defeats the purpose.
optionRationale.d: The 120-second default is valid, but the question asks for the setting that keeps routes only as long as needed while still covering the boot time, which 60 seconds does more precisely.

options.text: The peer changes its BGP state to `Idle` and starts its `RestartTime` timer, while the datapath continues to forward traffic with no disruption.

In the event of a Cilium Agent restart, the peering BGP router does not withdraw routes received from the Cilium BGP control plane immediately, and the datapath continues to forward traffic during the Agent restart, so there is no traffic disruption.
