stem: A cluster runs in Multi-Pool IPAM mode. A pod is created in a namespace that carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=green-pool, while the pod itself carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=blue-pool. Both pools exist and both have selectors that would match the pod. Which pool is the pod's IP allocated from?

options.text: blue-pool, because the annotation on the pod takes precedence over the annotation on the namespace
green-pool, because the namespace annotation is evaluated first
The default pool, because conflicting annotations are ignored
Allocation fails, because the pod matches more than one pool

explanation: The explicit pool annotation is the first item in the precedence order, and it may be placed either on the pod or on the namespace of the pod. The pod's own annotation is the one that names the pool, so blue-pool is used; the namespace annotation does not override it.

optionRationale.b: The namespace annotation is an alternative place to put the explicit pool name, not a higher-priority source than the pod's own annotation.
optionRationale.c: The default pool is only used when neither the pod nor the namespace has an explicit pool annotation, or when no selectors match.
optionRationale.d: The exactly-one-pool rule applies to matching pools via selectors; here the pool is named explicitly by annotation.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
You can explicitly name the pool for a pod using the ``ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=<pool-name>`` annotation, 
     either on the pod or the namespace of the pod.

stem: An engineer wants pods in namespace `empire` to draw IPv4 addresses from one pool and IPv6 addresses from a different pool, without relying on label selectors. Which annotations should be set?

options.text: ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool for both families, applied twice
ipam.cilium.io/ipv4-pool=<pool-name> and ipam.cilium.io/ipv6-pool=<pool-name>
ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" together with ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool
spec.podSelector and spec.namespaceSelector on the CiliumPodIPPool

explanation: The excerpt states that different pools can be specified for IPv4 and IPv6 using the ipv4-pool and ipv6-pool annotations. These can be placed on the pod or on its namespace.

optionRationale.a: The plain ip-pool annotation names a single pool; the per-family variants exist precisely to name different pools for each family.
optionRationale.c: require-pool-match only blocks allocation until a non-default pool matches; it does not select per-family pools.
optionRationale.d: Selectors are the second precedence step, not the way to name different pools per IP family.

     ``ipam.cilium.io/ipv4-pool=<pool-name>`` and ``ipam.cilium.io/ipv6-pool=<pool-name>`` annotations.

stem: A CiliumPodIPPool defines both spec.podSelector and spec.namespaceSelector. A pod carries labels matching the podSelector, but its namespace does not match the namespaceSelector. What is the result when the pod requests an IP?

options.text: The pod gets an IP from the pool, because matching either selector is sufficient
The pod gets an IP from the pool only if it also carries the ip-pool annotation
The pod is not allocated an IP from that pool, because both the pod and its namespace must match their respective selectors
IP allocation fails with an error because the selectors conflict

explanation: When both selectors are defined, both the pod and its namespace must match their respective selectors for the pod to be allocated an IP from the pool. A namespace mismatch therefore disqualifies the pod from that pool.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt requires both to match, not either.
optionRationale.b: The annotation is a separate, higher-precedence mechanism; it is not a condition for selector matching.
optionRationale.d: Allocation failure with a logged error occurs when a pod matches more than one pool, not when a selector does not match.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
If both selectors are defined, both the pod and its namespace must match 
     their respective selectors in order for the pod to be allocated an IP from the pool.

stem: A pool's selectors are intended to match a newly created pod, but at the moment of IP allocation Cilium does not yet know about that pool. The pod has no explicit pool annotation. What happens, and how can the engineer prevent it?

options.text: Allocation fails; set ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" to allow the default pool as a fallback
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; set ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" on the pod or namespace to block allocation until a non-default pool matches
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; set spec.allowFirstIP to true on the pool to prevent this
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; nothing can change this behaviour

explanation: The excerpt states that when the pool is not known to Cilium at allocation time, whether from race conditions or misconfiguration, the pod receives an IP from the default pool. The require-pool-match annotation blocks allocation until the pod matches a non-default pool.

optionRationale.a: Allocation does not fail in this case; it falls back to the default pool, and require-pool-match blocks rather than permits the fallback.
optionRationale.c: allowFirstIP controls whether the first address of an allocated CIDR is allocatable; it has nothing to do with pool selection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly offers require-pool-match as a way to change this behaviour.

In the case that your pool is not known to Cilium at the time of IP allocation, either due to race conditions or 
     misconfiguration, the pod will be allocated an IP from the default pool.

stem: Two CiliumPodIPPool resources have overlapping selectors, and a pod matches both of them for the same IP family. What is the outcome?

options.text: The pod receives an IP from the pool with the lowest name in alphabetical order
The pod receives an IP from the default pool
IP allocation fails and an error is logged
The pod receives one IP from each matching pool

explanation: A pod must match exactly one pool for a given IP family. If it matches more than one pool, IP allocation fails and an error is logged, which is why overlapping selectors must be avoided.

optionRationale.a: No tie-breaking by name is described; multiple matches are an error.
optionRationale.b: The default pool is the fallback when no selectors match or no annotation is present, not when several pools match.
optionRationale.d: A pod does not receive an address from each matching pool; the multiple match is rejected.

stem: An operator changes the value of the ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool annotation on a pod that is already running, hoping to move it to another pool. What is the effect?

options.text: The pod is immediately re-allocated an IP from the newly named pool
The pod keeps its IP until the next restart, at which point the new pool is used
The change has no effect, because the annotations are only considered when a pod is created
The change causes IP allocation to fail and an error to be logged

explanation: The excerpt states that the annotations are only considered when a pod is created, and that changing the ip-pool annotation on an already running pod has no effect.

optionRationale.a: No re-allocation occurs for a running pod.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives no such restart behaviour; the annotation simply has no effect on the running pod.
optionRationale.d: An error is logged when a pod matches more than one pool, not when an annotation is changed on a running pod.

citations.quote:
The annotations are only considered when a pod is created. Changing the ``ip-pool``
annotation on an already running pod has no effect.

stem: A cluster runs in Multi-Pool IPAM mode. A pod is created in a namespace that carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=blue-pool, but the pod itself carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=green-pool. Both pools exist and both have free addresses. Which pool is the pod's IP allocated from?

options.text: green-pool, because the annotation on the pod takes precedence over the annotation on its namespace
blue-pool, because the namespace annotation is evaluated before the pod annotation
The default pool, because conflicting annotations cause the explicit pool selection to be ignored
Neither pool: allocation fails because the pod matches two pools

explanation: The explicit pool annotation is the first item in the precedence order, and it may be placed either on the pod or on the namespace of the pod. The pod's own annotation is the one that names the pool for that pod, so green-pool is used. The failure case for matching more than one pool concerns label selectors, not annotations: a pod must match exactly one pool for a given IP family, and overlapping selectors are what cause allocation to fail.

optionRationale.b: The namespace annotation is an alternative place to put the explicit pool name, not an earlier step in the precedence order; the pod's own annotation names the pool.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the precedence order makes conflicting annotations fall back to the default pool; the default pool is used only when there is no explicit annotation and no selector match.
optionRationale.d: The 'exactly one pool' rule applies to matching pools via selectors; overlapping selectors are what make allocation fail, not an annotation on the pod.

stem: An operator is creating a CiliumPodIPPool with a /24 IPv4 CIDR and wants the very first address of that CIDR to be handed out to pods rather than reserved. Which field must be set to true when the pool is created?

options.text: spec.allowFirstIP
spec.allowLastIP
spec.ipv4.maskSize
spec.ipam.pools.requested

explanation: By default the first and last address of each allocated CIDR from a CiliumPodIPPool are reserved. Setting spec.allowFirstIP to true when creating the pool makes the first address allocatable independently of the last. Note that this field, like spec.allowLastIP, is immutable, so it must be set at creation time.

optionRationale.b: spec.allowLastIP controls the last address of the CIDR, not the first.
optionRationale.c: maskSize sets the size of the per-node PodCIDRs carved from the pool; it does not control whether the first address is reserved.
optionRationale.d: spec.ipam.pools.requested is a field of the CiliumNode resource listing per-node pool requests, not a field of CiliumPodIPPool.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
By default, the first and last address of each allocated CIDR from a
``CiliumPodIPPool`` are reserved and cannot be allocated. Set
``spec.allowFirstIP`` or ``spec.allowLastIP`` to ``true`` when creating the pool
to make either address allocatable independently.

stem: A cluster's nodes each have a different default gateway address, and the network team does not want to enumerate every node's peer address in the Cilium BGP configuration. They add a peer named "tor-switch" with peerASN 65000 and set autoDiscovery mode to "DefaultGateway" with addressFamily ipv6. What must the ToR switches be configured with so that Cilium's nodes can establish sessions?

options.text: A static neighbor entry for every Cilium node address, listed individually under the peer group.
A "bgp listen range" covering the relevant IP prefix, so the switch accepts sessions from a range of addresses.
A separate peer group per Cilium node, each with its own local ASN.
An eBGP multihop configuration with a TTL greater than one on each Cilium node.

explanation: Default gateway auto-discovery removes the need to know each node's exact peer address, but the ToR switch must be told to accept dynamic neighbours. The excerpt states that ToR switches must be configured with "bgp listen range" to support dynamic BGP neighbours, which lets the switch accept sessions from a specific IP prefix range.

optionRationale.a: This is precisely what auto-discovery is designed to avoid; the switch listens on a prefix range instead of knowing each node address.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt requires each ToR switch to be configured with the same local ASN, not a per-node peer group with differing ASNs.
optionRationale.d: Multihop TTL is not mentioned anywhere in the requirements for default gateway auto-discovery.

attachments.title: Peer configuration using default gateway auto-discovery
attachments.body:
peers:
 - name: "tor-switch"
   peerASN: 65000
   autoDiscovery:
     mode: "DefaultGateway"
     defaultGateway:
       addressFamily: ipv6  # Can be "ipv4" or "ipv6"
   peerConfigRef:
     name: "cilium-peer"

stem: An engineer applies the peer configuration below on every node in a cluster. On one node the default gateway for the IPv6 address family is a link-local address. What is the outcome for that node?

options.text: Cilium establishes the BGP session using the link-local address as the peer address.
Cilium falls back to the IPv4 default gateway and establishes the session there.
The link-local address is not supported as a default gateway, so no session is established on that basis.
Cilium establishes the session but ignores the peerConfigRef session parameters.

explanation: The excerpt closes with an explicit limitation: a link-local address as default gateway is not supported. A node whose discovered IPv6 default gateway is link-local therefore cannot use it for auto-discovered peering.

optionRationale.a: Directly contradicted by the stated limitation on link-local default gateways.
optionRationale.b: Nothing in the excerpt describes falling back to the other address family; the address family is fixed by the configuration.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the peer configuration referenced by peerConfigRef is used for session parameters, with no exception for link-local gateways.

peerASN, with the address family set under peerConfigRef.

stem: After the peer configuration with autoDiscovery mode "DefaultGateway" is applied, what does Cilium do on each node?

options.text: It discovers the default gateway for the specified address family and establishes a BGP session with it, using the peer configuration referenced by peerConfigRef.
It waits for the ToR switch to initiate a session and then adopts the switch's session parameters.
It peers with every address in the ToR switch's listen range simultaneously.
It discovers the default gateway but requires a manually created session before traffic flows.

explanation: The excerpt lists the behaviour once the configuration is applied: Cilium determines the default gateway for the specified address family on each node, automatically establishes a BGP session with the discovered gateway, and uses the peer configuration referenced by peerConfigRef for session parameters.

optionRationale.b: Cilium establishes the session itself rather than waiting to be contacted.
optionRationale.c: The listen range is a switch-side setting for accepting dynamic neighbours; Cilium peers with the discovered gateway.
optionRationale.d: The session is established automatically, not manually.

router bgp 65100 with neighbor CILIUM peer-group and bgp listen range fd00:10:0:1::/64 without a peer group reference.
router bgp 65100 with a separate peer group per Cilium node and no listen range.

optionRationale.c: The example binds the listen range to the peer group with peer-group CILIUM.
optionRationale.d: Per-node peer groups and the absence of a listen range contradict the stated requirements.

stem: A platform team wants Cilium's BGP control plane to announce Service virtual IPs to an upstream router so that clients outside the cluster can reach those Services directly. Which combination of fields must appear in a CiliumBGPAdvertisement resource to achieve this?

options.text: Set `advertisementType` to `Service` and set `service.addresses` to one or more of `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` or `ExternalIP`.
Set `advertisementType` to `PodCIDR` and set `service.addresses` to `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` or `ExternalIP`.
Set `advertisementType` to `Service` and set `service.addresses` to `IngressIP`, `NodePort` or `ExternalIP`.
Set `advertisementType` to `Service` and set `service.addresses` to `ClusterIP` only, because the other address kinds are advertised automatically.

explanation: The excerpt states that to advertise the service virtual IPs you specify the `advertisementType` field as `Service` and the `service.addresses` field as `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` or `ExternalIP`. The selector then narrows which Services are covered.

optionRationale.b: `PodCIDR` is not the advertisement type used for Service virtual IPs; the excerpt names `Service` as the value of `advertisementType` for this purpose.
optionRationale.c: `IngressIP` and `NodePort` are not among the address kinds listed; the permitted values are `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` and `ExternalIP`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt presents `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` and `ExternalIP` as alternatives you choose from, not as something advertised automatically alongside `ClusterIP`.

The node's primary interface subnet, so that the whole subnet is routed to the advertising node.

stem: An engineer applies the CiliumBGPAdvertisement shown in the attachment. Which Services will have their virtual IPs advertised?

options.text: Services whose labels satisfy the `matchExpressions` entry requiring the label `bgp` to have the value `blue`.

stem: An engineer configures Cilium to advertise a Service's virtual IP from every node in a large cluster so that traffic is spread across nodes. The upstream router supports ECMP. What should the engineer confirm with the network administrator before enabling this?

options.text: That the router's ECMP path limit is high enough for the number of nodes advertising the VIP, since exceeding it is possible when advertising from many nodes.
That the router accepts /24 prefixes, because Cilium advertises the whole Service subnet rather than individual VIPs.
That the router can perform DNAT on the Service VIP, because Cilium does not translate traffic for advertised VIPs.
That the router supports BGP graceful restart, because Cilium withdraws and re-advertises the VIP on every node failover.

explanation: Advertising the same virtual IPs from multiple nodes lets ECMP load-balance traffic to the Service, but many routers cap the number of ECMP paths they can hold. Advertising from many nodes may exceed that cap, so the limit should be checked with the network administrator first.

optionRationale.b: Cilium advertises exact routes for the VIPs as /32 or /128 prefixes, not a broader subnet prefix.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes direct access to the Service from outside the cluster via advertised VIPs and says nothing about the router performing DNAT.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium 1.18. An engineer applies a CiliumNetworkPolicy that uses the fromRequires field to establish base label requirements for endpoints labelled env=prod. What is the status of this field in that release?

options.text: It is deprecated, and it has been removed as of Cilium 1.19.
It is fully supported and is the recommended way to express base label requirements.
It was removed in Cilium 1.17 and replaced by fromEndpoints.
It is only honoured for egress policies, having been dropped for ingress.

explanation: The fromRequires and toRequires fields are deprecated as of Cilium 1.17.x and have been removed as of Cilium 1.19. On a 1.18 cluster the field is therefore deprecated but not yet removed, so a policy using it is on borrowed time.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states the fields are deprecated as of 1.17.x and removed as of 1.19, so they are not a recommended construct in 1.18.
optionRationale.c: The removal is stated as of Cilium 1.19, not 1.17; 1.17.x is when the deprecation began.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt treats fromRequires (ingress) and toRequires (egress) symmetrically and gives no indication that fromRequires was dropped for ingress only.

stem: An engineer wants any endpoint carrying env=prod to be reachable only from sources that also carry env=prod, and wants this requirement to hold regardless of what other ingress rules in the cluster allow. Which field establishes such a base requirement, and what does it do on its own?

options.text: fromRequires; it sets constraints that must be met for the selected endpoints to be reachable, but grants no access by itself.
fromEndpoints; it both sets the base requirement and grants access to matching sources in a single rule.
fromRequires; it grants access to every source that matches the requirement, without needing any further rule.
toRequires; it sets the ingress base requirement, while fromRequires is reserved for egress.

explanation: The fromRequires field establishes label requirements which serve as a foundation for any fromEndpoints relationship. It is a list of additional constraints which must be met in order for the selected endpoints to be reachable, and these constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves — traffic is only allowed when rules matching fromEndpoints are also present.

optionRationale.b: fromEndpoints is the rule that grants access; the base requirement is the job of fromRequires, and the excerpt explicitly says fromRequires needs to be combined with other rules.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that fromRequires does not grant access privileges by itself and that the rule allows nothing on its own.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt pairs fromRequires with fromEndpoints for ingress and toRequires with toEndpoints for egress, so the roles are the other way round.

be met in order for the selected endpoints to be reachable. These additional
constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves, so to allow traffic
there must also be rules which match ``fromEndpoints``.

stem: A scalability test creates 250 CiliumNetworkPolicies in a single namespace, each selecting all pods in that namespace and each allowing a disjoint set of ports. After all 250 are in place, what is the effect on the memory usage of the Cilium agents?

options.text: Memory usage grows roughly linearly with the number of policies, because each policy adds entries to the eBPF policy maps.
Memory usage is not significantly affected, because the eBPF policy maps have a constant size once a pod is initialized.
Memory usage stays flat only while the policies are L4; adding L7 rules causes the policy maps to be resized per policy.
Memory usage drops, because the policies are merged into a single map entry per namespace.

explanation: The report states that increasing the number of policies does not have a significant impact on Cilium's memory usage, since the eBPF policy maps have a constant size once a pod is initialized. The 250 policies therefore do not inflate memory in proportion to their count.

optionRationale.a: This is the intuitive but wrong assumption the report explicitly rules out: the maps are of constant size once a pod is initialized, so policy count does not drive memory growth.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt makes no distinction between L4 and L7 with respect to map sizing; the constant-size statement is given for the eBPF policy maps generally.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt describes merging policies into one map entry per namespace; the maps are simply of constant size.

stem: During a scalability test, 250 CiliumNetworkPolicies are created sequentially with `kubectl create`, so the convergence time cannot be computed properly. The report suggests an alternative so that convergence time can be measured. Which change does it recommend?

options.text: Create the policies in parallel rather than sequentially, so that all 250 arrive at the agents at the same moment.
Use a single CiliumNetworkPolicy with multiple policy rules defined under the `specs` field instead of the `spec` field.
Split the 250 policies across several namespaces so that each agent receives a smaller batch.
Replace the CiliumNetworkPolicies with CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicies so that a single object covers all pods.

explanation: Because the 250 policies were created sequentially, the report says convergence time cannot be properly computed, and that this could be done by using a single CNP with multiple policy rules defined under the `specs` field rather than the `spec` field.

options.text: Add a matchExpressions entry with key io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster and operator Exists to the toEndpoints selector.
Add a matchLabels entry setting io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster to the local cluster name.
Leave the selector unchanged and set the cluster-name ConfigMap option to a wildcard value.
Add a toEndpoints entry for each remote cluster, each with io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster set to that cluster's name.

explanation: The excerpt shows a policy that explicitly allows pods to communicate to all clusters by adding a matchExpressions clause with key io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster and operator Exists to the toEndpoints selector. Because policies otherwise select endpoints from the local cluster only unless one or multiple clusters are specifically targeted, the Exists expression is what widens the selection to every cluster.

options.text: Because each component can only have one Prometheus scrape and port annotation, so Envoy needs its own service.
Because Envoy metrics are only exposed when ServiceMonitor is disabled, and the annotations are removed otherwise.
Because the headless service is required to give the Cilium agent pods a stable cluster IP for scraping.
Because Prometheus can only discover pods, not services, through the `kubernetes-pods` role.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the additional headless service is needed because each component can only have one Prometheus scrape and port annotation, so the Envoy port cannot simply be added alongside the component's own annotation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not tie Envoy metrics to the ServiceMonitor setting in this way.
optionRationale.c: A headless service deliberately has no cluster IP, so this contradicts the term used.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not claim Prometheus can only discover pods; it describes the headless service as carrying the scrape annotation.

stem: An engineer configures Prometheus with a `kubernetes-pods` job using the `pod` role and the relabel rules shown, expecting Cilium and Envoy metrics to be picked up automatically. Which relabel configuration makes that automatic discovery work?

options.text: A `keep` rule on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape` with regex `true`, plus a `replace` rule combining `__address__` and `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` into `__address__`.
A `keep` rule on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` with regex `true`, plus a `replace` rule writing the port into `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape`.

A `drop` rule on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape` with regex `true`, plus a `replace` rule combining `__address__` and `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` into `__address__`.
A `keep` rule on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape` with regex `true`, plus a `replace` rule writing `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` into the `job` label.

explanation: The excerpt shows the `scrape_configs` snippet in which a `keep` action filters on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape` with regex `true`, and a `replace` action uses `__address__` together with `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` to set `__address__`. With that configuration Prometheus picks up the Cilium and Envoy metrics automatically.

optionRationale.b: The keep rule is applied to the scrape annotation, not the port annotation, and the replace rule targets `__address__`.
optionRationale.c: A `drop` action would discard the very pods carrying the scrape annotation.
optionRationale.d: The replace rule sets `__address__`, not the `job` label.

attachments.title: Prometheus scrape configuration
attachments.body:
scrape_configs:
 - job_name: 'kubernetes-pods'
   kubernetes_sd_configs:
   - role: pod
   relabel_configs:
     - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape]
       action: keep
       regex: true
     - source_labels: [__address__, __meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port]
       action: replace
       regex: ([^:]+)(?::\d+)?;(\d+)
       replacement: ${1}:${2}
       target_label: __address__

stem: A platform team runs the Cilium Gateway API implementation and wants to route traffic to a multi-cluster service through an HTTPRoute. Which backend reference does the route need in order for Cilium's Gateway API implementation to accept it?

options.text: A backendRef of kind ServiceImport whose ServiceImport carries the annotation multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service and is associated with an underlying Service
A backendRef of kind Service with the group multicluster.x-k8s.io, pointing at the local headless Service
A backendRef of kind EndpointSlice, since Cilium resolves all multi-cluster backends through EndpointSlice objects
A backendRef of kind ServiceImport with no annotation, because Cilium derives the backing Service automatically from the ServiceImport name

explanation: The excerpt states that the Cilium Gateway API implementation only supports MCS-API implementations that use an underlying Service associated with a ServiceImport, and that the ServiceImport must carry the annotation `multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service`. The sample HTTPRoute therefore uses a backendRef of group multicluster.x-k8s.io and kind ServiceImport.

optionRationale.b: The backendRef in the sample uses group multicluster.x-k8s.io with kind ServiceImport, not a plain Service in that group.
optionRationale.c: EndpointSlice is mentioned only in connection with alternate Gateway API implementations that rely on it, not as a backendRef kind for Cilium's own implementation.
optionRationale.d: The annotation multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service is explicitly required on ServiceImport resources; it is not derived automatically.

attachments.title: HTTPRoute using a ServiceImport backend
attachments.body:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
   name: rebel-base-mcsapi
   namespace: default
spec:
   parentRefs:
   - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
     kind: Gateway
     name: my-gateway
     namespace: default
   rules:
   - backendRefs:
     - group: multicluster.x-k8s.io
       kind: ServiceImport
       name: rebel-base-mcsapi
       port: 80
     matches:
     - method: GET
       path:
         type: PathPrefix
         value: /

It supports only MCS-API implementations from other vendors, not Cilium's own

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with VXLAN enabled and the underlying network has an MTU of 1500. A KataPod is deployed and its inner eth0 receives the device MTU from the outer namespace, but the default route MTU is not carried over. What is the most likely consequence for traffic between this KataPod and traditional pods?

options.text: The KataPod's inner route MTU is silently raised to the device MTU, so no fragmentation occurs but throughput is capped.
Performance degradation or packet drops may occur due to multiple unexpected fragmentation.
Cilium refuses to attach the KataPod to the endpoint and the pod stays in Pending.
The outer eth0 device MTU is reduced by Kata to compensate, so the KataPod behaves identically to a traditional pod.

explanation: Kata copies only the outer eth0 device MTU into the inner namespace and ignores the default route MTU. Because the route MTU is not adjusted for the Cilium overhead, connections can suffer fragmentation, giving performance degradation or packet drops between traditional pods and KataPods.

optionRationale.a: Nothing in the excerpt says the route MTU is raised to the device MTU; the point is that the route MTU adjustment is ignored, which causes fragmentation rather than preventing it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes a performance and fragmentation problem, not an attachment or scheduling failure.
optionRationale.d: Kata copies the device MTU over; it does not reduce the outer MTU to compensate for the missing route MTU.

attachments.title: Kata networking behaviour
attachments.body:
However, during the inner Container Networking Namespace creation (i.e., the pod
inside the VM), only the outer ``eth0 device MTU`` (1) is copied over by Kata to
the inner ``eth0``, while the ``default route MTU`` (2) is ignored.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
only the outer ``eth0 device MTU`` (1) is copied over by Kata to
   the inner ``eth0``, while the ``default route MTU`` (2) is ignored. For this reason,
   depending on the types of connections, users might experience performance degradation
   or even packet drops between traditional pods and KataPod connections due to
   multiple (unexpected) fragmentation.

stem: An engineer wants to fix fragmentation for KataPods on a Cilium VXLAN cluster without affecting traditional pod-to-pod or pod-to-node traffic. Which approach does the documentation prefer, and why?

options.text: Lower the MTU in the Cilium ConfigMap, because it applies uniformly and is therefore the safest option.
Add an initContainer with NET_ADMIN to the KataPod deployment to adjust the route MTU inside the inner pod, because it is self-contained and does not harm other connection types.
Disable VXLAN and switch to WireGuard, because WireGuard adds no overhead to the route MTU.
Set the runtimeClassName to kata-clh, because that runtime automatically computes the route MTU from the device MTU.

explanation: The excerpt lists two workarounds and states that (b) is preferred: modifying the KataPod deployment by adding an initContainer with NET_ADMIN to adjust the route MTU inside the inner pod. This aligns the KataPod with other pods and, being self-contained in the KataPod, does not harm other connection types.

optionRationale.a: Lowering the MTU in the Cilium ConfigMap is workaround (a) and is explicitly not recommended because it affects all other communications through a lower device MTU on all Cilium-managed interfaces.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives WireGuard as an example of additional overhead (+80B), not as a way to remove overhead.
optionRationale.d: kata-clh is only the runtimeClassName used in the example deployment; the excerpt does not say it computes the route MTU.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
b. modify the KataPod deployment by adding an ``initContainer`` (with NET_ADMIN)
   to adjust the route MTU inside the inner pod. This would not only align the
   KataPod configuration to all the other pods, but also it would not harm
   all the other types of connections, given that it is a self-contained
   solution in the KataPod itself.

stem: On a cluster with only Cilium VXLAN enabled and an underlying network MTU of 1500, an engineer is writing an initContainer to set the route MTU inside a KataPod. Which value should the route MTU be set to?
explanation: The route MTU is computed as device MTU minus overhead. For VXLAN the overhead is 50B, so on a 1500 MTU network the route MTU is 1500B - 50B = 1450.

optionRationale.a: 1500 is the device MTU, not the route MTU; the route MTU must account for the VXLAN overhead.
optionRationale.c: 1420 corresponds to an 80B overhead, which the excerpt associates with WireGuard, not VXLAN.
optionRationale.d: 1550 adds the overhead instead of subtracting it.

attachments.title: Example KataPod deployment
attachments.body:
apiVersion: v1
   kind: Pod
   metadata:
     name: nginx-pod
     labels:
       app: nginx
   spec:
     runtimeClassName: kata-clh
     containers:
       - name: nginx
         image: nginx:latest
         ports:
           - containerPort: 80
     initContainers:
       - name: set-mtu
         image: busybox:latest
         command:
           - sh
           - -c
           - |
             DEFAULT="$(ip route show default)"
             ip route replace "$DEFAULT" mtu 1450
         securityContext:
           capabilities:
             add:
               - NET_ADMIN

stem: An engineer needs to determine the correct route MTU value to configure inside a KataPod. Where can this value be obtained?

options.text: By issuing ip route on a Cilium Pod or inside a traditional pod.
By reading the device MTU from the KataPod's inner eth0 interface.
By inspecting the Cilium ConfigMap for the default route MTU entry.
By running ip route inside the KataPod's inner namespace after Kata has copied the outer values.

explanation: The excerpt states the correct route MTU can be either manually computed or retrieved by issuing ip route on a Cilium Pod (or inside a traditional pod).

optionRationale.b: The inner eth0 only receives the device MTU, not the route MTU, so it does not give the correct value.
optionRationale.c: The ConfigMap holds the device MTU setting, not the computed default route MTU.
optionRationale.d: The inner namespace is exactly where the route MTU is missing, so reading it there does not yield the correct value.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
The correct ``route MTU`` value to set can be
   either manually computed or retrieved by issuing ``ip route`` on a Cilium Pod
   (or inside a traditional pod).

stem: When Cilium creates the outer Container Networking Namespace for a KataPod, which two actions does the Cilium CNI perform?

options.text: It creates eth0 with the underlying device MTU and adjusts the default route MTU to device MTU minus overhead.
It creates eth0 with the route MTU and leaves the device MTU at the Kata default.
It creates a veth pair inside the VM and sets the inner route MTU to match the outer route MTU.
It copies the outer route MTU into the inner namespace and disables fragmentation reporting.

explanation: On outer namespace creation Cilium creates the eth0 interface with the same device MTU as the detected underlying network or the MTU in the Cilium ConfigMap, and adjusts the default route MTU (device MTU minus overhead) for the Cilium configuration overhead.

optionRationale.b: The device MTU is set from the underlying network or ConfigMap, not from the route MTU.
optionRationale.c: Cilium does not set the inner route MTU; Kata ignores the outer route MTU when creating the inner namespace.
optionRationale.d: The outer route MTU is not copied into the inner namespace, which is the root of the fragmentation problem.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
1. creates the ``eth0`` interface with the same ``device MTU`` of either the detected
   underlying network, or the MTU specified in the Cilium ConfigMap;
2. adjusts the ``default route MTU`` (computed as ``device MTU - overhead``) to account
   for the additional networking overhead given by the Cilium configuration

stem: How does the Kata runtime's networking design differ from that of a traditional pod in terms of namespaces?

options.text: Kata runs the pod directly in the outer namespace with no additional namespace.
Kata adds an additional layer of abstraction inside the outer namespace by creating an isolated VM with an additional inner Container Networking Namespace to host the pod.
Kata replaces the Cilium-created namespace with a host namespace shared by all KataPods.
Kata creates the outer namespace itself and bypasses the Cilium CNI entirely.

explanation: Because of its different networking design, the Kata runtime adds an additional layer of abstraction inside the Container Networking Namespace created by Cilium (the outer namespace), creating an isolated VM with an additional inner Container Networking Namespace to host the requested pod.

optionRationale.a: Kata does create an additional inner namespace; it does not run the pod directly in the outer namespace.
optionRationale.c: The outer namespace is created by Cilium, and Kata adds an inner namespace rather than replacing it with a shared host namespace.
optionRationale.d: The outer namespace is created by Cilium, and the Cilium CNI performs actions upon its creation.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
the Kata runtime adds an additional layer of abstraction inside the Container
Networking Namespace created by Cilium (referred to as "outer"). In that
namespace, Kata creates an isolated VM with an additional Container Networking
Namespace (referred to as "inside") to host the requested Pod

stem: A platform engineer applies the following Gateway manifest to a cluster running Cilium. What address does the Gateway report once it has been reconciled?

options.text: 172.18.0.140, because spec.addresses takes precedence over the infrastructure annotation
172.18.0.141, because the io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips annotation is used and spec.addresses is ignored
No address is reported, because the two conflicting IP specifications cause the Gateway to fail validation
Both addresses are reported, because Cilium allocates one address per listener

explanation: When the io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips annotation is present in spec.infrastructure.annotations, it is the annotation that determines the address and the spec.addresses field is ignored. The documented output for exactly this configuration shows ADDRESS 172.18.0.141, so the value in spec.addresses (172.18.0.140) never takes effect.

optionRationale.a: This inverts the documented precedence: the annotation wins and spec.addresses is ignored, not the other way round.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes no validation failure; the configuration is accepted and simply resolves to the annotation's address.
optionRationale.d: The Gateway reports a single ADDRESS column value, and the excerpt shows only 172.18.0.141 for this manifest.

attachments.title: The Gateway under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
 kind: Gateway
 metadata:
   name: my-gateway
 spec:
   infrastructure:
     annotations:
       io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips: "172.18.0.141"
   addresses: # This will be ignored
   - type: IPAddress
     value: 172.18.0.140 
   gatewayClassName: cilium
   listeners:
   - allowedRoutes:
       namespaces:
         from: Same
     name: web-gw
     port: 80
     protocol: HTTP

If you are already using the ``io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips`` in the ``spec.infrastructure.annotations`` to 
specify the IP, the ``spec.addresses`` field will be ignored.

stem: An engineer wants to pin a Cilium Gateway to a specific IP address using the Gateway API's spec.addresses field. Which address type does Cilium support for this field?

options.text: IPAddress only
IPAddress and Hostname
IPAddress, Hostname and NamedAddress
Any type defined by the Gateway API specification

explanation: Cilium's support for spec.addresses is deliberately narrow: only the IPAddress type is supported, and the address is expected to come from LB-IPAM. Other address types permitted by the Gateway API specification are not handled.

optionRationale.b: Hostname is a Gateway API address type, but the excerpt states that only IPAddress is supported.
optionRationale.c: NamedAddress is not mentioned as supported; the excerpt restricts support to IPAddress alone.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly narrows the specification's set of address types to one, so not every type is supported.

citations.title: Gateway API Addresses Support
citations.quote: The feature only supports IPAddress type of addresses, and works with the LB-IPAM.

stem: A client pod called mediabot sends traffic to the nginx-service ClusterIP. You run `hubble observe --all` and see a flow from `default/mediabot` to `default/nginx-service:80` marked `pre-xlate-fwd TRACED`, immediately followed by a flow to `default/nginx:80` marked `post-xlate-fwd TRANSLATED`. What do these two events represent?

options.text: The datapath events before and after socket load-balancing translation between the service and the selected service endpoint.
A DNS resolution of the service name followed by the resulting connection to the backend pod.
A policy verdict denying the first flow and allowing the second flow after the endpoint is selected.
The reverse direction of an established connection, first traced and then translated back to the client.

explanation: Hubble prints datapath events before and after socket LB translation between the service and the selected service endpoint, which is exactly what the `pre-xlate-fwd` and `post-xlate-fwd` pair shows: the flow to the service address is traced, then the translated flow to the backend pod is shown.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes socket LB translation between service and endpoint, not DNS resolution; no DNS event appears in the output.
optionRationale.c: The events are marked TRACED and TRANSLATED, not as policy verdicts; the excerpt does not describe a denial.
optionRationale.d: The reverse direction is shown by the `pre-xlate-rev` and `post-xlate-rev` events, not by the forward pair described here.

stem: A client pod called mediabot is sending traffic to the nginx-service ClusterIP. You run `hubble observe --all` and see the flows, but the cilium agent logs contain the message `Failed to setup socket load-balancing tracing with Hubble.` You still want to see the pre- and post-translation datapath events for this socket. What should you do?

options.text: Trace the packets with `cilium-dbg monitor` instead, for example using `-v -t trace-sock`.
Re-run `hubble observe --all` with the `--all` flag removed so that only translated flows are shown.
Run `crictl inspectp -o=json $POD_ID | grep cgroup` on the node and re-enable Hubble socket LB tracing with the resulting path.
Use `kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=PodName:.metadata.name,PodUID:.metadata.uid` to map the socket cookie to the pod, then re-run Hubble.

explanation: The excerpt states that socket LB tracing with Hubble requires the cilium agent to detect pod cgroup paths, and that if the agent reports `Failed to setup socket load-balancing tracing with Hubble.` you can trace packets using `cilium-dbg monitor` instead. The example shows `cilium-dbg monitor -v -t trace-sock` producing the pre-xlate-fwd, post-xlate-fwd, pre-xlate-rev and post-xlate-rev events.

optionRationale.b: Dropping `--all` does not address the failure to set up socket load-balancing tracing; the excerpt offers `cilium-dbg monitor` as the alternative, not a different Hubble flag combination.
optionRationale.c: The `crictl inspectp` command is given only for gathering the cgroup path to include in a GitHub issue, not as a way to re-enable Hubble socket LB tracing.
optionRationale.d: The PodUID column is used to correlate a cgroup id with a pod's cgroup path; it does not restore Hubble socket LB tracing.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium 1.9 with default settings. A pod is selected by a CiliumNetworkPolicy that allows ingress on port 80/TCP from a particular client pod, and it is also selected by a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that denies ingress on port 80/TCP from that same client pod. What is the result for a connection from that client to port 80 on the server pod?

options.text: The connection is denied, because deny policies take precedence over allow policies.
The connection is allowed, because the allow policy is more specific than the clusterwide deny policy.
The connection is allowed, because deny policies must be enabled explicitly and are not active by default in 1.9.
The connection is denied only if the client pod is also selected by a policy, because the server pod stays in default-allow mode.

explanation: Deny policies take precedence over allow policies, and this holds regardless of whether the policies involved are Cilium Network Policies, Clusterwide Cilium Network Policies or even Kubernetes Network Policies. The allow on 80/TCP therefore cannot override the deny on the same port. Deny policies have also been available and enabled by default since Cilium 1.9, so no extra enablement step is needed.

optionRationale.b: Precedence does not depend on the scope or specificity of the policy: deny wins over allow whether the policy is a Cilium Network Policy, a Clusterwide Cilium Network Policy or a Kubernetes Network Policy.
optionRationale.c: Deny policies are available and enabled by default since Cilium 1.9, so the deny is active without any opt-in.
optionRationale.d: Pods enter default-deny mode as soon as a single policy selects them, so the server pod does not remain in a default-allow state once it is selected.

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:
Deny policies take precedence over allow policies, regardless of whether they
are a Cilium Network Policy, a Clusterwide Cilium Network Policy or even a
Kubernetes Network Policy.

stem: An administrator applies the following policy. Which statement describes its effect?

options.text: Ingress from the world entity is denied on all pods managed by Cilium in all namespaces, while traffic from everywhere else, including existing inter-cluster policies, is still allowed.
All ingress to every pod is denied, because the endpointSelector is empty and therefore matches everything.
Ingress from the world entity is denied only in the namespace where the policy is created, because it is a namespaced CiliumNetworkPolicy.
Ingress from the world entity is denied, and all other ingress is also denied because no allow rule is present.

explanation: The policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy with an empty endpointSelector, so it applies to all pods managed by Cilium in all namespaces. Its ingressDeny blocks the world entity, while the ingress rule allows the all entity, so traffic from everywhere except world continues to be permitted and existing inter-cluster policies are still allowed.

optionRationale.b: The empty endpointSelector widens the set of selected pods, but the policy denies only the world entity rather than all ingress.
optionRationale.c: The resource is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, not a namespaced CiliumNetworkPolicy, so its effect is cluster-wide.
optionRationale.d: The policy includes an ingress rule allowing the all entity, so other ingress is not denied.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "external-lockdown"
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}
  ingressDeny:
  - fromEntities:
    - "world"
  ingress:
  - fromEntities:
    - "all"

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:
The following policy will deny ingress from "world" on all namespaces on all
Pods managed by Cilium. Existing inter-cluster policies will still be allowed
as this policy is allowing traffic from everywhere except from "world".

stem: A team wants to write a deny policy that blocks requests to a specific URL path on an otherwise allowed service, and another that blocks traffic to a specific external domain name. What does Cilium support here?

options.text: Neither is supported: deny policies cannot enforce at Layer 7, so a URL cannot be specifically denied, and toFQDNs cannot be used to deny traffic to a specific domain name.
Both are supported, provided the deny policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy rather than a namespaced one.
Denying a URL is supported at Layer 7, but denying a specific domain name with toFQDNs is not.
Denying a specific domain name with toFQDNs is supported, but denying a URL at Layer 7 is not.

explanation: Deny policies do not support policy enforcement at Layer 7, which means specifically denying a URL is not possible, and they do not support toFQDNs, which means specifically denying traffic to a specific domain name is not possible either.

optionRationale.b: The limitation applies to deny policies generally; using a clusterwide policy does not add Layer 7 or toFQDNs deny support.
optionRationale.c: Layer 7 enforcement, including denying a URL, is explicitly not supported by deny policies.
optionRationale.d: toFQDNs, that is denying traffic to a specific domain name, is explicitly not supported by deny policies.

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:
Deny policies do not support: policy enforcement at L7, i.e., specifically
denying an URL and ``toFQDNs``, i.e., specifically denying traffic to a specific
domain name.

stem: A cluster runs in a datacenter and its BGP peering must detect peer failure as quickly as the timers allow. Which timer values should be configured in the peer configuration?

options.text: `holdTimeSeconds: 9` and `keepAliveTimeSeconds: 3`
`holdTimeSeconds: 3` and `keepAliveTimeSeconds: 9`
`holdTimeSeconds: 90` and `keepAliveTimeSeconds: 30`
`holdTimeSeconds: 9` and `keepAliveTimeSeconds: 9`

explanation: The documentation recommends lowering the HoldTimer and KeepaliveTimer in datacenter networks for faster failure detection, and gives the minimum possible values as `holdTimeSeconds=9` and `keepAliveTimeSeconds=3`.

optionRationale.b: The two values are swapped: 3 is the minimum for the keepalive timer, not the hold timer.
optionRationale.c: These are the defaults, not the lowered values recommended for fast failure detection.
optionRationale.d: A keepalive of 9 is not the minimum possible value given; the minimum is 3.

citations.title: Timers
citations.quote:
For example, you can set the minimum
possible values ``holdTimeSeconds=9`` and ``keepAliveTimeSeconds=3``.

stem: An engineer sets `connectRetryTimeSeconds: 5` on a BGP peer configuration to speed up reconnection after losing connectivity. What range of values can the actual ConnectRetryTimer take?

options.text: Exactly 5 seconds, because the configured value is used as-is
Anywhere from 5 up to but not including 10 seconds, because random jitter is applied internally
Anywhere from 0 up to but not including 5 seconds, because jitter is subtracted from the configured value
Exactly 10 seconds, because the configured value is always doubled

explanation: Random jitter is applied to the configured value internally, so the actual value used for the ConnectRetryTimer falls within the interval `[ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds)`. With a configured value of 5, that is from 5 up to but not including 10.

optionRationale.a: Jitter is applied internally, so the configured value is not used verbatim.
optionRationale.c: The interval starts at the configured value, not below it; jitter is not subtracted.
optionRationale.d: The upper bound of the interval is exclusive, and the value is not fixed at double the configured value.

citations.title: Timers

As random jitter is applied to the configured value internally, the actual value used for the
``ConnectRetryTimer`` is within the interval ``[ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds)``.

The HoldTimer and KeepaliveTimer
The HoldTimer and ConnectRetryTimer
All three timers, to their minimum values

explanation: For datacenter networks the recommendation is to set the HoldTimer and KeepaliveTimer to a lower value for faster possible failure detection. The ConnectRetryTimer is addressed separately, for fast reconnection after losing connectivity with the peer.

optionRationale.a: The ConnectRetryTimer is reduced to speed up reconnection after connectivity loss, not for failure detection.
optionRationale.c: The ConnectRetryTimer is not part of the failure-detection recommendation.
optionRationale.d: Only the HoldTimer and KeepaliveTimer are recommended for lowering for failure detection; the ConnectRetryTimer serves a different purpose.

stem: An engineer applies the following CiliumBGPPeerConfig to a BGP peer in a datacenter Kubernetes cluster. The peer session drops, and the engineer measures how long Cilium waits before attempting to reconnect. Which statement describes the delay that can be observed?

options.text: The delay is always exactly 5 seconds, because the configured value is used verbatim.
The delay is somewhere in the interval from 5 seconds up to but not including 10 seconds, because random jitter is applied to the configured value.
The delay is somewhere in the interval from 5 seconds up to and including 10 seconds, because random jitter is applied to the configured value.
The delay is 120 seconds, because connectRetryTimeSeconds is ignored unless the HoldTimer is left at its default.

explanation: The documentation states that random jitter is applied internally to the configured ConnectRetryTimer value, so the actual value used lies within the interval [ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds). With connectRetryTimeSeconds set to 5, the observed delay falls between 5 seconds inclusive and 10 seconds exclusive.

optionRationale.a: Jitter is applied internally, so the configured value is not used verbatim.
optionRationale.c: The interval is half-open: the upper bound, twice the configured value, is excluded.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt gives no such dependency; connectRetryTimeSeconds is a configurable timer in its own right, and 120 is merely its default.

   name: cilium-peer

stem: A node has an interface named lo carrying several addresses, including a loopback address and an IPv6 link-local address. A CiliumBGPAdvertisement selects that interface with advertisementType "Interface". Which addresses are advertised to BGP peers?

options.text: All IP addresses on the interface, each as an exact /32 or /128 route.
Only the loopback and IPv6 link-local addresses, since those are the stable ones.
The interface's addresses excluding those from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 ranges, each as an exact /32 or /128 route.
The interface's addresses aggregated into the smallest covering prefix for the interface.

explanation: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes, and addresses drawn from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 ranges are excluded from advertisement. So the remaining addresses go out as /32 or /128 prefixes, never as an aggregate.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly excludes several address ranges, so not every address on the interface is advertised.
optionRationale.b: It is the reverse: loopback and IPv6 link-local addresses are among those that are not advertised.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the addresses are advertised as exact routes (/32 or /128 prefixes), not aggregated.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote:
The interface IPs are advertised as exact routes (``/32`` or ``/128`` prefixes).
IP addresses from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 address ranges are not advertised.

stem: An engineer configures a CiliumBGPAdvertisement with advertisementType "Interface" for an interface that is administratively disabled. What is the result for that interface's IP addresses?

options.text: The addresses are advertised, because only the operational state matters.
The addresses are not advertised, because the interface must be administratively enabled and in operationally up or unknown state.
The addresses are advertised as a default route instead of exact routes.
Cilium enables the interface automatically so that its addresses can be advertised.

explanation: Advertisement of an interface's IP addresses requires the interface to be administratively enabled and in operationally up or unknown state. An administratively disabled interface does not meet that condition, so its addresses are not advertised.

optionRationale.a: Both conditions apply: the interface must be administratively enabled as well as operationally up or unknown.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says nothing about substituting a default route; interface IPs are advertised as exact routes.
optionRationale.d: Cilium does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces; the node administrator configures them.

citations.title: Interface IPs

    in order to advertise its IP addresses.

stem: Which advertisementType in a CiliumBGPAdvertisement is used to advertise IP addresses assigned on a local interface?

options.text: "Interface"
"PodCIDR"
"LoadBalancerIP"
"ClusterIP"

optionRationale.b: PodCIDR is not the type used for local interface addresses; the excerpt's example uses "Interface".
optionRationale.c: LoadBalancerIP is not the type used for local interface addresses; the excerpt's example uses "Interface".
optionRationale.d: ClusterIP is not the type used for local interface addresses; the excerpt's example uses "Interface".

stem: A cluster uses a multi-homing setup where a common node's loopback address must be reachable through several BGP sessions running over different network interfaces. Which Cilium capability supports this?

options.text: Advertising arbitrary IP addresses assigned on a local interface to BGP peers.
Advertising only the pod CIDR of the node to BGP peers.
Advertising only addresses that Cilium itself has assigned to interfaces.
Advertising the cluster's service VIPs to BGP peers.

explanation: Advertising arbitrary IP addresses assigned on a local interface is what makes multi-homing setups possible, where a common node's loopback address is advertised via multiple BGP sessions over different network interfaces.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes advertising interface IP addresses, not restricting advertisement to the pod CIDR.
optionRationale.c: Cilium does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces; the administrator configures them, yet they can still be advertised.
optionRationale.d: Service VIP advertisement is not what the excerpt describes for this multi-homing use case.

via multiple BGP sessions over different network interfaces.

stem: Who is responsible for configuring the IP addresses on an arbitrary local interface that is not owned by Cilium, before those addresses can be advertised?

options.text: Cilium assigns them automatically when the advertisement is created.
The BGP peer assigns them through the session.
The node administrator must configure them themselves.
The Kubernetes control plane assigns them from the pod CIDR.

explanation: Cilium does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces, so the node administrator must configure those addresses themselves.

 the node administrator must configure them themselves.

stem: In what form are interface IP addresses advertised to BGP peers?

options.text: As exact routes, using /32 or /128 prefixes.
As the natural prefix length of the interface's subnet.
As a summary route covering all interfaces on the node.
As a default route pointing at the node.

explanation: The excerpt states that interface IPs are advertised as exact routes, that is /32 or /128 prefixes.

optionRationale.b: The advertisement uses host prefixes (/32 or /128), not the subnet's natural prefix length.
optionRationale.c: No summary route across interfaces is described; each address is an exact route.
optionRationale.d: A default route is not mentioned; the advertisement consists of exact host routes.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote: The interface IPs are advertised as exact routes (``/32`` or ``/128`` prefixes).

stem: A node has a loopback interface named lo carrying the address 10.0.0.5/32, and the interface is administratively enabled and operationally up. A CiliumBGPAdvertisement with advertisementType "Interface" and interface name lo is applied. What does the BGP control plane advertise to peers for this interface?

options.text: The exact route 10.0.0.5/32.
The connected subnet route 10.0.0.0/24.
Nothing, because addresses on the loopback range are never advertised.
Nothing, because Cilium does not manage addresses on non-Cilium-owned interfaces.

explanation: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes, so a /32 address on the interface becomes a /32 prefix. The exclusion list covers addresses from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 address ranges — 10.0.0.5 is not in any of those ranges, so it is advertised. The fact that Cilium does not manage addresses on arbitrary interfaces only means the administrator must configure them; it does not prevent advertisement.

optionRationale.b: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes (/32 or /128 prefixes), not as the covering subnet prefix.
optionRationale.c: The loopback range is excluded, but 10.0.0.5 is a regular address, not a loopback-range address; the interface merely happens to be named lo.
optionRationale.d: Cilium not managing the addresses means the node administrator configures them; it does not stop the BGP control plane advertising them.

stem: An engineer wants to advertise the IP addresses of a local interface to BGP peers using the Interface advertisement type. Which condition must the interface satisfy for its IP addresses to be advertised?

options.text: It must be administratively enabled and in operationally up or unknown state.
It must be administratively enabled and in operationally up state only.
It must be a Cilium-owned interface with addresses managed by Cilium.
It must carry at least one address outside the loopback and link-local ranges, regardless of its state.

explanation: The interface must be administratively enabled and in operationally up or unknown state in order to advertise its IP addresses. Cilium does not manage addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned interfaces, so the node administrator configures them, but Cilium ownership is not a precondition for advertisement.

optionRationale.b: The unknown operational state is also acceptable, not only up.
optionRationale.c: Cilium explicitly does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces; the administrator configures them.
optionRationale.d: The interface state is a hard requirement; address ranges only exclude certain addresses from being advertised, they do not replace the state condition.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote: The interface must be administratively enabled and in operationally ``up`` or ``unknown`` state

stem: You are enabling TLS between a Cilium Gateway and the backend workload. You run a JSON patch against the backend deployment that adds a volume named secret-volume, mounting the example-cert secret at /etc/secret-volume, and adds two environment variables to the container. Which two environment variables does the patch add?

options.text: TLS_SERVER_CERT set to /etc/secret-volume/crt and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY set to /etc/secret-volume/key
TLS_SERVER_CERT set to /etc/secret-volume/tls.crt and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY set to /etc/secret-volume/tls.key
TLS_CERT set to /etc/secret-volume/crt and TLS_KEY set to /etc/secret-volume/key
TLS_SERVER_CERT set to /etc/secret-volume and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY set to /etc/secret-volume

explanation: The patch adds the secret's tls.crt key at path crt and its tls.key key at path key inside the mounted volume, then points TLS_SERVER_CERT at /etc/secret-volume/crt and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY at /etc/secret-volume/key.

optionRationale.b: The secret keys are tls.crt and tls.key, but the volume items map them to the paths crt and key, so the environment variables reference the mapped paths, not the original key names.
optionRationale.c: The environment variable names in the patch are TLS_SERVER_CERT and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY, not TLS_CERT and TLS_KEY.
optionRationale.d: The variables point at the individual files crt and key inside the mount, not at the mount directory itself.

attachments.title: Patch applied to the backend deployment
attachments.body:
- op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/volumeMounts
    value:
    - name: secret-volume
      mountPath: /etc/secret-volume
  - op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/volumes
    value:
    - name: secret-volume
      secret:
        secretName: example-cert
        items:
        - key: tls.crt
          path: crt
        - key: tls.key
          path: key
  - op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-
    value:
      name: TLS_SERVER_CERT
      value: /etc/secret-volume/crt
  - op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-
    value:
      name: TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY
      value: /etc/secret-volume/key

The port named https on the pod

explanation: The Service exposes port 443 under the name https, but its targetPort is 8443, so traffic reaching the Service on 443 is forwarded to port 8443 on the selected backend pods.

optionRationale.b: 443 is the port the Service itself listens on; the targetPort determines the pod port.
optionRationale.c: The manifest explicitly sets targetPort: 8443, so the port is translated rather than passed through unchanged.
optionRationale.d: The name https labels the Service port; the pod-side destination is given numerically by targetPort: 8443.

A replace operation on /spec/rules/0/backendRefs/0/name with value 443

optionRationale.c: The path targets the port field of the backend reference, not its name field.

stem: You are preparing the backend deployment to serve TLS. The patch mounts the example-cert secret as a volume. Which two keys of that secret are mapped into the volume, and to which paths?

options.text: tls.crt is mapped to path crt, and tls.key is mapped to path key
tls.crt is mapped to path tls.crt, and tls.key is mapped to path tls.key
crt is mapped to path tls.crt, and key is mapped to path tls.key
cert is mapped to path crt, and privkey is mapped to path key

explanation: The volume's items list takes the secret keys tls.crt and tls.key and projects them into the volume at the paths crt and key respectively.

optionRationale.c: The direction is reversed: tls.crt and tls.key are the secret keys, while crt and key are the resulting paths.
optionRationale.d: The secret keys are tls.crt and tls.key; cert and privkey do not appear in the manifest.

stem: You are enabling TLS between a Cilium Gateway and the `backend` Service. The backend container reads its certificate and key from files mounted from the `example-cert` Secret, and the Service has been updated so that its `https` port 443 targets container port 8443. Which BackendTLSPolicy correctly attaches the TLS configuration to that Service port and validates the backend certificate for `www.example.com`?

options.text: A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: www.example.com` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-ca` ConfigMap.

A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: www.example.com` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-cert` Secret.

A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: backend` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-ca` ConfigMap.

A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: www.example.com` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-ca` ConfigMap, plus a `port: 8443` field under `validation`.

explanation: The BackendTLSPolicy targets the Service by name and by the named port `https`, and its `validation` block names the hostname the gateway should expect from the backend together with a reference to the CA certificate ConfigMap. The certificate Secret is mounted into the backend container; it is not the CA reference in the policy.

optionRationale.b: `example-cert` is the Secret mounted into the backend container to supply the server certificate and key, not the CA certificate reference used for validation.
optionRationale.c: The hostname in `validation` is the name the gateway validates against the backend certificate, which the example sets to `www.example.com`, not the Service name.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt's policy has no `port` field under `validation`; the port is selected through `sectionName: https` on the `targetRefs` entry.

kind: BackendTLSPolicy
metadata:
  name: enable-backend-tls
  namespace: default
spec:
  targetRefs:
  - group: ''
    kind: Service
    name: backend
    sectionName: https
  validation:
    caCertificateRefs:
    - name: example-ca
      group: ''
      kind: ConfigMap
    hostname: www.example.com

stem: A colleague has mounted the `example-cert` Secret into the `backend` container and set the `TLS_SERVER_CERT` and `TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY` environment variables, but the Cilium Gateway still does not speak TLS to the backend. Which change completes the setup?

options.text: Create a BackendTLSPolicy targeting the `backend` Service on `sectionName: https`, with `validation` referencing the `example-ca` ConfigMap and `hostname: www.example.com`.
Add a `tls` stanza to the `backend` Service manifest so that the Service itself terminates TLS on port 443.
Change the `backend` Service so that port 443 targets container port 443 instead of 8443.
Add the `example-cert` Secret to the HTTPRoute `backendRefs` so the route can present the certificate to the backend.

explanation: Mounting the certificate and setting the environment variables only makes the backend capable of serving TLS. The gateway is told to use a TLS connection with the backend by a BackendTLSPolicy that targets the Service's `https` section and validates the backend certificate against the CA ConfigMap for the given hostname.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt adds no `tls` stanza to the Service; the Service change is only to expose port 443 with `targetPort: 8443`.
optionRationale.c: The Service is deliberately configured with `port: 443` and `targetPort: 8443`, matching the port the backend listens on; changing the target port is not part of the setup.
optionRationale.d: The HTTPRoute change in the excerpt is only to replace the backend reference port with 443; certificates are not added to `backendRefs`.

    app: backend
    service: backend
  name: backend
spec:
  selector:
    app: backend
  ports:
  - name: https
    port: 443
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8443

An Allow effect for the action `ec2:DescribeInstances` on the resource `arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*`.
An Allow effect for the action `s3:GetObject` on the resource `*`.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt uses the wildcard action `ec2:Describe*` with resource `*`, not a single action restricted to an instance ARN.
optionRationale.d: The permissions relate to EC2 describe actions, not S3 object access.

The Ingress has been rejected because `ingressClassName: cilium` does not match any installed controller, so no address will ever be assigned.
A LoadBalancer service is only created in shared load balancer mode, so the service you are seeing must be the shared `cilium-ingress` service in `kube-system`.
The address will only be populated once the `details` and `productpage` backend services are themselves changed to type LoadBalancer.

explanation: The example states that a LoadBalancer service is created automatically for the ingress, and that the cloud provider will provision an external IP address, which may take around 30 seconds. A pending external IP is therefore expected shortly after creation rather than a sign of failure.

optionRationale.b: The manifest sets `ingressClassName: cilium`, and the `kubectl get ingress` output shows the Ingress accepted with class `cilium` and an address, so the class does match.
optionRationale.c: The dedicated mode output shows `cilium-ingress-basic-ingress` as the LoadBalancer service; the shared `cilium-ingress` service in `kube-system` belongs to the other mode.
optionRationale.d: The backend services `details` and `productpage` are shown as ClusterIP services; nothing in the material requires them to become LoadBalancer services.
